360 cameras use two lenses to simultaneously record everything happening around you, then stitch it together with software. That means you never miss that shot, but because there are essentially two cameras in one, they are more expensive than their action-camera cousins. Right now, though, you can grab my top-pick 360 camera, the GoPro Max 2, for 40 percent off ($299).
The GoPro Max 2 (7/10 WIRED Recommends) is my favorite 360 camera, and that’s still true even with the release of the new Insta360 X6. The X6 is more versatile—it can serve double duty as an action camera and 360 camera better than the Max 2—but judged purely on video quality, I prefer the Max 2. And at this price, you can grab the Max 2 and a GoPro Hero 13 for just $30 more than the X6.
The Max 2’s dual 14-mm (35-mm equivalent) lenses each record to a 1/2.3-inch chip, yielding what GoPro calls “True 8K” video. The large sensors provide sharper, clearer footage than other 360 cameras, and advanced users can record 10-bit color in log for greater flexibility in post-production color grading. Don't want to futz with log video? That’s no problem, as GoPro’s natural-looking color rendition in the default color profile is still the best I’ve tested.
Sharing the same triple mounting system as other GoPros, the Max 2 uses folding fingers, a tripod hole, or a magnetic system. This means you can mount the Max 2 just about anywhere. It also has the simplest lens-cover replacement process if you scratch it (I’ve been using mine for a year now and have no scratches, but it’s nice to know you can easily fix any).
As an action camera, you get all the usual GoPro video modes, including HyperSmooth video stabilization, horizon leveling, TimeWarp time-lapse-style video, and more. The Max 2’s one shortcoming is audio recording quality—it’s not the best. The easiest fix is to get a Bluetooth mic, which you can then pair with the camera. Check out the deal on the DJI Mic 3 below.

What if I told you Brooks Running started out making ballet slippers and bathing shoes? Founded in 1914, the Seattle-based company spent decades making just about everything except running shoes, moving from baseball cleats to roller skates, football cleats and children’s shoes, and softball cleats. It wasn’t until 1972 that Brooks made running its focus, and the company has been refining the category ever since.
Brooks introduced one of the industry’s earliest uses of EVA foam, developed the first running shoe with a breathable GORE-TEX upper, and introduced the Kinetic Wedge, which was an innovative design catered to women’s anatomy.
So, while Brooks may not be the trendiest brand, it has built a reputation for dependable support, comfort, and durability. Here at WIRED, Brooks has plenty of fans, especially for trail running and gravel running. The company also offers apparel we regularly recommend, including sports bras, outerwear, and running bottoms.
Brooks Running shoes are relatively reasonably priced for performance running footwear, with many models hovering around $150. If you’re in the market for a new pair, I’ve rounded up the best Brooks Running promo codes and Brooks Running coupons worth checking out.
Score 20% Off Your First Order With Brooks Promo Code
If you’ve never ordered anything off Brooks’ website before, new customers get 20% off their first order after subscribing to emails. You can apply the one-time Brooks coupon code for top-selling shoes, like the Caldera 7 and Adrenaline shoes, along with other gear and apparel. It’s an easy way to save on some of their top products to take your road and trail running game to the next level.
More Brooks Coupons and Offers
Are you already a member of Brooks Run Club? If you sign up, you get member perks, like early access to sales, standard free shipping with no order minimum, and free express shipping on orders from Brooks. Membership also includes more runner-specific perks, like a free birthday gift, an opportunity to earn prizes by syncing your fitness tracker and contributing research to the Brooks team. You can also win a chance to visit the Seattle flagship store and have your gait analyzed by Brooks’ team. To join, visit Brooks Run Club and register for the Brooks promo code.
If you shop and buy a complete outfit in one transaction from one of Brooks’ recommended buying guides—like Warm Weather Running Outfits or Fall Weather Running Outfits—you can get 15% off automatically applied during checkout. This is a fantastic deal if you only just realized in the past 10 days that you’ve been running in hail in your tiny shorts and cropped sports bra.
Save on Our Favorite Brooks Running Shoes
Brooks makes so many iconic running shoes that it’s hard to list them all. I’m currently running in the Brooks Glycerin Max, which is one of the cushiest shoes that I’ve ever tried. I don’t feel particularly stable on uneven terrain, but the padding is noticeably springy and cushy if you’ve been putting in some serious miles. WIRED director Michael Calore is a fan of the Brooks Ghost line, and if you’re planning on hitting the trails in the cold, wet Pacific Northwest, I would suggest the Brooks Cascadia Gore-Tex. The Adrenaline is the company’s most popular shoe.
Preorder Your Favorite Glycerin Now
One of the most anticipated Brooks drops is the Glycerin line. These shoes are made to be durable, while allowing freedom of movement and flexibility. The cushioned shoes are comfortable for running and movement on many types of terrain. Tons of shoes in the Glycerin line are available to preorder, including the Glycerin Flex, Glycerin 23, and Glycerin GTS 23. Be sure to check out the Glycerin line to see which is best for you.
The Cascadia Elite Available Now
Brooks is constantly dropping new shoe styles, ensuring there’s a type of shoe for every runner. The new Cascadia Elite Brooks Running shoe is unisex and great for trail running: with PEBA cushioning, a Vibram Megagrip Elite outsole, and a MATRYX engineered woven upper with Kevlar fibers to help secure your feet firmly, no matter what terrain you’re traversing. This shoe has a light, springy cushioning that helps to propel you forward, whether that be from competitive trail racing, to Sub-ultras to VKs to ultras.
Upcoming Brooks Sale Events to Watch Out For
Do you have a runner in your life? The odds are, they’re taking stock of their winter apparel and shoes and trying to decide if these leggings are going to make it through another winter season. The best time to save is during seasonal sales, with discounts on footwear and apparel, including discounts on popular items like the Ghost 16 running shoes.
Do you have running military, nurses, or first responders in your life? Brooks Running also offers 25% off Brooks promo code full-priced items for verified community heroes. Sign up here.
Brooks Discount: Shop Pre-Owned Shoes at Brooks
If you’re looking for a new pair of shoes, but don’t have the cash to invest in a brand new, high-end pair, look no further than Brook’s restart page, where gently-used Brooks shoes are on sale for deeply discounted prices. They have both men’s and women’s sections, recently added shoes, and a breakdown of bestselling styles, including the Adrenaline, Ghost, Glycerin, and Hyperion.
Brooks Coupon: 20% Off Join the Brooks Run Club
If you’re looking to shop at Brooks, it’s a great idea to join the Brooks Run Club for additional perks and discounts. Some of the best things Run Club offers are discounts of 20% off apparel when you join and an annual birthday gift. You’ll just need to log in or join the club for the discount code.
Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program: 40% Off
If you’re a sports medicine professional, you can save big and get rewarded at Brooks Running. The Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program is a free membership program for eligible sports medicine professionals as a way to say thank you for the care they put into runners and athletes. All you have to do is verify your status by signing in or creating an ID.me account to verify the applicant’s qualifications. Then, you’ll get a steep 40% Brooks discount on the first $1,000 spent on eligible items on Brooks Running online orders (it resets every January 1).
Brooks Return Policy and 90 Day Wear Test
Brooks knows how important gear is for the athlete. So, you can take your Brooks gear for a 90-day trial run, and if you aren't satisfied, return them for free. If you’re at all unsatisfied with your Brooks purchase, you can return it for free, with no shipping or re‐stocking fees.

India – September 10, 2026: The group stage of fourth season of the Global Chess League (GCL), a joint initiative of Tech Mahindra and FIDE, in Bengaluru is heading to a nail-biting finale with just one game point separating the top three teams with just two rounds left to play.
Defending champions Alpine APL Pipers , FYERS American Gambits and Ganges Grandmasters now have 15 Match Points after 8 rounds with the first two slight ahead with 73 Game Points while the Grandmasters on 72.
Pipers and Grandmasters had a chance of taking sole lead on Thursday as they were scheduled to play two matches each.
Ganges Grandmasters began the day with a convincing 12-4 win over the Alpine APL Pipers with black pieces but went down 13-5 in the last game against the American Gambits.
Pipers went on to beat PBG Alaskan Knights 11-6 and CheQ Mumba Masters kept their chances of making the final alive with a 14-5 win over Triveni Continental Kings. They now have 12 Match Points and 73 Game Points to show for their effort.
The day began with the Ganges Grandmasters beating the Pipers without dropping a game.
Stavroula Tsolakidou began the Grandmasters march by inflicting a second loss of the tournament on Koneru Humpy. On the Superstar men’s board, two-time world cup winner Levon Aronian turned the tables on Anish Giri by making the most of an additional knight in the end game to win in 61 moves.
_“I got lucky, very lucky. But I always believed that that I can find the best moves despite playing very badly in the start. May be not losing the game was what I deserved but winning of course is a huge luck,”_ said *Aronian*, who was also adjudged the Player of the Match.
Aronian made it a double when he defeated Nihal Sarin of FYERS American Gambits in the last match of the day but his team lost four of the six matches and surrendered the advantage.
On the icon board, Candidates 2026 winner Javokhir Sindarov defeated Ian Nepomniachtchi, Daniil Dubov outplayed Leinier Dominguez Perez, Bibisara Assaubayeva handed Polina Shuvalova her first loss of the competition and Marc’andria Maurizzi claimed three points after Luke Leon Mendonca ran out of time on the prodigy board.
Earlier, Pipers had bounced back immediately after the reversal against the Ganges Grandmasters with world number one Magnus Carlsen proving too strong for Viswanathan Anand with white pieces. Koneru Humpy then registered her fourth win of the tournament, handing Nino Batsiashvili her first loss of Season 4.
Volodar Murzin then defeated Abhimanyu Mishra on the prodigy board in a time scramble to put the result beyond doubt. Only 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus managed to score four points for a win with black for the Alaskan Knights as Vidit Gujrathi ran out of time on the Superstar men’s board.
In the day’s other match, CheQ Mumba Masters kept their hopes of reaching the final alive with a thumping win over Triveni Continental Kings.
Playing black, the Mumba Masters won three of the six games with Alexandra Kosteniuk winning the only game for the Continental Kings. On the icon board, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave outplayed Alireza Firouzja and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov defeated Aravindh Chithambaram on the Superstar men’s board.
With Bardiya Daneshvar also winning on the prodigy board, the Mumba Masters took their game points tally to 73 from 8 matches with four wins.
Schedule for Friday, September 11:
5.00 PM: Triveni Continental Kings vs PBG Alaskan Knights
6.30 PM: Alpine APL Pipers vs FYERS American Gambits
8.00 PM: Ganges Grandmasters vs CheQ Mumba Masters

Meta is testing Community Notes in Latin America. Fact checkers are worried.
The company is suggesting that its work with traditional fact checkers could come to an end.
Meta is beginning its international expansion of Community Notes. The company said it is starting to test the crowd-sourced fact checks in 16 countries in Latin America more than a year after it rolled out the program stateside and ended its partnership with US-based fact checking organizations.
The company says it plans to take a similar approach with its initial tests in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela. The platform is starting to onboard contributors to who, if approved, will be able to write notes that add "additional context" to posts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. During the testing phase, contributors' notes will not be surfaced to users and "there will be no changes to third-party fact checking," Meta says in a blog post originally published in Spanish.
But the company goes on to suggest that it intends for Community Notes to eventually replace existing fact-checking arrangements in these countries. "When we're confident the product is working well and can be successful, we will look at fully launching – beginning to publish Community Notes and transitioning our third-party fact checking program," Meta writes, according to a translation provided by the company.
Unsurprisingly, Meta's move to potentially end fact checking in a large swath of Latin America has alarmed fact checking organizations. In a statement published by Poynter, the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) said it was "deeply concerned" by the news. "The community notes program alone is simply not adequate when it comes to reducing the impact of harmful falsehoods on its platforms," the group wrote.
The Oversight Board, which has previously warned Meta that expanding Community Notes outside of the US would come with "significant" risks, also seemed troubled. "We urge Meta not to consider community notes a direct replacement for factchecking, and to use all the tools that best address the challenge of misinformation on its platforms in ways that both protect free expression and address potential harms," the board said in a statement.
Earlier this year, the group published a 15,000-word policy advisory opinion on how Meta should handle Community Notes' international expansion. In it, the Oversight Board repeatedly stressed that Community Notes should not replace traditional fact checking. "One doesn't have to replace or substitute for the other, they can coexist," board co-chair Paolo Carozza told Engadget at the time. "And in some situations, there are really important reasons for them to coexist."
In its guidance, the board cautioned against bringing Community Notes to countries experiencing "high polarization," "protracted conflict" and those with a history of organized disinformation networks. Meta is disregarding that advice, according to the IFCN.
"Meta is testing its community notes in some countries that face precisely one or more of these circumstances. Nicaragua, for example, has abolished elections and is actively practicing arbitrary detention of political dissidents. Disinformation networks have been well documented in El Salvador and Ecuador. And Venezuela has been in an extended state of instability."
When reached for comment, Meta didn't address the criticism directly. A spokesperson said there were "no changes to our third-party fact checking program at this time." The company has said that Community Notes has been a success in the United States, where it has 1.4 million contributors.
Others have raised questions about the effectiveness of Meta's program compared with X. The publication Indicator found that only 3 percent of Instagram posts that were debunked by the AFP's US bureau since last April had also received a Community Note. That would suggest that Meta's crowd-sourced approach is missing a significant number of social media posts that traditional fact checkers believe are worth addressing.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Apple Event Live Blog: Here Comes the Folding iPhone
Get all the iPhone news as it happens. We’re reporting live from Apple Park, the company’s headquarters in Cupertino, California.
Good morning everyone! Welcome to our live coverage of today's Apple media showcase.
We will have two reporters on the scene at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, to bring you live coverage. You'll be hearing from Julian Chokkattu, Boutayna Chokrane, Lauren Goode, Reece Rogers, and Michael Calore throughout the event. We might have some special guests pop in as well. We’ll be posting frequent news updates here, with the highlights also going on our social platforms.
Apple's presentation begins at 10 am Pacific, 1 pm Eastern, and 6 pm in the UK. We have a complete rundown on how to watch the show and what to expect.
Come back approximately 30 minutes before the presentation starts—about 9:30 am in California—and you'll see the words on this page replaced by a feed of our live updates.
A Folding iPhone Today
The short version of what to expect: The folding variant of the iPhone should make its debut today. The word around Silicon Valley is that it’s expected to be named the iPhone Ultra and that it will likely cost more than $2,000.
We’ll probably also see a Pro version iPhone today, and we can expect the folding iPhone and the Pro models to go on sale later in September.
What about the base model iPhone 18? That might not arrive until early next year, though Apple might tease it today. The longer wait could be because of a number of factors, including rising manufacturing costs and the ongoing memory crisis affecting the whole PC industry. Also, delaying the next generation of cheaper iPhones—the 18, the 18e, and the Air—would give Apple an opportunity to promote its premium handsets more heavily.
It’s also likely we’ll see the newest Apple Watch and Watch Ultra models debut at today’s event.
Both the new iPhones and the new Apple Watches will be getting some additional capabilities enabled by Siri AI, the newest version of Apple’s artificially intelligent assistant. So, expect lots of talk about the beefed-up new chips in these devices as well as “on-device AI,” secure computing, and battery optimization. Siri AI is actually powerful and impressive in our testing of the beta version, but just like the various Siris that came before it, there are limits to how helpful it can really be in your day-to-day life.
Also notable is the list of things we’re not expecting: Apple’s various smart-home products that have been rumored to be close to release, including new HomePod speakers and a smart home device that’s used to interacting with Siri’s camera-based Visual Intelligence capabilities.
Along those lines are the rumored AirPods with tiny cameras in them that can be used, in conjunction with voice commands, to give Siri AI some additional context about what you’re looking at and inquiring about. Those earbuds might come today, but we could just as well see them at an additional event in late September or in October. (It’s likely the smart-home products will show up at the next event too.)
How to Watch
To watch the livestream, you can, of course, just hit Play on the video stream on this page. But it's better on the big screen.
You can watch it in your TV's YouTube app; just tune into Apple's YouTube channel. You can also watch it on Apple's own streaming app. If you have an Apple TV or any streaming box, just go into the Apple TV app. When you open the app, the livestream for the event should be displayed prominently right at the top. This works even if you don’t subscribe to Apple’s paid streaming service. Watching it on the television frees up your laptop screen so you can follow the live blog. Convenient!
We'll see you back here about half an hour before the event begins.

Mental health conditions that may develop following a traumatic incident could contribute to a higher risk of future cardiovascular issues such as non-fatal heart attack and stroke or a fatal cardiac event, according to new research.
"Traumatic events are common experiences and can include serious fires or explosions, physical assault, transportation accidents, the suicide or death of a loved one, and severe medical illnesses or injuries," lead author Jennifer A Sumner, an associate professor in the department of psychology at the University of California Los Angeles, said.
"Experiencing traumatic events can significantly affect mental health as well as cardiovascular health. Although most work to date has focused on PTSD and cardiovascular health, our research suggests that we should think about a wide range of mental health consequences when looking at cardiovascular disease risk after trauma," Sumner said.
The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, examined national health registries in Denmark, looking at 2,19,866 adults who did and did not develop major heart or brain conditions following a traumatic event.
About 44,000 of the 2,19,866 participants experienced a non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death between 1995 and 2019.
Researchers compared 1,75,872 people who experienced a trauma but not a cardiovascular event to peers who experienced a heart attack, stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death during the 24-year period.
A wide range of mental health conditions were considered as possible cardiovascular predictors, and machine learning was used to identify the 15 most important mental health disorder predictors of heart and brain outcomes.
Alcohol abuse was found to be the most important mental health risk linked to serious heart or brain conditions for men and women.
"For men and women, the most important psychiatric predictor of MACCE (major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events) was alcohol use disorders," the authors wrote.
"After a traumatic life experience, individuals may turn to alcohol to cope and help manage their emotions. Over time, this new behaviour might develop into alcohol abuse, thus increasing their risk of a serious heart or brain condition," Sumner said.
Mood disorders, including depression, were found to be strong indicators of post-traumatic psychiatric issues associated with cardiovascular outcomes for both men and women. However, mood disorders were a more prominent predictor for women, compared to men.
Psychological conditions that can arise after a traumatic event connected to a higher risk of heart and brain conditions in the future included PTSD, mental disorders caused by brain or physical issues, non-substance-induced confusion, different substance use disorders, personality disorders, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and anxiety disorders.

Inside the White House on 9/11
John McConnell on his memories of working in the White House on September 11, 2001. Plus: American Pastoral by Philip Roth.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
In this episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum is joined by John McConnell, the longtime senior speechwriter for President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney, to discuss their memories of September 11, 2001—25 years later.
Then, David ends with a discussion of American Pastoral, a novel by Philip Roth, and what we can learn about domestic terrorism from the book.
The following is a transcript of the episode:

But the flags are still flying. They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow. But tonight they’re high.

John and I spent much of the day together on 9/11, 2001—and we’ll be discussing what we saw, what we thought, what we felt, and what we did.

So that’s the news. I hope you will join me this coming Saturday and each successive Saturday for the second, shorter David Frum Show weekend episode.
And now my dialogue with John McConnell.

John McConnell: Hello, David. Great to see you.

And she said, Sure. Come at 8:30.
And so the next morning—you remember how we’d get to the office, and the president’s and vice president’s schedules would be under our doors. And I looked at it; it said, “Meeting with John McConnell, 8:30,” and I thought, Oh, well, it’s an official meeting, so I really better be there at 8:30 sharp. So I went over, and the vice president was there. Sean O’Keefe, who was at the time the deputy director of the budget, former secretary of the Navy, friend of Cheney’s, had popped in on Cheney after the senior staff meeting. and so he was in there, and I waited outside the door. And I was just chatting with the vice president’s secretary’s personal aide and the Secret Service man standing post.
And then about 8:46, I’m still waiting for the vice president. We’re seeing on television early reports that a plane has hit the World Trade Center, and so we’re just watching that and speculating what could possibly have gone wrong on this beautifully, perfectly clear late-summer day. I said, Sir, just need a couple minutes of your time to talk about this little thing we’ve got on Friday. He said, Sure; have a seat. But all we did was immediately turn to his television and just look at it. It was on, and so he was aware of what was happening in New York. And instead of talking about the matter I brought or hoped to raise with him, we just sat there looking at the TV, and it wasn’t very long until we saw the live image of the second plane coming in and slamming into the South Tower. And, of course, at that moment you realize that this is a terrorist attack.
And he picked up the phone, and the president, as you recall, was out of town. He was in Florida. The vice president picked up the phone and asked to be connected to the president, as I recall. Then he got out of his chair and went out to see Andy Card’s assistant, the chief of staff’s assistant, to tell him to get in touch when he could.

And at a certain point, I realized there were going to be some big, big discussions. I remember also the president being on the phone with the vice president, and I had my hands on Cheney’s desk, and he was on the phone with the president, and I couldn’t make out what was being said even though I was right there. And I picked up the phone, and I called my mom, who was here where I am today in northernmost Wisconsin, a place called Bayfield County. And I called her, and she said, Where are you? And I said, I’m in my office, and everything’s fine. And she says, Well, on television it says the White House is being evacuated. And I remember I kind of chuckled. I said, Well, I’m here. And nobody knows you better than your mother, and she knows my passive personality. She said, John, go out in the hallway and see if anyone else is there.
Frum: (Laughs.)
McConnell: And I said, Okay, okay. I will, I will, and I’ll call you. And I put the phone down, and I went out into the hallway. And sure enough, people were being told, Get out, get out.
And so I went down the stairs and then down outside, they call them the Navy Steps, which you know well, the steps from the Eisenhower Building going down. Basically directing you right into the West Wing there, across that little West Executive Drive. And I saw one of the vice president’s Secret Service men who I’d known for a long time, and he said, John, everybody’s got to get out of here. And I said, I’m going. And I remember thinking in that moment, I swear to God, I thought, That plane is filled with people. It’s about to slam into the White House, kill them all, and destroy the White House. I cannot believe this is the year 2001. And that was the instant thought that came to my mind. I just can’t believe this is happening.
And we later found out that it was thought for a while that that was the plane that ended up hitting the Pentagon, but the Pentagon had already been hit at that point. So that plane I saw over 16th had to be a diverted commercial aircraft. I just assume that’s what it was.
And so we’re out there. Nobody knows where to go. There’s no evacuation plan. The White House has never been evacuated. And so, I ended up just out—you know, you leave the White House complex, you’re on West Executive Drive, and then boom, there’s Lafayette Park. And if you walk for one minute, you’re on Connecticut Avenue. And that’s about where I met up with you, isn’t it, David?

So that morning, I volunteered to take my children, Danielle’s and my children, and this friend’s children, to drive them up to Rockville, which is a long drive. And then you’re coming back with the rush-hour traffic.

Frum: Yeah.
McConnell: And and then we—
Frum: How he had a phone connection, I cannot at this point understand. He must have been—
McConnell: Yeah, he was with, was he with Fox at the time? I can’t remember. Yeah.
Frum: Yeah. So we walked over to 11th and M, a building that is now demolished.
McConnell: 17th and M.
Frum: 17th and M. Yeah. And went up to the American Enterprise Institute, and they were all still there. This must have been about near 10:00.

McConnell: And when you and I arrived in the AEI, and I think by that point, we had intercepted Matthew Scully. And the reason I say that is Matthew remembers seeing Tony as well. Frum: Yes.
McConnell: And I remember the image in my mind was that it had gone over, that it had fallen over to the side. And that was the image that came to my mind before we saw it on the TV. And we walked over there, and I remember my first thought, I had no—it was on Scully’s pager, so I didn’t know where I was going. And, and we walk into this brand-new office building, gleaming, and we take the elevator.
And the White House—I don’t know what it’s like today, but in 2001 it was not as glamorous a place as The West Wing made it look. It was quite, you know, it looked like a—it didn’t have the state-of-the-art except in the president’s personal suite and the vice president’s personal suite. They were still using the big bulbous computer screens. There were very few flat screens. Everything was a little like a government-procurement office. (Laughs.) Which were much sleeker than anything that the government had to offer.
McConnell: Yeah, right. That’s right. And that’s where we spent the rest of the day.
Frum: One thing I remember also about that was walking in, and they were going to have some kind of lunch at Daimler Chrysler, and they prepared a spread of sandwiches. And there’s a big difference between government food culture and private-sector food culture. The government food culture in those days was much more turkey on white bread with mayo. And these were like arugula sandwiches. That was my first inclination, Oh, maybe this was not a secret CIA facility. (Laughs.) Or my first indication this is not a secret CIA facility, but they would still have been the turkey on white bread with mayo.
Frum: So that’s where we started to work. So by this time we are with Scully, and this is now, I would say, about 11:30 in the morning, I’m guessing. And we arrive there, and we start thinking about, What should the president say? And again, we don’t have a good ways of communicating with anybody. And the whole team is sort of distributed all over the place. Mike Gerson is stuck in traffic, I think, on I-395. That’s the head of the speechwriting office. We don’t know where Pete Wehner, who’s sort of the operational head of the speechwriting office—we don’t know where he is. And the plane is on its way from Florida to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, and that’s where the president makes his first stop of the day, and where he makes his first statement to the American people.

McConnell: I don’t remember watching the president’s statement, but surely we did. We were just kind of disoriented. But the thing about being a speechwriter in a moment like that, we’re the only ones who knew we were going to be needed. There are a lot of our colleagues—What are they going to ask me to do? Where when you’re in presidential speechwriting, on an event like this, we were trying to be helpful in writing some things down. I also remember [White House staff secretary] Harriet Miers was there, and I think Harriet reminded us that anything we generated that day, that even though we weren’t on White House property and White House facilities, that these were government records that we were generating. And reminding us of that. Keep your notes, and things like that.
Frum: I remember watching the president from Barksdale, and it was a military link. It was a poor link, and so it looked kinda like wavery. That it looks like the government has lost the ability to put out a clear TV image to the American people. And it looks like, you know, the government of the United States has really been knocked off its pegs—because he looks wobbly, he sounds wobbly. This is really bad.
McConnell: The one other thing I was gonna mention when we were putting these notes together, Mike had been on 395 trying to get into Washington. He saw that plane that hit the Pentagon. He saw it. And he had a conscious memory of looking into the windows of that plane, and he said he thought, It’s too low; it’s too fast. And in the time it took him to process that thought, it hit the Pentagon, which he did not see. He did not have a line of sight to where it hit the Pentagon. But he saw this thing.
Frum: Yeah.
McConnell: And I know it was a haunting, haunting experience for him.

And a Jewish day school would be on the list of targets you would have to—if there was any kinda local auxiliary. So when the car-bomb story made it seem like this was not just a remote event, there may have been people somehow in Washington itself, and then a Jewish day school would be as it always is a target to worry about.
The kids had been all taken into a gymnasium, and the windows had been shut. In those days, Jewish day schools didn’t—today, they all have blackout blinds and bulletproof glass, but in those days they didn’t. And so the kids were all put in the gym, and Danielle, there were a line of parents who all came to retrieve the children. She stopped by a local grocery store to get some emergency supplies, and everybody in our neighborhood seemed to be doing the same because the supplies were wiped out. And she called me, but she was able to get through to me at last at about 2:00. And that’s when I heard the news that Barbara Olson, the wife of Solicitor General Ted Olson, and a close friend of, I think, all of ours, was on the plane that hit the Pentagon. I think all of us knew many people who were affected by the day, but that was the first person that I heard directly. It was someone I knew well, who was killed on 9/11.
McConnell: Yes. Yes. Barbara was a good friend of mine too, and I had seen her not long before. And, of course, we all know Ted, the No. 3 man at the Justice Department. And you were the one who told me about Barbara. I remember that moment. And you realize there’s not a chance she made it.

And that was their only daughter, Gary and Jeanette Nelson, lifelong friends of ours. Anne Nicole Nelson went to my high school, my college, the only daughter. aAnd she may have been killed right away, because she was about right where the area where the—
But you remember, David, you and I had explicitly talked about this before we knew anything, before we knew anything about. Because at first, we were talking about how there could be 50,000 people in these buildings. And I said, David, we’re all going to know somebody. And it’s true. We all did.
And [New York City Mayor Rudy] Giuliani said that afternoon—he said the numbers are going to be overwhelming. Because—more got out than they thought. But it was just this foreboding thought that you have these images and everything, but these human stories that are going to be coming at us. And these moments of loss that are gonna be experienced not just by us, but by people who are even closer to the murders.
Frum: Well, the Barbara Olson story, I learned later some details that were especially heartbreaking. And again, this is going to be an old-timey detail, but in those pre-cellphone days, planes often had a single telephone on the plane that passengers could use with a credit card. It was very expensive, so they didn’t get a lot of use. But Barbara somehow was able to get access to the telephone, and to call her husband, Ted, solicitor general, and to tell him that the plane had been hijacked. And Ted, I remember him talking with us and saying—and he knew about the two planes, and he had to make a decision in that moment whether to tell Barbara the news of what the likely fate of her plane was. Or not to tell her, and to let her have another few seconds of hope. And I remember, I can hear his voice—he’s now passed too—saying, I felt I had to tell her. And so he told her what had happened, and he told her what he feared was probably going to happen. They had no idea of the target, but of the fate. And they said their goodbyes. And that was the end.
That’s one of the many, many heartbreaking stories of that day. One, again, that came close to home.
McConnell: Yeah. And then it was only days later that Ted was on Capitol Hill testifying, I think, in favor of the Patriot Act. And it was just days later when all these measures had to be taken, and this man was on duty and remained so.
Frum: Yeah. So the president flew from Barksdale, then, to Strategic Air Command near Omaha, Nebraska.
McConnell: Against his wishes, as we know.
Frum: Yeah.
And that’s where he spent most of the day as the world tried to figure out exactly what was the scale of this attack. What had happened, and what had not happened. Because there were so many rumors. As the car bombs on the Mall were one. I’m going to forget the others, but there were so many, of things that had happened all over the place.
McConnell: Well, yes. And I remember in those first few days just the rumors you’d hear. And I also remember not wanting to know what the rumors were.
There was one point where I was momentarily in the Oval Office with Mike, and I think Matthew was there. The president said, Would any of you guys have a home computer? And Mike said, I got a computer at home. He said, Well, why don’t y’all go to Mike’s house? And I thought, What’s this all about? And then Andy Card walked in, and he said, We’re not going to do it. And the president said, Okay, y’all can stay here.
But apparently they were contemplating an evacuation of the White House. And you remember there were a few times the building was emptied out.
Frum: Yeah. Anthrax.
So after the Barksdale communication, you and I and Matt—we wrote a number of drafts. And what I remember us doing was writing alternative versions. Again, we had very little information. We didn’t know what the president wanted. We didn’t know exactly what was happening.
I remember—and maybe this was all of us, or maybe it was just me—that I wrote speeches of varying degrees of matter-of-factness, rhetorical flights. I had, like, four versions of the same statement depending on—Here are four different ways of doing it. Well, that was the way I often worked in those days. You would say, You could do it this way; you could do it this way; you could do it this way. And I always thought it was that while you could pitch it, say—Well, we can do a more matter-of-fact, we can do a more rhetorical—but it was often helpful for people for whom words were not their first trade to see it. This is what a matter-of-fact version would look like. This is what a different version would look like. This is what an aggressive version would look like. This is what a lean-back, if we’re not going to take aggressive action. The speechwriters don’t decide what to do. They just decide how to describe what the president’s decided what to do.
McConnell: Well, I’m sorry to interrupt, but you were so good that way. Very, very few writers can get tone as well as you can. But sorry, sidebar.
Frum: Yeah. But that’s what I remember. Thank you for that. But I remember that’s what I spent the afternoon doing, is writing the same thing in, I think, four, maybe five different versions, which are probably in Harriet Miers’s notes somewhere.
And then we got word as sunset fell that the president was returning.
McConnell: And I didn’t expect that we would see him. And, of course, we didn’t. But you remember getting back to the White House, and the mess stewards, the Navy mess, they had never left.
Frum: Yeah. I do remember.
McConnell: These guys. They stayed at their posts. And there were men with long guns all over the White House lawn, and it was quite a picture.
Frum: Well, what I remember, that’s actually maybe one of my most vivid memories of the day, is stepping out of that building. And Washington is deserted, and there’s yellow tape everywhere marking off the streets, and there’s the National Guard and armored personnel carriers everywhere.
But the flags are still flying. They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow. But tonight they’re high, and they’re lit up. And this capital is that ghostly beauty of Washington at night, one of the most, maybe the most, beautiful city in America at night. And there are armored personnel everywhere; there are military everywhere.
And you may not share the view—this is my view, and I won’t attribute it to you. But if you’ve been to Washington recently, and you’ve had feelings about seeing armed men in the streets of the nation’s capital, and they seem like an unwelcome force, like something imposed from outside, just imagine the opposite. The farthest of looking at it, and saying, This is the armed forces of the United States, here to protect the nation’s capital. Thank God they’re here; how proud we are of them. How much we admire them; how grateful we are.
I remember later, just to flash ahead, talking to a National Guard commander saying that one of his biggest problems with his deployment in Washington was managing his troops’ weight, because local merchants kept bringing them donuts and cake and coffee and cookies. And after, like, the third round he had to say, No, no more cookies. No more cookies.
McConnell: Well, and you remember the president said the following week, just meditating on that day, and as you were noting—it was the perfect, perfect day. And then, remember the National Book Festival had been on the 8th. Saturday the 8th on the Mall; I think the 8th and 9th. And the National Book Festival would just spread out on the Mall, the lawn of the Library of Congress. People walking in and out of the Library of Congress building. And it was just free movement. And I think the president and Mrs. Bush went up there at one point and wandered around among the book festival.
And anyway, what the president said after the events—he said, Night fell on a different world.
Frum: Yeah. So it’s about 8:00 at night. We get into the White House. Again, and it’s a different White House. Because the security—although there was security before 9/11, a lot of security—it was different after. And it was already, it was instantly different.
So we didn’t go watch the president speak, which is what I think we normally would’ve done. Again, there were just many more barriers to moving around inside. And the president spoke to the nation, but still in a way that was a little punch drunk, in my opinion.
And I looked this up later. So, after the firing on Fort Sumter, President Lincoln’s first communication to the nation is a written proclamation that he issued three days after the firing on Fort Sumter. And after the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt’s first communication to the nation was his Day of Infamy speech. But Pearl Harbor was struck at dawn Hawaii time, which on Sunday, which is about midday Washington time Sunday. And the president spoke first thing Monday. So however many hours that is before the first communication. In—it’s not yet the social-media age, but it’s the cable-TV age, and the president has to speak the same day, immediately. And in a way, there isn’t really time. That isn’t enough time to organize what you’re going to say. And so even the 8:00 speech struck me as not the right tone, not the right message exactly.
McConnell: Well, and then it was Monday the 17th where we got the assignment to do the speech to Congress on Thursday. And that was, of course, that would be then September 20th. It was nine days after the events in question. And if you look at history, it feels like a long time. But he did have the speech at the National Cathedral on Friday, and the radio address. Which I don’t even remember what that—
Frum: Well, I want to put a break—again, I want to slow down here a little bit, because here are the things I remember that are signal events before the speech to Congress.
There’s the speech to the National Cathedral, as you said, which was, I thought, so—that was beautiful. This is not my own work. I’ll say, because my portfolio was domestic and economic, so I was spending all my time on, like, the stock market and the reopening of the airlines. So the speeches I’m about to praise, I had nothing to do with. That beautiful speech at the National Cathedral, which I think you and Scully mostly wrote. And then he went to New York to speak at Ground Zero. And that famous moment, “I can hear you,” that was, as far as I’m aware, completely improvised in the moment. And then—and I think this is the thing, I think, people don’t remember enough—that he went to the Washington mosque on Massachusetts Avenue, I think, again, before the speech to Congress. And stood with dignitaries local and national, and made a speech for tolerance.
And I just want to stress this point, because there is a lot of misremembering and I think a lot of misinformation about what it was like to belong to the American Muslim community after 9/11. There were a flurry of hate attacks after 9/11, in the immediate aftermath of 9/11. I remember, in fact, I think three of them were murders. Two of the murders were carried out by the same person. And the three victims—only one of the three was Muslim; one was Sikh, and one was South Asian of non-Muslim background. And then many other incidents of harassment and intimidation and insult and vandalism. But the president was so forceful condemning it that that flurry of hate-crime incidents—and three of them murders in the immediate aftermath—was quickly stopped.
And there is a dramatic drop-off between, after the month of September into October. I think the killings were in September and October. By January of 2002, the FBI is recording a steep drop, I think, of hate-crime incidents, from that last half of 2001. And that the leadership of President Bush and people like him really made an important difference in creating an atmosphere of tolerance and respect that is not as remembered as well as it should be.
McConnell: Well, that’s a nice point, David. And this is a great country, and no patriot is going to want to harm an innocent, unsuspecting person in response to something like this. I mean, this is the horror of 9/11, is that very thing: harming innocent, unsuspecting people. And President Bush in that sense spoke for the best in our country and brought out the best, as I like to think he always did, and I know that he tried to do.
Frum: Well, again, to conjure it up, so—President Bush is kind of an accidental president in a way. He lost the popular vote in the election of 2000. He becomes president, he wins the electoral vote, and everything teeters on the state of Florida, where, on a few dozen votes in the state of Florida—because in those days, every county got to design its own ballot, and many of the counties did a bad job. And there was recount upon recount, and tremendous ill feeling about it. And it left behind, I think, a shadow. I know he spent a lot of the first half of 2001 trying to find ways to broaden his support. There is an emphasis on education as an early initiative, because that had broad bipartisan support. You could pass it with big majorities of both Republicans and Democrats in both houses of Congress.
But still, there was a question mark over his presidency up to that moment. And I think there was this feeling of—would he measure up? Could this accidental president be someone who could speak for the nation after 9/11?
McConnell: Well, that’s right. And I remember Bob Dole candidly said, some months after that, he said—I think he was talking about September 14th, when Bush was on that flattened fire truck in New York City with the bullhorn, and didn’t even know he was expected to speak and had nothing prepared for him. And then had one of the iconic moments of his presidency—and Bob Dole said, that was like a second inauguration. (Laughs.) And it really was the man meeting his moment, and people getting a sense of him that they really hadn’t had or allowed. Or, in the case of many Americans, allowed themselves to have at that time.
Frum: Well, on his way to that moment, he landed in New York, and he was taken in a car to Lower Manhattan. And the emergency workers there are the firefighters, and a lot of, not onlookers because the area’s closed to the public, but there were a lot of people there. And they’re all cheering and waving and clapping and greeting him enthusiastically. And Mayor Giuliani, who was in the car with Bush—and Mayor Giuliani was a very different man in 9/11 from the man he is now—and I later heard that he had said to the president, You see all these people cheering for you? Not one of them voted for you.
McConnell: Well, and President Bush—you’ve heard him tell the story, David, and he repeated it in his book. He has a strong emotional memory of just one guy in a hard hat standing on a mound of rubble, making eye contact with him, and pointing his finger and said, “Don’t you let me down.”
Frum: (Laughs.)
McConnell: And it really, really touched his heart and stays with him to this day.
Frum: All right. So we have just a few minutes left. I want to flash forward; now look back on this from the perspective of 25 years. How did the country do? How did the Bush administration do? What did we get right? What did we get wrong? Do you have thoughts looking backward from a perspective of a quarter century on 9/11, and what it meant and what it led to?
McConnell: Nothing deep or profound. I grew up in the ’70s and ’80s. I remember once when I was about nine or 10 years old—I grew up in a town of 500 people in northern Wisconsin, and I have this memory of walking with one of my little friends around this little town on a summer day. And we agreed that we were probably never going to see a war in our lifetimes, because people, they don’t do this anymore. You know what I mean? That’s how things felt in the mid- to late ’70s. People aren’t going to fight wars anymore, big tanks and armies and all this stuff. And we just looked ahead to a future where that kind of tragedy and sorrow just wouldn’t fall on the human race like it used to. This is, you know, innocent kid stuff, right?
And the ’80s were pretty quiet. And you had the Cold War, but it’s a pretty, pretty quiet decade when you think about it. And so the point is—when 9/11 happened, that was very jarring for me, as it was for everybody. And you get this sense that the world—we might see a lot of things like this from now on, and we might see a lot of things like this inside the United States. That was my biggest fear, that the United States would, having found itself vulnerable that day, would continue to be. I didn’t think we had to be, but I was afraid that we might be.
And so when I look back, I think mainly of the president you and I worked for, and the responsibilities that we had. And there’s only so much that speechwriters can do. There’s only so much that’s on the page, and the rest is up to him. And when he did such a great job in those moments, it’s really because of him and the kind of man he was. And this was, as I said before, a man meeting his moment. And our country has not descended into the kind of fright and vulnerability that many of us feared could happen, and that’s not by accident. A lot of good decisions were made; a lot of difficult decisions were made that kept us safe. We could talk about any number of particulars and wars and things of that nature that have come since.
But by and large, I look back on that time as a pivotal point, a moment of great decision. And things were handled well by the people in power.
Frum: I will have a somewhat different view, which I’ll present on a later occasion. I’ll say just one thing as I think back on it. I think there are many might-have-beens in history, and I’m not a big believer in these alternative scenarios, because usually things that have big consequences don’t have happenstance causes. If the guns firing at Fort Sumter had missed, the Civil War would still have happened.
But one I do think about is, if [Osama] bin Laden had not got away in Tora Bora in December of 2001, if the United States and Britain and the many other allies who were there, and the Afghan partners of the United States—if they had succeeded in cornering him and killing him in Tora Bora at the end of 2001, would we have had the quarter century of wars in the Middle East that have since happened? His getting away caused an upping of the ante of American policy. The United States had to do something, and had failed to do in December 2001 the most necessary and logical and demanded thing. And so, sometimes when you fail to solve a problem, you redefine the problem to make the problem bigger.
It’s September 11th, 2026. The United States is at war with Iran; American troops have been engaged in anti-terrorist and counterterrorist operations all over the planet for a quarter century. The death toll has been high for Americans, and even higher for others. And I think that 9/11 of 2001 put us on this path. There was an exit in December of 2001, and we didn’t take the exit. We missed the exit. Not through anyone’s fault, or not through anyone’s intention. Maybe somebody’s fault. Not through anyone’s intention. We missed the exit, and here we are. And we’ll be talking about that more in the coming weeks.
And John, I thank you so much. Not only did I spend that day with you, I remember also very vividly spending my last day at the White House with you. We had lunch that day, and I remember going with you to the big bow in the South Lawn, the iron fence, and looking out and thinking, All my life I’ve wanted to look into this fence. I’ve had a year and a half of looking out of the fence, and now I’m looking out of it for the last time, with my good friend McConnell by my side. And for the rest of my life, I’ll be back to looking inside and trying to make sense of this with everyone else’s eyes of looking in.
But you, you’ve spent so much of your life inside, and your knowledge is so profound, and your heart is so big, and it was an honor to work with you and to be your friend.
McConnell: Thank you, David. It was an honor to be your colleague as well. It was a great time, and we’re so privileged to have had that experience.
Frum: Bye-bye.
McConnell: Thank you.

Frum: Thanks so much to my friend John McConnell for joining me today on The David Frum Show. This week’s book is also a contemplation of terrorism, but in this case, a contemplation of homegrown, domestic American terrorism. The book is American Pastoral by Philip Roth, published in 1997. In my opinion, probably his greatest novel.
American Pastoral tells a story of an American Jew whose daughter gets mixed up in extremist activity. The novel is narrated by a man named Nathan Zuckerman, who’s Roth’s recurring literary alter ego. And Nathan Zuckerman tells a story of his childhood friend, Seymour “The Swede” Levov, a golden-boy athlete from Zuckerman and Roth’s hometown of Newark, New Jersey. The Swede seems to have it all. He’s a former high-school sports star. He marries a Miss New Jersey. He takes over his father’s successful glove-manufacturing business, and he settles into an idyllic life in rural Old Rimrock, New Jersey. He has one child, an adored daughter named Merry, M-E-R-R-Y.
Merry becomes increasingly politically outspoken in the course of the 1960s, when the novel is set. She gets involved in radical causes. She becomes increasingly dogmatic. Merry has a speech impediment, and somehow that concentrates her rage into forms of action that are beyond speech. And ultimately, that expressed itself when, in order to oppose the Vietnam War, Merry plants a bomb in the local post office that kills a local doctor. Merry then disappears, goes underground, and The Swede spends years looking for her.
When he finally tracks her down, she’s back in Newark, New Jersey, living in terrible filth and squalor, and she has converted to a form of ultra-pacifism. She becomes a Jain, J-A-I-N, a religion from India that is so opposed to violence that it refuses to kill even an insect. And The Swede has to contemplate how his beloved daughter could swing from one extreme of murder to this other extreme of pacifism almost beyond reason.
The Swede, who’s had this perfect life—sheltered from everything, coasting on inherited prosperity and success on an American dream in a country that has been a golden land for Jews like himself—he has to confront this eruption of what Roth calls “the American berserk,” the country’s capacity to burst out from anybody’s planned order into these forms of strange, bizarre personal violence.
Roth is here describing something very real. I mean, I went through, did a quick scroll through incidents that reminded me of the story of Merry Levov—of privileged people, people at every American advantage who lash out, who would adopt some scheme of or some personal ideology of extremist hate, and then lash out in violence against others. There’s so many examples of this. Let me just mention a few that just come to mind in the course of an ordinary search.
Remember Elliot Rodger? Elliot Rodger was the son of a Hollywood director. He grew up in very comfortable circumstances. He developed this ideology of misogyny; incel, I think, is the term. Misogyny, violent hatred to women. He killed six people and wounded 14 in a rampage, leaving behind a manifesto justifying what he did.
Or Patrick Crusius. He was the man who turned a weapon on a parking lot in El Paso to kill 23 people, motivated by his “Great Replacement,” anti-immigrant ideology. He also acted alone, and he also had a comfortable middle-class upbringing in Dallas, Texas.
Or Luigi Mangione—this is a perfect example of this—who comes from a prominent family in Maryland, and he gunned down an insurance executive in New York City. Again, for some crazy, bizarre ideological reason all his own, that unfortunately has found resonance in some of the more malicious corners of online life.
Or Ayman Mohamed Ghazali; I’ve talked about him before. He’s the Lebanese immigrant who settled in Michigan, was given the opportunity to make a life for himself in America, given the amazing gift of American citizenship, and instead took guns to Temple Israel in West Bloomfield.
You know, these people all have motives. They may be diagnosable as having some kind of mental illness, but they’re not so delusional as not to understand what they’re doing. But they’re acting on some script, some sense of grievance—the American berserk that Roth talks about—that pushes them in these directions.
And notice something else. They all have these remarkable resources and freedom. They have the resources to acquire weapons, and they have the freedom to conduct their work without surveillance. There are many societies in which people like this would be caught early because they lived in more of a surveillance state. Americans have freedom, resources. They have the ability to become whoever they are. And for most of us, the ability to become whoever we are is a great gift. It allows us to realize ourselves in all kinds of ways, in ways that people could not realize themselves even in countries that are comparably free but are not as supremely abundant and affluent as the United States.
But when you’re given the right to be who you are, that reveals something in some people that is berserk, that is bad. It allows, it gives you more scope to be indulged in wickedness and cruelty and hatefulness, to come up with some crazy set of ideas all your own, or that link in some other way. And to act out against your fellows in ways that bring hurt and harm and sorrow and suffering to the human species.
America gives all of us the means to be ourselves, and the question we all face is: Who will we be?
That’s it for this week’s episode of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching. As ever, please, the best way to support the work of the show, if you can, is by subscribing to The Atlantic.
