Original | July 6 at 17:04 IST Pharmaceutical-sector focused AI startup Graph AI is in talks to raise $14 Mn (about ₹133 Cr) in a Series A funding round, sources told Inc42. The funding round will be led by US-based Insights Partners, and will also see participation from existing investors, including Bessemer Venture Partners, the sources added. However, the discussions are yet to be finalised, and the funding amount could change. Questions sent to Graph AI, Insight Partners, and Bessemer Venture Partners didn’t elicit any response till the time of publication. This comes over eight months after the startup raised $3 Mn in a seed funding round led by Bessemer. Founded in 2024 by Raghav Parvataraju (CEO), Vijay Ponukumati (CTO), Mohan Konyala (CPO), and Ashutosh Bordekar (CFO), Graph AI offers AI-native platform ‘Graph Safety’ to automate adverse drug event (ADE) monitoring, regulatory submissions, and aggregate safety intelligence for the pharmaceutical and biotech industries. Pharmacovigilance, which is mandated by global drug regulatory authorities, requires pharmaceutical companies to continuously monitor, detect, and report ADE across a drug’s entire lifecycle, from clinical trials to post-market use. The startup claims its flagship SaaS product Graph Safety, which is built on its graphx platform, unifies source, intake, case processing, aggregate reporting, signal detection, risk management, and regulatory compliance into one connected ecosystem. The product, which automates individual case safety reports (ICSR), is already live with enterprise customers. Graph AI is currently working on adding advanced capabilities to Graph Safety across the safety value chain. This comes at a time when AI adoption is transforming the drug discovery and safety landscape. Investors are actively backing AI-native startups as they look to capitalise on the opportunity the technology provides. For instance, AI-powered drug discovery startup Peptris raised ₹70 Cr (about $7.7 Mn) in a Series A funding round co-led by IAN Alpha Fund and Speciale Invest in February this year. Overall, AI funding is on the rise as its adoption is increasing across sectors. The funding raised by Indian AI startups surged over 4X YoY to $676 Mn during the first six months of 2026.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on how it proposed to determine whether packaged foods were “high” in sugar, salt or fat as part of its proposed front-of-pack warning labels, as it underlined that food safety was a cause of “national interest”.
The FSSAI had last month proposed prominent red warning labels on packaged foods high in added fat, added sugar or salt, marking a regulatory pivot after the top court questioned its reluctance to introduce such warnings.
In an affidavit filed before the court, the food regulator said the labels would take the form of a red hexagonal warning on the front of packages where a product was found to be high in two or more specified nutrients of concern — fat, sugar or salt. The thresholds would be based on those prescribed under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while examining the FSSAI’s affidavit, however, questioned how the regulator would determine the threshold beyond which a packaged food would be classified as “high” in sugar, salt or fat.
“If you ask them to put a label, say high in salt, high in sugar, high in sodium, high in potassium, how will you determine it? Have you laid down any guidelines?” the Bench asked.
Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, said the regulator was adhering to the guidelines issued by the ICMR-NIN.
The Bench was hearing a public interest litigation petition filed by non-profit organisations 3S and Our Health seeking warning labels on packaged foods to indicate high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fats. On Thursday, it indicated that it would soon pass a detailed order seeking further information from the stakeholders.
“We have done some homework and undertaken some study. We propose to pass an order calling for some further information from you. Study the order and come back with an appropriate further report,” Justice Pardiwala told Mr. Chahar.
‘Take orders seriously’
The top court also asked the regulator to take its directions “seriously”, stressing its concern over the impact of food safety standards on public health, particularly that of growing children.
“We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously... We expect one and all to extend cooperation in a cause which is in national interest,” Justice Pardiwala said.
‘Two-phase rollout’
The FSSAI had told the court that it intended to introduce the front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPNL) system in two phases to give consumers time to adapt to the new labels and the food industry time to reformulate its products. Under the first phase, the warning would apply to products high in two or more of the three specified nutrients, added fat, added sugar and salt, besides certain sweetened beverages. The second phase would extend it to products high in even one of these nutrients.
The Bench, however, questioned why a product would initially have to be high in more than one nutrient to attract the warning.
“It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?” Justice Pardiwala asked.
Taking the court’s suggestion into account, Mr. Chahar told the Bench that the regulator could consider introducing the warning labels “in one go”, rather than in two phases. This would effectively bring products high in even one of the three nutrients within the warning-label regime from the outset.
Senior advocate Devadatt Kamat, appearing for an intervenor, meanwhile argued that ultra-processed foods could not be placed on the same footing as other packaged foods, citing the example of snacks such as Kurkure on the one hand and eggs or salted cashews on the other. He urged the court to consider a more prominent warning for ultra-processed products.
“Ultra-processed food and packaged food... both cannot be equated,” Mr. Kamat submitted. Pointing out that red and green marks are already used to distinguish non-vegetarian and vegetarian products, respectively, he suggested that a different colour could be prescribed as a warning for ultra-processed foods.
The Bench said it would consider the suggestion and pass an order, which would be uploaded within a day or two.
Earlier, the court had questioned the FSSAI’s reluctance to adopt warning labels for foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat and asked whether pressure from food manufacturers was influencing the regulator.
“You don’t want people of this country to remain healthy? More particularly growing children?” the Bench had asked, warning the authorities that it was their “last chance” to rollout the warning labels.
The court had made clear that its concern was not about banning any particular food but ensuring that consumers, particularly children, knew what they were consuming before making a choice.

Kenya's foreign trader crackdown sparks fear among migrant communities
Kenya’s foreign trader crackdown sparks fear among migrant communities
NAIROBI, Kenya — In Kibera, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, it's another busy morning. People rush to work, hailing matatus along the roadside as vendors set up for the day.
But for foreign nationals who run small businesses here, it's far from business as usual.
Last week, President William Ruto ordered authorities to shut down small-scale businesses operated by foreign traders, saying such work should be left to Kenyans.
The president gave them until this week to comply, prompting fear among migrant communities.
At a matatu terminal in Nairobi, James Mogaka is already seeing the impact. He manages a hub for the country's ubiquitous minibus taxis and says many of the vehicles are owned or operated by foreign nationals.
"Today they have not come. Their vehicles are not here," he says.
Mogaka says one of his drivers is too scared to come to work and is worried about his wife, a Burundian national who runs a fruit business.
"The guy is even afraid that people might come to chase away the wife," he says. "I really don't know where we are heading."
The government announcement has left migrant communities anxious about the potential impact on their livelihoods and safety.
It also comes against a backdrop of rising tensions over migration and foreign-owned businesses in parts of Africa — from restrictions on non-citizens running certain businesses in Tanzania to a resurgence of xenophobic violence in South Africa.
The unease is palpable in Kenya, where many people affected by the directive were reluctant to speak to us on the record.
In Nairobi's central business district, the directive is drawing a mixed reaction.
Local trader Robert Kiberenge opposes the move. "The president is just trying to divert our attention from more pressing issues. We have no problem with foreigners doing small businesses in Kenya."
But there is also support for the president's move. Graduate Kiprono Kutuny is among those who back it.
"I concur with him. The government needs to protect the traders and small business people, but you find that these people who come from different foreign countries have taken these businesses and they are doing it in a cheap labor."
Kenya is East Africa's economic hub and is known for its relative political stability. The United Nations estimates put the number of international migrants living in Kenya at about 993,000 in 2024.
The government says the policy is intended to protect Kenyan traders in a crowded small-business sector, where competition from foreign nationals has become an increasingly contentious issue.
But economist Edward Kusewa says the President Ruto's directive is the wrong move. "I think it's very uncalled for."
Kusewa says the policy could undermine the principles of the African Continental Free Trade Area, which aims to ease the movement of goods and people across borders.
"These people contribute a lot to the economy," Kusewa says." They pay taxes directly and I think this is going to have an impact on the Kenyan economy."
Ruto faces voters next year, with the debate over who gets to operate small businesses unfolding against a backdrop of economic pressures and concerns over jobs and livelihoods.
As the government tries to reassure those affected, foreign nationals — many from neighbouring countries including Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo — have been turning to their embassies for help securing documents to return home.
On Tuesday, in an effort to ease concerns, the government gave undocumented East African nationals 90 days to obtain or update the documents required to stay and do business in Kenya.
But for many, the fear of what comes next has already taken hold.

Jimmy Kimmel is interviewing James Talarico today but his interview will only stream on YouTube after the late-night host said pressure from the FCC has prevented Disney from airing it on ABC.
The Texas Democrat, who is running for Senate, responded to the news and called the move the “most dangerous form of cancel culture”.
“Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” Talarico told MS NOW’s Symone Sanders Townsend on The Weeknight. “People at the top, powerful politicians, powerful media executives, censoring what we watch, what we read, what we say. And that, again, should be a concern to everyone who believes in the First Amendment and believes in the freedom of speech.”
Talarico, however, remained optimistic that the interview may well end up on ABC at some point. “I’m still hopeful that we can have this interview on the air. So we’ll see what happens tonight,” he added.
Watch on Deadline
This comes after Kimmel revealed on his show on Wednesday night that the President and the FCC has “threatened” him, the show, the network and local affiliates.
“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead,” Kimmel said.
This was a similar situation that the Democrat faced on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.
Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, also weighed in on the news.
“This is now the second time in a matter of months that a late-night host has disclosed they had to bury an interview because of FCC intimidation, and there is no way to know how many other editorial decisions across the country have quietly been shaped by this same pressure. No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview. Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office,” she said.

US existing home sales hit weakest pace in over a year
Contract closings slipped 2 per cent to an annualised rate of 3.98 million in August, as would-be buyers wait for relief on mortgage rates
Sales of previously owned homes in the United States slowed last month to their weakest pace in more than a year, as would-be buyers waited for relief on mortgage rates before purchasing.
Contract closings slipped 2 per cent to an annualised rate of 3.98 million in August, data released on Thursday by the National Association of Realtors showed. Last month marked one of only two times since the autumn of 2024 that sales have dipped below 4 million.
The disappointing figures reflect a housing market in desperate need of a catalyst. Home price growth has cooled off from the pandemic era, when annual increases ran into the double digits, but affordability concerns remain a material headwind for buyers.
The median sales price rose 1.6 per cent from a year ago to US$429,100, extending a streak of annual price increases dating back to mid-2023.
Mortgage rates, now at their highest levels in more than a year, also provide a disincentive to move, especially for people who refinanced a few years ago at borrowing costs less than half that. Nationwide, less than a quarter of outstanding mortgages have rates above 6 per cent, according to a recent housing report from Apollo Global Management.
“Mortgage rates and home sales move in opposite directions, so it’s not surprising to see a mild dip in home buying activity due to high mortgage rates,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement.

Xiaomi has landed in fresh trouble in India. The serious fraud investigation office (SFIO) has reportedly recommended a probe into alleged irregularities in the smartphone maker’s business model and compliance with the foreign exchange management act (FEMA). According to Reuters, SFIO has recommended a detailed investigation to examine the movement of funds by Xiaomi. The agency has also reportedly called for probing whether the company sought mandatory investment approvals after India tightened scrutiny of Chinese investments following border clashes between the two nations in 2020. Sources reportedly said that the Centre is examining the memorandum that was drafted in May this year. Based on the report, the proposed investigation would examine: Xiaomi's foreign investors and beneficial ownership Movement of funds between Xiaomi and related entities Whether required government approvals were obtained for investments post 2020 Possible violations of India's foreign direct investment (FDI) rules Whether financial statements and auditor reports contain material mis-statements The company's relationships with sellers and ecommerce platforms As per the report, the SFIO proposal said that it was recommending action against Xiaomi based on complaints and inputs received from the commerce ministry. It also called for "coordination" between other government agencies to flag overlapping violations. While the proposal did not specify the information that SFIO had reviewed, the agency, however, reportedly dished out a 21-point investigation framework with methodology and plan of action, including possible summoning of company executives if needed. "The inquiry should specifically cover whether preferential and exclusive launches of Xiaomi products on selected e-commerce platforms .... defeated the intent of the FDI policy applicable to ecommerce (companies)," SFIO reportedly said in its recommendations. Inc42 has reached out to Xiaomi for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response. However, a Xiaomi spokesperson told Reuters that the company has not received any notice or communication from the SFIO. “We accord paramount importance to the laws of the land and comply with them fully at all times,” the company reportedly added. The development comes as Xiaomi continues to be under regulatory scrutiny in India, with authorities examining alleged FEMA violations and customs-duty evasion. In January 2022, the government issued three show-cause notices to the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and sought ₹653 Cr in customs duty for the period between April 2017 and June 2020. In addition, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in 2022 seized ₹5,551 Cr from Xiaomi India's bank accounts under FEMA norms, alleging that the company had illegally remitted money overseas as "royalty". The development also comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit India over the weekend to attend a BRICS summit.

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

In a parallel universe, this week is Harry Brook's first as England's new Test captain.
There are numerous reasons why it will be Joe Root, rather than Brook, leading England into a new era against Pakistan at Headingley: the timing of Ben Stokes' retirement, Brook's workload as white-ball captain and Root's surprise willingness to resume the job among them.
Inescapably, there is also what happened during the winter, when Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington on the eve of a one-day international against New Zealand.
In June, Brook said it would be an "honour" to be asked to succeed Stokes. Almost two months later, he does not know if the Wellington incident has cost him the top job, at least for now.
"I dunno," he tells BBC Sport. "I honestly don't know. I don't really look at it like that.
"The decision to make Rooty captain is the right one. I'm actually really excited to see what he can do. He's definitely the right man to take over that job. I'm really looking forward to working alongside him."
For some, Brook became the poster boy of everything they disliked about the Bazball era, both for what happened off the field and for the way he plays the game on it.
At this point, it's probably worth noting that no man has scored more international runs across formats since Brook made his Test debut in 2022. Of all players to have batted at least 20 times in Test cricket for England in the past 60 years, no one has a higher average than Brook's 53.04.
Brook has occasionally done himself no favours, but there is also something uncomfortable about the narrative that surrounds the 27-year-old, especially in a sport that struggles with elitism.
He often speaks about how he is living his dream - his parents have told him he has been talking about playing for England since he uttered his first words.
But not everything about playing for England is a dream. Scrutiny, criticism and the court of public opinion. Brook had the lot after the Wellington misdemeanour became public knowledge.
"It was a tough period, especially when I was at home, getting ready to face the media," he says.
"I feel like the character that I showed throughout that period to go out there and still perform and lead the white-ball side fairly well - I was proud of myself and the team.
"I don't want to say it's helped me, but it's made me realise how big it is to be England captain. It's not just the leadership on the field. It makes a massive difference if you can lead with responsibility off the field."
Amid the Wellington fallout, Brook led England to important ODI and T20 series wins in Sri Lanka, as well as the semi-finals of the World Cup that followed. His own form was superb. In the maelstrom, he drew on an experience from three years earlier.
In 2023, his only season in the pressure cooker of the Indian Premier League (IPL), Brook struggled. After his one significant score for Sunrisers Hyderabad - admittedly an unbeaten century - he said he was glad to "shut up" supporters that had been "slagging me off".
"I got into a little bit of a rabbit hole with scrutiny and social media when I was at the IPL," says Brook.
"It didn't help me as a person on the field or off the field. I decided to, not stay away from social media, but also not go out of my way to look at it.
"On the other hand, I actually feel it's a little bit of a compliment if people are giving me scrutiny and have an opinion about my game.
"I know it's not a nice thing to see people slagging you off, but it means people care and people think I can put in a better performance than I have done that day."
There are comparisons that can be drawn between Brook and Stokes. Maverick players from working-class backgrounds, often finding themselves outnumbered by the well-to-do members of the dressing room.
But, like Stokes, Brook is authentic in the way he plays and speaks, even if that can get him into trouble. One example would be Brook's "who cares" line about batters being caught in the deep after an ODI against Australia two years ago.
"I would say that I'm an extremely honest person," says Brook. "I'm honest with myself and honest with my game.
"A lot of people say honesty is the best policy. I probably have got into trouble a few times being too honest."
Authenticity bleeds into Brook's batting, for better and worse. He is probably the most thrilling batter to wear an England shirt since Kevin Pietersen and no batter with at least 3,000 Test runs has scored more quickly than Brook, whose strike rate is almost 87 runs per 100 balls.
But Brook can delight and frustrate in equal measure, nowhere more so than on an Ashes tour when an average just under 40 was a disservice to his ability.
Costly crimes included his drive at Scott Boland in the calamitous second-innings collapse in the first Test and trying to hit Mitchell Starc for six over extra cover in the first innings of the second Test. "Shocking shots" were how Brook described them in Australia.
"If supporters get frustrated, imagine how frustrated I get," says Brook.
"It's something I've been really trying to work on, trying to assess conditions quicker, and read the surface better. To go out there knowing what shots are going to be hard and what is going to be easier.
"I practise every single shot and have done since the age of eight. In the nets, I'd do a 360 challenge with my dad. He'd throw balls and I'd have to try to hit it to a certain place: that corner, then that corner.
"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games."
At the end of that Ashes, Stokes pulled Brook aside to tell him his Test average could be as high as 65 or 70.
Though Brook says it's "not that easy", Stokes' point is only a select few have Brook's talent, and he might not be making the most of it.
"Yeah, maybe," says Brook. "I'm definitely not the finished article and maybe never will be."
And, when Brook says he knows what it is like to be a disappointed supporter, he pulls out his own example from when he was 16 years old, one that goes some way to explaining why he has grown so close to Brendon McCullum.
"I remember as a kid going to watch Baz play at Headingley for Warwickshire and Matthew Fisher got him out in his first over. I was absolutely devastated. I'd only gone to watch him," says Brook.
"After he got out I said to my dad, 'Can we just go home'. I kind of understand it as a fan of cricket."
Brook grew up at Burley-in-Wharfdale Cricket Club, where his entire family is part of the furniture.
Brook's father David recently had his 50th birthday party at the club, while Harry still nets there and gets along to watch while he can.
A scholarship to Sedbergh School - "posh", in Brook's words - was where he honed his game, with 6.20am nets run by former Kent player Martin Speight. Speight remains one of Brook's closest advisors.
Challenged to improve his conditioning as a teenager, Brook has worked hard on his fitness as a professional.
He used the time when he missed England's tour of India in early 2024 - his grandmother Pauline died in March that year - to get back on track after he had "slipped on the wrong path".
"I wasn't as good an athlete as I could have been," says Brook. "I went on meal plans, I went to the gym and ran, with schedules from the strength and conditioning coach.
"When I came back, I felt like I was seeing the ball a hell of a lot easier. The pace of a delivery felt slower. It helped to bat for longer periods of time and run twos better.
"It made a massive difference to my fielding as well. I just think it was a vital area of my career so far that I've improved on and it's made a massive difference."
When he was named as England white-ball captain last year, Brook pulled out of the IPL and remains banned from the competition as a result.
"Not really," says Brook, on suggestions of regrets over his exile from cricket's most lucrative tournament.
Club cricket, school, fitness and no franchise gigs apart from The Hundred are all parts of what Brook has put into his England career.
He may not be Test captain now, though he knows there is a good chance the job will come. When it does, Brook will have a better understanding of what it means to be captain because of his experiences of the past year.
"There are little things you learn throughout your career," he says. "Obviously, the past few months have been on quite a high scale.
"Having that responsibility now has made a massive difference for me. There is the potential I could be captain, but at this moment in time all I'm focusing on is trying to win a few games of cricket. I will be 1,000% behind Rooty and I'm really looking forward to what this Test side can do."
And, in the tough moments, Brook's England career never stopped being his dream.
"I'm an extremely upbeat person. I'm always happy," he says. "Even when things are bad, I think there's no point dwelling on things. You've got to be happy.
"I'm in a very privileged position to be able to say I do something I love as a job. I refuse to call it a job, but I'm doing something I love for work. That is a dream come true.
"Every time I step over the white line, it's always a phenomenal feeling to be able to say, 'This is my life.'"

Zelenskyy visits Canada to seek further military support for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Canada for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was in Canada on Thursday for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney, his latest international trip aimed at locking in future support for the fight against Russia’s invasion.
Ukraine is under pressure from Russia’s air war, which is using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defenses. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the upcoming winter as part of its campaign to demoralize civilians, Ukrainian officials say.
“The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter,” Zelenskyy said of his Canada trip in a social media post. “We will discuss how to strengthen our resilience, support our people, and ensure that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs to defend itself.”
Canada and European countries are sending their own weaponry to Ukraine and are also buying American weapons for Kyiv under the so-called Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL. The United States under President Donald Trump has stopped donating weapons to Ukraine.
“Canada has consistently provided Ukraine with concrete support, and this visit is about taking that cooperation further,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who was also on the trip, said on X.
Recent U.S. efforts to stop the more than four years of fighting have delivered no significant breakthrough, although Washington-brokered talks between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv are expected to continue.
Zelenskyy’s arrival on Wednesday night in Calgary, Alberta, came the day after his flight from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion.
The aerial drone battle between Russia and Ukraine has grown in scale since Russia’s all-out invasion in February 2022. Ukraine’s neighbors Romania and Moldova, and other European countries, have reported repeated drone incursions.
A Ukrainian sea drone wounded 28 people, including two children, on the waterfront in the Russian city of Sochi, local officials said. They said that beach infrastructure had been damaged but did not provide further details.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Thursday that its forces shot down 448 Ukrainian drones overnight. The drones were destroyed over 13 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Caspian seas, the ministry said.
Falling debris from a Ukrainian drone set fire to a home in Russia’s southwestern Voronezh region, killing one woman and wounding two other people, local Gov. Alexander Gusev said Thursday.
Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure targets supporting the war effort over the past 24 hours, including a refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and a port in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said Thursday.
Targets in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan and Bryansk regions were also hit, he said.
Those targets were hundreds of kilometers (miles) apart, underlining the scope and scale of Ukraine's domestically developed long-range drone technology that has unsettled Russia.
The previous day, Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery more than 3,000 kilometers (1,800 miles) from Ukraine in Siberia, Ukraine’s General Staff said, confirming earlier reports.
Meantime, Russian forces launched 149 drones, many of them jet-propelled, at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said Thursday.
One person was killed and two others wounded in a Russian drone attack on the Kyiv region on Thursday morning, regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
At least 16 other civilians were wounded in other Ukrainian regions, according to local authorities.

With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.
The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.
Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade
Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.
Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.
If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.
Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?
We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.
All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.
While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.
The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.
All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.
To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Apple has taken its time with its first foldable, enabling it to learn from the best folding phones already on the market. Eschewing the more prevalent book- and flip-style foldables, Apple has gone with a passport-sized form factor for the iPhone Duo, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current favorite). The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.
The iPhone Duo has a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating for solid dust and water resistance. But at 254 grams and 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded, the Duo is not the slimmest or lightest foldable around (the Fold8 is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded).
Foldables don’t have as much space for cameras, so the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). But it has room for the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.
Where Apple will likely add a lot of value to the foldable phone category is with its software design. Controls have been pushed to the side and stacked vertically to free up more screen real estate. Apps offer plenty of split-screen support, and transitions between displays look slick. Apple has also included features that take advantage of the fact that you can prop the Duo open on a table or nightstand, so there’s StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you.
Who it’s for: You want something different. You’re curious about folding phones or already convinced they’re great and can’t wait to experience Apple’s take.
The iPhone 18 Pro is similar to last year’s 17 Pro, with a 6.3-inch display, though the Dynamic Island has been slightly slimmed and can now show three Live Activities notifications at once. It keeps the same aluminum unibody, with Ceramic Shield on the back glass, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and an IP68 rating. Black is back, and there’s also a new Burgundy color, alongside Glacier and Silver. Those colors look more uniform than the 17 Pro’s two-tone finish.
Two standout upgrades stand out: the new A20 Pro chipset is faster and more power-efficient, and the main camera now has a variable aperture. The A20 Pro also enables better on-device AI and is aided by a redesigned vapor chamber to keep it cool while it works. Apple reckons you can expect 34 hours of video playback; that’s three hours more than the 17 Pro.
The camera introduces a physical lens aperture. Like the pupil of your eye, the aperture is the lens opening that lets light in. A bigger aperture can let in more light for better photos when it’s darker, and a smaller aperture can help you avoid overly bright photos when the sun is shining. But the aperture also impacts depth of field, so a bigger aperture can help you achieve that bokeh blurred background effect for a portrait photo, while a smaller aperture can help retain detail across a wider landscape shot. The camera app has new features and controls to help you take advantage of it.
Who it’s for: You don't want a big phone, but you want full-strength Apple silicon, a top camera, and all the latest features.
If foldables aren’t for you, the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the biggest screen you can get at 6.9 inches, and it is a battery-life beast. Apple says you can get up to 43 hours of video playback out of a full charge; that’s a six-hour increase on last year’s already impressive 17 Pro Max. It has the same design and colors as the regular Pro, just bigger.
You also get the new chip and variable aperture camera. Both Pro models now boast a versatile triple 48-megapixel camera system with pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. The class-leading video capture goes up to 4K at 120 fps. The iPhone 18 Pro phones are the right pick for photographers and videographers.
Who it’s for: You want the best Apple has to offer, including a big screen and long battery life, in a familiar form factor.
How to Get the iPhone 18 Unlocked
It makes sense to buy your iPhone unlocked, since it's much easier to switch carriers or use an international eSIM when you travel. The iPhones sold through Apple's storefront are unlocked, so Apple.com is the best place to buy them. During a preorder period, you can only purchase a newly announced iPhone from Apple.
Don't forget to take advantage of Apple's promotions: You get three free months of Apple One, which includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, Apple Arcade, News+, Apple Fitness+, and extra iCloud storage. Just watch out, because it will auto-bill you after the trial. Set a reminder to cancel if you don't want to continue subscribing to these services.
- The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256 GB
- The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256 GB
- The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256 GB
Apple has some financing options. If you have an Apple Card, you can pay for your iPhone over 24 months at 0-percent APR, and most carriers offer financing deals, too. Apple also offers Apple Upgrade, enabling you to lease your new iPhone from $35 a month for 24 months for the entry-model iPhone 18 Pro (12 months starts at $50 a month). We don’t think it’s a good deal, but if you’re tempted, remember you must return it in good condition (AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss costs an extra $15 a month).

All of a sudden, French entrepreneur Hèlene Huby is seemingly everywhere.
This week she is serving as one of two envoys, alongside astronaut Thomas Pesquet, at a high-profile International Space Summit convened by French President Emmanuel Macron. The government’s website for the event describes her as chief executive of “the fastest-growing space company in Europe.”
Also this week, that firm, The Exploration Company, announced a significant capital raise of $450 million in Series C funding. Although not spectacular by the standards of some US space businesses, this is the largest-ever Series C funding round by a Europe-based space company, and likely the largest funding round ever raised by a female-led company in Europe.
And Huby has arrived on center stage in the European space community at a time when there are increasingly urgent questions about the ability of the continent to navigate a future in space as commercial startups in the United States and China race ahead.
A lack of ambition
So many of the biggest European space projects of this decade feel dated. The flagship rocket, the Ariane 6 vehicle, is flying. But its costs are high, it is fully expendable, and its flight rate of 10 launches a year feels antediluvian in the megaconstellation era. Europe’s response to SpaceX’s Starlink constellation is a project called IRIS², which is already years behind schedule and has seen its estimated cost balloon to more than $15 billion before much metal has even been cut.
From civil projects, such as space-based data, to military applications, Europe seems to be fighting a losing battle on almost every front. All of this makes Huby refreshing because she is honest about the situation and has big ambitions. She seems to be one of the only people in Europe who recognizes these problems, speaks publicly about them, and is trying to do something about it.
After working for the traditional European space industry for about a decade, at heavyweights Airbus and ArianeGroup, Huby founded The Exploration Company five years ago. Initially, the company focused on building a relatively small cargo capsule to deliver supplies to, and return from, low-Earth orbit. This work has resulted in the Nyx spacecraft, which is now undergoing NASA safety reviews for a cargo mission to the International Space Station as early as November 2028.

China snaps up 1 million tons of American soybeans in massive trade surge ahead of Xi Jinping visit to Washington
China has bought around 1 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this week
China has procured approximately 1 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans this week, four traders told Reuters, as the world's top oilseed buyer steps up purchases ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington later this month.
The recent acquisitions bring Beijing's total purchases of American soybeans to nearly half of the 25 million tons the White House said China committed to buying annually through 2028.
While the orders could help bolster trade and diplomatic ties with Washington, the buying also coincides with tightening global oilseed supplies amid dwindling inventories in top exporter Brazil.
"There have been more purchases made by Sinograin in the past few days," said one Asia-based trader. "They have been buying before Xi's visit to U.S."
State-owned buyers Sinograin and COFCO did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported sales of 340,000 tons of U.S. soybeans to China, alongside an additional 100,000 tons to undisclosed destinations.
China maintains a 10% additional tariff on all American goods, including agricultural products, following a tit-for-tat trade conflict last year. A reduction in the soybean tariff could encourage private Chinese crushers to return to U.S. supplies after tariffs largely shut them out of the market.
Following a meeting between the two leaders in May, Washington said China had agreed to buy $17 billion worth of non-soy U.S. agricultural goods annually through 2028, while upholding its pledge to purchase 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans each year over the same period.
In late July, President Donald Trump said Xi would visit Washington on September 24. China has not confirmed the visit date or the volume of any planned purchases of U.S. soybeans or other agricultural commodities.

Jadavpur University (JU) saw night-long rampage and vandalism on August 20, when a mob, armed with sticks and rods, allegedly stormed the campus.
The violence followed a heated altercation late on August 19 between activists from the Akhil Bharaitya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) from the university’s engineering department and members of the Left-wing student outfit, Democratic Students’ Federation (DSF), and other student organizations. The ABVP alleged that its members were assaulted and that several workers required hospitalisation. Students from the engineering faculty disputed the claim and offered a counter-account of the incident.
By midnight, an armed mob allegedly entered the campus, apparently seeking to avenge the earlier altercation. The attackers tore down and set fire to placards, festoons and flags belonging to various student organisations active on the campus. The mob also surrounded Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building, trapping students inside.
The violence was captured by CCTV cameras installed across the university campus. Students and journalists also recorded several videos of the incident. Alt News accessed multiple such recordings and analysed them to establish the identities of those involved in the ruckus.
What happened at JU: A Blow-by-Blow Account
Around 9:30–10:30 pm on August 19, the DSF-run Faculty of Engineering & Technology Students’ Union (FETSU) held a general body meeting on the campus. The meeting had been announced through the union’s social media account.
ABVP and the allied Right-wing student outfit, Nationalist Students’ Front (NSF), opposed the meeting, citing a Calcutta high court ruling that no activities could be undertaken from student union offices until fresh student union elections were held. According to students present, ABVP and NSF members were outnumbered and were forced to leave the spot. A few DSF members were also injured in the ensuing scuffle.
Ayantik Pal, a third-year B Tech student who attended the meeting, said the GB meeting had been convened to elect signatories for the union’s email ID, Facebook account and bank account. Since the last FETSU election was held in 2020, he said, the meeting was intended to allow the union to continue its functioning.
According to Pal, ABVP activists at the meeting repeatedly objected that it was illegal. He said they nevertheless participated when names for the signatories were being proposed, before becoming agitated as the meeting progressed. They allegedly abused some students, calling them “Naxals” and “Maoists”, following which a scuffle broke out.
Accounts diverge over what happened immediately afterwards.
According to students, Nikhil Das, an ABVP research scholar and president of the organisation’s JU unit, attempted to enter the undergraduate and postgraduate students’ GB meeting and allegedly tried to provoke a confrontation. Students said they intervened to stop him, escalating the situation. They alleged that three DSF workers were injured in the assault by ABVP activists and that one was taken away towards the Sulekha Crossing. ABVP denied these allegations.
ABVP, meanwhile, claimed that Das was assaulted during the GB meeting and subsequently had to be hospitalised at KPC Medical College and Hospital. BJP MLA from Jadavpur Sarbari Mukherjee visited him at the hospital. Students alleged that during the visit, she threatened that ABVP and BJP workers would retaliate if those accused in the assault did not surrender. She later repeated this on camera.
Around midnight, a crowd of approximately 50–60 people gathered outside Gate 4 of the university, which is the only entrance that remains open at night. By around 12:30 am, the group entered the campus.
Pramita Basu, an undergraduate Philosophy student, said that after 7 pm, everyone entering the campus is required to show an ID card, including hostel residents. However, according to her, the crowd entered without being stopped by the guards stationed at the gate.
The group moved from Gate 4 towards the Science-Arts crossing, where some wall graffiti was allegedly damaged, before turning towards Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building. Videos from the night accessed by Alt News show some members of the group carrying saffron flags.
Meanwhile, students who had remained on campus after the earlier confrontation gathered inside Aurobindo Bhavan. According to them, they had decided to stay back until morning because they had heard that ABVP activists were looking for them outside the university.
Pal said an all-faculty GB meeting was also convened that night, with students from the arts, science and engineering faculties discussing what to do next. Around 12:30 am, he said, a university staff member alerted them that a mob had entered the campus and advised them to protect themselves.
“Within minutes, we saw a stream of mobile flashlights coming towards Aurobindo Bhavan from the side of the green zone. A few students present at the green zone were thrashed by this mob,” Pal said.
The students then woke the guards at Aurobindo Bhavan, obtained the keys and locked themselves inside, according to Pal.
The crowd that reached the building tried to break through its collapsible gates but failed. It then tore down red flags, festoons and posters belonging to student organisations and set them on fire outside the administrative building. Students trapped inside alleged that members of the crowd abused them verbally, threw stones and eggs at the building, and attempted to throw burning flags inside. Footage of the episode was broadcast live on television and recorded by students and journalists.
The violence continued until around 2 am. Around the same time, another group gathered outside Jadavpur police station and allegedly attempted to breach the entrance to the university’s main hostel, located next to the police station.
At the protest, ABVP West Bengal leaders were reportedly heard telling the media that the organisation was “putting the last nail in the coffin” of the “Dimagi Naxals” and would carry out “surgical strikes” at Jadavpur University to suppress them.
By around 2:30 am, the crowd had dispersed. The students who had taken shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan began leaving the campus at around 5 am.
Alt News procured a third CCTV footage from University sources, where several persons of interest can be spotted as present on the campus on the night of August 20.
The confrontation did not end with the dispersal of the mob.
Around noon the following day, the Student Federation of India (SFI) and other Left student organisations held a protest near the Lenin statue at Jadavpur 8B bus stand. Kolkata Police barricaded the area and stopped the protesters from proceeding towards the university. Around 2 pm, an ABVP rally that began from Golpark reached Gate 4 of the university. Students inside the campus also gathered in response. As Gate 4 was kept locked to prevent outsiders from entering, a face-off between the two groups on either side of the gate ensued.
During the confrontation, members of the ABVP crowd were seen standing on the historic university emblem designed by artist Nandalal Bose as they attempted to cross the closed gate and enter the campus.
Visuals of Rajyeshwar Sinha, a professor of Bengali at JU, holding the partially damaged University emblem went viral.

ABVP Denial
Directly denying any role of ABVP, the outfit’s central working committee (CWC) member Subhabrata Adhikary said on a talk show on ABP Ananda, that ABVP had no connection with the rampage at Jadavpur University on August 20. When pointed out by the anchor that people in the mob were holding ABVP flags, Adhikary said, “It doesn’t prove anything. SFI workers have done the vandalism while holding ABVP flags”. When asked if ABVP was condemning the night-long violence, he again said, “It is clear that ABVP has no connection with the incident.”
Talking to The Times of India, south Bengal ABVP secretary Neelkantha Bhattacharya, too, denied his presence during the campus violence. However, he then said, some of ABVP boys entered the campus “out of over-enthusiasm. The gate was open. We just pushed inside. I went at most 10 steps inside the university to get them out”.
Adhikary, on the other hand, contradicted his own statement on ABP Ananda, and told TOI, “I was standing right by the gate. I have no connection with the mob. After hearing about the situation, I went there to ensure that no untoward incident happened. ABVP has no involvement in any vandalism.”
CCTV and Video Footage Disprove ABVP Claims
Alt News examined CCTV footage from the intervening night of August 19-20 and identified several prominent ABVP faces and BJP-linked political figures on the campus.
1. Subhabarta Adhikary
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 (Captured by a camera fixed on the external wall of PG Arts building)
As the gate opens at 12.38.17 am, Adhikary is one of the first persons to enter the campus, followed by a crowd. When the group nears a large white SFI banner, he is seen saying something in an animated manner. Within seconds, others in the crowd tear down the banner. It is not clear whether he instructs them to do it or tries to dissuade them.
2. Neelkantha Bhattacharya
Visible in JU CCTV footage-2 (Captured by a camera installed on a pole at the science-arts crossing).
Around 12:40 am, Neelkantha Bhattacharya is seen carrying a rod or a stick while instructing a group. In the same footage, at the 12:39:22 am mark, Subhabrata Adhikary is seen next to him. They are in front of the PG science building. At 12:40:28, the two once again can be seen together. This time Bhattacharya is carrying sticks in both hands.
It is worth noting that Bhattacharyya first told TOI that he was not present on the campus. Then, he claimed, he had barely taken 10 steps inside the gate. The distance from Gate 4 to PG Science building, according to Google Maps, is over 360 feet, i.e., about 110 meters.
3. Somsurya Banerjee
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Banerjee, an NSF activist, is spotted on the campus around 1.14 am on August 20. Banerjee had earlier courted controversy by claiming that cows were slaughtered within the University during Iftar.
4. Aditya Mondal
Visible in footage captured by Mrittika TV, a local media outlet.
The portal captured the exact moment when the crowd entered the campus, in a livestream. Although the video was later deleted from the page, Alt News accessed the footage. In that video, (embedded in the story above) Aditya Mondal, the ABVP candidate for the recently held election to internal complaint committee (ICC) of the Arts Faculty, was spotted near the PG science building. The wall had an SFI graffiti, where a person was seen urinating on the Nazi Hakenkreuz. The writing next to it said, ‘Break Fascism with Red’. Mondal was seen with a group that tried to rub the symbol off. Mondal can be heard saying, “The left-naxals had insulted the symbol of India, Swastik. We are correcting it.”
5. Partha Chakraborty
Visible in the footage captured by students stuck inside Aurobindo Bhavan, during the rampage.
Partha Chakraborty, a Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM) worker from the Dhakuria area, was also present at the scene. In videos captured by the students stranded inside Aurobindo Bhavan, he was seen burning flags of SFI and other Left organizations in front of the collapsible gate of the building, and throwing the burning flags inside. Three days later, on August 23, he was seen with BJP’s losing candidate from Kasba assembly Sandeep Banerjee and South Kolkata Yuva Morcha leader Shatadru Ghoshal.
6. Abhijeet Roy (Raja)
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Another prominent face identified in the footage from that night is Abhijeet Roy alias Raja, the election agent of Jadavpur MLA Sarbari Mukherjee. In a video posted on social media, Roy was seen standing with a group outside Gate-4, with one member holding an ABVP flag. ABVP leader Neelkantha Bhattacharya is part of the group. Roy’s entry into the campus was also captured on CCTV footage. He is seen interacting with a group of men with former VC Buddhadeb Sau standing at an arm’s length.
7. Buddhadeb Sau
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3.
The most talked about entry on that eventful night was perhaps that of Buddhadeb Sau, professor of mathematics and ex-VC of the university. Sau’s presence raised eyebrows not only for the fact that it is unusual for an academic of his stature to be on the campus past midnight, but also because of his Sangh connections. He is associated with the RSS-backed Akhil Bhartiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), and represented the organisation at a joint press meet held by Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh JU unit, ABVP JU unit and ABRSM JU unit, held after the campus violence.
Sau can be spotted in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3. In the JU CCTV footage-1 feed, he is seen entering the campus through a side gate at 12:39:44 am, and exiting through the same gate at 12:44:35 am. For the entire duration, he stood in front of the security guards’ room, occasionally speaking to others. From 12:44:09 till his exit 26 seconds later, he is seen watching others tearing down what appears to be political flags put up on Gate-4.
Sau is seen once again in JU CCTV footage-3. This time he was captured by the camera installed on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4, at 1:06:33 am. This time also, he is seen standing in front of guards’ room.
Asked about his presence during the rampage, Sau told TOI, “I went to the spot as soon as I received news of the disturbance. No one from the authorities was present there. I was concerned. I told the police to get additional cops to manage any potential flare-up. Once the group retreated and the situation was brought under I returned to my quarters. I went and tried to protect the students; is that my crime?”

Trump gives nonsensical answer when quizzed about delay for his $5,000 ‘dividends’
The White House has offered few details about the plan to send $5,000 checks to Americans after the midterms
In a recent interview, President Donald Trump offered a vague answer when asked about the timing of the $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks he said his administration would send to Americans after the midterms.
The Republican, who outlined the plan last night at the GOP’s midterm convention in Texas, spoke with Fox News’ Laura Ingraham about the check plan after his speech.
In a preview clip of their interview, which will air in full on Thursday evening at 7 p.m. Eastern time, Ingraham asked the president why he was promising to send the checks after the midterms if the money was available now.
“Because the Democrats can’t do it. Because with them, it’s negative growth. With us, it’s so positive,” Trump said. “So, we’re taking in $21 trillion. No country has ever taken in anywhere near that. It’s four or five times higher than the next one. All because of that beautiful word you and I love more than most others, tariffs.”
(It is unclear what $21 trillion the president was talking about, but neither his tariffs nor investment commitments to the U.S. have brought in that much money.)
During his speech, the president said the checks would go to all American adults and were contingent on voters helping Republicans keep their majority in Congress, a pitch critics said resembled buying support ahead of the November elections.
“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said during his remarks.
The White House did not provide additional details about the plan when asked for comment by The Independent.
“President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle told The Independent in a statement.
Trump has repeatedly floated payments for Americans that have never arrived, including $2,000 checks tied to tariff income, $5,000 checks from DOGE savings and federal funds for healthcare spending. During the Wednesday night speech, Trump compared the payout to the administration’s $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” checks for American military service members.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election … because Republicans (and America) will win!” Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote on X after the speech.
Trump ally Elon Musk faced allegations of vote-buying during the 2024 election, which he denied.
During the presidential race, Musk, a prominent Trump surrogate and donor, carried out a $1 million-per-day sweepstakes for voters who signed a petition supporting the U.S. Constitution. Critics said the scheme was a thinly veiled attempt to buy a Trump win.
During the pandemic, Democrats campaigned on proposals for a $2,000 stimulus check.

The presence of E. coli and coliform bacteria in bottled drinking water in Kochi, Keralam, has prompted authorities to take measures to address contamination risks and ensure water traceability. The Kochi Corporation is planning to make it mandatory for hotels to use only Kerala Water Authority (KWA) water, which would help ensure the use of safe water and enable traceability.
Chairperson of the Health Standing Committee Seena Teacher said the decision was taken after inspections found contamination in water used at some hotels.
“The idea is to make them use only KWA’s water, thereby ensuring the veracity of the source of the drinking water. We have plans to create a QR code for this, through which they can get water from the KWA using the My Kochi mobile application. We will also hold a meeting with the stakeholders to trace the source of the water and take necessary action,” said Ms. Seena.
The contamination was observed in the samples collected from eateries as part of the surprise checks carried out jointly by the Health Department, Kochi Corporation, Food Safety Department and police.
Food Safety Assistant Commissioner Jose Lawrence said that while inspections are periodically carried out at the water bottling units in the city, the presence of E. coli was not observed. “We carry out checks in packaged drinking water (water bottles) from random locations. In this light, we will focus more on the cans as well. We recently received a complaint from the Kalamassery area about fungal growth in a can from a supplier. Test results are awaited,” said Mr. Lawrence.
The most probable number (MPN) of coliform bacteria detected in the samples ranged from 17 per 100 ml to 1,600 per 100 ml. According to experts, the MPN should be zero in drinking water and the high MPN values indicate faecal contamination and render the water unfit for human consumption.
More checks sought
According to Kerala Hotels and Restaurants Association (KHRA) representatives, more inspections need to be carried out to find the source of contamination.
KHRA State president G. Jayapal said that only packaged water with Indian Standards Institute (ISI) marking is used in hotels. “We will be directing all hoteliers to procure water from reputed agencies,” said Mr. Jayapal.
Not dismissing the chances of such contaminated drinking water cans entering into households, Consortium of Flat and Villa Owners Association, Kerala State chairperson Saju Abraham said awareness among the end user was crucial.
“While KWA’s water is used in apartment complexes, a significant percentage of the residents rely on canned water. Tracing the source of the water used by these agencies as well as tankers is important,” said Mr. Abraham.
