In September 2026, a rumor circulated online about a black bear that apparently took a wounded raccoon, and later a wounded fox, to a wildlife center where the bear itself had been treated.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) said:
The first time, nobody believed it. Security cameras at a wildlife center captured a black bear approaching a rear entrance carrying a wounded raccoon in its mouth. It placed the animal gently beside the door. Then disappeared into the woods.
[…]
Several weeks later, cameras recorded a bear approaching a side entrance with an injured fox. Same careful approach. Same gentle placement near the door. Same quiet exit into the trees.
Both animals were found alive and received treatment.
Workers compared the two recordings. Both bears had the same unusual white mark on their chest. Same bear. Two deliveries. Two injured animals brought to the one place that could help them.
Staff searched old photographs and records of bears previously treated at the facility. That's when everything clicked.
Years earlier, the same bear had been rescued, treated at that very wildlife center, and released back into the wild. He had been a patient there. And now he was bringing patients back.
Officials believe the bear remembered where it had once been helped and returned because it somehow understood that injured animals would be safe there.
Other Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same text. The black bear story also appeared in a YouTube short (archived).
Snopes readers sent emails and searched the website wondering whether the story was true.
There's no evidence supporting the rumor that a black bear took a wounded raccoon and a fox to a wildlife center it had previously received treatment at. It was posted online by a page with a history of posting heartwarming — though fictitious — animal stories generated with artificial intelligence tools.
As such, we've rated this claim false.
We searched Google for "bear brought raccoon to wildlife center" and "bear brought fox to wildlife center," and also searched DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo using the same phrases. None of the searches yielded credible evidence supporting the story's veracity.
Snopes also used Google Lens to conduct a reverse image search on multiple different images posted alongside the story purportedly taken at the unidentified wildlife center.
That search revealed the story appeared to originate from the Facebook page StoryTime, which posted (archived) prior to the other social media posts linked in this fact check.
StoryTime's history
Snopes has been fact-checking StoryTime's animal rumors for more than a year. The page frequently posts fictitious, AI-generated animal stories supported by AI-generated images that are usually purposefully grainy and/or blurry, all meant to generate clicks because of their surprising or heartwarming nature.
At one time, the intro section on StoryTime's Facebook page read, "story (noun) - an account of imaginary or real people and events told for entertainment." At present, the page's intro section reads, "Animal rescue storytelling from around the world 🌎🐾 Real moments, inspired stories, and emotional second chances ❤️."
Facebook users can subscribe to the page using real money, which gives the page incentive to continue pumping out the animal stories it's known for, regardless of their reality.
AI-generated text
StoryTime's version of the claim begins with the headline "Wildlife Center Releases Statement After Bear Saves Two Injured Animals." StoryTime, much like the other Facebook pages telling the story, doesn't name the wildlife center or the worker quoted, or describe any geographic details about where these events took place. (Even without those identifiers, the wildlife center's statement, which isn't directly quoted in the post, should have showed up in search engine results, if real.)
When we input the text of StoryTime's version of the claim and that of another version of it into Pangram, which is widely considered the most reliable AI-text detection tool available as of this writing, it concluded that 100% of both versions were written or assisted by AI.
It's important to note that even the best AI detection tools can be fallible. Snopes cautions against using them to find definitive answers on the authenticity of texts or images without additional corroborating evidence.
AI-generated images
Each of the four Facebook posts linked in this story uses a different pair of images of the black bear carrying the raccoon and fox to the wildlife center, which is already a major red flag for the tale's authenticity.
In one version, the size of the object at the bottom left of the building's wall is sized differently in the pair of images presented.
In another version, the building is different in each of the two images presented. The bottom of the pair appears to depict a door opening inward from the right even though the door's handle is on its left side.
In a third version, the building and its door are once again inconsistent from one image to the other.
In StoryTime's version, neither the building, the stone patio nor the gravel-covered grounds around the building are the same between the pair of images.
The general lack of consistency between images is a telltale sign of AI generation, as artificial intelligence tools usually generate each image from scrap and therefore sometimes struggle in keeping details consistent when trying to emulate multiple images of the same place.
StoryTime does not keep its DMs open, leaving Snopes unable to contact the page for comment. StoryTime has not replied to past attempts by Snopes to contact the page's administrators, either.

How the WNBA became a political prop in the culture wars
The Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA) is having a landmark year. Viewership and attendance are up, team valuations are soaring and the league just signed a massive $3.1 billion media rights deal.
Journalist Sabreena Merchant, who covers the WNBA for The Athletic, says in many ways the league is in a better place than ever: "There's so much talent. The quality of play in the league is better than it ever has been. The playoff field is really exciting and it's kind of open. So no one really knows who's gonna win the title in 2026."
But Merchant also acknowledges that the league has become embroiled in controversy and culture wars. According to Media Matters, since June 25, Fox News has dedicated at least 206 segments to the WNBA, largely aimed at stoking tensions related to race and trans athletes.
"Everything in the WNBA seems to take on a political lens far beyond what is actually happening on the court," Merchant says. "And I think it's because people see an opportunity to use the league as a political prop."
The management of the Chicago Sky has disclosed that it is enlisting help from national security experts in an effort to protect its players off the court. Meanwhile, league commissioner Cathy Engelbert recently announced her plans to step down at the end of the calendar year.
"There is just a lack of control of the narrative of the WNBA, and I don't think the commissioner is entirely to blame," Merchant says. But, she adds, "I think they want a commissioner who is better able to control the story around the WNBA and prevent it from being a political prop in all of these culture wars."
Interview highlights
On why physicality in the WNBA has become a talking point
I think part of it is an element of misogyny. There's a segment of the population that thinks that it's protecting women by preventing them from being in any spaces where they may be, I don't know, like beaten up a little bit, like on a basketball court. There's a lot of people who don't think that women should be engaging in physical labor, which athletics very much are. And that is the undercurrent to me of any objections towards physicality in women's pro-athletics because a lot of people don't believe women should be playing professional sports as is.
On claims that Indiana Fever player Caitlin Clark, who is white, gets special treatment from the league and from the NBA
Caitlin is sort of the golden goose that came in in 2024 and created this rocket ship of popularity that the league has experienced ever since. When we talk about viewership records, those tend to involve games that include the Indiana Fever. Her WNBA draft was the most viewed. When she participated in the All-Star game, that was the one that caused record attendance. Sort of an understanding that this is where our bread is buttered, let's make sure to take care of this, and that's something that [NBA Commissioner] Adam Silver has at least publicly made clear that he is worried about the treatment that Caitlin Clark gets — that's not a sentiment that Cathy Engelbert has publicly expressed, but based on the way players' relationships are with the commissioner, there seems to be a sentiment that certain players have better access to things than others.
On the perception that Black players on opposing teams disproportionately defend Clark
There is a perception that I see online and get in my email inbox from fans that Clark is defended more tightly by Black players because they resent the attention that she gets by WNBA marketers and all of the fandom that she has brought in. … The data does not suggest that at all. Caitlin Clark draws more fouls than any other guard in the league. And yes, she has more usage. She has the ball in her hands more often. But she is still getting to the line and drawing fouls at a higher rate than other players at her position. So to suggest that she is getting played more physically, maybe that's the case. But she's also receiving the fouls because of that and earning the free throws as a result. …
The WNBA has historically been built on the back of Black women. Most of the great players in the league have been Black women and the fandom has been a safe space for marginalized communities like Black women, like LGBTQ women. And things started to change when Caitlin Clark came into the league and brought in a new fandom that, didn't have those identities. She is a straight, white woman from middle America. And it's not as if the WNBA hasn't had white superstars before. ... But Caitlin still is kind of unique in the grand scheme of the WNBA because she has a fandom that didn't relate with her because of those marginalized identities. ... The majority of players in the WNBA are Black, so she is going to be defended by a lot of Black players.
On Sophie Cunningham's statement on trans women in WNBA
In July of this year, ESPN released a profile of Sophie Cunningham, an athlete on the Indiana Fever, who has monetized being Caitlin Clark's teammate better than anybody else. ... She has taken advantage of every opportunity to increase her popularity by being on the Indiana Fever. … In this profile that was written about her, she has a line in the middle of it where she says that she doesn't believe that trans women belong in girls sports. And she was asked about that after the profile came out and doubled down on her statement saying that she wants to protect young girls in sports.
In doing so, Sophie became the first active professional women's athlete to express these sentiments about restricting transgender women from women's sports. And a lot of people latched onto her as this avatar of this particular viewpoint of keeping women's sports exclusively for cisgender women. ... As of now, the WNBA doesn't have an expressed policy about transgender athletes in their league. In the CBA [collective bargaining agreement], it says that you have to be a woman to play in the WNBA, but it doesn't go on to define what a woman is.
The WNBA has never had a transgender player in its history. They've had a couple of non-binary players, both of whom were assigned female at birth. There have never been any eligibility concerns about transgender women wanting to enter the league. The NCAA doesn't even currently allow transgender athletes to play, so it's hard to see where the pipeline would come from. It's a question it's really never had to confront. So it's a theoretical issue at this point, one that the WNBA is not currently presented with.
On concerns about the quality of the officiating in the WNBA
It is universally acknowledged by white players, Black players, straight players, gay players alike that WNBA officiating is not as good as the quality of play in the league. They don't have full-time officials. The training process is such that the good ones from the G League end up going to the NBA, and the less good ones end up go to the WNBA. For a long time, it was even written that when officials went from the WNBA to the NBA, they were being promoted. So they are not even getting the best quality officials in this league. A lot of them have to referee college basketball as well during their offseason. So they're sort of picking up two different sports at the same time, because college rules are a little bit different than the WNBA rules.
On WNBA players supplementing their salaries overseas
Prior to the collective bargaining agreement that was instituted during the 2026 offseason, the average salary for a WNBA player was a little over $100,000 ... and that necessitated a lot of players to play overseas during their WNBA offseasons. ... And that means that players are competing year-round, not giving them a lot of time to rest, recover their bodies, work on their games even, or spend time with their families and loved ones during their break from their WNBA season.
For the majority of the WNBA's history, players made more money on their overseas contracts, whether that was playing in Russia or Turkey or France or Italy or Australia, compared to their WNBA contracts. I mean, it got so ridiculous at points that a player like Diana Taurasi, after winning a WNBA title in 2014, goes to play in Russia during that offseason and then her team says, we're going to pay you a million dollars not to play on the WNBA this year, just so you can rest and be ready for our next season. And so she sits out instead of defending her title and makes ten times as much money as she would for not playing as she would by playing.
The new collective bargaining agreement has created an average salary of about $600,000 now for WNBA players. ... And there is a revenue-sharing component in the CBA such that as the WNBAs revenue rises, whether that's more media money, more ticket money, any sort of revenue that the league brings in, that would create a corresponding change in the WNBA salaries.
Monique Nazareth and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

The United States has now named six Chinese AI firms accused of waging industrial-scale attacks distilling US frontier AI model capabilities and perhaps sparing billions in Chinese development costs.
In a joint release Tuesday, the National Security Agency (NSA), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) alleged that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI have been attacking US models since at least late 2024. The firms “likely” acted with “Chinese government awareness” when extracting capabilities from US models, including variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok, agencies said.
“China-based AI companies that conduct industrial-scale distillation against US AI models see significantly shorter AI development timelines and reduced financial expenditures in training a frontier model,” agencies said.
All American AI firms must work with the government and US allies to end the alleged theft threatening the US lead in the AI race, the agencies said. That will require coordinated action across the AI ecosystem to combat the “aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale that extract restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities of US frontier AI models.”
Attack methods include “exploiting AI model inference APIs” by bulk-buying fake accounts, agencies said. Not registered to legitimate users, these swarms of fraudulent accounts execute “highly coordinated queries featuring identical or similar prompt texts,” which range “from thousands to millions on similar topics.”
Another common method is using prompt injection techniques to jailbreak models, including crafting “prompts forcing models to reveal their hidden [chain-of-thought] reasoning,” agencies said. For example, “DeepSeek employed prompts instructing models to imagine and articulate the internal reasoning behind completed responses and write it out step by step.”
Fixes may frustrate AI users in US
To encourage firms to work together, agencies recommended mitigations that would supposedly make it harder for Chinese firms to steal from US models.
First, AI firms must improve detection of sophisticated campaigns that allegedly use tens of thousands of accounts relying on “a gray market of proxies” to evade geographical restrictions and “route distillation requests through multiple pathways to gain unauthorized access.”

Empty seats and technical glitch mar ‘Trump-a-palooza’ and the president’s wild speech
President Donald Trump tries to claim arena ‘packed’ for Republican midterms convention – but urges crowd not to go to the bathroom in case media report otherwise
President Donald Trump’s speech on the opening night of his Republican midterms convention in Dallas, Texas, was marred by a bad technical glitch and large sections of empty seating, despite his insistence the arena was “packed.”
The two-day “Trump-a-palooza” summit had threatened to be a disaster before it began, with many congressional Republicans making their excuses and declining to attend and the timing of the televised event likely to cost it viewers, given that it clashed with the NFL season opener.
When the president finally took to the stage at the American Airlines Center, he bragged about the size of the crowd inside the 21,000-capacity venue, only for his boast to be contradicted by photos and video posted on social media by attendees like Liz Landers of PBS, who panned her camera to reveal blocs of vacant seats.
“Not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” the president insisted. “We have an amazing response. They love our party. They love what we’re doing.”
Among those fact-checking Trump’s declaration was Reuters White House correspondent Nandita Bose, who posted a view from her seat with the caption: “Trump keeps talking about the arena being full and obsessing over capacity.
“It isn’t. The upper decks are empty, large stretches of the side sections remain sparsely filled, and even with Trump onstage the arena is clearly not at capacity.”
The problem worsened as the president’s speech dragged on well beyond its planned 45-minute duration.
“As President Trump passes the 90 minute mark of his speech and insists nobody has left the arena, it’s clear that lots of folks have left the arena,” posted Garrett Haake of NBC News.
“Trump’s gaslighting on full display to the few people who are still there,” wrote anti-MAGA pundit Ed Krassenstein, reposting Haake’s footage.
“He’s literally trying to convince a half-empty stadium that they are filled. And most of them probably believed him.”
The president actually attempted to fend off such criticism during his speech, joking with the crowd about not going to the bathroom in case the media took a picture of their empty seat.
Trump began his first term by picking a fight with journalists about the size of the crowd that attended his January 2017 inauguration and more recently claimed that his Great American State Fair on the National Mall was attracting huge numbers of visitors, despite plenty of evidence to the contrary.
Also going viral from Dallas were posts about the huge screen positioned behind Trump, which began glitching unnervingly as the president began to speak, flashing up rapid-fire clips of speakers who had already appeared, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and UFC fighters Justin Gaethje and Bo Nickal.
The error was filmed by several journalists, who swiftly uploaded the evidence to social media, offering coverage from different vantage points.
Trump’s speech itself was as wild as expected, seeing him attempt to blame opposition Democrats for the ongoing affordability crisis, demand that Republicans push through his preferred voting reforms and claim he won the 2020 election he lost to Joe Biden.
He also promoted his stalled White House ballroom and championed Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, albeit by calling him ugly.
“He may not dress right,” Trump said of his party’s candidate. “He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen, but you know what he is?
“He’s the greatest attorney general in America, and he deserves to be your next senator.”
To make amends, the president also referred to Paxton’s rival, Democratic rising star James Talarico, as “weird-looking.”
Trump’s most eye-catching claim of the night was his promise to give voters $5,000 checks as a reward for the GOP maintaining control of the House of Representatives and Senate in November.
The pledge is already inviting questions as it would likely cost as much as $1.3 trillion dollars to execute and may not in fact be legal, drawing accusations of vote-buying.

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma and former India cricketer Sunil Gavaskar on Thursday launched the Guwahati International Marathon.

SC clears Bilquis Mir as chief coach for Indian kayaking team, quashes J-K HC order
The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Jammu and Kashmir administration to issue international water sports coach Bilquis Mir a no-objection certificate and relieving order by September 15, clearing the way for her to join the Indian national kayaking and canoeing team for the Asian Games in Japan.
Mir, a physical education teacher with the J&K Youth Services Department, has been appointed chief coach to assist the national team for the Asian Games, which begins on September 19.
A bench comprising Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi allowed an appeal filed by the Indian Kayaking and Canoeing Association against an August 11 order of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
The Supreme Court also set aside the J&K government’s June 19, 2026 order denying Mir permission to take up the assignment on the grounds of pending departmental inquiries and service conditions.
Highlighting the time-sensitive nature of elite sport, the bench observed that sporting schedules could not be subjected to ordinary administrative delays.
“Sports administration necessarily involves strict timelines. Selection, training camps, qualifying events and international competitions operate upon fixed schedules which cannot be postponed to await completion of ordinary administrative processes,” the court said.
Under the directions, the J&K administration must complete the necessary formalities by September 15, enabling Mir to join the national camp and travel with the team to Japan.
The court also directed that Mir’s absence while on national duty should not be treated as unauthorised absence.
However, it clarified that the judgment does not give government employees a general right to claim deputation or foreign travel and does not prevent the administration from continuing disciplinary proceedings against Mir in accordance with law.
Mir had been selected by the association in February 2026 to prepare the national team. Administrative delays had earlier resulted in her missing an assignment as chief finish line judge at the World Cup in Hungary in May.
The court said sending the matter back to the administration at this stage would effectively deny Mir meaningful relief before the Asian Games.
It also criticised the administration for issuing its June 19 rejection while an interim court direction dated May 6 was still in force.
“An order of a constitutional court, for so long as it remains operative, binds the parties to the proceeding,” the bench said.
The Supreme Court, however, left untouched the High Court’s direction to the Centre to frame an enforceable statutory framework for government employees who are outstanding sportspersons or coaches.

Iran Signals Readiness to Escalate Fight in Face of Rising U.S. Pressure
The Iranian government is taking an increasingly aggressive approach as it confronts a growing economic threat and worries that its grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, analysts say.
Iran has signaled that it is willing to escalate its fight with the United States, with senior leaders issuing increasingly sharp warnings in recent days after attacking American warships for the first time.
The country’s leaders are taking a more aggressive approach as Iran faces mounting economic pressure and they worry that their grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping. The American blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to ship oil, its main money source. And in effect, Iran sees escalation as the primary leverage it has against the United States, analysts said, warning that the recent clashes could reignite a full-blown war.
The U.S. military said Tuesday that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attempted strikes on a U.S. Navy warship, while Iran said it launched strikes at a base used by American forces in Jordan in response. The attacks occurred three days after Iran made its first known attempt at striking an American military vessel.
On Sunday, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s lead negotiator and the speaker of Parliament, told lawmakers that the era of “proportionate responses” to American attacks was over. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, also announced plans to impose a “restricted zone” for shipping in the Persian Gulf that would go beyond the country’s efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has largely withstood the heavy military campaign launched by the United States and Israel in February. But the war of attrition in recent months has created an economic threat that is now pushing the government to intensify its rhetoric and attacks.
An American naval blockade has prevented Tehran from exporting much of its oil, the country’s main source of revenue, making a longstanding economic crisis even worse. On Tuesday, the government raised some gasoline prices because of fuel shortages, a move that is expected to further roil a country already struggling with soaring inflation and unemployment, and a rapidly depreciating currency.

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate running for senator in Texas, has spoken out after ABC pulled his sit-down with Jimmy Kimmel over FCC concerns. The interview will instead be posted to the “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” YouTube channel on Thursday night.
“Government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party,” Talarico told MS NOW, calling the FCC’s threats against certain broadcast programs (including ABC’s “The View”) “the most dangerous form of cancel culture.”
“People at the top, powerful politicians, powerful media executives, censoring what we watch, what we read, what we say,” Talarico continued. “That, again, should be a concern to everyone who believes in the First Amendment and believes in the freedom of speech.”
Popular on Variety
He told Symone Sanders Townsend of MS NOW’s “The Weeknight” that he still has hope ABC will air the Kimmel interview across its broadcast channels. “I’m still hopeful that we can have this interview on the air,” he said. “So we’ll see what happens tonight.
Kimmel announced on his show Wednesday night that ABC had decided to preempt his chat with Talarico because of concerns about Trump’s FCC, which is led by Brendan Carr. The government agency is currently locked in a dispute with ABC over whether “The View” qualifies as a “bona fide news program” exempt from the “equal time” rule. Ultimately, Colbert put his Talarico interview on YouTube, with the clip garnering 9.5 million views. The Talarico campaign raised $2.5 million in the 24 hours after Colbert revealed he was barred from airing the interview.

Liverpool began its Champions League campaign with a 2-1 comeback win over Atletico Madrid at Anfield on Wednesday, with Alexis Mac Allister scoring the decisive goal in the second half.
Marcos Llorente had given Atletico an early lead before Dominik Szoboszlai restored parity shortly before the interval. Mac Allister then completed the turnaround with a powerful effort from outside the box.
The result gave Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola a winning start in his first Champions League match in charge, although the victory was tempered by an injury to new signing Bradley Barcola, who was forced off with a calf problem.
Liverpool started brightly, with Alexander Isak going close after a quick break led by Szoboszlai. But the home side’s attacking approach also left space at the back, and Atletico took advantage.

Julian Alvarez, making his first start of the season, opened up the Liverpool defence with a pass that released Llorente, who finished confidently past Alisson Becker. Alisson then produced a sharp save to deny Alvarez from distance before Liverpool began to work its way back into the match.

President Donald Trump often refers to the affordability crisis as a hoax. His White House may not agree.
Trump called the crisis a "fake" Democrat-created issue on the first night of the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention this week in Dallas. But the remark sits awkwardly beside months of White House messaging that has treated affordability as one of Trump's central economic promises.
In his speech, Trump blamed former President Joe Biden for runaway inflation and said affordability concerns were fake "because I'm bringing the prices way down." In the same speech, he promised that every adult US citizen would receive a $5,000 dividend from tariff revenue if Republicans won the midterms — a form of stimulus which economists expect would further exacerbate inflation.
Trump claimed that "food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down," even as consumer prices have increased by 4.3% since January 2025, with groceries up 3.4% and gasoline up 31% amid the ongoing crisis in Iran. This isn't the first time Trump has brushed off affordability concerns, as the administration has at times taken a deal-with-it stance on high prices.
In November 2025, Trump told Fox News that Democrats "have this new word called 'affordability,' and [Republicans] don't talk about it enough." Days later, he called affordability a "con job," adding that his party "did a great job on groceries and affordability," and were "victors on affordability."
By December, Trump was trying to have it both ways. In a speech in Pennsylvania, he said, "I have no higher priority than making America affordable again," but also described affordability as Democrats' "new word" and said, "they always have a hoax."
The White House's own messaging has told a different story Just a few days later in December, it acknowledged in a post that affordability is "finally trending in the right direction." As part of the affordability push, the administration pledged to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, open "Trump accounts" that allot $1,000 to children born between 2025 and 2028, and ban institutional investors from purchasing single-family homes.
Trump's State of the Union address also outlined ways to relieve pressure on US households, such as tax incentives for American-made cars and no tax on tips or overtime. In April, Trump signed an executive order expanding access to retirement savings by offering up to $1,000 in matching contributions for lower-income workers without employer-sponsored plans. A White House press release in August outlined how major retailers, energy companies, drug companies, and automakers have slashed prices on thousands of goods.
That mix of messages captures the tension in Trump's economic pitch heading into the midterms: He wants credit for bringing prices down while rejecting the premise that affordability remains a crisis.
For voters still feeling squeezed, that may be a hard balance to sell.

It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple iPhone Duo
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
iPhone 18 Pro
As predictions suspected, Apple is not releasing its base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They come with Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Adjustable Aperture
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple Watch
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
AirPods 5
Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.
The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.
Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

Coach crash kills several people in Swiss Alps
- Published
A tourist coach has crashed in the south-eastern Swiss Alps, leaving several people dead and several injured, local police say.
The bus overturned between Susch and Zernez in the Graubünden - also known as Grisons - region late on Thursday afternoon.
A large team of rescuers equipped with several helicopters was deployed to the scene.
Some 48 Dutch passengers were on board the bus, according to a spokeswoman for the General Dutch Association of Travel Companies on behalf of tour operator OAD.
The spokesperson told Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf they could not yet say how many people had been killed or injured.
Images on Swiss news sites show a coach lying on its side beside a narrow country road on which stand numerous ambulances while groups of rescuers work at the scene.
The coach reportedly left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.
Zernez is the entry point for visitors to the Swiss National Park, a vast Alpine reserve stretching more than 100 sq km (40 sq miles) across the mountainous Engadine valley.

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.

Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.
The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.
But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.
Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.
“What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.
Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.”
While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”
Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.
She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”
Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.
Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”
Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”
He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”
There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.
Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.
The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.
Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.
“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”
Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”
They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”
Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.
Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.

Jeff Bezos’ Washington Post assures everyone talk of AI killing humans is nothing to fret about
The news outlet, whose owner recently co-founded an AI company, instead warned about looming government overreach against Big Tech
A Washington Post editorial invoked the Bible to downplay the potential threat posed by artificial intelligence and instead warned of looming government overreach against Big Tech — while failing to note that billionaire Post owner Jeff Bezos recently co-founded an AI company.
The unsigned editorial, published Wednesday evening under the headline “AI hysteria jumps the shark,” came in response to comments in which current and former Anthropic employees said people working on AI projects “earnestly believe” the technology could kill all humans within 10 years.
“Scripture warns against false prophets,” the Post's editors wrote. “The Gospel of Matthew says that no one but God, ‘not even the angels of heaven,’ knows the day or hour of the end times.”
The editorial, posted outside the news outlet’s formidable paywall, also condemned the “chilling sweep” of legislation proposed by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Democratic Rep. Greg Casar of Texas to pause advanced AI development and ban “artificial superintelligence.”
“Politicians should not seek to regulate a fast-moving technology they don't understand,” the editors wrote.
The editorial made no mention of Amazon founder Bezos, who bought the Post for $250 million in 2013 and last month ranked No. 10 on Time's list of the most influential people in AI.
The magazine cited his role as co-founder and co-CEO of the AI startup Prometheus, which was launched in November 2025 and valued at $41 billion in June, with Bezos telling CNBC that its work “will make it much easier for engineers to design physical objects.”
A Post spokesperson didn't immediately respond to an inquiry from The Independent regarding the editorial's apparent lack of full disclosure.
The editorial came as Bezos — whose Blue Origin space company reportedly holds about $1.1 billion in federal contracts — has significantly softened his stance against President Donald Trump, with whom he feuded during Trump's first term over the Post's coverage of the White House.
Amazon, where Bezos is executive chairman and owns nearly nine percent of the company's stock, donated $1 million toward Trump's 2025 inauguration, which he attended with future wife Lauren Sánchez.
The company also gave an undisclosed amount to help fund construction of the president's controversial $600 million White House ballroom, and spent $40 million on a widely panned documentary about first lady Melania Trump that IMDb says grossed about $16.7 million worldwide.
The Post has also been undergoing a period of upheaval under Bezos, including the loss of about 300,000 subscribers and associate editor David Maraniss, a 48-year employee, after the owner vetoed a 2024 endorsement of Vice President Kamala Harris over Trump and ended the paper's practice of endorsing candidates.
The Post lost another 75,000 subscribers early last year after Bezos said its opinion pages would only promote “personal liberties and free markets,” leading to the resignation of top opinion editor David Shipley.
His right-leaning successor, Adam O'Neal, announced his resignation in July, telling colleagues it was best for him and his family, according to The New York Times.
Several high-profile opinion columnists, including Pulitzer Prize winners Eugene Robinson and Jonathan Capehart, have also resigned or taken buyouts since the libertarian shift in the Post's editorial tone.
The spark for Wednesday's AI editorial was a series of Tuesday social media posts in which Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said he'd resigned his position after three years “doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic.”
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he wrote.
Coxon also said, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
In response, Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger, who holds the title of alignment science lead, wrote, “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
“I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he added.
Spokespersons for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to inquiries from The Independent.
The posts followed similar warnings about the potential impact of AI from major tech figures including Elon Musk, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, a retired computer scientist who's been called the “godfather of AI.”
A 2024 survey of more than 4,000 AI researchers around the world found that only 3 percent “were most worried about the long-term, speculative scenario in which advanced, out-of-control AI poses a threat to human existence,” according to Responsible Ai UK, a group of British academics.
The most frequently cited concerns about AI were malicious use, misuse, misinformation and the impact on jobs, RAiUK said.
The Post's editorial came as polls have consistently shown that about seven in 10 Americans oppose AI-related data centers in their communities.
It acknowledged that predictions of people being killed by AI were “concerning” but said they “merit a certain skepticism.”
“People working at the frontier may know more than most about what today’s models can do. But that does not give them special knowledge of what machines that do not yet exist will someday become — or how society will adapt to the challenge,” it said.
The editorial also held out the promise of “the many potential upsides of AI, such as the developing breakthrough medicines.”
But left unsaid were the results of a May study, published by leading medical journal The Lancet, in which Columbia University researchers found that the rate of fabricated sources in biomedical papers surged 1,200 percent from 2023 to 2025, according to the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy.
The authors offered several possible explanations, including intentional misconduct, but noted that previous studies found that up to 69% of AI-generated references in “biomedical contexts” were made up.

Adrian McElwee, son of the filmmaker Ross McElwee, was such an interesting child, full of precocious wisdom. For instance, when his father asked young Adrian during a seaside trip, “Why do you think you like fishing so much?” the boy spontaneously replied, “I don’t know. I just love the deep surprise of the ocean.”
The elder McElwee would include his son in many of his films and later, when Adrian entered adulthood, they worked together on documentaries. But Adrian’s fate was not to be a happy one. The boy who displayed such joy and promise as a child experienced periodic depression as an adult and slipped into drug addiction.
In McElwee’s documentary Remake, which just aired on the PBS series POV, he explores his relationship with Adrian and his son’s struggles after he came of age, which culminated with Adrian’s untimely death at the age of 27. The film has won awards around the world including the Impact Golden Globes Prize for Documentary at the Venice Film Festival, the ReFrame Award for Creative Use of Archive at IDFA in Amsterdam, and the True Vision Award at True/False in Columbia, MO.
Watch on Deadline
McElwee joins the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss the film and what he learned about himself during the making of Remake. No film could be more heartbreaking, yet there are touches of humor throughout. The director tells us about striking that delicate balance and whether he sees this as his final film.
Music Box Films acquired Remake and the company also released a restored version of McElwee’s 1985 documentary Sherman’s March, the film that launched his career and inaugured a new style of documentary filmmaking where the director – through on camera commentary and voice-over – guides the viewer through the subject matter. The influence of that style can be seen in many successive films including You Can See Everything, which just premiered at Telluride, and The Oldest Person in the World, directed by Sam Green. On the pod, McElwee talks about the making of Sherman’s March, which becomes a significant storyline in Remake.
That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
- Published
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.
Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?
F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.
Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?
This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.
Madrilenos know how to make sport great
Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.
They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.
Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.
But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?
"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.
"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.
"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."
"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.
"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."
Welcome to Madring
As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.
The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.
This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.
"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.
"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.
"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.
"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'
The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.
As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.
But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.
Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?
"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.
"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."
Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.
A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.
It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. It's a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, impossible to sit on.
"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.
Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.
"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.
"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.
"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."
What could happen in the race?
Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.
"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.
"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."
Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.
"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.
"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].
"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."
Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.
"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."
Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.
"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.
"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."
