- In August 2026, a claim spread that McDonald's lost a lawsuit against the TV chef Jamie Oliver, who — according to posts — proved that the fast food chain's food was "unfit for human consumption" because it was "highly toxic." The claim is unproven.
- Snopes previously investigated a variation of this claim in 2018 and 2026. We found then and now that Oliver said in a 2011 TV program that beef trimmings used for a product he called "pink slime" were "not fit for human consumption." We found no evidence that he specifically called McDonald's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic," as the posts suggested.
- The American Meat Institute, a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry, said in 2012 that beef trimmings used to make "pink slime," which it calls Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, were edible.
- 
However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode where Oliver discussed "pink slime" to see if he specifically mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether Oliver has ever called the fast food chain's food "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" or whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver and are waiting for responses.
A claim (archived) circulated on Facebook in August 2026 that fast food chain McDonald's lost a lawsuit against the TV chef Jamie Oliver after Oliver proved its food was "unfit for human consumption" because it was "highly toxic."
For example, one Facebook user wrote:
McDonald's loses lawsuit against chef Jamie Oliver, who proved that the food they sell is unfit for human consumption because it is highly toxic.
Chef Jamie Oliver won a lawsuit against the world's largest fast-food chain. Oliver demonstrates how hamburgers are made.
According to Oliver, fatty cuts of meat are "washed" with ammonium hydroxide and then used to fill the hamburger patties. Even before this process, the TV presenter says, this meat was unfit for human consumption.
Oliver, a radical activist chef taking on the food industry, says: "We are talking about meat that is sold as dog food and then served to humans. Aside from the quality of the meat, ammonium hydroxide is harmful to health." Oliver calls it "the pink slime process." What sane person would put a piece of meat soaked in ammonium hydroxide into a child's mouth?
Similar claims circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim, which we previously reported on in July 2026 and January 2018.
The claim contained three parts: that McDonald's sued Oliver, that Oliver made the comments about "pink slime" and that Oliver's alleged comments were specifically about McDonald's.
We found no evidence in online searches (archived, archived, archived) that McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver. AFP Fact Check reported in December 2021 that Oliver had never taken legal action against McDonald's.
According to an excerpt of a 2011 episode of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," Oliver said that the meat used to produce a specific type of beef product that the celebrity chef called "pink slime" was "not fit for human consumption."
McDonalds reportedly ceased using "pink slime," which is also known as Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, in their food in 2011, as we noted in 2018 when we fact-checked a previous version of this claim. Oliver did not mention McDonald's specifically in excerpts of the 2011 episode of "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" that Snopes reviewed.
However, because we could not access a full version of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question to see if it mentioned McDonald's, we leave this claim unrated.
Snopes contacted Oliver and McDonald's to ask whether McDonald's ever lost a lawsuit involving Oliver, whether Oliver had ever proved McDonald's food was "unfit for human consumption" or "toxic" and to ask whether McDonald's used Select Lean Beef Trimmings in 2026. We await replies to our queries.
Oliver's allegations
In the first episode of the second season of his program "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution," in which Oliver attempted to reform school lunches and fight obesity in the U.S., the celebrity chef held a demonstration where he showed children and adults where on a cow different cuts of meat came from.
According to a segment of the episode (archived) that an internet user uploaded to YouTube in 2016, after spray-painting prices on a live cow to show where various cuts were found, Oliver then addressed what happened to the remainder of the animal.
He said (time code 00:01), "The public loved seeing that, that, equalling a steak. They never for a minute thought I would clear all the meat and cuts away and introduce them to a new world of food. It's called pink slime."
Oliver added (time code 00:12), "When you've broken down a whole beast, you're left with trimmings. You know, in my industry, we call those trimmings [BLEEP]."
Speaking to a crowd of people, Oliver described the trimmings used for "pink slime" as (time code 00:36) "not fit for human consumption."
Oliver went on to say that processing plants took trimmings that were "not fit for human consumption," separated the meat from the fat, killed harmful bacteria using ammonium hydroxide and sold the end product, which he called "pink slime," as human-grade food. Ammonium hydroxide is a watery solution that can be used to regulate acidity in food or in hair dye or cosmetics.
In an excerpt from the program included in a 2012 CBS report, Oliver said (time code 00:32), "We're taking a product that would be sold at the cheapest form for dogs, and after this process we can give it to humans."
(Snopes could not locate a complete video of the "Jamie Oliver's Food Revolution" episode in question. The clips we have found online appeared genuine and did not indicate any signs of possible manipulation.)
FDA says ammonium hydroxide 'generally safe'
Around 11 months after Oliver's episode discussing "pink slime" aired, the American Meat Institute President J. Patrick Boyle issued a statement to say that Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings was "a safe, wholesome and nutritious form of beef" that helped prevent food waste by utilizing trimmings that would otherwise go to waste.
The institute is a trade association that represents processors of meat and poultry.
Boyle's statement said, similarly to Oliver's demonstration, that processing Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings involved first separating the meat from the fat and using "food grade ammonium hydroxide gas" to destroy bacteria before blending the product into foods like ground beef.
However, he denied claims that the trimmings used to create Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings were not edible. The statement said:
Some recent media reports created a troubling and inaccurate picture, particularly in their use of the colloquial term 'pink slime.' The fact is, BLBT is beef. The beef trimmings that are used to make BLBT are absolutely edible. In fact, no process can somehow make an inedible meat edible; it's impossible. In reality, the BLBT production process simply removes fat and makes the remaining beef more lean and suited to a variety of beef products that satisfy consumers' desire for leaner foods.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which regulates ammonium hydroxide use in food, says the ingredient is "generally recognized as safe." This was also the case when we last reported on these claims in 2018.
In sum ...
While Oliver did call the cuts of meat used for Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings "not fit for human consumption" and claimed (time code 00:59) the product was "admitted to being in at least 70% of ground beef products" in a 2011 program, the episode excerpts Snopes reviewed did not show him specifically accusing McDonald's of using the product or calling the fast food chain's products toxic.
McDonald's said in a 2013 statement it had not used Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings in its products since 2011.
We found no evidence that McDonald's had lost a lawsuit involving Oliver since then. Given the prominence of McDonald's and Oliver, such a lawsuit would have been widely reported by reputable sources. That was not the case.
While the FDA generally recognizes ammonium hydroxide, which is used to process Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, as safe, reporting by the publication Food Safety News claimed that fast food giants like McDonalds, Taco Bell and Burger King had all stopped using the product by January 2012.
Both ABC, which broadcast Oliver's program, and Oliver himself have faced lawsuits over their coverage of the product.
ABC settled out of court in 2017 in a $1.9 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Beef Products Inc., a producer of Boneless Lean Beef Trimmings, over Oliver's program and other stories the network had reported about the product in March and April 2012.
A man who Beef Products Inc. laid off after negative press heavily affected the company's sales sued Oliver, ABC and other defendants in 2012. He dropped the case in 2013.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Weeks after suspending production of select cars in India, Vietnamese EV maker VinFast is now reportedly eyeing the development of two new electric vehicles for the Indian market. As per a report by Reuters, VinFast is currently in initial discussions with suppliers in India for the two new models, internally codenamed VF X and VF Y. Inc42 has reached out to VinFast for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response. The two models mark a shift in VinFast's India strategy, with the company looking to develop vehicles specifically for the Indian market instead of adapting its global models. The VF X is expected to be positioned as an affordable compact EV with a targeted price below $12,000, the report added. As per a report by Autocar India, the EV maker has also filed design patents in India for the facelifted versions of its VF6 and VF9 electric SUVs. The EV cars are some of its most sought after cars internationally. For the Indian market, the models could potentially get revised lighting elements, new alloy wheels, among other upgrades. VinFast appears to be changing its India strategy after reassessing the economics of localising its global models. The development comes days after reports suggested that the company is halting its production in India. However, a VinFast representative told Inc42 that it will continue CKD assembly of these models at its Thoothukudi plan. To note, VinFast has committed to invest $2 Bn in India as it seeks to establish the country as a global manufacturing hub. The company had commissioned its Thoothukudi facility, with the first phase involving an investment of up to $500 Mn. The Thoothukudi facility currently has an initial annual capacity of 50,000 vehicles, which is planned to be scaled to 150,000 units. It currently focuses on assembling the VF 6 and VF 7. The strategic reset comes as VinFast has started gaining traction in the Indian EV market. The company retailed 2,198 electric passenger vehicles in August, its highest monthly sales since entering India, as per industry data. Its sales rose 44% from 1,531 units in July, giving it a 7% share of the electric passenger vehicle market. “Recently, we have been actively engaging with local suppliers and have organised consecutive supplier conferences in both Vietnam and India, with the participation of more than 300 Indian suppliers, to explore deeper cooperation opportunities and promote localisation,” the representative added. The recent strategic shift comes at a time when the company is doubling down on the Indian EV market commercially. Earlier in June, the company also forayed India’s electric ride-hailing market with the launch of its Green SM Limo service in Delhi NCR. Green SM, owned by VinFast parent Vingroup, operates an all-electric fleet comprising VinFast's Limo Green, a seven-seater electric vehicle. The EV maker was also planning to enter India’s electric two-wheeler (E2W) market this year, following the launch of its VF6 and VF7 electric SUVs in the country in 2025.

- The claim that serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, who cannibalized parts of his victims' bodies, said he didn't eat people with tattoos because "tattoos taste terrible" is unproven.
- The rumor stems from numerous posts on Instagram and Facebook affiliated with tattoo artists or tattoo parlors of a meme facetiously encouraging people to get tattoos.
- We looked through numerous recorded interviews and FBI reports about Dahmer and found no evidence he ever mentioned tattoos in connection with his crimes.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In August 2026, an online quote spread online claiming serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, who ate the flesh of some of his victims, said he didn't cannibalize people with tattoos because the ink tasted bad. The rumor spread on Instagram, Reddit and Facebook.
Snopes readers have been sending us this particular Dahmer anecdote for years. Some asked us to confirm whether Dahmer actually said, "I ate someone with a tattoo once. Made the meat taste like s***." A post on Instagram stated Dahmer said that "tattoos taste terrible" and used it facetiously to encourage people to get tattoos and save themselves from cannibals.
(Instagram user @dark_grey_tattoo)
Snopes looked closely at interviews, FBI reports and documentaries detailing Dahmer's crimes and found no evidence he ever made such a comment. We did find, however, that the claim is often posted by tattoo artists and studios as an advertisement encouraging people to get tattoos. Until we learn more, we will leave this claim as unproven.
Dahmer killed 17 young men and boys over the course of 13 years. In 1992, he was convicted of murder and handed 15 consecutive life sentences in prison. Two years later, another inmate beat him to death.
In interviews with the news media and FBI agents, Dahmer spoke of eating his victim's hearts, livers and thigh meat, and one time ate a bicep as a way of keeping them "a part of me." FBI agent Robert Ressler interviewed Dahmer, who described his actions as a "perverse sexual practice."
In 1993, Inside Edition conducted an interview with Dahmer while he was in prison. He didn't say anything about tattoos.
The Netflix documentary series "Conversations with a Killer: The Jeffrey Dahmer Tapes" shed more light on his inclinations. Interviews with law enforcement showed he liked certain body types and offered to take his victims' photographs. In one instance he cut off and preserved a victim's head and genitals. He also took photos of body parts of victims he liked. Dahmer described having sex with the insides of a person in his interview recordings with investigators.
We were unable to find evidence that Dahmer confessed a preference for eating untattooed skin in any of those sources.
Snopes has covered numerous claims about Dahmer, including the true story of how Milwaukee police returned a victim, Konerak Sinthasomphone, to Dahmer after accepting the serial killer's explanation that the injured 14-year-old boy was his lover.

In his address at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai today, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra urged businesses in the fintech sector to double down on AI, tokenisation and quantum computing to enhance financial inclusion while building consumer trust. Malhotra said India’s digital finance transformation had achieved scale, but its greatest achievement was normalising digital payments in the country. This transformation, which is largely driven by public-private partnerships, has promoted responsible innovation while maintaining public confidence in the country’s financial system. However, he said the next phase of growth must see the industry focus on taking financial services deeper into the last mile, particularly to customers and businesses that traditional financial institutions struggle to serve economically. “Reaching the last mile while serving the informal sector through micro-insurance, small pensions and small-ticket credit, and providing credit to women entrepreneurs, MSMEs, and small and marginal farmers in India’s villages and tier III and tier IV towns is a task that traditional banking and financial service providers alone struggle to accomplish economically,” Malhotra said. He said fintech companies can help bridge this gap by using tech to make smaller-ticket financial products viable for underserved customers, while also expanding access to credit, insurance and pension products. RBI Gov Calls For Tech To Be Built On A Foundation Of Trust The governor stressed that fintech growth must be accompanied by greater focus on consumer trust, data protection, cybersecurity and operational resilience. He urged fintech companies to treat customer data as a “fiduciary responsibility” and ensure that innovation does not come at the cost of trust in the financial system. He reiterated four specific objectives for fintechs — consumer service, meeting unmet financial needs like access to credit, enhancing operational efficiency, and curbing financial frauds. Malhotra linked technological deployment to systemic trust and security, warning that rapid execution without building confidence is unsustainable. “Trust is not just a marketing strategy. It is an operating discipline built transaction by transaction. It takes years to build … but it can at the same time be lost in a single episode over minutes,” he added. The RBI governor also highlighted several key moves for the financial sector that he considered critical to building trust, including: Managing risks like bias, exclusion, cybersecurity and privacy while adopting AI Act as a data fiduciary by collecting data while ensuring it is not misused outside of the consumer consent framework Taking on systemic responsibility as a business grows by ensuring operational resilience, business continuity, and cybersecurity proportional to their scale Engaging transparently with regulators through sandboxes and pilots, rather than exploiting gaps to scale first and later seeking forgiveness During his GFF 2026 inauguration address, Prime Minister Narendra Modi also outlined the aforementioned four objectives for the fintech sector. PM Modi also called for fintech companies to “move beyond payments”, underlining the next opportunity lying in segments like credit, insurance and pensions. He also called to take financial services to sections of the population that have historically had limited access to formal banking. RBI’s Role In Developing India’s Fintech Ecosystem The RBI governor noted that Indian fintechs can build for the world to make the country a leader in global finance. “Many emerging economies face challenges which are very similar to ours. Our solutions for financial inclusion, affordable payments, digital identity, interoperable infrastructure, and trusted innovation can be appropriately repurposed for wider global adoption,” he said. The RBI is working towards this by not just regulating the fintech industry but working with it as a strategic partner to leverage technology, Malhotra added. Accordingly, he announced that the central bank would recognise the Unified Fintech Forum (UFF) as the second Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO) in the fintech sector, after the Fintech Association for Consumer Empowerment (FACE). “These initiatives reflect our belief that regulation and innovation are not opposing forces, but they are mutually reinforcing pillars of a resilient financial ecosystem,” he added. The RBI is now focusing on digital public infrastructure, regulatory frameworks and engagement with the fintech ecosystem to support responsible innovation in the fintech segment. In line with this, Malhotra announced that the RBI and SEBI would unveil a framework for tokenisation of corporate bonds today as another step towards advancing this goal. “The Reserve Bank remains committed to this dialogue through our sandbox, our innovation hub, and our openness to engage with this ecosystem. I would ask in turn that this festival’s innovators treat trust not as a constraint on innovation, but as its very purpose,” he added. UPI Launches Today Additionally, Malhotra today unveiled UPI Tap & Pay, a new feature enabling users to make UPI payments by tapping NFC-enabled smartphones on compatible Point-of-Sale (POS) terminals. He also launched the AI-powered MyUPI platform built on NPCI’s Small Language Model (FiMI). The suite provides a single view of transactions and AutoPay mandates across banks and apps. Its key features include safety controls like declining transactions in case of a compromised account, delinking a mobile number for receiving payments, getting contextual information about a payee before making a payment, real-time chargeback for eligible transactions, and transaction replays to automatically repeat past transactions. Besides, he also unveiled an AI-powered support mechanism to UPI users, MyUPI. Built on NPCI’s FiMI model, the platform gives users a unified view of their UPI transactions and AutoPay mandates across banks and UPI apps. MyUPI also adds safety and control features, including a Safety Switch that lets users request the decline of UPI debit transactions if they suspect their account has been compromised.

Tamil Nadu recorded nearly 45,000 fewer births in 2025 than the previous year, with the number of births falling by 5.3% from 8.47 lakh in 2024 to 8.02 lakh, pointing to a continuing decline in births in the State.
The decline comes against the backdrop of a long-term fall in fertility in the State. In 2026, five lakh-odd births were recorded so far, according to Civil Registration System data.”
While the decline in births reflects a broader demographic transition, with implications for the workforce and ageing population, experts say greater attention must be paid to education, childcare, social security, elderly care and standard of living.
T. Sundararaman, former executive director, National Health Systems Resource Centre, said the total fertility rate among women of reproductive age fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in Tamil Nadu nearly 20 years ago. “We continued to have a positive population growth rate because of population momentum. We have now moved beyond this phenomenon and a decline in the population is likely to occur,” he said.
S. Irudaya Rajan, chairperson, International Institute for Migration and Development, Thiruvananthapuram, pointed out that Tamil Nadu is better placed compared with Kerala, which has recorded around three lakh births.
“There will be no short-term impact. The State government can focus on creating a productive, healthy population of eight lakh-plus by investing in quality education over the next 20 to 25 years. The focus should be on quality rather than quantity,” he said.
“First of all, there is no need to worry about the low fertility rate or the decline in births,” Padmavathi Srinivasan, independent research consultant in demography, said, adding: “This opens up opportunities to increase and improve the standard of living and enable people to better access the State’s resources. The State government should seize this opportunity and capitalise on low fertility.”
Observing that politicians would worry about what would happen to the State’s labour force, she said, “but this is the time to focus on education and employment opportunities. Tamil Nadu is a prosperous State, but this prosperity needs to translate to better living standards.”
“It would be an injustice if the State focussed on increasing fertility and channelled government funds towards it. Rather, it should focus on the existing population, especially the youth. The State should pay attention to the foundations, such as quality education and the nutritional status of children. There are still pockets of people living in poverty, those who have no access to opportunities and have not benefitted from the State’s economic growth.”
Financial incentives to reverse low fertility rates have never worked, as evidenced in many developed countries, she said, asking: “So, why go down that route, when there are much more pressing issues we need to tackle.”
Professor Rajan said the State government’s “Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam”, under which one-gram gold rings will be gifted to babies born in government hospitals, is unlikely to help increase births. Increasing maternity leave to women government employees for a third child cannot be considered a meaningful incentive, he believed.
Policies alone will not help much. At best, they may add another 5,000-odd births, he said. “Children are assets, but when you ask couples today, many consider them liabilities. This mindset should change. Increasing the fertility rate is not simple, given factors such as delayed marriages. To motivate young couples to have children, we need out-of-the-box, innovative ideas.”
Priority areas
Professor Sundararaman said increasing longevity means that there will be more people aged 65 or 70 and above. “At the same time, we will have less working age population and a larger elderly population that needs to be cared for. This has already happened in most developed countries that have stronger social security systems and better elderly care,” he said.
“I am less worried about productivity and more concerned about social security and elderly care. We need policies that anticipate these changes,” he added.
Efforts simply to increase childbearing are unlikely to work. What can make a difference is providing child care support for the first two children, he said. “We need to have innovative thinking and creative community-based efforts for elderly care. Our priorities should include elderly care, social security, child care support, good quality primary education and measures that make it easier for working women for childcare. Funds should be better utilised to establish facilities, such as creches for working women,” he added.

ARPA-H, the government agency that funds cutting-edge health research, plans to commit $62.7 million to develop artificial intelligence bots that direct treatment of heart failure. Among the goals of the program, called ADVOCATE, is to produce partially autonomous AI devices authorized by the Food and Drug Administration to help treat patients, including assessing symptom severity, prescribing drugs, and ordering lab tests.
ARPA-H on Wednesday announced the first batch of awards to health tech companies Atman Health, UpDoc, Tempus AI, and teams from Stanford University, Duke University, and the Kaiser Permanente health system. ARPA-H may still fund additional teams. The amount committed for the first year is $33.7 million, and the remainder may be renegotiated up or down.
Many of the 6.7 million Americans with heart failure don’t get optimal treatment because of difficulty accessing specialists, and the hope is that AI agents developed with ARPA-H funding can help address the gap, especially in rural and other underserved settings.

For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom. The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero, an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles. It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book. Nevertheless, Ellis’s renown skyrockets. By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers (American Psycho, The Rules of Attraction) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs.
Regardless of how you felt about his work—and readers had all sorts of opinions—his success couldn’t be denied. “If you were not a supporter of the Brat Pack, you simply had to accept us anyway,” he writes in his 2005 novel, Lunar Park, which is narrated by a semifictional version of himself. Such white-hot notoriety was rare in his time, and it’s rarer now. While a book can become a hit in many ways, you’re only young once—and though we’ve all been told about the virtues of writers who labor away unappreciated until they finally get their moment, it’s hard not to be a little envious of the ones who’re able to enjoy their spoils before knee pain sets in. It didn’t matter that, when I finally read Less Than Zero after college, I thought it was a relic best left in its era—the work of a poser trying too hard to convince readers of his secret depth. Ellis’s early works felt too significant, too settled, for me to really say much about; disputing him would have been like arguing with a redwood tree.
His reputation as a hedonistic provocateur made the release of his 2023 novel, The Shards, somewhat of a surprise, at least to me. On its face, The Shards is an autofictional murder mystery starring a teenage version of Ellis who, at the start of his senior year of high school, suspects that a new classmate is responsible for a series of gory killings around the school’s ritzy Sherman Oaks neighborhood. Novel-Ellis is working on an early draft of Less Than Zero, drawing from his own party-heavy lifestyle. The sensationalistic violence and substance-fueled navel-gazing—all of that sounds like a typical Ellis novel. Yet The Shards is not celebratory or defiant. It’s narrated by a much older Ellis, who looks back on his youth with regret and shame—about his closeted homosexuality, about his formative and long-dead teenage friendships—and rips apart his own mythos from the inside.
Parts of The Shards read like they could have used a more punitive editor—it’s a little long, and Ellis describes himself as “keyed-up” a few too many times. Yet the book’s hefty length—594 pages in hardcover—is conducive to novel-Ellis’s obsessiveness as he combs through memories for hidden meaning and tries to identify each emotion he felt during this chaotic time period. “The facts from that fall were receding from memory but being seventeen actually became clearer to me emotionally,” he writes. “I realized I had needed this distance of forty years to finally begin writing the book.” Now, he suggests, he can admit that Less Than Zero was indeed an act of mimicry—that he’d copied that book’s numbed affectation from a classmate. The cynicism of his early work had put me off, but here he seemed weary enough to let down his guard and, perhaps, tell a version of the truth.
The Shards has now been adapted for FX by Ryan Murphy, whose campy and provocative shows (Glee, American Horror Story, Feud) have helped define TV in the 21st century. In many ways, it’s a natural match. Murphy’s eye is consistently drawn to beauty, and to the machinations and aspirations of the rich. And though his scripts can be plenty outlandish, he knows when a performer should play it straight.
The early episodes seem to preserve much of Ellis’s plot. We begin by meeting Bret (played by Igby Rigney), an aspiring novelist and senior at the prestigious Buckley School in Sherman Oaks. Bret has recently started dating Debbie (Hayes Warner), a bottle-blond socialite; along with another couple, Susan (Kaia Gerber) and Thom (Graham Campbell), they constitute a glamorous foursome. Beneath this picturesque front is a more complicated reality. Susan and Thom may look like the perfect prom queen and king, but she’s grown restless in their relationship. And while Bret is quietly in love with Susan, he’s also been hooking up with some of his male classmates and wondering how to take advantage of the fact that Debbie’s father, Terry (Wes Bentley), a well-connected (and seemingly gay) movie producer, appears interested in giving him his big break.
These delicate dynamics are unsettled by the appearance of a mysterious new transfer student, Robert (Homer Gere), who looks like he walked right out of an Armani advertisement. Bret is transfixed by his new classmate and is convinced that he’s seen Robert before, at the movies, where he made an indelible impression. But Robert becomes strangely defensive about the encounter, and insists that Bret must have made a mistake. His denials and secretive behavior lead Bret to suspect that Robert is connected to the Trawler, a yet-unidentified serial killer who’s been targeting local teenagers. Bret’s obsession with proving his guilt slowly spins out of control.
Gruesome deaths, a pulsing ’80s soundtrack, dramatic conversations about people’s hidden motivations—it should be fun, and it sometimes is. As Robert, Gere conveys an alluring darkness; you can’t take your eyes off him, and neither can the show’s characters. Gerber’s Susan is beautifully nonchalant, a quality that propels her into Robert’s arms. (Gere and Gerber are the respective children of Richard Gere and Cindy Crawford, who used to be married.) And Jordan Roth is ridiculous but memorable as Steven, Terry’s assistant, who seems to be manipulating everyone behind the scenes.
Yet Murphy makes a subtle tweak that changes The Shards completely. The novel is told from the first-person perspective, which allows an older Bret to constantly remark on the described action with the benefit of time and perspective. Here, that framing device is snipped entirely. Bret still narrates, but voiceover-Bret is not Bret Easton Ellis, the middle-aged author of American Psycho who’s now looking backwards. It’s just Rigney, who plays young Bret, speaking from a vague near future, and sometimes obnoxiously. “Kids today have it fucking easy,” he sneers, which is new writing.
The elision of this metafictional narration is paired with a lot of new plot. Ellis co-wrote the first two episodes before being sidelined in a reported power struggle. (He has not promoted the show on his personal Instagram, nor did he appear at a glitzy launch party in July.) The other episodes depart drastically from the book’s structure. Murphy tacks on stray storylines: a dance competition on an American Bandstand–type local TV show, for instance, and a kidnapping plot involving a foulmouthed classmate who has what seems to be a form of Tourette’s. One episode has the characters monologuing at one another in Shakespearean verse while dressed in costume. The add-ons are tonally confusing and parceled out inconsistently. Some moments are played for show-stopping drama, only to be immediately abandoned. Other confrontations have the taste of corny reality TV, and the ’80s references are often played for laughs.
A blunter way of saying this: The new stuff is awful, and a waste of time. The show expands Bret’s outer world at the cost of his inner life (and screen time, as Rigney disappears for long stretches), but that outer world isn’t very interesting. The novel’s emotions have been strip-mined, leaving only the surface tensions of vain teenagers. Many TV adaptations of literature miss the mark, because the visual medium isn’t always well suited to novelistic storytelling, which can be both wide-angled and highly internal. But this misfire bears a particular irony. Since Less Than Zero, Ellis has been trailed by critics saying his work is shallow and trades in shock value. The Shards show unfurls as if all of those put-downs were true, as though the book is little more than a collection of unsettling murders, great outfits, and hot people being mean to one another.
Two comments about the making of the show—both from that launch party—reveal something about what went awry. The first comes from Murphy, speaking about what drew him to the book: “I knew the songs, I knew the clothes, I knew everything because I had lived it. It was my time.” The second is from Roth, speculating on the show bringing about a trend revival: “Love Story got us our ’90s nostalgia, and Shards brings us our ’80s nostalgia.”
The former comment is Murphy viewing The Shards as his story, not Ellis’s—a tricky approach for a book that’s so explicitly personal. The latter is, I think, deeply cynical about the point of a show like this. Even when The Shards invites us to laugh at its characters, it does so through the prism of “Weren’t the ’80s crazy?” The emotions are blustery, but not intimate; the narration has been edited for cool concision. In the book, novel-Ellis narrates about Robert: “The boy aroused something primal in me that I had never felt before—I wanted him immediately, I needed to be his friend, I had to make contact, I had to see him naked, I had to own him.” In the show, this confessional surge has been drastically pared back, keeping Bret’s messy feelings at a distance.
Regret and shame, the novel’s animating sentiments, are not sexy; I’m sure the actors had more fun overindexing on the ’80s of it all. The end result, though, is the transformation of a great novel into a bad show, one that Murphy wants to run for two more seasons. Let’s hope not. Although Ellis is often nitpicky about adaptations of his work—he’s never come around to the wonderfully caustic movie version of American Psycho—he’s right to distance himself from this one. “It was nothing like the book,” Bret narrates in both the show and the novel, after coming out of a screening of The Shining. “I felt cheated.” It’s quietly tragic that the same thing has happened here.

What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.
Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.
Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.
“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.
The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.
Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.
Betel nuts are actually the seeds of the Areca catechu palm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.
Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.
The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.
To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.
“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.
“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”
While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.
Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.
“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.

Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
Wide-ranging partnership to cover trade, investment, energy and critical minerals
Canada and Ukraine were bound together more tightly on Thursday with the signing of a long-term strategic and political partnership that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries.
The countries signed a declaration to establish a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said the war in Ukraine is at a turning point where some of its uncrewed systems are now reaching hundreds of kilometres inside of Russia.
He also acknowledged the heavy toll Russia's stepped-up missile and drone campaign is having on Ukraine, especially Kyiv which has been under relentless night and day bombardment.
"Canada will always stand in solidarity with Ukraine," Carney said alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary.
"Canadians understand in our bones the importance of your struggle. There is no qualification to our commitment. Because your cause — freedom, democracy, sovereignty — is our cause."
Ripping a page out of Ukraine's wartime experience, Canada plans to create its own drone marketplace where individual military units can reach out to companies to quickly fulfil their needs.
"This is a key part of our plan to build the industrial capacity to produce millions of drones within the next two years," Carney said.
At the moment, the Canadian military has only 2,000 drones — of all types — in its inventory.
The governments also plan to partner Canadian and Ukrainian companies to build drones.
"As a result, Canadian industry will learn from the most battle-tested developers on earth," Carney said.
Canada and Ukraine are also forging a long-term partnership to jointly produce uncrewed systems, counter-drone technologies, munitions and artificial intelligence technology.

Zelenskyy called it a "very important package" and a decision that could affect the lives of Ukrainians.
"I'm very happy to be here among friends," the Ukrainian president said prior to the signing of the agreement. "Thank you for your support, supporting Ukraine, Ukrainians, our children, our sovereignty."
Carney also announced that Canada will contribute to the Ukraine Energy Security Fund to repair energy infrastructure, increase storage capacity and power hospitals. To help Ukrainians get through the winter, Canada will provide over $430 million in loan guarantees for gas purchases.
In addition, Canada is putting $350 million toward an air defence package. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created a shortage of air defence missiles that has directly affected Ukraine.

The 1987 ghost: Vande Mataram row and why Omar Abdullah won't let Congress call the shots in J&K.
The latest Congress-National Conference (NC) clash may have begun with a song, but it is really about something much older: who gets to set the political terms of the alliance in Jammu and Kashmir?CM Omar Abdullah and NC president Farooq Abdullah stood through the full rendition of Vande Mataram on Wednesday at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar. The song was played in its complete six-stanza version, lasting about three minutes and 10 seconds, in line with the Centre's new protocol.
This was in sharp contrast with the Congress's stand. Its grand-old party has reaffirmed its 1937 decision to restrict public rendition at party events to the first two stanzas, arguing that the later verses sit uneasily with the pluralist ethos of the freedom movement.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal subsequently said the full version "sits uneasily" with the syncretic and pluralist ethos envisioned by India's freedom fighters and urged allies to stand by the Congress position.
Venugopal called on allies to honour the wisdom of the freedom fighters
The NC was quick to respond, saying the J&K government was only fulfilling its official duty. "After legislative enactment by Parliament, singing Vande Mataram and standing for the song has become a statutory obligation (mandatory legal duty) regardless of the ideological position of any party, group or alliance," said National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq.A day later, CM Omar Abdullah also defended the move and said the issue had been needlessly politicised.
"This is not just for Jammu and Kashmir; it applies to the entire country. In states governed by the Congress, the same will happen at government functions," he said."This is now a statutory obligation. Even today, at the closing ceremony, a Union minister will be present. The national anthem will be played there, and the national song will be played too," he added.The Vande Mataram row is the latest in the list of NC-Congress differences that have surfaced post-election. However, in J&K, the dispute carries an additional historical charge.The NC has spent decades constructing its political identity around a particular proposition: New Delhi can be a partner, but it cannot be the political proprietor of Kashmir's choices.That is where the ghost of 1987 enters.
One alliance, two political vocabularies
The Vande Mataram dispute has once again exposed an asymmetry that has repeatedly surfaced between the two parties.Congress has to balance its position across India. For Abdullahs' NC, the principal political constituency remains rooted in J&K, where questions of identity, autonomy, federalism and the relationship with New Delhi carry a much more immediate electoral meaning.
Congress and the National Conference have had a stop-start relationship since 1965
It is also why the latest row is not an isolated irritant in the alliance.In December 2025, for instance, Omar Abdullah explicitly distanced the NC from Congress's "vote chori" campaign, saying Congress was free to choose its own agenda but that it was not automatically the agenda of the INDIA bloc. With this, Omar tried to assert his party's political autonomy within the alliance.And that has been the recurring pattern.
The alliance and an unequal power equation
The 2024 assembly election gave the NC-Congress relationship a new lease of life, but it also made the asymmetry between the two parties stark.The alliance crossed the majority mark with 49 seats, with the NC winning 42, Congress six and CPM one. The BJP emerged with 29, PDP three and independents seven.The pre-poll negotiations themselves had not been effortless: the parties agreed that NC would contest 51 seats and Congress 32, while several constituencies remained "friendly contests".The campaign also revealed the limits of joint ownership. Congress and NC leaders did not always campaign together. In Sopore, where the two allies were in a friendly contest, Rahul Gandhi and Omar Abdullah campaigned for their respective candidates separately.During the campaign, Omar Abdullah had publicly noted that Rahul Gandhi should dedicate more campaign time and effort to the Jammu region in addition to Kashmir to maximise electoral impact.Omar himself gave the practical reason for the alliance during the campaign: it was intended to prevent a hung assembly and give voters an alternative.
What Omar Abdullah had said in 2024
The alliance won the election, and the next question was: what does each side get to claim as its own?The first major post-election rupture came even before the new government had settled in.Omar Abdullah became CM in October 2024, but Congress chose to stay out of his ministry, citing restoration of statehood as its priority. While Congress backed the NC government from outside, its absence highlighted a strategic divide within the alliance. Omar had to engage with Delhi to govern the Union Territory, while Congress sought to pressure the Centre from outside. That difference in approach has repeatedly resurfaced.
Statehood: Common demand & source of friction
In July 2025, Congress announced protests in Jammu, Srinagar and Delhi and Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge wrote to PM Narendra Modi seeking legislation to restore J&K's statehood. The NC leadership was irritated because the announcement had not been coordinated with the ruling party. Some NC leaders described Congress's campaign as counterproductive and even as "sabotage" of the government's own efforts.Omar's objection was that Congress had launched the campaign without informing or consulting the NC, leaving its alliance partner caught off guard.The difference is clearer on Article 370. The NC's 2024 manifesto explicitly called for the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A and reversal of the changes made after August 2019. Congress has similarly opposed the 2019 constitutional changes, but in its recent campaigns placed greater emphasis on the restoration of statehood.Omar reiterated in the J&K assembly in February that his government remained committed to restoring special status, even as statehood remained an immediate demand. By July 2026, he was also linking the restoration of statehood to any future discussion on J&K's earlier constitutional position.This has given the two parties different political priorities.
The Rajya Sabha dispute
In October 2025, the disagreement moved from ideology to seats. J&K was electing four Rajya Sabha members. The NC, which had emerged as the dominant party in the assembly, initially discussed leaving one seat for Congress.Talks failed.The NC eventually fielded candidates for all four seats after Congress decided not to contest the fourth seat it had been offered, arguing that it was not among the "safe seats" it had sought.Omar's response was strikingly matter-of-fact: "So be it."The NC-Congress disagreement ultimately cost the alliance a clean sweep, with the BJP winning the fourth seat Congress had declined to contest.
We felt that the best chance of winning that seat was with the Congress, and they felt otherwise. So be it.
Omar Abdullah on RS seat deadlock
The ghost of 1987
To understand why the NC may be particularly sensitive to questions of control, one has to go back not merely to 1987 but to 1984.Farooq Abdullah's government was dismissed on July 2, 1984, after 12 NC legislators defected. Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Farooq's brother-in-law and leader of the defecting group, formed the government with Congress support. Contemporary accounts described the episode as a central-government intervention in Kashmir politics; Farooq called the dismissal unconstitutional.For the NC, this was not an abstract constitutional episode. It was a direct lesson in the vulnerability of a regional government to New Delhi's political machinery.Then came 1986.Rajiv Gandhi and Farooq Abdullah reached an agreement that brought the two parties together electorally. A Human Rights Watch report noted that the accord deepened a sense of betrayal among many Kashmiris, who saw Farooq Abdullah compromising with the same Congress party that had pushed him out of office two years earlier.
1987: The alliance that became a warning
The NC-Congress alliance won 66 of J&K's 76 assembly seats in 1987. But the result was overshadowed by the emergence of the Muslim United Front as an opposition platform, arrests of its candidates and workers, and widespread allegations of electoral rigging. Human Rights Watch later described the election as a turning point that contributed to widespread disillusionment with electoral politics.The significance of 1987 for the NC, therefore, is about the political memory it created. A generation of Kashmiri activists came to believe that the democratic route had been closed to them, a perception that became part of the backdrop to the insurgency that followed.The episode also left an enduring paradox. Congress was simultaneously the NC's electoral partner and a major force at the Centre. That history helps explain the NC's instinct to work with Congress while resisting any perception that Delhi is dictating its regional agenda.That distrust predates the 1980s. In 1953, Sheikh Abdullah was dismissed and arrested after his relationship with the Union government deteriorated. The circumstances were very different, but the political memory was similar: central intervention could reshape J&K's politics. For the NC, unlike many other regional parties, Congress's centralising past is therefore not distant history but part of its own political inheritance.
2009-14: History managed, but not erased
The two parties showed they could overcome that history after the 2008 assembly election. The NC won 28 seats and Congress 17, and the parties formed a coalition government with Omar Abdullah as CM in 2009.But the partnership remained contested. Differences over AFSPA, administrative issues and governance repeatedly surfaced. In 2011, Congress called for consensus on AFSPA while Omar maintained that the state government was an important stakeholder.By 2014, the alliance had run its course and Congress chose to contest the assembly election separately. NC leaders argued that the association with a centrist national party had diluted the party's pro-Valley credentials, with one senior NC leader calling Congress a "very bad alliance partner".
The 1987 ghost & real test of alliance
While 1987 may still shape the NC's political instincts, it would be too simplistic to link every present-day disagreement to that history. The political and constitutional context has changed; however, the experience remains part of the backdrop to the relationship.
The lesson for the NC, as we saw in the last election, has not been to avoid Congress, but to work with it where interests converge while retaining its own political space.The Vande Mataram dispute, therefore, is less significant in itself than what it reveals about continuing differences over statehood, Article 370, seat-sharing and the balance between Congress's national strategy and the NC's regional politics.The alliance can survive such differences, but the interesting question now is how durable it will be, which willdepend on how well the two parties manage their competing political priorities.

Officials should be held accountable for the continued “illegal detention” of activists and workers in connection with a stir seeking wage hikes in Noida in April, several lawyers, activists and professors demanded at the Press Club of India on Thursday.
The call came following the Allahabad High Court’s ruling on September 2 that quashed the detention of 25-year-old Delhi University law student Akriti Chaudhary under the National Security Act (NSA) in connection with the stir.
At least 15 workers and eight activists, including former journalist Satyam Verma against whom provisions of the NSA have also been invoked, continue to be in jail in cases filed by the Uttar Pradesh police.
The court had come down heavily on Gautam Buddha Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam, who had issued the order to detain Ms. Chaudhary. It observed that Ms. Roopam “desired to make an example” out of the petitioner.
Demanding accountability from officials involved in the case, senior journalist John Dayal said: “Even if it is the daughter of the CEC (Chief Election Commissioner) or the CJI (Chief Justice of India), they must be held accountable for their actions.”
“The court verdict in Akriti’s case questions the functioning of Gautam Buddha Nagar DM Medha Roopam and this applies to most officials across the country. Just as Swatantra Bhardwaj (who was arrested in connection with the alleged assault on the father of a student during a protest at Jantar Mantar in July) boasts about his crimes calling BJP leaders ‘big brothers’, U.P. Police functions with the arrogance that the government and administration are their ‘big brothers,” Mr. Dayal said, adding that police reforms are needed in the country.
Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan said the quashing of Ms. Chaudhary’s NSA detention is “symptomatic of the winds of change” blowing through the country. “The students, youth, and working people of the country are on the streets demanding accountability from the government and the administration. It has put more pressure on the judiciary to give judgments in favour of the people,” he said.
Keshaw, an activist associated with the Campaign for Release of Activists and Workers of Noida (CaRWAN), said the High Court flagged discrepancies in Ms. Chaudhary’s detention order and termed the State’s version a “concocted story”.
“The Commissioner of Police, Laxmi Singh, had claimed at the outset that they had ‘strong electronic and videographic evidence’ to nab the ‘masterminds’. Yet, even after five months we do not see any concrete evidence being presented against any of the activists or workers,” he said.
“DM Medha Roopam, who has been reprimanded and fined by the Allahabad High Court, has written in the same document in which she approved the NSA detention that the workers’ agitation can affect capital investment and portray a harmful image of the industrial area. Is she not declaring loyalty to the industrialists of Noida whose exploitation led to the workers taking to the streets in the first place?” he said.
Mr. Keshaw also referred to a video that surfaced in which U.P. Police can be allegedly seen planting the phone of a detained activist at her home. “During police custody, they brought Srishti to her home to ‘recover evidence’. The footage clearly shows them placing her already seized phone and a book in her house and ordering her to take it, so they can capture it on video. Seeing the cameras, they abort their mission and even try to break the cameras,” he said.
Other speakers, including former JNU professor Arun Kumar, and lawyer Manik Gupta, representing the activists in courts, said the government was not ready to accept that there was skyrocketing inflation in the country and worsening workers’ conditions, which led to the protest. “After what happened in the Strait of Hormuz, the prices of LPG cylinders went up in India. Workers who earn ₹10,000-12,000 a month cannot afford to buy cylinders,” Mr. Kumar said, adding that around 94% of workers in India are employed in the unorganised sector.
“Whenever we apply for bail, new sections and new FIRs are added. The NSA is invoked. The accused are brought to court after custodial torture, in chains,” Mr. Gupta alleged. “It is fortunate in the current regime in U.P. that they were not killed in an encounter. All grounds for invoking the NSA have fallen apart in the court. No claim is backed by evidence,” he said.

D2C fashion and accessories startup Theater has raised ₹75 Cr (around $7.8 Mn) in a Series A funding round led by investment firm Niveshaay. The round also saw participation from new investor Physis Capital and existing investors, including Prath Ventures, the startup said in a statement. It valued the startup at a post-money valuation of ₹410 Cr (about $43 Mn). Theater plans to deploy the fresh capital to expand its offline retail footprint across Tier I and II cities. It will also invest in brand-building initiatives, including celebrity partnerships and marketing campaigns. Theater is looking to combine its digital-first operations with an expanding physical retail presence as it seeks to build a nationally recognised mass-premium fashion brand. Founded in 2021 by Sarthak Aggarwal, Vikram Jain, Karan Jain and Shruti Aggarwal, Theater offers footwear, stockings, perfumes, and bags. The startup focuses on cruelty-free fashion and accessories positioned between imported luxury products and mass-market offerings. The company claims to have grown eightfold over the past two years while maintaining a focus on profitability. However, it did not disclose its revenue or profit figures in the statement. Theater previously raised $1.5 Mn in a pre-Series A funding round led by Prath Ventures in September 2024. Theater competes with the likes of FableStreet, Miraggio, Huemn in the Indian apparel space, which is projected to reach $117.05 Bn by 2034. The funding comes as a growing number of Indian D2C fashion and lifestyle brands are expanding beyond online channels and building omnichannel businesses. Startups are increasingly using physical stores to improve brand discovery and customer experience while continuing to leverage ecommerce for scale. For instance, D2C lifestyle brand Salty recently raised ₹30.1 Cr in January to expand its product portfolio, strengthen its ecommerce and quick commerce presence, and set up a flagship store. In March, omnichannel streetwear brand Bonkers Corner raised $15 Mn to fuel its offline expansion plans.

The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, a new report warned on Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last year.
With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025 and thousands of aid workers losing their jobs, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report.
In 2025, only those whose lives were in immediate danger became the focus, while support for longer-term issues and the ability to recover from crises was drastically scaled back.
Jennifer Doherty, co-author of the report produced by the humanitarian organisation Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap), said: “The impacts were not felt equally. The combination of reduced funding and restrictive politics meant women, children, elderly people and displaced people were especially hardest hit.”
Doherty, who said up to 23% of humanitarian staffing was estimated to have been lost in 2025, said: “Specialised services closed and targeted support became harder to sustain.”
According to the report, funding fell to an estimated $33.3bn (£24.6bn) in 2025, from a peak of $47.5bn in 2022.
While USAID sustained the most dramatic cuts, with a 55% reduction in 2025, there were also cuts by other leading donors, with 13 of the top 20 reducing their aid donations last year.
The report also highlighted the growing pressure from governments on how aid could be spent, such as the US spending freeze on programmes considered driven by diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
The aid cuts also meant that for the few people who did receive support, the targeted amount for each person dropped from $178 in 2021 to $90 in 2025, despite the actual needs of each person having risen to $255.
An aggravating factor was that governments not only failed in their duties to protect civilians but were also often actually endangering people. States were responsible for 64% of attacks on healthcare workers and largely responsible for violence that affected aid workers through the use of airstrikes.
Yemen was one of the countries badly affected by aid cuts, with nutrition worsening and diphtheria cases rising because vaccination campaigns were suspended.
Mohammed Bahashwan, Action for Humanity’s country director in Yemen, said diminishing levels of aid were exacerbating the crises faced by families.
“Problems are not occurring separately. A family may have lost its income, be unable to afford food, have a malnourished child and still need to travel considerable distances or pay costs they cannot afford to access healthcare,” he said.
The report said there were examples of the humanitarian system mobilising to support those most in need, often led by local aid organisations, and of diaspora networks stepping in. But it also said the international system did not coordinate well with these networks and that it was often local aid organisations and staff who were worst affected by cuts.
Meg Sattler, chief executive of the Vienna-based organisation Ground Truth Solutions, which carries out regular surveys of people who need aid, said there should be more focus on localisation because the international humanitarian system had not adapted fast enough or pushed back against the cuts and stipulations imposed by the US.
“We have definitely spoken to people feeling the pinch of this contraction. It is especially causing distress where aid is now considered ‘life-saving only’ and isn’t letting people do things such as send their kids to school or save to start a business – things that would help them be less reliant on aid in the future,” she said.

What Bush Understood That Trump Doesn’t
The leaders of the American right have embraced the false idea that the United States is at war with Islam.
The current New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, has affronted one of his predecessors, Rudy Giuliani, by taking the inflammatory step of deciding to attend the city’s 9/11 commemoration. “It offends me,” Giuliani proclaimed earlier this week on Newsmax.
One might suspect that the nature of Mamdani’s offense lay in his being a politician who is associating himself with a day that Giuliani prefers to associate with Giuliani. But the former mayor proceeded to lay out a much darker rationale. “They’re taking over certain parts of America and certain parts of Europe. They have every desire to take us over. This is not ‘they want to be just another religion,’” he said of Muslims. “Mamdani is a clear, a clear supporter of that. All of the Muslims he supports are murderers!”
Like many of Giuliani’s utterances, this one has no connection to reality. Yet his assertion that Mamdani harbors some secret desire to conquer the United States in the name of Islam, that his religion is the skeleton key to a web of sinister motivations, is now treated on the right as almost banal. A quarter century after 9/11, delirious anti-Muslim bigotry is almost routine in the political rhetoric of many conservatives.
The conventional account of Donald Trump’s political career explains his rise to power as a populist revolt against Republican orthodoxy. The GOP elite had lost touch with their base by endorsing immigration reform, free trade, or forever wars in the Middle East, which created an opening that Trump exploited.
That story is largely true, but it misses an important issue. The President George W. Bush–era Republican Party after 9/11 insisted that the United States was at war not with a religion but with an idea. America opposed radical Islamism, not Islam. We stood for freedom as a universal human principle.
Not all voters on the right accepted this formulation. Some believed that the United States was at war with Islam itself. By 2007, conservative Republicans viewed Islam negatively by a margin of more than 30 points; Democrats, independents, and moderate Republicans all held net-favorable views. Ten years later, nearly 80 percent of Republicans believed that the values of Islam were at odds with American values. One of the most important and ominous notions that Trump has seized upon and legitimized is that Muslims are inherently un-American.
Anti-Muslim sentiment sprang up organically in the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, but Bush’s forceful defense of pluralism confined it to the rantings of Ann Coulter, Michael Savage, and other fringe reactionaries. After Coulter called on the United States in 2001 to “invade their countries, kill their leaders and convert them to Christianity,” National Review dropped her column. As Bush passed from the scene and was replaced by Barack Obama, some right-wing-outrage entrepreneurs recognized an opportunity to redefine the War on Terror as a war against Islam.
Trump himself was among the first to see the opening. In 2010, a right-wing backlash arose in opposition to a proposal for a Muslim cultural center, modeled on the YMCA or a Jewish community center, in downtown New York. The most hysterical opponents depicted the center, which planned to call itself Park51, as a “victory mosque” celebrating the destruction of the World Trade Center. Other conservatives merely insisted that it was “insensitive” for Muslim Americans to open a center in the general neighborhood of Ground Zero.
Trump inserted himself into the controversy, proposing that he purchase the property to halt construction on the putatively offensive site. In his offer letter (which, naturally, he made public), Trump called it a “very serious, inflammatory, and highly divisive situation that is destined, in my opinion, to only get worse.” David Letterman asked him, “Does this, in fact, suggest that we are officially at war with Muslims?” Trump, who was still in the formative stage of his transition from celebrity to right-wing rabble-rouser, replied, “Well, somebody knocked down the World Trade Center.” He later added, “Somebody’s blowing us up. Somebody’s blowing up buildings, and somebody’s doing lots of bad stuff.”
Trump’s first campaign was pockmarked with undisguised bigotry against Muslims. He falsely claimed that Muslims in New Jersey had cheered the 9/11 attacks en masse, and he called for surveillance of mosques, a database of Muslims in America, and a ban on Muslims entering the United States. He associated the sitting president with Islam by incessantly using his middle name.
He has continued to attack Muslims as disloyal or un-American. He falsely claimed that Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, a Democrat, had praised al-Qaeda, and he demanded that she and Reprepresentative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, both of whom are U.S. citizens, be sent “back from where they came.” He insinuated that Mamdani has no right to reside in the United States: “A lot of people are saying he’s here illegally.”
The through line connecting these smears is the assumption that Muslims cannot be Americans, even if they arrive legally, even if they are born here. Trump has made this point explicitly and told Sean Hannity in 2016, “Assimilation has been very hard. It’s almost—I won’t say nonexistent, but it gets to be pretty close. And I’m talking about second- and third-generation. They come—they don’t—for some reason, there’s no real assimilation.”
This sort of rhetoric has grown so common that episodes such as the uproar against Mamdani have come to feel like normal politics, rather than paranoia and rank discrimination. The New York Post alone has published at least eight stories (as of press time) hyping the Giuliani-fueled controversy.
Some relatives of 9/11 victims have claimed that Mamdani’s presence at the observance would be a distraction (even though mayoral attendance has been a regular feature throughout its existence). Others have depicted their anger as a protest against Mamdani’s current agenda. “It’s not about his religion or where he came from. It’s about the policies he has today,” one explained. Is it the plan for free buses? The pied-à-terre tax?
That Mamdani wishes to attend the ceremony and has denounced the 9/11 attacks as heinous terrorism ought to serve as satisfactory evidence that, whatever shortcomings he may have, he is not a supporter of al-Qaeda. Indeed, it might well be offensive if Mamdani did not want to attend the ceremony. The New York Post would need to publish phone-book-size editions to convey its full outrage.
The logic of Islamophobia rejects out of hand that it is possible for Mamdani to oppose terrorism. 9/11 was, in this view, a battle in a war against Islam, so he is, by dint of his faith, the enemy. Thus, his desire to commemorate the tragedy, like Muslims’ desire to have a YMCA of their own in New York City, must be understood as revealing hidden malevolence.
If you had asked Bush after 9/11 to imagine a future within his lifetime in which New York had a Muslim mayor who would join the city in mourning the attacks, he’d surely have considered it the ultimate vindication of the ideals he sought to foster. But Republicans have rejected Bush’s understanding of 9/11 and its meaning in favor of Trump’s.
The events of the past decade, and especially the past six months, have clarified that the primary grounds for this repudiation does not seem to be Trump’s abhorrence for wars of choice in the Middle East. It is that Bush denied and suppressed contempt for Muslims, while Trump has honored and nurtured this hatred.
