The book Intangible Cultural Heritage under National and International Law: Going beyond the 2003 UNESCO Convention published in 2020 is edited by Marie Cornu, Anita Vaivade, Lily Martinet and Clea Hance is based on the Osmose project initiated in 2014 to study the legal regimes established in different countries to safeguard the ICH. The editors and their team coordinated an international study on the ICH in about 26 countries. A comprehensive questionnaire was circulated among informed members in these countries to elicit information regarding the comprehension and negotiation of the pertinent national laws and how these national laws were modified, or may be retained, in light of the provisions of the UNESCO convention of 2003. After collecting the responses to the questionnaire, the editors have categorized, commented and expanded on the responses under several broad heads like environment and the ICH, interaction between the national and the international laws, the national and international tools for the safeguarding of the ICH, and, importantly, the judicialization of the ICH. All complexities involved in the institutionalization of laws at the local, national and international levels about the ICH are put forward in a transparent manner without prejudice or unconditional bolstering of the clauses of the UNESCO Convention. This is the first such comprehensive study on the connection between the international legal framework and the national legal instruments for safeguarding the ICH.
The UNESCO convention of 2003 on the Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) is an important milestone in the discussion on the global ICH. There was a tacit recognition of the fact in organization of the Convention that cultural diversity and heritage are an equivalent of the environmental biodiversity. Both are sine qua non for the material and spiritual welfare of the human beings. A community loses its bearings without the notion of heritage. Soon after the convention, the member states of the United Nations ratified the convention. Subsequent to the ratification, measures as envisioned in the convention were thought about, deliberated at the national level and sought to be put into practice. India also became a signatory to the UNESCO convention of 2003 and ratified the convention in 2005. The 2003 convention provided a broad framework about the nature, definition, implications and the necessity of the safeguarding of the ICH. To that end, following the convention, an inter-governmental committee for the safeguarding of the ICH was constituted at the international level under the aegis of the UNESCO, which in turn led to the creation of inventories at the national level, and the procedure for inscription in the list of the ICH. There is already a procedure for the inscription of the ICH item in the UNESCO, however, now, after the ratification of the 2003 convention by member states of the United Nations, inscription processes were initiated at the nation level.
To say that the member states ratified the UNESCO convention does not imply that prior to the Convention there was no mechanism in place to safeguard the ICH. The different nation states had created mechanisms to protect the intangible cultural heritage. The Convention reenergized efforts in this direction, and provided a clear and comprehensive framework to understand the nature and implications of the ICH, in addition to providing an international legitimacy to the notion of the ICH by instituting discussion on a prestigious global platform. In different countries the nomenclature was variegated and often confusing. In some countries, the term, ‘cultural heritage’ was used, in others the terms like, ‘folklore’ or even ‘folk culture’ or ‘popular culture’ were used. A colorful array of terms and expressions were used to discuss the heritage elements and those who practiced these aspects of the heritage. In some countries the term ‘heritage holders’ was used for the communities dealing with a particular heritage, in others the expression used was the ‘living communities’. The UNESCO convention of 2003 for the first time clubbed all these words, phrases and terms together, and used the umbrella term Intangible Cultural Heritage. No doubt there were linguistic and cultural problems in merging the divergent usages, however, countries since the ratification have tried to bring their nomenclatures in line with the widely accepted intangible cultural heritage, and then branching away from it to create sub sets.
An important dimension that the book discusses is the judicialization of the ICH before and more so after the UNESCO 2003 Convention. The terrain of the ICH is not devoid of the tedious lawsuits. The interests of the heritage holders and the evolving laws about animals and environment have often clashed, resulting in the bitter litigation process. Hence, some rituals which are part of the heritage of a community are often seen at odds with the evolving dynamics of the animal rights. For example, to give just one instance, among scores of others from the 26 countries studied by the editors, bull fighting may be a longstanding game associated with some communities in Europe, but in the contemporary discussion about animal rights, the game is seen as an anathema, an eyesore to those who plead for the rights of the animals, especially in the scenarios where the threat of physical violence is patent. Same applies to cockfighting. There are several such case studies, where the notion of heritage has had a head on collision with the current delimitation of the rights of animals. Some of the ICH have met with stiff resistance when it comes to their inscription in the inventories at the national level. A number of inscriptions have been challenged and had to be removed from the inventories. The inventories, by the way, are at the local level as well, in some countries. The ICH and the mechanisms to protect it is a fraught territory with contesting claims of the stakeholders and the legal machinery.
The judicialization is no debilitating bar to the rich inventories that have been created hitherto. The field of the ICH is vast and heterogenous, with the scope to nurture traditions that have stood in good stead of the communities they are a part of, in shaping their identities, perspectives on life and the world and lending a sense of stability and continuity.
The book is a good resource for scholars of different fields like heritage studies, humanities, anthropology, history, law etc. With the presentation of actual comparative case studies from countries that have ratified the Convention, the understanding of the ICH becomes clearer. In Kashmir, the need for sound legal instruments to safeguard the ICH is needed more than ever before, for the threat of extinction to the ICH is imminent, with an emergent and striking cultural gap between generations. A legal instrument can provide the pivot for identifying and creating the perimeters of the ICH, with an assurance of transference of the same to the future generations.
Dr. Javaid Iqbal Bhat, Associate Professor, South Campus, UoK

Stronger-than-normal El Nino alarms scientists over Galápagos wildlife and forests
The prediction that this season’s El Nino will be stronger than normal has alarmed the Ecuadorian scientific community
QUITO, Ecuador -- The prediction that this season’s El Nino phenomenon will be stronger than normal has alarmed the Ecuadorian scientific community, which has warned of its impact on the flora and fauna of the Galapagos Islands, home to the highest concentration of species not found elsewhere on Earth.
The archipelago of more than 230 islands — of which only four are inhabited — is located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) off the coast of Ecuador.
The climatic phenomenon occurs periodically and in the equatorial Pacific is characterized by an increase in sea temperature and intense rainfall. Its strength is determined by measuring the water temperature in that area and comparing it to the normal average. If it is 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) above normal, it is considered “very strong.”
The sea temperature will be about 2.2 degrees Celsius (4 F) above normal, according to the latest projection from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which means that “the impact will be significant,” said Franklin Ormaza, a professor and researcher at the Faculty of Maritime Engineering and Marine Sciences of the Higher Polytechnic School of the Coast (ESPOL).
Animals and fish will be at risk because as the water temperature rises, “plankton, algae, and smaller fish species, which are food for larger marine animals, practically disappear,” explained Washington Tapia, director of Biodiversa Ecuador, a conservation organization in the archipelago, to the AP.
He specified that the species most at risk are the iconic Galápagos penguins, blue-footed boobies, petrels, flightless cormorants, albatrosses, and even sea lions. Coral colonies could also be seriously affected, as could tuna fishing.
In the absence of food, “animal colonies stop reproducing,” disperse in search of food, and die of starvation in the process, explained scientist Gustavo Jiménez, from the Charles Darwin Foundation.
If the phenomenon occurs with the expected magnitude, the archipelago’s vertebrate population could decrease by at least 20% this year, Jiménez added.
One of the most closely monitored species in the islands, the Galápagos penguins, serves as a marker of the impact of this climate phenomenon on the archipelago’s fauna.
According to data from the Charles Darwin Foundation, after the 1998 El Nino — one of the most powerful and destructive cycles — only 400 of the 1,300 existing Galápagos penguins remained.
If El Nino strikes with the expected force, the last three remaining Scalesia forests could be at risk of disappearing, scientist Heinke Jager of the Charles Darwin Foundation said.
Opuntia cacti, which grow along the seashore, would also be threatened.
These plants, found only in the Galápagos Islands, support various ecosystems of insects, birds and other smaller plants that are part of the archipelago’s unique biodiversity.
Jager explained that “these species need human support” because the heavy rains brought by El Nino will cause the territory they occupy to be overrun by invasive plants, such as blackberries, which have shorter reproductive cycles.
Therefore, they have organized a plan that includes the eradication of invasive plants, the collection of seeds and the creation of nurseries to conserve threatened species. The Ecuadorian government, foundations, and nongovernmental organizations working in the archipelago are participating in the program.
The Galápagos Islands were declared a Natural World Heritage Site in 1978 for their unique animal and plant species, which served as the basis for the English scientist Charles Darwin to develop his theory of evolution.

Modi-Xi bilateral meet set for Day 1 of BRICS Summit on Saturday
Xi Jinping's attendance at the 2026 BRICS Summit in Delhi will be his first visit to India in nearly seven years.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will hold a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Saturday, September 12, on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit 2026 in New Delhi.
Xi Jinping's attendance at the 2026 BRICS Summit in Delhi will be his first visit to India in nearly seven years. The Chinese president's visit also comes as both Delhi and Beijing work towards renewing their ties after years of strain caused by border tensions.
Deep Dive
Along with a bilateral with Xi, the prime minister will also meet with Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian and Russian president Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in the national capital.
Modi and Xi met in the Russian city of Kazan in October 2024, soon after the two sides reached an understanding on ending the military standoff on the LAC. The two leaders also held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Tianjin last August.
At the 2026 SCO Summit, the two leaders exchanged a brief word during the annual family photo in Bishkek.
Xi Jinping's India visit
Last month, it was reported that the Chinese President was likely to come to New Delhi to attend the BRICS Summit. With this now confirmed, Xi is also expected to be accompanied by a large delegation.
This will also mark the first time that the Chinese President has travelled to India since October 2019, when he came to Mamallapuram in Tamil Nadu for the second informal summit with Modi.
However, six months later, India-China relations hit a six-decade low over incursions by Chinese troops in the Ladakh sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC).

The recurring nightmare that haunts British 9/11 survivor who escaped south tower
Janice Brooks escaped the 84th floor of Two World Trade Center on 11 September 2001 after the first plane struck next door. Sixty-one of her colleagues did not make it out alive. She tells Caspar Barnes her story
For the past 25 years, Janice Brooks has been reliving the same recurring nightmare.
She is standing in a building in the middle of New York’s Hudson River looking across at the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center. There are no buildings in the middle of the Hudson River – this is how she knows she’s dreaming.
Halfway up one of the towers she sees a man standing in the huge void left in the building by a plane. He has curly black hair and is wearing a blue shirt and a tie. The man cannot stop looking over his shoulder at a wall of flames inching towards him.
Ms Brooks can see the sweat forming on the man’s brow as he edges towards the drop. The man looks down, bends his knees as if about to jump, and then, “Boom,” Brooks claps, “I wake up.”
She is one of the few people who walked away from the 11 September terror attack, making a miraculous escape from the 84th floor of the south tower. Sixty one of her colleagues weren’t so lucky.
Aged 41 at the time, she had moved to New York just three weeks earlier, accepting her dream job as an executive assistant at Euro Brokers at Two World Trade Center. She had already spent a decade in London working for the brokerage firm and had built up close relationships with many of her colleagues.
On the previous Friday night, four days before the attack, Ms Brooks climbed to the top of her 110-storey office building – once the world’s tallest buildings – to take in the view of the city she now called home.
Wind ruffled through her short-cropped hair as she looked down onto the Brooklyn Bridge, turning to see the sunset glinting off the Empire State Building. Her new adventure was just getting underway and she smiled to herself.
On 11 September at 8.46am, when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the north tower, all passengers aboard were killed instantly. The plane severed all three staircases in the skyscraper, trapping an estimated 1,400 people above the 91st floor. None of them survived.
Ms Brooks had been at her desk in the adjacent tower when the first plane struck. Her 84th-floor office faced away from the north tower so she did not see the Boeing 767 aircraft but she heard the explosion. “I could see paper and dust swirling in the air through the windows,” she remembers.
Lower Manhattan was filled with construction sites at the time and she initially thought that was where the noise had come from. This seemed to happen all the time in New York and nobody paid much attention, she says. But this bang was much louder than anything she had heard before.
She went to check with her colleague, Brian Clark, who told her not to panic and promised to investigate. Ms Brooks went back to her desk but soon heard a man’s voice shout, “Everybody out.”
She grabbed her things to go but, before leaving, she hesitated. “Better call the London office to keep them in the loop,” she thought. When the receptionist put her through to the managing director in London, Brooks was casual over the phone, “ Not really too sure what's happening, but I'm getting ready to leave,” she said.
“F****** hell, Janice. A plane's gone into the building, get the f*** out of there!” her boss shouted down the line. The London team over 3,500 miles away already knew more about what was going on 200 yards away from where Ms Brooks was sitting. They had been watching in horror as the news was unfolding on TV.
“I don't remember hanging up. I just remember grabbing my bag and running,” Ms Brooks says. She ran through the dealing area to the main corridor where the designated fire marshals, Steve Chucknick and Jose Marrero, were ferrying people towards the staircase. Both men lost their lives that day.
In the stairwell the chatter was amiable, as if they were simple taking part in a fire drill. People were swapping stories from the weekend, what restaurant they’d tried, or the play they had seen on Broadway. Ms Brooks fell in with a colleague from the dealing floor, a man she recognised but whose name had not stuck yet. He recommended Ms Brooks might want to remove her high heels, which she promptly did.
They made it down to the 72nd floor when the first announcement came over the PA system from a Port Authority official. “We have been asked not to evacuate Two World Trade Center. The space is being used on the plaza for those being evacuated from One World Trade Center. This building is stable. Please return to your office,” Ms Brooks remembers.
For some, this announcement would turn out to be a death sentence.
“Your attention, please, ladies and gentlemen. Building Two is secure. There is no need to evacuate Building Two. If you are in the midst of evacuation, you may use the reentry doors and the elevators to return to your office. Repeat, Building Two is secure.”
On hearing the announcement, Ms Brooks and a dozen others walked down to the nearest bank of elevators in Morgan Stanley’s offices on the 70th floor. They waited to take the elevator back up to their office. Luckily for Ms Brooks, that elevator never arrived.
After a few minutes of repeatedly pressing the elevator button, the group decided to walk back up the stairs. At this point, it was still thought that a small plane had flown into the first tower by accident, that perhaps the pilot had suffered a heart attack. It only became clear that America was under attack at 9.03am, when United Airlines Flight 175 crashed into the south tower.
Ms Brooks and her group had been moving through an adjoining corridor from one stairwell to another, likely on the 76th floor, when the second plane struck.
“There was this almighty bang, the lights went off. I could feel stuff falling down from the ceiling. A couple of the girls at the front fell to the floor,” Ms Brooks says. She could feel the building swaying for about five seconds.
The badly wounded started to emerge from the offices closest to windows. The first woman Ms Brooks encountered had glass in her hair and cuts all over her face.
“Her arm was cut almost neatly, actually from her shoulder to her elbow,” Brooks says. One of the guys took his t-shirt off and wrapped it around her arm, tying it in a knot under her armpit. Half of her foot was missing.
One man had a large shard of glass lodged in his chest that people were helping him extract. Another woman had blood running into her eyes from a cut on her head. “She had long, dark hair and when she shook her hair, glass showered everyone,” Brooks says.
They searched desperately for a way down. They returned to the stairwell they had just ascended but it was gone. “There was just blackness and dark,” Ms Brooks says. After the second plane struck, only one of the three stairwells in their tower remained undamaged.
Ms Brooks’s group managed to find their way through the smoke and rubble to another stairwell. The lights were on and they could see pieces of ceiling, plaster and concrete littering the stairs. There was a broken pipe gushing water down the stairs.
The woman with the severed foot and badly injured arm was trailing blood down the staircase. Ms Brooks remembers walking barefoot through it, trying to stay calm and suppress her screams. Her colleague, whose name she still didn’t know, helped calm her down.
This colleague, Bob Mahon, played an instrumental role in getting the group safely to the bottom. When her pain became too much, Mr Mahon carried the injured woman down the last 10 storeys on his back.
At the eighth floor, they encountered three firefighters ascending, who looked them up and down, noting the walking wounded, then continued silently upward to their fate.
When Ms Brooks eventually reached the bottom of the south tower there were still firefighters, police and Port Authority workers streaming into the building. At the entrance to the south tower, a burly New York cop told her and Mr Mahon, “Keep your head down, don’t look up, and run.”
They ran past St Paul’s Chapel into Vesey Street and kept going until they could see the Brooklyn Bridge. Then, for the first time, Ms Brooks turned to look at the Twin Towers. “I couldn’t believe what I was seeing, where our floor should have been there was a huge gaping hole, and I could see smoke and flames,” she says.
Mr Mahon asked her the time. It was 9:43am. The tower they had just escaped collapsed just 16 minutes later at 9:59am. More than 600 people died, including 61 of their Euro Brokers colleagues – a fifth of the New York branch. Some 30 minutes later, at 10:28am the north tower come crashing down, taking with it more than 1,400 lives. The official death toll for the September 11 attack is 2,977 people.
Ms Brooks now lives in a cottage in Norfolk, in the east of England, with her dog Jesse. Twenty-five years since 9/11, one third of Americans are unlikely to remember the attacks. Around the world, more than half of the population is too young to have a memory of it.
Some years Ms Brooks feels like the date can pass without even an acknowledgement of the attacks. September 11th is not taught in the school curriculum in Britain.
Now aged 66, Ms Brooks works with a charity called Since 9/11, through which she gives talks at schools to educate those born after the attacks about their significance. She does not like reliving that day but in retelling her story, she hopes to bring listeners closer to the event, to personalise the tragedy so that its scale can be understood.
“For me, these talks help to keep the date alive, to keep not only my friends but everyone that died on September 11th alive,” she says.
Each year, as autumn approaches again, her nightmare with the man in the Twin Towers comes back to her more frequently. In a bid to understand that lone man is, Ms Brooks has seen a psychiatrist, who told her she needed to find an ending for this man – to forge a narrative for him that she can wholeheartedly believe and then finally put this nightmare to bed.
She has tried a couple of variations. Perhaps she knew this man with the curly black hair and the tie. Perhaps he does not jump, and he gets to safety.
Recently she was speaking at her local church about September 11th. After she had finished, a member of the audience approached her. “You know that man in the nightmare is you, Janice?” the audience member said.
She reflected on this in the weeks after. But the nightmare persists.

Govt tightens e-commerce rules to curb deceptive pricing, search practices
The changes, incorporated in an amendment to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, were announced by the consumer affairs department on Thursday
The government will impose regulatory changes on e-commerce companies beginning January 1, 2027, requiring online marketplaces to integrate with the National Consumer Helpline (NCH), a government grievance portal, and crack down on misleading search results and deceptive price discounts.
The changes, incorporated in an amendment to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, were announced by the consumer affairs department on Thursday, which said they would strengthen consumer protection while balancing the need for ease of doing business.
Integrate with National Consumer Helpline
The government said every e-commerce entity would have to become a partner in the convergence process of the NCH, integrating platforms more closely with the government’s consumer grievance redressal mechanism. Under the amended rules, e-commerce entities would have to give a complainant a copy of the complaint as recorded by the platform’s grievance officer.
The move comes amid a large volume of complaints linked to online commerce.
Of the 17,71,622 grievances received under NCH in 2025, 5,11,196, or about 29%, were related to the e-commerce sector, the department said.
Bars manipulation of search results
Under these provisions, platforms would be barred from manipulating search results in a manner that misleads users or adversely affects the relevance of results to their queries. Sponsored listings will have to carry clear and prominent disclosures, making it easier for consumers to distinguish paid placements from organic search results, a government statement said.
The rules also tighten requirements around advertised price reductions. Where a price cut is announced, platforms will have to display both the reduced price and the prior price, defined as the lowest price at which the product or service was offered during the preceding 30 days.
Covers dark patterns
The government has also brought dark patterns under a stricter compliance framework. E-commerce entities will have to comply with the 2023 guidelines on prevention and regulation of dark patterns, conduct an annual self-audit and prominently display a certificate of compliance.
Dark patterns are design tactics on a web page intended to lure consumers into making a choice or making a transaction they never intended to.
Marketplace platforms will also have to provide consumers with key product and transaction information, including best-before/use-before dates, return and refund terms, warranty, delivery and payment details.
The amended rules also restrict the use of consumer information without the consumer’s express and affirmative consent.
Another provision bars marketplace entities from collecting bundled fees for services unrelated to the e-commerce platform, with an exception specified for loyalty or membership programmes.
For imported products, platforms will have to disclose importer details and the country of origin, giving consumers more information about the products they purchase.

Quick Answer
John Ternus faces the tough task of balancing Steve Jobs’ product-first innovation with Tim Cook’s business success. As Apple’s new CEO, he must revive innovation, fix its AI struggles, manage rising costs, and keep Apple at the top.
It is September, and around this time of year my stories usually start with “Tis the iPhone season” (not kidding, you can check). While the new iPhones are still coming early in September, this story is not about the iPhone but rather about the people behind it, or rather Apple in general.
After 15 years of taking care of CEO business, Tim Cook finally bid farewell to Apple. On his last day in the role, on 31 August 2026, he penned an emotional memo addressed to “Team”. Cook has not cut ties with Apple completely but will now serve as the Executive Chairman of Apple’s Board of Directors.
John Ternus has taken over the reins as Apple’s new CEO. He has been with Apple since 2001 and has climbed the corporate ladder, all the way from being a member of the product design team to the CEO position in 2026. In case you do not know him well, we got you covered.
A full circle moment for Apple
This change in command feels like Apple’s life has come full circle. The company was started/ headed mainly by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, who were known as product people through and through. It seemed to be teetering on the verge of closing down when Jobs returned to turn it around in 1997. He was succeeded by Tim Cook, who, as Jobs himself mentioned, is “not a product person” but focused more on scaling the business and made Apple the first trillion-dollar company in the world under his tenure. And now Cook has given the Apple empire to Ternus to take care of.
Many believe Ternus has been handed a golden spoon— Jobs laid the groundwork in his second coming, made products that became aspirational and industry benchmarks, and then Cook followed by scaling the business in a way no one had ever imagined could be done. Many think Ternus can just pass his tenure enjoying the fruits of their labor.
I respectfully would like to disagree. If anything, I believe he has an uphill battle in front of him.
From Jobs to Cook – from being insanely innovative to being a world champ
Steve Jobs focused on products and features that were not created to blend in. Under him, Apple’s product portfolio was slim and streamlined. People who have recently started following tech may find it hard to believe, but under Steve Jobs, Apple back then was generally launching just one iPhone a year. Just one. The idea was to focus on user experience, bringing out products that made the lives of its users easier, developing interfaces that would make using a device a simple process – in short, innovation that would make a difference. Apple was actually ‘thinking different’.
Under Tim Cook, that rulebook was respectfully thrown out of the window. Whatever Jobs did, it seemed Cook was doing the opposite. From launching just one iPhone a year, Apple started to launch multiple ones, sometimes more than once a year. It also had multiple watches, earbuds, headphones, iPads, iMacs, MacBooks, Mac Minis, HomePods, and, believe it or not, even a cleaning cloth (there are two generations of it now). It is safe to say Apple’s product portfolio expanded (some would say “exploded”) under Tim Cook.
It may have gotten extremely hard to keep track of all of Apple’s products, but under Cook, Apple became the most valuable company in the world. During his time as CEO, Apple’s shares went up a whopping 2,275 percent! When Cook gained control in 2011, Apple was valued at USD 350 billion (a very healthy number), and with his strategy of diversifying the portfolio and expanding into new markets, Cook took Apple all the way up to a valuation of USD 5 trillion, becoming only the second company in history to do so (Nvidia was the first).
Jobs and Cook thus both played very vital but very different roles in making Apple what it has become today. One focused on innovation, the other on expansion.
Ternus has got some big shoes to fill
Now, Ternus has stepped into the CEO’s role, and he has some really big shoes to fill. Not just in terms of his immediate predecessor, but the one before him too.
Let me explain: Ternus is a product person, and for all these years when Cook was in the office, many Apple purists were disappointed by his constant efforts to make the brand more mainstream. Cook’s efforts were not about making the brand more accessible or democratizing it (even though the number of Apple products has vastly expanded, they still remain premium), but were more about relentlessly releasing products and their variants. While this did increase Apple’s revenues and profits exponentially, many believed it had deflected the brand from its core values, the values Jobs believed in: innovation, user experience, and product design. According to many critics, Apple’s designs became repetitive, software became buggy, and its innovation arc felt more like a flat line of late, with the odd bump here and there.
So naturally, now that Ternus has assumed office, this lobby has new hope. Hope that perhaps as a “product person,” he will take Apple back to what they insist were its ‘golden days’ under Jobs. That he will channel all of Apple’s energy into making more innovative products and not just products that seem to exist to make numbers.
What this lobby, however, forgets is that Jobs is not the only legacy Ternus has to live up to. Cook may have done things very differently (some might say he really did ‘think different’ but in a different sphere of business), but under his leadership Apple soared and found its way to the top. Today, it stands at the very pinnacle of the tech world; some would even say it is the most important company in the world. While topping this would be difficult, Ternus can certainly not let it slide off this pedestal.
Now it’s Ternus’ turn to think different
This means John Ternus basically has to find a balance between the Jobs method and the Cook method or come up with something completely new. And that too at a very difficult time for the industry. With demand for memory driving up prices of all things tech – smartphones, laptops, computers, hard drives – it will be a challenge for Ternus to manage prices, even while bringing in the big sales numbers that many now associate with Apple. There is also the matter of Apple’s struggle with AI for the past couple of years, which has become quite a spectacle, one which Ternus needs to solve as soon as possible.
Many would kill to be in Ternus’ position, as it seems like the guy has got it all made and simply has to carry it forward, but if you ask me, I do not envy him his place or task. He has to deal with the shadows of two illustrious predecessors and an industry crisis, as well as a deeply polarised community, apart from, of course, intense competition from the likes of Microsoft, Google, Meta and Samsung. To be fair, it was not easy for either Jobs or Cook. Jobs took over Apple in 1997, with many confident that the company would not last another year. When Jobs passed away in 2011, an equally large number of people felt that a non-product person like Cook would not be able to succeed. Both of them defied their detractors and added a new dimension to Apple in different ways. It is Ternus’ turn to put his own spin on Apple. It will not be easy. Will he, too, Think Different, differently? Only time will tell.

Paris Saint-Germain began its pursuit of a third successive Champions League title with a commanding 6-1 win over Slovan Bratislava at the Parc des Princes on Wednesday.
Ferran Torres marked his European debut for PSG with a hat-trick, while Ousmane Dembele scored twice and provided an assist as Luis Enrique’s side dominated from the opening stages.
Dembele put PSG ahead in the 17th minute after Nuno Mendes’ powerful effort came back off the post. The France international controlled the loose ball before finishing past goalkeeper Dominik Takac.
PSG doubled its lead soon after. A deflected effort from Dro Fernandez fell kindly for Dembele, who headed home his second of the night.
Torres, who joined PSG from Barcelona during the summer, made it 3-0 in the 31st minute after meeting a cross from Dembele.
The Spaniard then almost returned the favour, playing the ball across goal for Dembele, but Takac diverted the forward’s effort onto the underside of the crossbar.
PSG continued its dominance after the interval. Torres scored his second just two minutes into the second half after a strong run by fellow new signing Maghnes Akliouche created the opening.
Mendes later had a goal ruled out for offside before Torres completed his hat-trick by turning in Dembele’s corner with his knee.

Slovan, coached by former Manchester City and Barcelona midfielder Yaya Toure, managed a consolation through Suleiman Camara, who finished well to reduce the deficit.
Fabian Ruiz restored PSG’s five-goal advantage late on, reacting quickest to a loose ball inside the penalty area to make it 6-1.
The result provided PSG with a comfortable start to the league phase as it looks to become only the second club in the modern Champions League era to win the competition three years in a row, after Real Madrid’s run from 2016 to 2018.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

After nearly 900 years in France, the Bayeux Tapestry is welcoming visitors in London. The rare loan lets visitors see the famous embroidery at the British Museum. Its stitched scenes bring England’s medieval past and the Battle of Hastings to life. But history can feel distant when it appears only through dates, names and textbook chapters. The Bayeux Tapestry brings that past closer through colourful pictures stitched onto cloth. Made during the 11th century, it tells a story of ambition, conflict and power. Here are 5 reasons why seeing this remarkable work offers a memorable historical experience. The embroidery shows events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. Its story leads towards the Battle of Hastings, where William defeated King Harold. Instead of reading battle summaries, visitors can follow the action through connected scenes. Ships are prepared, armies travel, and rival claims to England’s throne drive the story. This makes a complicated struggle easier to understand, even without much knowledge of European history. The tapestry tells its story through pictures, making it approachable for ordinary viewers. One scene follows another, helping visitors understand how events develop across the cloth. Edward the Confessor’s funeral appears alongside preparations for William’s invasion and Harold’s final battle. The people, ships and buildings give viewers plenty to notice beyond the main action. Looking closely becomes an exercise in discovering details, rather than simply remembering important dates. The cloth stretches almost 70 metres while its height is only around 50 centimetres. That unusual shape allows a long historical story to unfold across one continuous surface. Following it means moving through the narrative rather than viewing a single framed picture. Its scale also highlights the effort needed to plan and complete such detailed work. Even before understanding every scene, visitors can appreciate the patience behind this enormous creation. Despite its name, the Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery, rather than a woven tapestry. Its makers stitched dyed wool onto linen to create figures, objects and scenes. Many scholars believe it was made in England, possibly in or around Canterbury, and probably by women. It encourages appreciation for skilled hands whose individual names have not survived alongside their work. The embroidery does more than show battles; it presents disputed claims about royal power. Harold’s oath to William remains an important example of its complicated political story. Historians also debate what Edward’s deathbed scene suggests about his preferred successor. These questions remind visitors that surviving accounts do not always provide complete answers. Seeing the tapestry encourages curiosity about whose version of history we inherit. TOI correspondent from Washington:
 The Trump administration’s homeland security image targeting the generic “Mr Singh” has struck a particularly sensitive nerve in the Sikh community, whose members have become a highly visible presence in American trucking, business, and indeed in public life. However, the post was later deleted.
There are no federal statistics identifying truck drivers by religion, but the North American Punjabi Trucking Association (NAPTA) estimates that Sikhs account for roughly 20% of US truck drivers and about 40% on the West Coast, putting the number of Sikh truckers nationally at about 150,000.
The community’s influence extends beyond driving. Many early drivers became owner-operators and eventually fleet owners. NAPTA says its membership includes about 1,400 companies operating more than 9,000 trucks, while industry estimates have put the share of US trucking companies controlled by Punjabi/Sikh operators as high as 20%. The figures are estimates, not government census data, but underscore the scale of the community’s entrepreneurial network.
Also read: ‘Get off our roads, Mr Singh,’ US homeland security poster ignites backlash over targeting of Sikhs
Trucking offered many immigrants a relatively accessible path from employee to business owner: a driver could accumulate capital, buy a truck and eventually build a fleet. 
The industry also generally accommodated Sikh articles of faith, including turbans and uncut hair. Established Punjabi networks, family businesses and a shortage of American truck drivers helped fuel the community’s expansion.
Its presence is visible along the nation’s freight corridors. At Exit 360 on Interstate 80 in Nebraska, for example, the Akal Travel Center, or dhaba, has become a familiar marker of the Punjabi-American trucking ecosystem.
The history of Sikhs in America also complicates any portrayal of “Singh” as synonymous with a foreign newcomer. UC Davis’ Punjabi and Sikh Diaspora Digital Archive records four Sikh men arriving in San Francisco on April 6, 1899, in the first documented record of South Asian pioneers in California. Early Punjabi migrants worked in agriculture, lumber and railroads and quickly established communities across the West.
They also encountered hostility. In 1907, white residents attacked South Asian workers, mainly Sikhs, in Bellingham, Washington, amid broader anti-Asian agitation. UC Davis records several such attacks and notes that most of the early South Asian pioneers were Sikhs, some of whom predated the arrival of Europeans on the east coast.
For Sikh-Americans whose families have been in the country for generations, the DHS image therefore raises concerns that a surname is being used as shorthand for an entire community, blurring distinctions among citizens, permanent residents, legal immigrants and people in the country unlawfully.
Ranjeev Singh Puri, a Michigan Democrat, said Wednesday that the post had particularly personal resonance. “As a proud Sikh-American, my middle name is Singh. So are my sons’. It is not a punchline, it is a surname carried proudly by millions of Sikhs worldwide, generations of whom have served this nation, built businesses, and strengthened the fabric of our democracy,” Puri said, calling the DHS post “xenophobia dressed up as public policy.”
The controversy also puts a spotlight on prominent Sikh Republicans. Harmeet Dhillon, who serves as Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, and Nikki Haley, the former South Carolina governor and former US ambassador to the United Nations, had not publicly commented on the matter at the time of writing.
Sikh-American political and civic visibility extends well beyond trucking. In 2004, Chirinjeev Kathuria became the first Indian-American to run for the US Senate while wearing a turban. Other prominent Sikh-Americans include World Bank President Ajay Banga and former US Attorney for the Southern District of New York Preet Bharara, neither of whom carries the Singh surname.
For Sikh community veterans, debates over immigration enforcement, commercial driver’s licenses, English proficiency, licensing fraud and highway safety are legitimate. But they say the argument changes when a federal agency turns a surname shared by millions of people into a symbol of incompetence. For a community that has spent more than a century establishing itself on American roads, farms, businesses and institutions, that distinction matters.

Man 27, charged in stabbing inside Edmonton Sikh temple
Accused was granted statutory release from federal prison day before attack
Nearly three weeks since two men were stabbed inside a Sikh temple in Edmonton, police have laid criminal charges in the case.
In a news release Thursday, police said Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, has been charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm, two counts of possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, and mischief.
Sim-Pelletier was charged on Sept. 4 and his next court appearance is scheduled for Friday, police said.
“This investigation is complex and involves numerous investigative steps that we are still diligently working to complete,” Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart, with the EPS Investigations Branch, said in the statement.
In a news conference Thursday, Stewart said the accused remains in custody in a federal institution.
Stewart said the charges against him were not announced immediately as the investigation continued. He noted that there was no concern for public safety as the accused remained in custody on a previous warrant.
He said police have been in contact with both victims in the stabbing and have confirmed they are recovering from their injuries and he thanked temple staff for being exceptionally helpful during the course of the investigation.
Stewart said police continue to investigate a possible motive,but there is no evidence to support hate crime related charges at this time.
The attack
Police said the accused, who had been released from a federal prison outside the Edmonton region the day before, entered the Nanaksar Gurdwara on Aug. 21 during morning prayers.
Police said the man entered attempted to access the prayer area when he was confronted by staff.
The victims, aged 51 and 75, were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries after the attacker was wrestled to the ground by temple attendees and arrested by patrol officers.
The violent incident inside the sprawling temple on the northeastern outskirts of the city has prompted widespread condemnation from political leaders and Sikh community advocates and raised questions about the release of federal offenders who may pose a risk to public safety.
Sikh communities have documented a rise in recent discriminatory threats and attacks.
During a news conference last month, police said the suspect had a “significant” history of violent crime dating back more than a decade.
The accused had just served a sentence for aggravated assault and assault on a peace officer.
He had been held in custody these past weeks on a warrant issued for his failure to report to his designated Edmonton halfway house in the hours before the attack.
Statutory release 'not a choice'
In her statement condemning the attack last month, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the stabbings should serve as a reminder of the need for federal bail and parole reform.
In a statement to CBC News on Aug. 24, the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) stated that the suspect had been discharged from custody on statutory release — a policy which means federal officials have little leeway over his removal from custody.
“Statutory release is not a choice or discretionary decision by CSC — it is required by law after an offender serves two-thirds of a fixed-length federal sentence, with the offender being supervised in the community under conditional release,” the statement reads.
Statutory release requires the Correctional Service of Canada to release most federal prisoners into the community under supervision.
Unlike day and full parole, statutory release is not subject to decisions by the Parole Board of Canada but inmates released under the federal policy are required to report regularly to a parole officer and remain subject to conditions.
Most offenders qualify, with the exception of those serving a life sentence or an indeterminate sentence because of a dangerous offender designation issued by the court.
'Where the chain breaks down'
Michael Spratt, an Ottawa-based criminal defence lawyer with APG LLP, told CBC News last month that statutory release laws are "very, very effective" overall, but questioned systemic enforcement when breaches occur.
When an offender breaks release conditions — such as failing to report to a halfway house — infractions are reported quickly, Spratt noted.
He said public scrutiny should focus on how fast law enforcement responds to issue warrants and apprehend individuals in breach, he said.
“The public is rightly concerned when someone does offend on statutory release or on bail," Spratt said.
"We often focus on the tragedy of the offence, but we don't focus on the police response … quite often that's where the chain breaks down.”

- Microsoft GameInput SDK 3.5 introduces a new companion helper for PS5's DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers.
- The update lets PC developers tap into DualSense features like adaptive triggers, the RGB light bar, player LEDs, and more.
- However, this does not add system-wide native support for the PS5 DualSense controller on Windows.
Microsoft has released GameInput version 3.5 on PC, introducing support for Sony’s PlayStation 5 DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers on Windows. This update lets PC developers access DualSense’s landmark features, including the RGB light bar, adaptive triggers, and more such functionalities.
Microsoft GameInput 3.5 Expands DualSense Support for PC Developers
To begin, GameInput 3.5 allows developers to tweak adaptive trigger sensitivity, weapon feedback, and vibration effects, and enable player LEDs and the microphone mute LED. This could give PC developers more opportunities to replicate the kind of DualSense integration as seen in PlayStation titles like Saros and Ghost of Yotei.
According to Microsoft GameInput’s GitHub, here’s a list of all the new controls added with the latest 3.5 version:
- Added support for Agility SDK style side-by-side deployment.
- Added support for XInput and background GIP raw device reports.
- Added companion header for PlayStation 5 DualSense features
- Updated public header and static library (lib) license to MIT.
- Fixed issues with input loss after suspend/resume on Xbox.
- Fixed missing display names for input devices on Xbox.
- Fixed PlayStation®5 DualSense Edge® input duplication for some Windows.Gaming.Input games.
- Stability and performance improvements.
Microsoft GameInput 3.5 does not add system-wide native support for the PS5 DualSense controller. Instead, developers can use Microsoft’s new companion header to communicate with the controller through GameInput and send the required output data.
For now, the implementation is built around USB-format reports, while Microsoft has not indicated that the same functionality works over Bluetooth. GameInput 3.5 also addresses the DualSense Edge’s duplicated input problem, as seen in select Windows.Gaming.Input games.
This isn’t Microsoft’s first attempt to bring DualSense functionality to GameInput. Earlier versions added advanced haptics while GameInput 3.3 introduced gyroscope support.
The 3.5 version builds on those capabilities by giving developers a dedicated helper for sending DualSense output commands to implement features such as adaptive triggers, haptics, and controller lighting in future PC games.
This should make it easier for PC developers to take advantage of the DualSense controller features. That said, Microsoft has been busy not only in the PC gaming space, but also on its own platform.

Adityanath recalls GB Pant's role in Kakori case, land reforms on 139th birth anniversary
Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Thursday paid tribute to Bharat Ratna Pandit Govind Ballabh Pant on his 139th birth anniversary, recalling his contribution to India's freedom struggle, governance, land reforms and resolution of linguistic tensions after Independence.
Adityanath and Uttar Pradesh Finance Minister Suresh Khanna attended a programme in Lucknow where floral tributes were paid to Pant, the first chief minister of Uttar Pradesh.
Describing Pant as a distinguished lawyer and freedom fighter, the CM recalled his role in defending revolutionaries prosecuted by the British government following the 1925 Kakori train action.
"In 1925, when the British government registered a case against the revolutionaries in connection with the Kakori train action, Pandit Govind Ballabh Pant was the great leader who became the revolutionaries' lawyer and fought their case with full strength," he said.
Adityanath said Pant played an active role in India's freedom movement and gave up his position as premier of the erstwhile United Provinces to participate in the struggle against British rule.
"In 1937, he was elected as the premier of Uttar Pradesh, but soon after, he resigned from his post and moved forward to fight for the freedom movement," he said.
After Independence, Pant became the first CM of Uttar Pradesh in 1947 and worked to establish a model of good governance in the large state, which at the time included present-day Uttarakhand.
"As the first CM of Uttar Pradesh, he began efforts to present the administration of such a large state as a model of good governance. He worked for its economic advancement and for the interests of every section of society," Adityanath said.
He said Pant introduced several reforms during his tenure, particularly highlighting his land reform initiatives.
"Among the many reforms he brought, the model of land reforms that he presented was particularly important," Adityanath said.
Pant later served as Union home minister, where he played a significant role in dealing with linguistic tensions and other challenges confronting the newly independent country.
"In 1954, he became the Union home minister. At that time, there were linguistic conflicts in the country and attempts were being made to create new divisions in society. He played his role with great wisdom in finding a solution to these issues," Adityanath said.
He also credited Pant with helping Hindi become the official language of the Union.
Pant was born in Almora in present-day Uttarakhand and studied law at Muir College, Allahabad University, where he was awarded the Lumsden Medal for academic excellence.
He served as premier of the United Provinces from 1937 to 1939 and became Uttar Pradesh's first chief minister after Independence, serving from 1946 to 1954. He later served as Union home minister from 1955 to 1961.
Pant was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 1957. His policy priorities as Uttar Pradesh chief minister included abolition of the zamindari system, forest conservation, women's rights, economic stability and protection of vulnerable sections.

New Delhi: India plans to bring all sterile drug products under a central licensing system, tightening oversight of injectables and other medicines, after about 240 injection samples were found to be not of standard quality in fiscal 2026, according to two officials familiar with the matter.
The proposal would shift products that are currently licensed by state authorities to the Central License Approving Authority, or CLAA, system, the official said, who didn't want to be named, citing rules. It would require amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, and is aimed at replacing a fragmented licensing system with uniform requirements for approval and inspection across the country.
About 240 injection samples were found to be not of standard quality in 2025-26, excluding other sterile dosage forms, according to a government document reviewed by Mint. It cited recent quality problems in India and abroad, including contamination reported in metoprolol injection and an adenosine injection solution.
“A centralized licensing and regulatory system for the entire country is a welcome step that will help ensure uniform manufacturing standards across the nation, without being vulnerable to individual state licensing variations,” said Dr Rajeev Jayadevan, a public health expert and former president of the Indian Medical Association’s Kochi chapter.
“These sterile products, by their very nature, require stringent adherence to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP). Any lapse in quality can have serious consequences for patient safety,” the document said.
The government’s concern is that the split can result in differences in how applications are assessed and manufacturing facilities are inspected across states. The document said the review of applications for additional products after an initial license is particularly inconsistent.
“It is proposed that all sterile drug products, irrespective of category, be brought under the CLAA scheme,” the document said. The change would expand the scope of the central licensing system and allow applications and related regulatory processes to be handled through the government’s online ONDLS portal.
The proposal comes as India seeks to strengthen confidence in the quality of medicines made for both domestic and overseas markets. India’s generic injectable market was valued at about $3 billion in 2024 and is estimated to reach $7.6 billion by 2033, according to India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF), making quality oversight increasingly important as production expands.
Queries emailed to the health and family welfare ministry, the office of the Drugs Controller General of India, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd., Cipla Ltd., Mankind Pharma Ltd. and Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. remained unanswered till press time.
Industry experts backed the move, saying stronger oversight would help raise quality standards.
“Quality is the fundamental license to operate in the pharma industry. All steps, both at the central and the state level, are in the direction to advance the quality agenda for patient care,” said Sudarshan Jain, secretary general of the Indian Pharmaceutical Alliance, which represents 23 leading pharmaceutical companies.
Medical experts said the need for tighter oversight is particularly important for sterile medicines. “Unlike a tablet or syrup taken by mouth, a medicine bygiven as an injection bypasses several of the body’s natural and powerful protective barriers,” said Dr Jayadevan.
A contaminated injection can introduce harmful material directly into the bloodstream, potentially causing severe or fatal complications, he said.
“I strongly support tighter central regulatory oversight for sterile injectable products, particularly given that these medicines are administered directly into the body and any failure in sterility or quality can have serious and potentially systemic consequences for patients," said Nikhil K Masurkar, CEO of Entod pharmaceuticals, which manufactures ophthalmology solutions.
“Eye drops are already required to comply with stringent sterility and manufacturing standards and their risk profile and route of administration are fundamentally different from injectable medicines. A risk-based regulatory framework that differentiates between sterile injectables and other sterile dosage forms would, in my view, strengthen patient safety without creating unnecessary regulatory duplication or delays for established, compliant manufacturers,” he said.

Don't buy the 'regular' AirPods 5
The first time you need to adjust volume, you’ll wish you’d spent that extra $20.
Before yesterday, I wasn't expecting new AirPods during the iPhone Duo event. When Bloomberg finally committed to an AirPods 5 prediction the morning of the show, I knew the updates would be minor at best. For various reasons, including the lack of spicy rumors, it just didn't seem like Apple had anything groundbreaking to add to its base-level AirPods lineup. As it turns out, it didn't.
I will concede that the upgrades to the model that Apple is now calling AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case are notable. And doing so for $149 when the comparable AirPods 4 model was $179 is commendable. I already know how much the swipe gestures for volume control will improve the experience. I say this as someone who constantly tries to swipe the stems of the AirPods 4 every time I wear them. I've definitely been AirPods Pro-pilled there. Live Translation is also a substantial addition, no doubt about that.
My issue isn't that the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case exist, it's that Apple is also selling the "regular" AirPods 5 for only $20 less. Sure, the most affordable model now has active noise cancellation (ANC), Live Translation and the same increased water resistance (IP57) as the new $149 set. (I'll save any arguments about 50 percent better ANC performance for my upcoming review, but on paper, that enhancement seems modest at first glance.) There simply isn't enough differentiation between the two models now to warrant the basic set's existence. And if you don't want ANC at all, the AirPods 4 are already gone from Apple's website.
Since that's the hill I'm willing to die on, I'll also argue that $20 isn't enough of a difference to make this a tough decision. Just spend the extra money for all of the added features that the new model with the extremely silly name offers. Trust me, the first time that you need to adjust the volume and swipe on a non-responsive AirPod stem, you will regret not doing so. At some point, that extra hour of battery life will likely come in handy, and it's a lot more convenient to plop an AirPods case down on a MagSafe or Apple Watch charger than to reach for a USB-C cable. You also never know when you'll wish your AirPods case had a speaker to assist with Find My search and rescue missions.
The entry point should be a regular AirPods 5 option for $99. A $50 difference makes more sense, and it was the variation between the two models in the AirPods 4 lineup. I would be totally fine with that base version not having ANC to get the price down. In fact, I'd argue Apple would have a more compelling AirPods earbud slate with the normal, non-ANC AirPods 4 at $99, the ANC AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case (which would could thankfully just call AirPods 5) at $149 and the AirPods Pro 3 at $249. Three different enough models at three different enough prices would make a trio where customers would have a decision to make. Plus, that would set things up nicely for the camera-equipped AirPods Pro that are rumored to be coming early next year.
And Apple, please, don't call them AirPods Pro 4 with Visual Intelligence.

Switzerland publishes 200-page dossier on Nazi war criminal Mengele
Swiss federal intelligence has released a 200-page dossier on Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, known as the "Angel of Death" for his horrific experiments at Auschwitz
BERLIN -- The Swiss federal intelligence service on Thursday published a 200-page dossier on the notorious Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, the German doctor known as the “Angel of Death” for conducting horrific medical experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz.
During World War II, Mengele served at the Auschwitz extermination camp in Nazi-occupied Poland, where about 1.1 million people were killed, approximately 1 million of them Jews. He became infamous for carrying out brutal medical experiments on inmates, including children, under the guise of scientific research.
After the war, Mengele obtained a Red Cross travel document under a false identity, allowing him to leave Europe. Like many former Nazi officials, he spent years in hiding in Latin America while being pursued internationally for his crimes. He drowned in 1979 while swimming on the coast of Brazil.
The documents released by Swiss authorities include material provided to police suggesting that Mengele may have returned to Switzerland after initially fleeing Germany, or may have been planning to enter the country under a false name, according to the German news agency dpa.
Historians seeking to establish whether Mengele spent time in Switzerland while being pursued as a war criminal, without Swiss authorities catching him, had long sought access to the files.
Swiss authorities had maintained that the documents should remain sealed until 2071 on security grounds and to protect individuals named in them.
Historian Gérard Wettstein successfully challenged those restrictions before the Federal Administrative Court, leading to the online publication. Some sections have been redacted to protect sources and the personal data of third parties, authorities said.
The dossier was compiled by the police service of the federal prosecutor’s office, a predecessor of Switzerland’s federal intelligence services, and transferred to the Federal Archives in 2001.

N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
- Published
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) says North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex.
The new building is said to be capable of housing up to twenty-eight centrifuge cascades, which are used to enrich uranium.
The nuclear watchdog's director, Rafael Grossi, called the continuing production of weapons-grade material a cause for "serious concern".
The IAEA also reported that Pyongyang has started operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site. These findings, drawn from satellite imagery, point to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure.
In a statement published earlier this week, Grossi said that there was a new building in Yongbyon. The agency, which was expelled by Pyongyang in 2009, does not have inspectors in North Korea but relies on satellite imagery to carry out assessments.
The IAEA had first reported on the existence of the building in June this year, according to a report released on 28 August. The report said that leader Kim Jong Un had on 3 June reportedly visited a "newly inagurated nuclear materials production factory", which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility.
Kim had then praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the IAEA report.
The IAEA also said there were indications that operations had started at another encirhment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it detailed.
The report relied on satellite imagery, open-source information, and photographs in state media.
"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," said Grossi in a statement released earlier this week.
The IAEA had said in April this year that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.
In August, South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, proposed talks with North Korea on officially ending the war between the two countries, adding that this could serve as a forum for discussing "effective ways to halt the advancement of the North's nuclear capabilities".
North Korea has yet to respond to the proposal.
North Korea declared itself a nuclear power in 2022 and vowed never to relinquish its weapons, of which it is estimated to possess dozens.
Lee previously said Pyongyang was producing 15 to 20 more warheads annually, telling the BBC last year he would back a deal between US President Donald Trump and Kim to freeze production.
