On 06 September 2026, a nearly 30-year-old five-storey building housing a boys’ PG collapsed in Delhi’s Satya Niketan area near Delhi University’s South Campus, killing seven people, including five students, while 12 people were rescued. The building was reportedly undergoing renovation work in the basement, where water had accumulated, and authorities are investigating whether this contributed to the collapse. Police arrested the building owner, Hariram, his wife, Urmila, and son, Mahesh, while the MCD suspended five South Zone officials over alleged lapses. The Delhi High Court has also ordered an audit of PGs and hostels following the incident (here, here, and here).
In the aftermath of this incident, several videos (here, here) are being shared on social media, claiming to show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan.
Fact: To sum up, none of the videos show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. The first video shows the demolition of an unauthorised building in Jasola, Delhi, while the second shows a building collapse in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
In our investigation, we found (here, here, and here) that the video is not related to the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. The video shows the MCD demolishing an unauthorised four-storey residential building in Jasola, southeast Delhi, after it began tilting dangerously.
Video 2
In our investigation, we found (here, here) that the video is from Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. The video shows the collapse of a severely dilapidated building on Jama Masjid Road, near Humsafar Marriage Hall in the Sadar tehsil area, amid incessant rainfall. According to the District Magistrate, the building had been inspected and found to be in an extremely dilapidated condition. The administration had sealed the building on 04 September 2026 and restricted movement around it as a precautionary measure. The building collapsed on 05 September 2026, but no casualties were reported as the premises had already been sealed.
To sum up, none of these visuals show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan.

All the Places Trump Was on 9/11
The president’s latest version doesn’t square with the facts.
Updated at 4:30 p.m. ET on September 9, 2026
Where were you on 9/11? Every American old enough to remember the day has an answer to that question. President Trump has several.
At a ceremony honoring first responders and victims’ families yesterday, Trump offered an elaborate account of where he was in the hours and days after nearly 3,000 Americans were killed. “I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened, and they had no hesitation; everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. Wasn’t too much we could do, I’ll be honest. It was raw—nobody had seen anything like it, ever.”
The story presents significant problems in terms of its relationship to reality. Listeners could be forgiven for interpreting Trump’s remarks as a reference to his whereabouts on the day of the attack itself. (The president clarified that timeline last night: “I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.) It is true that two days after the attack, on September 13, Trump was interviewed by reporters while walking in Lower Manhattan. The president has previously made variations of the same claim—that he and the employees he sent downtown helped clear rubble in the days following the attack. “Everyone who helped clear the rubble—and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit” was his version of it on the 2016 campaign trail. But supporting evidence is scant, and the whole account is likely an exaggeration. Richard Alles, a retired New York City Fire Department deputy chief who had a supervisory role in the efforts, said in 2019 not only that he never witnessed Trump at the site, but that the account doesn’t add up: “He was a private citizen at the time. I don’t know what kind of role he could have possibly played.” And, Alles added, if Trump had indeed sent workers, as he has claimed, there would be a record of it: “Is there a chance he was ever down there by himself and I didn’t know it? It’s possible, but I know of no one who ever witnessed him there.”
Nevertheless, Trump pressed on, veering into territory even further detached from verifiable fact. The U.S. Steel Building—a skyscraper in Lower Manhattan known today as One Liberty Plaza—was “really creaking,” Trump said at yesterday’s ceremony. “I’ll never forget: two firemen. We thought it was coming down on top of us and two firemen—big, strong guys. And I’m not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arms, said, ‘Gotta get outta here.’ And they literally lifted me up—this is not easy to do; I’m big. They lifted me up, and they started running with me. I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself.’ But they were amazing, but they thought it was coming down. It didn’t come down: U.S. Steel.”
There was, in fact, public concern in the days following the attack that the building at One Liberty Plaza could collapse. But the notion that Trump was inside the building and rushed out by firefighters has not been corroborated by any evidence. The president has offered versions of the same account before, though in less colorful form. In 2016, he told a story about being evacuated by firefighters—but in that rendition, it took place “a couple of days” after the collapse, and the U.S. Steel building was “not so far from us” when the two “massive guys” grabbed him. “I never knew I could run that fast,” he said then. In 2021, Trump likewise recalled two firemen grabbing him after hearing “creaks.”
Trump’s whereabouts on September 11 are no mystery. They are fairly well documented by his own prior statements about watching the attacks unfold from his home in Trump Tower, about four miles north of the Twin Towers. For those who have reason to doubt Trump’s statements, his whereabouts are also documented on video. “I have a window that looks directly at the World Trade Center, and I saw this huge explosion,” he said in a phone interview with a New Jersey news channel on 9/11. “For years, I’ve looked right directly at the building—I’d see the Empire State Building in the foreground and the World Trade Center in the background—and now I’m looking at absolutely nothing. It’s just gone, and it’s just hard to believe.”
Trump’s view may have been clear, but his recollection of September 11 has been murky, as reporters have tracked for more than a decade.
Sometimes, in his accounts, he watched the second plane hit the World Trade Center from his apartment in Trump Tower; when he called into the live broadcast that day, he did not mention having witnessed the second jet. Sometimes, he claims to have personally seen people jumping from the Twin Towers. “I have a window in my apartment that specifically was aimed at the World Trade Center,” he said in 2015 on the campaign trail, “and I watched as people jumped.” In his TV interview the day of the attack, he didn’t see those scenes himself but talked to someone who had. “I have somebody that was down there who witnessed at least 10 people jumping out of the building from 70 and 80 stories up in the air,” Trump said.
The president has also embellished what he saw in news coverage on that day, most notoriously claiming to have seen widespread celebrations by Muslim residents in New Jersey. “I watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down,” he said in a 2015 stump speech. “And I watched in Jersey City, New Jersey, where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down.” That claim has been thoroughly disproved. A professor who spent months combing through news reels and video archives from that day found one possible instance that could slightly resemble those events—a few Arab American teenagers who briefly gathered in front of a library in South Paterson in a way that could be seen as celebratory.
Even the live phone interview Trump participated in on the day of the attack contains inaccuracies. On the call, Trump said that one of his buildings was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan: “Forty Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan,” he said when asked whether his property had been damaged. “When they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” But as The Washington Post documented, using data from the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, neither claim was true. Forty Wall Street was the tallest building for only about two years and that was in the 1930s, before Trump was born.
At the center of yesterday’s ceremony was an important honor—one that Trump had promised to bestow months prior. Welles Crowther, who was first identified as “the man in the red bandana” in a 2002 New York Times story, rescued more than a dozen people from the South Tower before being killed when the building collapsed. His parents, who had given him a red bandana as a boy and knew that he always carried it with him, were able to recognize him by that detail and confirmed through the survivors that their son had helped them. Crowther was an equities trader and a volunteer firefighter, and he was 24 years old when he died. While posthumously awarding the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Crowther, Trump drew the focus to himself, comparing his own fame to that of the fallen hero: “The Man in the Red Bandana, he’s become more famous than me—I don’t like it. Very unhappy. But he’s become much more famous than me.”
When the president has brought up 9/11 lately, the remark has usually been severed from the attack, its victims, or its perpetrators. This year, Trump has tended to mention the day in the context of lambasting political opponents. He’s invoked it on several recent occasions—alongside World War I, World War II, and Pearl Harbor—when arguing that the attack and all three of those historical calamities are dwarfed by the danger communism poses to America today.
Critics have noted that other presidents, both Republican and Democrat, might have faced months of blowback—if not the end of their political careers—were they caught exaggerating or outright inventing aspects of their experience on one of the most catastrophic days in American history. But Trump has rarely if ever paid a real political price for misleading statements. In a second term marked by his fixation on his legacy, Trump’s relationship with history has often involved “taking bits and pieces from a grab bag and turning it into a story that’s useful to him—either politically useful, as in the case of his fabrication about Muslims celebrating 9/11, or making himself the center of a story that obviously he was not the center of 25 years ago,” Tim Naftali, a presidential historian at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs, told me. The fabrications are unlikely to stop, he said, especially as the president ages. “It doesn’t happen the same to all men in their 80s, but we may see more of this: new recollections about the past that we’ve never heard before, because they never happened,” Naftali said. The White House did not address my specific questions about the president’s most recent claims, but Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that the president “was relaying his experience of a city reeling” from the attacks.
September 11 continues to be a point of tension about what the government owed, and continues to owe, those who were most affected. The mayor’s office released more than 170,000 pages of city records this week showing that city officials misled New Yorkers about air quality following the attacks. And the health toll continues to grow; the number of 9/11 survivors receiving assistance for cancer treatment roughly tripled over the past five years, according to a Washington Post analysis of reports by the World Trade Center Health Program, which funds health care for responders and survivors. Twenty-five years later, Americans everywhere will pause to remember what the nation lost that day—both those who suffered directly and those who lived through it by watching the tragedy unfold from the safety of their homes, much as Trump did.
This article originally stated that Welles Crowther was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor. In fact, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special.
The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be
Android foldables have done most of this before, but rarely looked so good doing it.
If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design.
More has been made of Apple’s efforts to eliminate the foldable display’s crease, which seem to have been largely successful. Apple attributes it to a 100-component hinge, custom adhesives that allow the display layers to “glide” over one another, and a matte finish that reduces glare and reflections to make the crease harder to spot. Trying the phone at Apple’s event yesterday, Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel said that you can’t really see the crease, but that “if you go looking for it, you can definitely feel one.”
It sounds, and looks, impressive, but Apple is far from the first to do it. Samsung made great strides in eliminating the crease on its Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to new titanium display layers. Before that, Oppo all but eliminated its Find N6 crease by using 3D printing to fill the minute gaps across the hinge. I’d have to see all those phones side by side to see which crease is subtlest, but even if Apple does win, it won’t be by much.
None of the iPhone Duo’s other standout hardware features are true firsts either. Google beat it to an IP68 rating, now even surpassed by Honor’s IP69. Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have all offered stylus support before — though Samsung has since dropped it. Samsung also moved on from the under-display selfie camera, which has always been hamstrung by poor photo and video quality and a distractingly visible patch on the screen.
In other ways, the hardware even feels behind the competition. The Duo is the thickest of this new wave of wide foldables, though at 5.2mm when open it’s still thinner than the iPhone Air. The weight is a more obvious issue: The 254g Duo is 26 percent heavier than the Z Fold 8 — a 53g difference — which is going to be pretty noticeable. You have to go back to 2022’s Z Fold 4 to find a Samsung foldable that’s heavier, TriFold excluded.
There’s also no evidence that Apple has adopted silicon-carbon batteries yet, which have allowed Samsung, Motorola, and other Android manufacturers to fit bigger capacities into the smaller spaces of foldable phones. Apple says the phone should still deliver a full 24 hours of regular use, but Honor’s Magic V6 uses silicon-carbon to deliver two days of life.
The rear cameras are pretty basic too, with a pair of 48-megapixel shooters and no telephoto. That’s almost an exact match for the cameras on the Z Fold 8, but Google, Motorola, Xiaomi and others are now providing capable triple cameras across their foldable lines, and the iPhone Duo already lags behind.
It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them
None of this is to say that the Duo looks like a bad piece of hardware. Every foldable phone is a compromise, and Apple has picked a similar set of compromises to Samsung in order to get this phone out the door at $1,999. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them.
Where that might change is the software. Google has made an effort to make Android more flexible and adaptable to suit folding phones, while OEMs deliver custom solutions to push things further, but none have rewritten the rulebook quite like Apple.
The version of iOS 27 running on the iPhone Duo isn’t the same as on other iPhones, but it doesn’t match the iPad either. The biggest change takes the dock from the bottom of the display and lays it out vertically along the right-hand side. The Dynamic Island is turned vertical and thrown in here too, while the status bar collapses into a small circular icon in the top-right corner. This big change is bolstered by clever little touches throughout, like a dynamic blur effect that shifts as you open the screen, creating a fluidity no Android foldable has so far matched. It’s a total transformation of the iOS layout that specifically has foldables in mind.
The point of all that change is to ensure consistency between the outer and inner screens. Open the iPhone Duo on the homescreen and almost everything will stay in place, making the move between screens feel seamless. That effect won’t hold in full-screen apps of course, which will adapt to fill the space, but that right-hand UI rail will be fixed. Locking the whole phone interface to the right-hand edge doesn’t sound great for left-handed users though, who are likely to find the Duo unusually awkward to use unless Apple adds the option to flip everything to the other side.
StandBy mode has also been retooled for the Duo. Prop the phone down half-open and it will enter StandBy, letting you use it as a digital photo frame, smart display, or just get quick access to a few key widgets, like the clock. Finally, the $2,000 alarm clock you’ve always dreamed of.
Not everything is as ambitious. Multitasking looks limited so far, with the option to run two apps in split-screen, including two windows of the same app, and save pairs to reopen together. Android rivals offer similar, but support three split-screen apps at once, and often more sitting in flexible, resizeable floating windows.
But Apple’s software power doesn’t only lie in its OS. It’s the only phone manufacturer with the influence to shift the app ecosystem at large, and with the Duo it hopes to push third-party developers to adopt its best foldable features. It already showed off Netflix, Slack, and Zoom apps with custom Duo support, in some cases adapting dynamically depending on how flexed the hinge is.
Android foldable features are still rare, with most apps simply changing size to fit the varying screens. Even that has its limits — I found a few apps ran awkwardly on the Fold 8’s short outer display. Apple is likely to have an easier time ensuring developers optimize their apps to suit both of the Duo’s displays.
Most apps do little else to take advantage of dual displays, multiple cameras, or semi-open states like a tented mode. A few video apps adapt their playback controls when foldables are half-open, but that’s about it so far. Of course, some of those app developers might take their iOS foldable features and eventually roll them out to Android too, so Apple’s advantage might not last forever.
It’ll take more time with the Duo to see exactly how it stacks up against the latest models from the Android side of life. So far it doesn’t look like Apple has surpassed its rivals on the hardware side, but its total control of software may give it an edge regardless.

Hong Kong court convicts publisher of deterring reporter from taking union role
A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal of deterring its reporter from taking up a trade union role
HONG KONG -- A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal of deterring its reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The court acquitted Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. of the charge of dismissal over the union role.
Former WSJ reporter Selina Cheng, also chairperson of the trade union Hong Kong Journalists Association, launched a private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. after losing her job in July 2024.
Hong Kong, once considered a bastion of press freedom in Asia, has seen its media landscape change drastically in recent years, including the forced closure of news outlets and the prosecution of newsroom leaders.
Principal Magistrate David Cheung convicted the defendant of the first charge but said the defense has raised sufficient reasonable doubt for the second charge.
Cheng earlier said her supervisor told her that her participation in the union election was problematic and that the supervisor needed to discuss the issue with the Journal management in New York and Dow Jones’ in-house lawyers. Cheng said she was told that her union role would be incompatible with her employment.
Dow Jones pleaded not guilty last year to two charges under the city’s Employment Ordinance, each carrying a maximum fine of 100,000 Hong Kong dollars (about $12,750). The first charge alleges the company had prevented or deterred Cheng from exercising union participation rights. The second alleges the company terminated her employment for exercising those rights.
During the trial, the defense tried to convince the court that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and argued the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defense also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.
Cheng’s termination in 2024 alarmed many journalists, especially given that foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets in Hong Kong.
After Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020, two local news outlets known for critical coverage of the government, Apple Daily and Stand News, were forced to shut down following the arrest of their senior management.
Jimmy Lai, founder of Apple Daily, was sentenced to 20 years in prison in February. His staffers received prison terms ranging from six years and nine months, to 10 years.
Hong Kong, a former British colony returned to Chinese rule in 1997, ranked 140th out of 180 countries and territories in Reporters Without Borders’ latest World Press Freedom Index, down from 18th out of 139 regions in 2002.

Don’t appease One Nation on migration, Malinauskas warns
The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has iwarned the Albanese government not to join the “madness” of cutting migration to appease One Nation.
In a speech in Sydney last night, Malinauskas – whose grandparents migrated to Australia after the second world war – said the wave of populist politics has “more than arrived in Australia”, but the government should push back.
Above all else, [we must] preserve our strong migration program … The correct political response to anti-immigration politics and populists is not appeasement.
More troubling is the prospect of mainstream politics entering a political race to the bottom for who can cut migration numbers the most. This is not unfortunate – this is madness.
There could be no greater act of national economic self harm at this time than to slash migration numbers for political purposes.
He also warns against cutting international student numbers, calling it “crazy”.
Imagine if we did this to the mining industry, there world be an ad on every television station and mobile phone about how we’re killing the goose that lays the golden egg. It is crazy.
‘We need to explain Australia doesn’t have a migration crisis’: Malinauskas
Peter Malinaukas says he understands the concerns of Australians worried about migration and the housing shortage in Australia, but that the answer is politicians need to explain there is a housing crisis not a migration crisis happening.
He tells the ABC’s AM program that Australia will soon have more people over 65 than under 15 and migration will be essential to replace the ageing workforce.
We need to explain that Australia doesn’t really have a migration crisis so much as a housing crisis. If we have a housing crisis, we would do well to focus our skills policy on making sure that we’re bringing in the very workers that we require in the housing construction industry. You know, Australia’s got a massive shortage of almost every trade.
Everyone, I think, accepts that it needs to be a well-calibrated, balanced migration program. My point is that we haven’t seen much evidence in the political discourse in this country in the last few years making the case for migration. Just to be seeing be a lot of culture wars being executed against migration. And I think that’s self-defeating, and we’ve got a responsibility to stand up against it.
But when asked what the magic number is for a well-balanced migration program, Malinauskas won’t say.
Instead of coming up with an arbitrary number and then cutting different parts of the migration program, Malinaukas says governments should work from the ground up, determining the skills shortages, and growth in regional areas, and then coming up with a target.

In Victoria a car is stolen or broken into every 43 minutes: data
Melbourne recorded more insurance claims for stolen and broken-into cars than all other Australian capital cities combined, according to the Insurance Council of Australia.
Property crime data released by the ICA showed Victoria had the highest rates of car theft and home burglary claims in the country in the last financial year. Analysis of Insurance Statistics Australia (ISA) data showed that there were more than 12,300 claims – costing insurers $244m – lodged in the state for cars stolen or broken into.
In the same time period, every other state and territory recorded a decline.
The ICA’s chief executive, Andrew Hall, said in Victoria a car was stolen or broken into every 43 minutes while a home is broken into every two hours.
The insurance data shows Victoria has a crime problem, and it is being felt directly by households, businesses and communities.
The ICA has called for a statewide strategy and better intelligence sharing, the establishment of centrally coordinated clean-up arrangements, and the abolishment of stamp duty on business, home and contents insurance products.
It also called for improving insurance affordability for healthcare professionals, community organisations and live music venues by “modernising civil liability laws”.

Australia should ‘put shoulder to the wheel’ on multilateral diplomacy: Rudd
Tom McIlroy
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd is in Canberra for a round of high-profile speeches this week, marking his return to Australia after serving as ambassador to Washington DC.
Rudd spoke at the Australian Institute of International Affairs on Wednesday night and will be at the National Press Club today.
He said Australia must continue to push multilateral diplomacy, even as Donald Trump withdraws the US from a range of important global institutions. Australia, as a leading middle power, should promote the United Nations system, which has support across Asia and Europe, according to Rudd.
There remains an opportunity for Australia, in partnership with other middle powers around the world, to put our shoulders to the wheel in supporting those UN multilateral institutions which now find themselves under financial and institutional pressure as a result of the US withdrawing.
Australia remains active in the UN, the IMF and the World Bank. We remain active in the G20 and in APEC.
We remain active in major regional institutions, such as the Pacific Islands Forum, where the government has once again registered a remarkable series of foreign policy achievements.
Rudd said this kind of serious engagement would “put flesh on the bones” of the plan outlined by the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at Davos earlier this year.
And it would mark a deeply practical contribution to sustaining the multilateral rules-based system as America resolves its internal domestic debate on its future posture within it.

The MAGA Movement Is Splintering Without Charlie Kirk
A year of feuds among MAGA figures shows how much the movement depended on Kirk personally.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
When Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, many of his allies on the right memorialized him as a hero of free speech and the founder of an enduring political movement. Critics on the left tended to emphasize his long history of offensive remarks and dismiss him as little more than a troll.
With a year of distance, neither view appears complete. Since his death, the MAGA movement has stumbled: Its factions are bickering, and Republicans are facing potentially disastrous midterm elections. President Trump seems disconnected from his base and reality. The current plight points to Kirk’s rare ability as a political node, someone who united otherwise disparate forces under one umbrella—and also to how much the movement depended on Kirk personally.
Just how fragile a peace Kirk had managed to keep became clear three months after his killing, at an annual conference of Turning Point USA, the organization he’d co-founded. At the summit, feuding parties each tried to claim Kirk’s endorsement of their views. Ben Shapiro, the Daily Wire impresario, used the occasion to blast the broadcaster Tucker Carlson for conducting softball interviews with anti-Semites and other white supremacists. Citing Kirk’s stiff-arming of the Hitler-admiring influencer Nick Fuentes, whose followers were sometimes ejected from Turning Point events, Shapiro assailed Carlson for giving Fuentes a platform. Carlson mounted a counterattack in that evening’s keynote speech, arguing that it was Shapiro who was betraying Kirk’s commitment to open debate.
These conflicts among leading right-wing figures have continued ever since. Kirk’s widow, Erika, now leads Turning Point and is well-regarded, but she does not seem to have the muscle that her husband did to quell conflicts. Carlson has become a furious critic of Trump and has vowed to create a rival political movement (although his ability to follow through is in question). Candace Owens, another prominent media personality, has become a proponent of conspiracy theories about Kirk’s death and has baselessly suggested at various times that the Israeli or French governments or “Egyptians” were involved. Fuentes has become a more influential commentator, but overall, MAGA media figures are seeing splintering audiences.
No movement leader is as important as Trump, but the president has also had a tumultuous year. He is obsessed with building a ballroom at the White House—in part as a legacy project, but also perhaps because Kirk’s assassination and the attempts on his own life have instilled an understandable sense of paranoia that makes having a secure space at his residence feel imperative. As Trump has become more cloistered and withdrawn from public appearances, he has lost touch with his base, and he is pursuing an unpopular long-term war in Iran that betrays his campaign platform and writing off voters’ concerns about the economy and inflation.
These dynamics, along with the natural pendulum swing against the sitting president’s party in midterm elections, mean that Republicans have bleak expectations for November. Not only are Democrats leading in polls of the generic House ballot and gaining in several Senate forecasts, but GOP voters are less enthusiastic than their Democratic counterparts. The problems are particularly acute among young voters. Although that group is typically heavily Democratic, Trump nearly matched Kamala Harris’s showing with the demographic in 2024, for which Turning Point received a great deal of credit. Today, however, young voters disapprove of Trump by wide margins—even greater than the general population. Young people who voted for Trump are also more likely to regret their vote than older ones, a recent Navigator poll found. Young men have turned against the president more than almost any other group has.
What’s notable is that this drop in support and enthusiasm for Trump and Republicans comes at the same time that Turning Point is growing. As Reuters reported today, the organization has expanded since Kirk’s death, especially on campuses, but the people flocking to these chapters aren’t uniformly loyal to Trump. Turning Point could yet be an important presence in the midterms. The group was central to the Trump campaign’s plan for voter turnout in the 2024 election, helping deliver the president his first popular-vote victory among his three tries. Wired reports that Turning Point once again plans to spend large sums on field operations from now until the midterms.
Kirk’s legacy on free speech and debate also remains up for grabs. As I wrote shortly after the assassination, an ironic phenomenon was emerging in which Kirk was being praised for his commitment to open discourse at the same time that right-wing figures were attempting to stifle any criticism of him. Some professors who were fired or punished in that period have since been reinstated or paid damages, but Trump and his allies have abandoned even a perfunctory commitment to free speech.
Many of the tensions on display today have always been present in the MAGA movement. Trumpism is a big tent; it includes populists and plutocrats, isolationists and interventionists, and a dozen more dyads. The seams would inevitably have become visible at some point, but in retrospect, Kirk appears to have helped stave that off by maintaining connections across many factions and the sway to keep figures such as Fuentes outside. In his absence, the conflicts have come into the open.

Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman has faced intense criticism from Democratic Party figures and progressive activists after making a surprise virtual appearance at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas.
The Democratic senator used the video address to praise his Republican counterpart, Senator Dave McCormick, and signal his willingness to work with US President Donald Trump on industrial policy. The move triggered an immediate backlash within his own party, according to a report by The Hill.
Fetterman delivered the approximately one-minute address virtually while standing outside a major steel-processing facility in Pittsburgh. Wearing his trademark casual clothing, he described himself as a “common sense Democrat” and sought to distance himself from what he characterised as the extremes within his party.
He also praised McCormick as a close friend and said he intended to work to protect the US steel industry alongside Trump.
Fetterman’s appearance was greeted enthusiastically by conservative delegates at the convention. His willingness to praise a Republican senator and express support for working with Trump was viewed by attendees as evidence of bipartisan cooperation.
Within Democratic circles, however, the reaction was sharply different.
Party leaders and progressive activists quickly condemned the senator's decision to appear at the Republican gathering. Some of the strongest criticism came from Pennsylvania state Representative Malcolm Kenyatta, who issued a particularly harsh rebuke of Fetterman's address.
According to statements published by news agencies, Kenyatta remarked, “John Fetterman is the laziest Benedict Arnold America has ever seen. He didn’t even have it in him to get off his couch in his million-dollar penthouse to kiss Donald Trump’s ring in person. He phoned it in, just as he has every day as our senator. John should do his job or resign.”
Political analysts and commentators have also questioned whether Fetterman's increasingly independent positioning reflects the priorities of the voters who sent him to the US Senate.
The controversy has highlighted broader tensions within the Democratic Party as it attempts to preserve its coalition ahead of the crucial 2026 midterm elections.
With control of the US Senate expected to be closely contested, strategists are examining whether Fetterman's increasingly conservative rhetoric could further distance him from Democratic voters or create problems for the party's efforts to retain or expand its Senate numbers.
Fetterman's supporters argue that reaching beyond the traditional Democratic base and appealing to independent and cross-party voters can be crucial in politically competitive states such as Pennsylvania.
Critics, however, say publicly embracing Republican politicians and echoing elements of the Trump administration's message could weaken Democratic unity and undermine the party's broader legislative strategy.
The dispute reflects a larger debate within the Democratic Party over how far its candidates should move toward the political centre as they seek to compete in battleground states.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): To modernise the state’s public passenger transport system into a secure, smooth, and eco-friendly network, Chief Minister Mohan Yadav will inaugurate the two-day 'Yatri Transport Vision Summit-2026' on Friday at the Brilliant Convention Centre.
Transport and school education minister Uday Pratap Singh will also attend the event, where private bus operators, policymakers, transport experts, state transport undertakings (STUs), and tech leaders will gather to brainstorm.
Organised under the theme 'New Thinking, New Path, New Madhya Pradesh,' the summit aims to accelerate a public-private partnership (PPP) model, advanced IT infrastructure, and a green mobility ecosystem through the Madhya Pradesh Passenger Transport and Infrastructure Limited (MPYPIL).
During the summit, CM Yadav will oversee several major inaugurations and releases, including an Industry Expo, the MPYPIL logo and booklet launch, a Summit Souvenir, and a Mobility Hackathon.
Industry giants and technical experts to join
The summit will gather private bus operators, policymakers, transport experts, state transport undertakings (STUs), and tech leaders. Participating industry players include Tata Motors, EKA Mobility, Volvo-Eicher, Switch Mobility, Greencell Mobility, Rapido, Chalo Mobility, Amnex, IOCL, and SBI. Key institutions and think tanks, such as WRI India, BITS Pilani, CEPT Ahmedabad, KPMG, and DIMTS, will also contribute technical guidance.
Eight sessions to shape policies
The conference will feature eight dedicated sessions to shape future policy actions. The session topics include: MP Mobility Vision 2030, Future-Ready Infrastructure, Financial Viability, Employment & Entrepreneurship, Safety and Reliability, Data-Driven Operations, Green Mobility, and Integrated Ticketing ('One State, One Journey').

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!
Yesterday’s Massive Student Protest Delivered The Final Verdict:
Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.
ALSO READ: The fictional strikes on the Karachi port and what it says about Indian media
A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.
Check the thumbnails in the compilations from 2022 below. Each and every bulletin represented by these thumbnails was on communal issues. All on News 18:
Hosted by Aman Chopra:
Shows hosted by Amish Devgan:
The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.
"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.
He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the party's first-ever midterm election convention, when the balance of power could change in the US government.
Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran. On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East.
"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."
He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".
He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons.
At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".
In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".
Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".
The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from fuel to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings - and pressure from those within his party, including devout supporters, to quickly end the war.
Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing their control on Congress.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Aitchison is one of five changes to the England team that beat France in Bordeaux last time out.
Scrum-half Natasha Hunt makes her comeback from a knee ligament injury that has kept her out of action since the win over Ireland in April, while fellow World Cup winner Tatyana Heard makes her first Test appearance of the year after recovering from a foot injury.
May Campbell, whose five previous England appearances have come off the bench, makes her first Test start with resources stretched thin at hooker.
Amy Cokayne will miss the match through injury and Connie Powell is recovering from ankle surgery, while Lark Atkin-Davies is on maternity leave having had a daughter in June.
Their absences mean back-up hooker Bryony Field, who plays alongside Campbell at Saracens, is set to win her first senior England cap from the bench, where Hannah Botterman, who has not featured since 2025's World Cup final win, and Morwenna Talling are primed to make returns from injury.
Gloucester-Hartpury's Mia Venner, who finished joint top of last season's PWR try-scoring charts, come in on the wing.

IM Aswath S completed the requirements to become India’s 98th Grandmaster after scoring his third and final GM norm at the Pune International Grandmaster Round Robin Tournament on Wednesday.
The 17-year-old from Nagercoil needed to win his final-round game and did exactly that, beating FM Kannan Vaidyanathan with the black pieces to finish the tournament with 7/9 points. His title push came in a period of rapid growth for Indian chess, with Harshavardhan G.B. having become the country’s 97th GM shortly before him.
India’s Grandmaster story began with Viswanathan Anand in 1988. Nearly four decades later, the country is now two short of the 100-GM mark, with Tamil Nadu continuing to produce the largest share of India’s elite chess players (35).
Here’s a look at the 98 Grandmasters India has so far:
1. Viswanathan Anand, 1988: This is where the Indian GM story starts. Anand became the country’s first Grandmaster and later carried Indian chess into the world elite.
2. Dibyendu Barua, 1991: Barua became India’s second Grandmaster, three years after Anand, and the title was a big moment for Bengal chess as well.
3. Praveen Thipsay, 1997: Thipsay was later recognised more for his coaching and analysis.
4. Abhijit Kunte, 2000: Kunte was one of the early names from Maharashtra on India’s GM list.
5. Krishnan Sasikiran, 2000: Sasikiran was one of the strongest players after Anand’s generation paved the way. He became a regular part of Indian teams.
6. Pentala Harikrishna, 2001: Harikrishna was among the first Indians after Anand to become a long-term elite player. He later crossed 2700 and stayed around the top level for years.
7. Koneru Humpy, 2002: Humpy became India’s first woman to become a Grandmaster. She has been one of the biggest names in women’s chess for more than two decades.
8. Surya Shekhar Ganguly, 2003: Ganguly added another strong name to Bengal’s chess tradition.
9. Sandipan Chanda, 2003: Chanda was part of the early-2000s batch that made the Indian GM list grow faster.
10. R.B. Ramesh, 2003: Ramesh earned the GM title as a player, but is better known as one of India’s most important coaches, training R, Praggnanandhaa and R. Vaishali.
11. Tejas Bakre, 2004: Bakre became Gujarat’s first Grandmaster.
12. Magesh Chandran Panchanathan, 2006: Magesh Chandran was part of the Tamil Nadu group that continued to add depth to Indian chess.
13. J. Deepan Chakkravarthy, 2006: Deepan Chakkravarthy’s title added to Tamil Nadu’s growing chess strength.
14. Neelotpal Das, 2006: Neelotpal Das became another Grandmaster from Bengal. His title came in the same period when Bengal had a good run of strong players.
15. Parimarjan Negi, 2006: Negi was one of India’s first big teenage GM stories. He became a Grandmaster at 13, before later moving away from full-time chess.
16. G.N. Gopal, 2007: Gopal became Kerala’s first Grandmaster. It was an important moment for chess outside India’s more established centres.
17. Abhijeet Gupta, 2008: Abhijeet was one of India’s strongest young players at that time.
18. Subramanian Arun Prasad, 2008: Arun Prasad was another Tamil Nadu player to make the GM list. He has been a regular in the Indian tournament circuit.
19. Sundararajan Kidambi, 2009: Kidambi is known not just as a player, but also as a chess thinker and writer.
20. R.R. Laxman, 2009: Laxman added another Tamil Nadu name to the list.
21. Sriram Jha, 2010: Sriram Jha was one of the experienced Indian players to reach the GM title. He later worked in coaching players as well.
22. Deep Sengupta, 2010: Deep Sengupta became another strong Grandmaster from Bengal.
23. Baskaran Adhiban, 2010: Adhiban became a Grandmaster and crossed 2700; he was known for his fearless style of play.
24. S.P. Sethuraman, 2011: Sethuraman became another Grandmaster from Tamil Nadu. He has also won the national title.
25. Harika Dronavalli, 2011: Harika became India’s second woman to become a Grandmaster. She has been one of the most consistent Indian players in women’s chess.
26. M.R. Lalith Babu, 2012: Lalith Babu had been a strong player in the Indian circuit for years.
27. Vaibhav Suri, 2012: Suri was one of the Delhi players to join the GM list. He has been part of India’s strong open-tournament generation.
28. M.R. Venkatesh, 2012: Venkatesh is another Grandmaster from Tamil Nadu. He has been active both as a player and mentor.
29. Sahaj Grover, 2012: Grover was a strong junior before completing the GM title. He was one of the notable Delhi names of that period.

Trump faces accusations of bribery after promising to pay Americans $5,000 each if Republicans win midterms
The president offered few details of the plan but said the money would have to be spent in America
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration would pay a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” to each American adult if voters help Republicans keep their congressional majority through the 2026 midterms.
“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said of the plan during his speech at the Republican midterm convention in Texas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”
The president offered few details of the plan, but he said the funds would have to be spent in America. He argued the checks would be a reflection of the country’s economic success under the Trump administration and the funds collected as a result of the president’s tariffs.
The Republican called the offer the “best part” of his much-anticipated convention speech, and he compared the payout to the administration’s $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” checks for American military service members.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
Commentators accused the president of attempting to bribe voters to back Republicans, who are forecast to suffer heavy losses in November.
In a post on X, reporter Sam Stein accused the president of describing “openly bribing people to vote for Republicans.”
Such a plan would likely cost more than $1 trillion.
Trump has repeatedly floated sending money to Americans under various payment plans, only for the funds to never materialize.
On the campaign trail, the Republican said the government or insurers would be mandated to pay “all costs” associated with in vitro fertilization, though no such program has been instituted.
Similarly, the president endorsed a proposal to return 20 percent of the savings from the White House’s DOGE cost-cutting program to Americans through checks as high as $5,000, but that plan didn’t pan out either.
There have also been substantial delays in refunding U.S. businesses that paid Trump administration tariffs that were later struck down by the Supreme Court.
Direct payments to Americans have occurred in the past. During the depths of the Covid era, the federal government and state governments sent payments to U.S. citizens to offset the economic difficulties of the pandemic.
Trump ally Elon Musk faced allegations of vote-buying during the 2024 election, which he denied.
During the presidential race, Musk, a prominent Trump surrogate, carried out a $1 million-per-day sweepstakes for voters who signed a petition supporting the U.S. Constitution. Critics said the scheme was a thinly veiled attempt to buy a Trump win.
In June, a federal judge ordered Musk to testify about the giveaway in the face of proposed class-action lawsuits.
