Meta has launched its new Muse assistant, marking the company’s first real foray into AI-powered productivity tools. The company says its AI agent can “take the busywork off your plate” by helping you with online shopping, emails, trip-planning, and more. I decided to try out the new tool and see how well it performed — especially from a company that previously prioritized entertainment over productivity. Though the AI assistant generally worked as I expected it to, the unnerving amount of information it autonomously gleaned about me largely overshadowed my experience.
Meta’s Muse AI works and creeps me out
Muse rattled off very specific interests linked to my Instagram account.
One of the first tasks I assigned Muse, which carries out actions using a cloud-based virtual computer, was to sort through my Gmail inbox and delete messages I don’t need. That required me to connect Muse to my Google account and give it permission to access, read, and delete emails. The process didn’t go smoothly on mobile; the Google sign-in screen kept glitching and returning me to the Muse website instead of the app. I eventually got it working on my laptop, where it deleted thousands of promotional emails and updates. I didn’t feel good about permitting Muse to view all of my emails given Meta’s track record on privacy over the years.
Meta says it designed Muse to only exchange data with third-party apps “that’s needed for them to work for you.” The company also says that it doesn’t share your information with advertisers. I still felt uneasy, but I pushed on anyway, linking my Amazon account to Muse. I asked the AI agent to pick out workout tops for me based on a specific size, style, and colors. Before placing the order, Muse noticed I had other items in my cart and asked if I wanted to remove them. The consideration pleasantly surprised me. Once I signed off on the purchase, it proceeded to successfully buy only the tank tops.
Shifting gears, I tried out some of Muse’s other capabilities, which allow it to generate AI podcasts similar to Gemini Notebook, create images and videos, as well as develop interactive webpages or documents called “artifacts.” Muse denied my requests to generate images of a “cartoon mouse with red pants” and a “cartoon guy with a red hat, blue overalls, brown hair, and a mustache.
However, it readily generated a video and several images of a product launch event featuring devices with Apple’s logo when asked. In one image, Muse created what looks like an iPhone-like foldable, an Apple Watch, and AirPods. Each device is propped up on a stand with Apple’s logo on it, while a presenter stands in front of a backdrop plastered with the company’s recognizable bitten apple. The phone even included Apple’s native app icons on the fake iPhone, though it hallucinated and named the App Store “Photos,” while calling Maps, Music, and the actual Photos app “Calender.” Muse refused to generate an image of an “Apple CEO.”
Then things got weird. I tapped over to the “Feed” tab, where Muse generates a news feed of sorts based on a text prompt. I submitted the prompt that Meta includes by default: “Make me a feed about my interests. Keep the tone clear and direct. Ensure it is quick to skim. Try to avoid clickbait.” It returned several AI-generated summaries of current events, including blurbs about Apple’s iPhone Duo launch event, the dangerous surf hitting California’s coast, and tankers destroyed in the Iran war. The app also listed several news stories from the state where I’m currently visiting my family, which Muse admitted it pulled from the shipping address on my Amazon order.
I dove deeper from there and asked Muse what else it might know about me based on the Instagram and Facebook accounts I signed up to use the AI agent with. It rattled off my very specific interests, ranging from anime and CrossFit to Labrador retrievers, Florida wildlife, and ’90s/2000s nostalgia — many of the same topics that frequently pop up in my Instagram Reels feed.
Curious, I asked Muse to tell me where it got that information. “Honestly, Instagram doesn’t show you that exact list anywhere in the app — I read it through the account’s API data, which surfaces more than the UI does,” Muse wrote. “The closest thing you can see yourself is your ad topics… That shows the topics advertisers can target you with, and you can remove ones you don’t want or choose to see less of them.” I checked the “Ad topics” list in my Instagram settings menu, and while it does include some vague categories, like workouts, music, and electronics, it’s not the same level of detail that Muse provided. The Verge reached out to Meta about the data Muse can access inside Instagram and Facebook but didn’t immediately hear back.
Like some of the other agentic AI tools I’ve tried out, Muse does a decent job at performing low-stakes tasks. I also like that it generates a running list of “ideas” that give personalized suggestions on how to use the tool, like providing side-by-side comparisons of products, finding and cancelling forgotten subscriptions, and keeping track of the next release of Pokémon cards. Muse keeps a running list of “goals” to complete based on your conversations with the AI agent, too.
Muse delivered on its promise of handling life’s more mundane tasks in the background, but the level of personal details Muse scooped up from sources unavailable even to me was enough to leave me with an uneasy feeling about letting Muse sort through personal emails and handle my credit card. That level of suspicion is going to be the real hurdle for Meta to overcome.

Primark will offer home delivery in Great Britain for the first time as the fast-fashion retailer seeks to revive flagging sales.
The company, which already offers a click and collect service, has long avoided home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders.
However, the clothing chain, which will spin off from its owner Associated British Foods (ABF) next year, disclosed on Thursday that it had acquired an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield and would offer home delivery “in the future” in the UK, except for Northern Ireland.
“Primark’s digital maturity, including the success of click and collect, and online market developments, mean there is now the opportunity for profitable growth through the home delivery channel,” it said in a statement.
The push into home delivery came as the company told investors that it expected Primark’s sales to drop 3% in its quarter ended on 12 September, with the UK and Ireland up 0.4% but continental Europe down 4.3%.
George Weston, the chief executive of ABF, said Primark’s trading in Europe “remained challenging”, but the initial customer reaction to its “iconic value” campaign – in which it cut prices across hundreds of autumn and winter products – had been encouraging.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at the broker AJ Bell, said Primark, faced with slowing sales, “clearly had no choice but to adapt to the modern retail world” and adopt online delivery.
Shares in ABF, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, fell by almost 10% on Thursday, taking its year-to-date fall to 14%.
Analysts at the broker Jefferies, an investment bank, said Primark looked particularly vulnerable as it started its final quarter of the year.
“In an environment with rising concerns over both the health of the consumer and of industry input cost challenges, Primark continues to be among the most disadvantageously positioned clothing retailers,” they said.
The news comes as Primark prepares to split from its parent company ABF, the owner of Twinings tea and Kingsmill bread. The demerger, which is likely to complete in December 2027, is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9bn, and the food business £4bn.
Weston, a member of the billionaire family that controls ABF and who is the long-term chief executive of the group, is to lead the food business after the demerger.
Eoin Tonge, an experienced former ABF, Marks & Spencer and Greencore finance director, will remain as chief executive of Primark.
The fashion chain, which was founded by Arthur Ryan under its Irish brand name, Penneys, in Dublin in 1969, opened its first shop in Britain in 1974, in Derby. It employs more than 80,000 people around the world.

Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
- Published
Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.
A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg.
"We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government.
"All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."
The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.
Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.
At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.
Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling.
The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.
While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.
There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.
But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.
Sharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.
Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.
The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.
At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.
A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.
Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng.
"The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.
Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest.
"[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."
Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.
Another survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.
Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself.
"We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says.
"People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them.
"Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."
It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.
The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.
Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.
The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.
Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.
But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994.
"Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.
Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive.
"Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.
Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past".
"Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen.
"So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.
But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".
The TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.
But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.
The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.
When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.
For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma.
"Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng.
"Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

Mohammed Kounain Quraishi on Thursday scored a century on day five of the Duleep Trophy final for East Zone against South Zone in Chennai.

LinkedIn beat two lawsuits over its practice of scanning users’ browser extensions, with a judge granting the Microsoft subsidiary’s motion to dismiss the cases. The users who sued LinkedIn failed to adequately allege that they have standing to sue because neither asserted that they “had browser extensions installed that conveyed private information to LinkedIn,” ruled Judge Vince Chhabria in US District Court for the Northern District of California.
In his ruling on Tuesday, Chhabria gave the plaintiffs leave to amend their complaints but said he doubts they can make a plausible case. “Given LinkedIn’s further arguments that users voluntarily download browser extensions, which by their nature intentionally expose data to websites, it seems unlikely that the plaintiffs will ever be able to allege a privacy violation, much less prevail at the end of the day,” Chhabria wrote.
California residents Nicholas Farrell and Jeff Ganan separately filed class actions against LinkedIn in April, seeking to represent themselves and other LinkedIn users. Ganan’s attorney, J.R. Howell, said he is evaluating whether to bring the claims in a California state court, which has different requirements on standing, or to appeal the US district court ruling in the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.
“The federal court determined that it lacked jurisdiction to hear the LinkedIn users’ claims,” Howell told Ars today. “The court did not adjudicate whether LinkedIn’s surveillance practices were lawful. The ruling is not a vindication of the mass surveillance program alleged in our complaint.”
“BrowserGate” stems from dispute over scraping
As we wrote in April, the plaintiffs filed their lawsuits after a report alleged that “LinkedIn Is illegally searching your computer.” LinkedIn did not deny that it scans browsers to identify extensions and already disclosed in its privacy policy that it uses cookies and similar technologies to collect information about each user’s “web browser and add-ons.”
The so-called “BrowserGate” report was issued by a German entity called Fairlinked, which describes itself as a trade association and advocacy group for commercial LinkedIn users. It appeared to be run by the same people behind Teamfluence, an Estonian software company that sued LinkedIn in Munich after its CEO was banned by LinkedIn.

NAIROBI – In a school for the deaf in Kenya, children signed their excitement as a team demonstrated how a robotic arm could revolutionize their studies.
Roughly 300,000 children in the east African nation are deaf or hard of hearing, according to the Kenya Society for Deaf Children, but just 20,000 were enrolled in schools as of 2024.
Kenyan startup ZeroBionic, co-founded by 22-year-old Norah Kimathi, hopes to tackle some of the educational difficulties they face.
It has built a mechanical hand that can translate a teacher’s voice into sign language in real time, allowing deaf children to learn alongside their hearing counterparts.
For the students at the Kasarani Treeside Secondary School for the Deaf in Nairobi, there is another element of the technology that is even more promising.
The robotic arms are trialed by deaf teachers to record and store signs using a bodysuit, which ZeroBionic imported for the task.
In the process, they are building a database of technical terms — drawing on English, American and Kenyan signs — that is helping to expand the language and make it easier for deaf children to learn and communicate.
“The biggest challenge we faced actually was in Africa we don’t have a standardized African sign language dataset,” Kimathi said at the company’s tiny lab in Nairobi.
“No one else had built this on the continent ... We had to start from scratch,” she said.
Many deaf children in Kenya learn a patchwork of makeshift signs, and the local dialect lacks many technical terms used to teach subjects like math and biology.
Sharon Mumbe, 19, one of the students at the deaf school, says it gives her “hope for the future.”
“I’ll be able to understand different concepts better,” she said.
Numerous prototype limbs litter the surfaces in Kimathi’s lab.
The team works with Africa One, a humanoid robot they built, to refine and expand the signs their mechanical arms are able to produce.
Everything has been designed and built in-house, using recycled materials to reduce costs and the environmental impact, produced using 3D printers that thump away constantly in the background.
Each hand costs roughly $350 and can last for up to two years. They are already in 78 schools across Kenya.
They boast a 92% speech-to-sign accuracy rate, and Kimathi says the results have made all the long hours in the lab worthwhile.
“We know we’re going to put a smile on someone else’s face,” she said.

Rubio visits Ecuador as Trump-friendly leader helps the US counterdrug push in the region
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visits Ecuador on the second leg of a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders
QUITO, Ecuador -- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visits Ecuador on Wednesday on the second leg of a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to President Donald Trump, especially in the administration's push to crack down on drug trafficking.
After spending Tuesday in Colombia meeting with new conservative firebrand President Abelardo de la Espriella, Rubio was traveling to Quito for talks with Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, who has rapidly embraced the Trump administration’s get-tough stance on counternarcotics operations and illegal immigration.
Ecuador has struggled to contain drug violence since 2021 as rival cartels partner with local gangs and battle for control of routes and coastal ports used to smuggle cocaine. The country is wedged between Colombia and Peru, the world’s top cocaine-producing countries.
Under Noboa, Ecuador has become a strong U.S. partner in counterdrug efforts in the region.
Coinciding with Rubio’s trip, U.S. forces intercepted and sank a vessel on Tuesday that Washington said had links to the Ecuadorian criminal group Los Choneros. It was the sixth such operation in less than two weeks and the second in as many days.
Unlike in U.S. strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in Latin American waters that began in September 2025, people aboard the floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities.
It appears to be a shift after a series of strikes on boats over the year has killed at least 227 people, whom the Trump administration accused of being “narcoterrorists” without providing evidence. The U.S. military carried out at least two of those deadly strikes last month.
In public remarks Tuesday in Barranquilla on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, de la Espriella and Rubio both extolled a resurgence in U.S.-Colombia ties, starting in the security sector where cooperation had lagged under the previous Colombian leadership.
“We have a lot of common interests with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements,” Rubio said of the three countries he is visiting. “It’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with U.S. and U.S. interests.”
From Quito, Rubio will travel to Lima, Peru, where he will see new Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori.

In my job as a product reviewer, I have learned to fear large boxes. Each one that arrives, whether an office chair or a pellet smoker, might mean anywhere from 20 minutes to multiple hours scratching my head at arcane diagrams, while bent upside down trying to find the right place to put a screw without dropping it.
And so the four-step instruction manual on the Vari Ergo electric standing desk was a source of immense relief. Ever since the Texas-based standing desk company first started rolling out standing desk conversion kits in the early 2010s (then under the name Varidesk), Vari has put a heartening emphasis on ease of assembly. This is an underrated quality, one that goes along way toward forging a good relationship between me and my furniture.
By the time I had the Ergo upright and plugged in, 10 minutes out of the box, my desk and I were pretty much good buddies. It’s a relationship that has continued apace over multiple months of testing.
The Ergo is sturdy, easily (and quietly) adjustable across a broad range of height from 25 to 50 inches, and somewhat elegant in a minimalist way. It doesn’t have any drawers, and I might want better cable management, but the Ergo otherwise covers most every base I need covered from a standing desk.
The Basic Specs
| Height range: 25 to 50.5 inches | 
| Desktop sizes: 54 x 26 | 
| Memory Presets: Four | 
| Load: 200-pound operational load | 
| Weight: 104 pounds | 
| Warranty: Lifetime | 
An Affordable, Compact Option
The Ergo’s virtues are quite simple: The desk is sturdy on its T-shaped legs, with minimal wobble. It adjusts easily, with a relatively quiet dual-motor system, across a broad range from 25 inches to 50 inches high. The warranty is for life, at least on manufacturing defects under normal operation.
The desk’s three-stage, T-bottomed legs mean the desk stays stable even at its top height—a problem among some desks in the lower price range, and I’m able to set four different pre-set heights. In practice, this is one more than I even need: I have mine set for seated typing, face height for Zoom calls, and standing height.

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

Reliance Jio has introduced a new pricing structure for rich communication services (RCS) business messaging, allowing brands to send marketing, transactional and one-time password (OTP) messages to iPhone users on its network. The new rates came into effect on September 1, as per an ET report citing emails sent by the company to businesses. Marketing messages will cost ₹0.27-0.30 per message, while transactional messages will be charged at ₹0.25 and OTPs at ₹0.11-0.16 per message. The new pricing replaces Jio's earlier flat RCS tariff of ₹0.08-0.10 per message, as per the report. The development follows Apple's expansion of business RCS support on iPhones in partnership with telecom operators. Unlike Apple's consumer RCS implementation, which enables messaging between individuals across iOS and Android, business RCS allows companies to send application-to-person (A2P) messages to customers. Apple has supported RCS on iPhones since iOS 18, although availability depends on mobile operators. Jio was among the first operators in India to bring RCS to iPhone users through its partnership with Apple in 2025. Jio already offers RCS-based business messaging through its Jio Business Messaging platform. The service enables businesses to send branded and interactive messages, including rich media, carousels and action buttons, directly to customers' native messaging inboxes. Jio describes the platform as being powered by RCS, through partnerships with Google and Apple. Therefore, the latest development marks an expansion of Jio's existing RCS ecosystem into commercial business messaging for iPhone users, rather than the introduction of a new Jio-Apple RCS partnership. Apple is gradually rolling out business RCS in other markets, including the US, UK, Germany, France and Spain, through partnerships with local telecom operators. However, the commercial pricing is set by individual telecom operators rather than Apple or Google, as per reports. Jio's move could give businesses another channel for customer communication as they increasingly rely on rich messaging services for marketing, transaction updates and authentication. RCS offers features such as verified business profiles, images, videos, carousels and interactive buttons, while being delivered through the native messaging application. Jio's business RCS offering also supports both Android and iOS users on its network. The move comes as RCS adoption grows in India. According to data cited by Infobip, RCS interactions in the country increased 108% between H1 2025 and H1 2026, with financial services and fintech companies accounting for more than three-fourths of RCS traffic. Inc42 has reached out to Jio for comment. The story will be updated if the company responds. The development comes at a time when Jio Platforms is gearing up for a major public market debut. The company has received SEBI’s approval for an IPO which could probably be one of the largest IPOs to hit the Indian markets till now. The company filed its DRHP with the SEBI for a fresh issue only IPO in June, proposing raising fresh capital by issuing 27 Cr equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each. The company plans to use the net proceeds to prepay or repay, in full or in part, certain borrowings of its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited (RJIL), as well as for general corporate purposes. Of the total amount that would be raised via the IPO, ₹27,500 Cr would be used towards the prepayment of certain outstanding borrowings of its material subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd.

2030 Winter Olympics boss departs amid turmoil
- Published
Edgar Grospiron has left his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
The departure of Grospiron, the 1992 Olympic moguls champion, was confirmed at a meeting of the committee's executive board on Thursday, marking the latest setback in the event's troubled governance.
In a statement, the organising committee said: "His decision to leave the presidency is part of a deliberate, organised and fully assumed transition, taken in the interests of the project and its governance.
"It reflects a shared desire with stakeholders to enable the organisation to quickly enter this new operational phase."
Confirming his departure via a post on LinkedIn, Grospiron said his decision followed "months of tension".
"I draw the conclusion that the conditions are not met for me to continue this," he wrote.
Grospiron's tenure, which began in February 2025, has been plagued by internal turmoil and logistical challenges.
In February 2026, chief executive officer Cyril Linette left the committee, citing "insurmountable disagreements" with Grospiron.
Linette's departure followed a number of other high-profile resignations, including chief operating officer Anne Murac and communications director Arthur Richer.
Budget cuts have plagued the planning process, with Grospiron admitting in February they had "little time, little money".
However, he remained confident he could "deliver a Games that will honour our vision and ambition" provided there was "serenity" and "continuity" from the organising committee.
In May, the committee was forced to shelve the Games' 'ice sports hub' in Nice after the city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow OGC Nice's Allianz Riviera Stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.
The ice events will now be hosted in Lyon, with the exception of speed skating, which will take place in Heerenveen in the Netherlands.
Two months later, following a tense board meeting in July, French Olympic Committee president Amelie Oudea-Castera told La Tribune Dimanche, external that they were "once again facing governance problems".
Despite another departure from the organising committee, French sports minister Marina Ferrari says there is "no concern about what comes next".
"The bid is continuing to move forward," she told reporters. "Our teams are mobilised and working. We are confident about the future of the Alpes project."
The International Olympic Committee praised Grospiron's "crucial work in laying the foundations for the success" of the Games.
"The IOC will continue working in close collaboration with the organising committee to build on the solid foundations that Mr Grospiron has laid," the statement added.

On the intervening night of June 18 and 19, Jalil Akhtar, an elderly Muslim man, from West Bengal’s Bagroi village in Karandighi block of Uttar Dinajpur district, was woken up from sleep and picked up by Dalkhola police from his home, his family alleged. Other members of his household, sleeping in the same home, came to know of his arrest only the next morning.
The 66-year-old man, whose name appeared in both the 2002 and 2026 Special Intensive Revision (SIR) lists, was allegedly arrested on grounds of “being a Bangladeshi”, his family told Alt News. After spending nearly three months in various holding centres and judicial custody, when Akhtar was produced before additional chief judicial magistrate (ACJM) of Islampur court on Wednesday, September 2, the investigating officer of the case gave a written declaration that identity documents submitted by Akhtar were valid. However, Akhtar has not yet been granted bail, the court is expected to hear the matter next on September 10.
During his nearly three-month-long incarceration, Akhtar was kept in two holding centres, and then lodged in Islampur jail, until, his family claimed they were told he would be deported to Bangladesh. They further alleged that during the entire duration, police failed to prove that Akhtar’s citizenship and legal documents were fake, raising questions over why the arrest was made in the first place when his name appeared in the latest SIR list.
“My brother is an Indian, we have all the documents and he has never even seen the Bangladesh border. Yet, he was arrested, kept in holding centres and jailed on a mere suspicion of being a Bangladeshi, which the police could not even prove. Was he held for so long just because we are Muslims and live in a border district with significant Muslim population?” asked Motiur Rahaman, Akhtar’s cousin.
‘Picked up at Night without Family Being Informed’
According to his family and locals, Akhtar slept on a cot in front of his single-room home. His wife, Taufa Bibi, woke at dawn on June 19 to find him gone. She initially assumed that he might have gone to offer ‘Fazr Namaz’, but began to panic when she found his kurta hanging from the family closet.
Motiur was first to launch a hunt for his cousin, a landless villager who was entirely dependent on his two migrant worker sons. Describing the long fight in detail to Alt News, Motiur said he assembled a crew of fellow villagers and they scoured through the entire neighbourhood including forest areas through the day. They were eventually informed by a local that a police vehicle had entered the village the previous night.
Upon calling one of his sources at the recently established Bazargaon police camp, which falls under Dalkhola police station, Motiur learned that the police had picked up a man from his village the previous night, allegedly identifying him as an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant. The group then reached the police outpost, and found Akhtar sitting on the floor of the lock-up, bare bodied, as the police, Motiur claimed, did not even allow him to wear his kurta while nabbing him.
Motiur further alleged that, as per Akhtar’s recollection of the arrest to his family, the police held him at gunpoint, apparently to keep him silent while taking him into custody from the densely populated area.
The Family’s Fight To Prove His Citizenship
“In the police camp we tried to reason with the officer in charge that Jalil Akhtar’s name was not only in the 2026 SIR list, but was also in the 2002 list, so he should be released. The police retorted saying ‘don’t you people dare to threaten me, those days of threatning are over…now the government has changed,” claimed Motiur.
Another officer of the outpost reportedly told Motiur to give them some time to verify the documents and if everything came out clean, his cousin would be released. However, the same morning, Akhtar was moved to a holding centre in Nizampur near Chakulia.
To establish his Indian citizenship, Akhtar’s family began gathering every document they could find. According to his family, they obtained the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list, both of which included Akhtar’s name. They also collected land deeds linking Akhtar to his father, Rousan Ali, as well as a residence certificate issued by the Bazragaon-2 panchayat, stating that Akhtar was a permanent resident of the panchayat area.
On July 9, they visited Dalkhola police station and submitted the documents for verification. Before that, they had also approached the district superintendent of police’s (SP) office. On both occasions, the police asked them to allow time for the documents to be verified and assured them that no harm would come to Akhtar if he was indeed an Indian citizen. According to his family, the police also said they were under “considerable pressure from higher-ups to identify and deport those deemed to be illegal Bangladeshi migrants”, and that they were only acting as per orders.
‘An Attempt To Send Him To Bangladesh’
However, as days went by, Akhtar remained under police custody and shifting between holding centres. Dulal Rajbanshi, organiser of the Votadhikar Surakkha Samanway Samity, an organisation formed to help those whose names were deleted in the 2026 SIR, helped Akhtar’s family. “We were able to prevent the police from sending Jalil Akhtar into Bangladesh twice. When they failed to send him into ‘no man’s land’, the police eventually filed a false FIR and produced him before the court,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, Akhtar was moved to another holding centre near Phulbari border crossing near Siliguri, allegedly to send him to Bangladesh. The state police keeps the detainees at temporary holding centres, before handing them over to the BSF for deportation into Bangladesh, Rajbanshi claimed. He said that in Akhtar’s case, first the police handed him over to the BSF, who took him towards Phulbari to apparently deport him.
“We were informed by local sources that Akhtar was moved from the Nizampur holding centre and taken towards Phulbari on July 6. The next day, we reached Uttar Dinajpur district magistrate’s office in Raiganj, who asked us to immediately contact the SP in Islampur,” he said.
“We travelled a 110-kilometre distance from Raiganj to Islampur, where again, the SP said that he needs time to investigate, as there is “immense pressure from above to deport illegal Bangladeshis”. However, we were later told that Akhtar was brought back to the Chakulia holding centre. It was unclear what happened after this, and which border they took him to in order to attempt deportation the second time.”
However, acting on the SP’s direction, the group then met Dalkhola police station’s inspector-in-charge (IC) in the following days. “The IC asked us whether we could bring any relatives of Akhtar to the police station for verification. By that evening, we had brought even his 90-year-old aunts and all other relatives to the station. But the police did not meet them, instead, they collected the death certificate of one of Akhtar’s brothers,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, the BSF often selects a favourable point along the border to ‘pushback’ alleged Bangladeshis, sometimes at gunpoint. “Currently, the Border Guard Bangladesh and Bangladeshi villagers are on high alert to prevent any pushback from India. As a result, many people are getting stranded in no man’s land, as neither country is willing to take them in. Akhtar’s family was wary of this exact fate,” he claimed.
According to Motiur, the IC also mentioned “immense pressure”, stating that the police were already “holding a list of 500 names whom they have to deport and 50 more were recently added”.
‘It Is Better If They Kill Me’
In the meantime, Akhtar’s family visited him at the detention centre. According to Motiur, Akhtar broke down completely. “My brother kept saying, what will I do if I am sent to Bangladesh? I don’t know anybody there. I have never been to that country. I can’t even beg there. It is better if they kill me than push me into Bangladesh,” Motiur said.
According to the family, a Border Security Force (BSF) team also visited their home to investigate the matter. “The BSF team came and spoke with us. They were infuriated by the state police’s actions — or lack of investigation — and told us that they would not deport an Indian citizen. At least the BSF came to the village to investigate. Nobody from the state police even cared to do that,” Motiur claimed.
On July 20, villagers organised a protest against Akhtar’s arrest in the nearby Rasakhowa Haat. However, before the programme could start, police intervened and dispersed them, they alleged. The next day, Rajbanshi alleged, the administration again attempted to send Akhtar into Bangladesh.
“On July 21, we received information that he had once again been moved from the Nizampur holding centre. We got the news around 2 pm and, by 4 pm, had organised a press conference at the Uttar Dinajpur Press Club in Raiganj. We shared information about the press conference across social media. We were worried that police might announce that he has gone missing. The next day, on July 22, police informed the family that they would produce Akhtar before the Islampur court,” claimed Rajbanshi.
Discrepancies between FIR and Police Submission
As per the FIR lodged against Akhtar by Dalkhola police, he was picked up from Nizampur around 1:05 am on June 20. Nizampur is also where, according to his family, he was subsequently held at a holding centre — the location is around 35 km from Akhtar’s home.
Motiur alleged that upon prodding the police on who lodged a complaint against Akhtar, police refused to reveal the name of the complainant. According to the FIR, Akhtar was detained at the Nizampur centre along with two other “illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”. The FIR states that all three detainees are from “AndhaRahamatpur village of Thakurgaon district of Bangladesh”. It is claimed that this was revealed by Akhtar himself during interrogation.
The FIR further states that Akhtar crossed the Hili-Malda border and entered India around 24 years ago. However, the documents submitted by his family before the court show that his name appears in both the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list. In both documents, his father’s name is the same. If the police account is accurate and Akhtar entered India only around 23-24 years ago, it would be impossible for his name to have appeared in the 1995 voter list, nearly three decades ago, and subsequently in the 2002 SIR list.
Alt News has seen the case diary submitted by police in court on August 5. It says Akhtar voted in 1982 elections as well, although it does not clarify which elections and where. The submission also mentions that during investigation, police had been told by locals that coming to Uttar Dinajpur in 1982, Akhtar worked as a rikshaw puller in Delhi and does not speak proper Bengali. These statements directly contradict the FIR claim that he entered India around 24 years ago and does not establish any link between Akhtar and Bangladesh.
According to the police’s submission, Akhtar was born in either 1959 or 1960 and first appears in official records in 1982. No records relating to him from before 1982 could be found, the police said. They also claim that he failed to establish a credible link with Raushan Ali, whom he identifies as his father, through land records or other documentary evidence.
However, Rajbanshi claimed that Akhtar was not required to produce his parents’ birth records to establish his Indian citizenship. “Under the Indian Citizenship Act, a person born before 1987 does not need to show the birth records of their parents to prove their Indian citizenship. The 2002 and 2026 SIR exercises were also meant to identify and remove illegal entries from the electoral rolls. Akhtar’s name appears in both lists. Yet he continues to be detained, merely to serve what appears to be the BJP’s political agenda,” he said.
The September 2 Hearing
As per legal records, the police postponed the bail hearing four times stating that they need more time to verify the documents. During the hearing on September 2, the additional chief judicial magistrate and the defence counsel asked the police to testify whether the documents provided by Akhtar were valid. The police ultimately confirmed the documents were legitimate.
According to Akhtar’s lawyer, Firoz Ahmed, the police deliberately avoided telling the court whether the former’s documents were genuine. “The ACJM pressed the investigating to state whether Akhtar’s documents are genuine before carrying on with the investigation. Even then, the IO remained silent,” he said.
Later, however, the police stated in a report submitted in the late afternoon that Akhtar’s voter ID and PAN card were genuine Indian documents, and that his records in the 1995 voter list and 2002 SIR list were also genuine. “They are awaiting an email response to verify the authenticity of his Aadhaar card, so they could not say anything about it,” Ahmed added.
“As his birthplace and his current residence are different, and fall under different police stations, the police are now harping on that, as if relocating to another place is a crime,” Ahmed alleged.
“The police had been given a target to identify and round up Bangladeshis, and they are targeting any vulnerable person they can find. Since Akhtar was born in another village, around four to five kilometres from ours, and is extremely poor and owns barely any land, it is easy for the administration to portray him as a Bangladeshi, citing a lack of evidence,” Motiur alleged.
Dalkhola Police’s Response
Alt News spoke to Sankha Chatterjee, IC of Dalkhola police station. Upon being asked whether Akhtar was arrested at gunpoint as alleged by his family, he said, “A lathi is enough for us to arrest a 66-year old. We don’t need a gun for it. As for the family’s allegation, tell them that we used a Bofors cannon to take Jalil Akhtar in custody.”
He further said that police had submitted their findings before the court. “Now it up to the court to decide whether Jalil Akhtar is an Indian or a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or a Cuban citizen. According to our investigation, we couldn’t find any documents of Jalil Akhtar till the age of 21. All his documents are from the age of 22 till 66,” said the officer.
Alt News asked about the discrepancies between the FIR and the case diary submitted by the police before the court, however, the officer’s response did not clarify the aforementioned loopholes. Chatterjee simply said: “I don’t want to get political, but if you come to Uttar Dinajpur, I can show you people who have voter cards and other documents of both India and Bangladesh. It’s better not to get into how they were able to cross over to this side.”
Motiur, Rajbanshi and Akhtar’s family claim their efforts have helped prevent Akhtar’s ‘pushback’ till now. But the family’s ordeal is far from over. They still do not know when, or whether, he will be freed from detention and his name will be cleared in this ‘test of citizenship’. For the family, what began as an effort to establish his identity has become a prolonged battle against an administrative process that they believe is inherently designed against them.

Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).
JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.
JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.
The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.
CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.
According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.
The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.
Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.
The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.
Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”
Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”
Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.
She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.
Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.
The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.
During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.
But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.
Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she and was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”.
Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets.
“The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.
The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.”
HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020.
Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.

Armand ‘Mondo’ Duplantis is the headline act as the world’s top-ranked track-and-field athletes gather for this weekend’s inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest, where they will compete for unmatched prize money totalling USD 10 million.
From Friday, some 381 athletes from 65 federations will gather for three nights of competition at the Zsivotzky Gyula Nemzeti Atletikai Kozpont stadium that hosted the World Championships in 2023.
Automatic qualifiers for the season-ending Ultimate event include 26 Olympic champions from the 2024 Paris Games, 26 world champions from Tokyo last year and 25 Diamond League winners from the 2026 season, along with the best performers of the year based on the world rankings qualification system.
There are no quotas for countries, with inclusion based solely on performance.
“We have created the Ultimate to ensure every athletics season culminates with a major global championship - one with real meaning for the athletes, fans, media and broadcasters,” said World Athletics president Sebastian Coe, with 2026 having neither a World Championships nor an Olympic Games.
“Our North Star is to maximise our global broadcast audience, and so it is unapologetically made for TV to engage broadcasters in a new way to help further elevate national heroes.”
On the track, the two semifinals in the 100m, 200m, 400m, 800m, 100m hurdles/110m hurdles and 400m hurdles will feature eight athletes, and the top four in each will make it through to the final. The 1,500m, 5,000m and relay races will be straight finals.
All field events will be straight finals, although there is no place for shot put, discus or women’s hammer throw.
The horizontal jumps, with the men’s triple jump a notable absence, and throws will feature four rounds, with each of the eight athletes guaranteed two attempts.
Everyone’s a winner
Each Ultimate winner will receive the top prize of $150,000, a sum World Athletics said was a game-changer in a sport often seen to be underfunded.
But every athlete will earn: an eighth-placed finisher in an individual event, for example, will bag USD 10,000.
“We have a USD 10million prize pot where every athlete who competes goes home with something,” said Coe, of the 28 disciplines delivered in a fast-paced, made-for-television format.
World and Olympic pole vault champion Duplantis, who improved his own world record to 6.31m earlier this year, will face a field that includes Emmanouil Karalis, who has cleared 6.20m this season and arrives in Budapest as the Diamond League champion.
Duplantis withdrew from the Brussels Diamond League finals as a precaution when tightness in his leg resurfaced, raising questions over how fit he is coming into Budapest.
Several of this season’s other world record-breakers will also be in action: Ja’Kobe Tharp in the 110m hurdles, US teammate Masai Russell in the 100m hurdles and Brazil’s Alison dos Santos in the men’s 400m hurdles.
Other Olympic champions entered include Gabby Thomas, Marileidy Paulino, Keely Hodgkinson, Yaroslava Mahuchikh, Letsile Tebogo and Ethan Katzberg, while world champions Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, Oblique Seville and Collen Kebinatshipi are also among those set to compete.
The middle-distance programme is particularly attractive, with the women’s 800m featuring world leader Audrey Werro, Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol.
Missing from the track, however, will be injured Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles and Olympic and world long jump gold medallist Tara Davis-Woodhall, who sustained a concussion in a car crash last week.
“We want to bring our fans athletics as they have never seen it before -- with the best of the best athletes in our sport competing head-to-head in a passion-fuelled, high-octane festival of sport, with sound, light and innovation,” said Coe.
“This is the holy grail of all sports -- how do you reach out to all audiences in a way that is familiar to them?” he told AFP.
Duplantis said the championship will be “the ultimate high in a year when we do not have a World Championships or Olympic Games”.
“Even with fewer events, there will still be 26 individual events taking place over just three nights -- the pace will be insane.”

Union Minister for Civil Aviation K Rammohan Naidu on Thursday assured the Central government’s full support for developing tourism in Andhra Pradesh. He also announced that new airports and introduction of seaplane services were being planned to make travel to tourist destinations faster.
Speaking at the 41st Annual Convention of the Indian Association of Tour Operators (IATO) under the theme “India – The World’s Next Tourism Opportunity,” Mr. Rammohan said that Andhra Pradesh possesses abundant natural, spiritual, and cultural resources necessary to transform it into a world-class tourism destination.
He highlighted that the State is home to numerous hidden tourism gems, and that air connectivity to major tourist destinations across the State—including Visakhapatnam—was being strengthened.
He said: “Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu firmly believes the future belongs to the tourism sector and is prioritising it with special attention.
Minister for Tourism Kandula Durgesh said: “Seven special tourism circuits have been planned for the river Godavari Pushkarams in 2027. These circuits encompass the Pancharama Kshetras, Shakti Peethas, Devi Kshetras, Vaishnava Divya Kshetras, Godavari Heritage Temples, Pushkar Ghats, and the Akhanda Godavari regions.”
He said that tourism packages have been designed to connect various destinations, including the historic Havelock Bridge, Papikondalu, Pushkar Ghats, Harathi venues with pilgrimage sites such as Antarvedi, Vadapalli, Appanapalli, Mandapalli, Samarlakota, Draksharamam, and Palakollu.
Mr. Durgesh announced that the State government was working towards strengthening Andhra Pradesh into a pivotal and premier tourism destination on India’s tourism map.
Earlier, to mark the commencement of the convention, the dignitaries unveiled the ‘Indian Association of Tour Operators Manual Book.’ Mr Durgesh also launched the poster for ‘The Godavari Calls’—a prestigious initiative by the Andhra Pradesh Tourism Department designed to bring spirituality, culture, and heritage together on a single platform, much like the Kumbh Mela. The Minister added that the poster highlights the significance of the Godavari Pushkaram, scheduled for 2027, and provides details regarding tourism circuits.

Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.
With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.
These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.
Get More Personal Context
You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).
It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.
This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.
Ask About Anything on the Screen
Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.
So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.
The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).
Write and Edit Text Anywhere
The old Siri could generate text for you, but it offloaded the job to an integrated ChatGPT plug-in. With Siri AI, no third-party help is needed, and you can use it for things like text messages and emails.
Just call up Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri" or tapping on the Write with Siri link, then tell it what you want to say or describe the edits you'd like it to make. You can instruct it to make your messages sound more or less formal, to expand or shorten sections of text, or to turn quick notes into full paragraphs and sentences.
You retain final approval over what's written, and can continue to make manual or AI-generated edits as you go. Siri AI lets you review all the changes and jump backwards and forwards through your different revisions.
Do More Inside Your Apps
Not only can Siri AI access more information pulled from your apps, it can now take more actions inside these apps. You’re able to create calendar events or switch playlists just by talking or typing to the digital assistant.
Some of this was already possible with the earlier incarnation of Siri, but now you can go deeper and do more inside your apps, and you should be able to use a wider range of natural language prompts to get stuff done—just as if you were talking to a real human assistant you'd handed your phone over to.
You might see some suggestions for actions pop up as well—so if someone texts you a date and time, you’ll see Siri inviting you to create a calendar event. Over time, deeper hooks into third-party, non-Apple apps should show up too.
Get at All Your Chats With the Siri App
For the first time, Apple's digital AI assistant has its own app. Launch it from the home screen to access your Siri AI conversation history and sync your queries and requests across different Apple devices.
Compared to the likes of Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT, this is something Siri AI has been sorely missing, and it gives you another way of launching chats with the assistant: Open up the dedicated app rather than invoking it with a voice command.
Also, look out for what Apple calls "broad world knowledge" in the new Siri AI. Roughly translated, stand-alone queries about the history of Rome or how to fix a leaky faucet should bring up more informed, complete responses in the app.
Customize Siri’s Pace and Expressivity
This final tip needs even more computing resources, so it’s only for the most powerful devices—the 2026 iPhones, as well as the iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air—as far as iPhones go.
The actual feature is being able to adjust the tone, speed, and what Apple calls the "expressivity" of Siri AI's spoken responses to you. In other words, you can tweak the personality of the assistant to some extent, as well as switch between voices.
To find these new options, open up Settings on your iPhone and tap Siri. You can customize Siri AI in other ways from this same screen, including changing the AI’s default voice and choosing how long to keep chats stored in your history.
