England's push for two-day win halted by weather
- Published
Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day two of five)
Pakistan 133 (Shakeel 43; Tongue 4-42) & 52-2 (Robinson 2-10)
England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148)
Pakistan are 268 runs behind
England's charge towards a two-day win in the final Test against Pakistan was only halted by rain at Edgbaston.
The tourists were battling for survival on 52-2 - 268 adrift of making England bat again - when the bad weather intervened for a second and final occasion in Birmingham.
The time was 17:07 BST. With the possibility of an extra half an hour available to force a result, play could have continued until 19:00 if conditions had allowed.
Given the fragility of the Pakistan batting - the tourists have not reached 200 or batted for more than 51 overs in the series - there was a real possibility England would earn victory inside two days after Ollie Robinson reduced the visitors to 0-2.
Instead, the players will return on Friday, when England will complete a 3-0 series clean sweep.
The eventual outcome of this match was barely in doubt when England began Thursday on 156-4, leading by 23.
Contributions of 75 from Harry Brook, 69 by Jamie Smith, 65 scored by Dan Lawrence and 50 from Robinson pushed England to 453, a huge first-innings lead of 320.
The only disappointment was that no England batter pushed on to make a century, meaning Ben Duckett's ton against New Zealand at Trent Bridge will remain the home side's only hundred of the summer.
No let up from England
One of the criticisms of the previous England regime, under captain Ben Stokes and coach Brendon McCullum, was their inability to finish series strongly.
England have lost the final Test in each of their past six series. Some of their worst performances in the Bazball era came in dead rubbers after a series had been won, notably at home to Sri Lanka in 2024 and away to New Zealand later the same year.
Stokes often said he did not like the word "ruthless" and there were plenty of times his side lacked ruthlessness. On this occasion, Root's England are showing their ruthless side.
The quality of the opposition should be taken into account - Stokes' England would have comfortably beaten this poor Pakistan side. The hosts also had the better of the conditions on Thursday, batting under blue sky then bowling when it got dark overhead.
But, under Root, England are showing a new-found calmness, along with a willingness to find the right tempo to their batting. The way they extended their lead on the second day was an example of a more mature approach.
And, in Robinson, they have a bowler in the form of his life, a purple patch England will hope carries through the winter and to next summer's Ashes.
Batters impress but miss out on hundreds
Given England's dominance over Pakistan, it is curious that none of their batters have registered a century in the series and now will not get another chance.
Duckett's sole ton means England will end a six-Test home summer with their fewest number of individual hundreds.
Brook, Lawrence and Smith all impressed, and all will be disappointed they missed out on three figures.
A stand of 86 between Brook and Lawrence was full of intent at the beginning of the day, with Lawrence the aggressor. Busy running was a feature of the stand, until Brook attempted a needless single to mid-wicket and was run out at the non-striker's end.
Lawrence has made three half-centuries since being recalled at the beginning of this series, probably enough to earn a place in South Africa in December. This is his 17th Test and he gave an audible cry of frustration when he chopped on off Mohammad Imran, extending a wait for a maiden hundred.
Smith suffered a tough Ashes tour, yet has shown signs of rehabilitation with bat and wicketkeeping gloves this summer. On a ground where he has had plenty of previous success, he muscled the ball through the leg side before he offered a tame return catch to Razaullah.
Robinson can do no wrong at the moment. He swiped through the leg side, including a massive six into the Hollies Stand, for his second half-century in Test cricket. Robinson's previous 50 came against India in Ranchi in 2024, his last before being dropped. Now he is indispensable.
Even Jofra Archer got involved, heaving two sixes of his own. He was left unbeaten on 32 when last man Josh Tongue was caught behind.
England denied chance to build on Robinson strikes
Pakistan's innings began after tea, leaving England one session to produce the first two-day finish in a Test in this country since 2000.
With Jordan Cox keeping in place of Smith, who has a bruised finger, Robinson made the sort of start that made a two-day finish a real possibility.
From the first ball of the innings, Saim Ayub needlessly edged to Brook at second slip. In the same over, Abdullah Shafique's crooked bat resulted in an edge to Root at first slip.
To their credit, Azan Awais and Shan Masood survived 12 overs in the gloom, even if Masood survived a tough chance to third slip Duckett off the bowling of Gus Atkinson.

Gujarat Assembly passes bill making licences mandatory for livestock feed
Gujarat Assembly passed a bill making licences mandatory for livestock and poultry feed manufacture, storage and sale, with penalties for substandard feed.
The Gujarat Legislative Assembly on Thursday unanimously passed a bill making licences mandatory for the manufacture, storage and sale of livestock feed, poultry feed and mineral mixtures in the state, with penalties prescribed for substandard and adulterated feed.
The Gujarat Livestock Feed, Poultry Feed and Mineral Mixture (Regulation of Production, Storage, Distribution, Sale and Quality Control) Bill, 2026, provides for a fine of up to ₹5 lakh and suspension of a licence for up to one year for manufacturing substandard feed. Misleading branding can attract a fine of up to ₹5 lakh and suspension of a licence for up to three years.
Manufacturing or selling adulterated feed, where no animal death occurs, can lead to cancellation of the licence, imprisonment for up to one year and a fine of up to ₹5 lakh. If an animal dies because of adulterated feed, the licence can be cancelled and the offender can face imprisonment of seven to 10 years and a fine of up to ₹10 lakh.
Gujarat agriculture and animal husbandry minister Jitu Vaghani, who introduced the Bill, said manufacturers would have to comply with standards prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). The legislation also provides for periodic testing and analysis of feed samples and prescribes requirements for packaging and labelling to prevent misleading claims and branding.
Vaghani said the legislation was based on the World Health Organization’s “One Health” approach and was intended to protect livestock farmers and manufacturers that complied with quality standards. He said the government would take action against businesses that compromised on feed quality.
The minister said the licensing process would be online and faceless to prevent unnecessary harassment of businesses. Farmers preparing feed for their own livestock and feed produced for research purposes have been kept outside the scope of the law.
The government said the legislation was aimed at protecting the health of Gujarat’s livestock population, which includes more than 106 lakh buffaloes and 96 lakh cows, besides sheep, goats and poultry, and at improving milk productivity.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Tim Scott mocked for over-the-top Trump event speech: ‘An SNL cold open’
One commentator compared Scott’s speech to something from a ‘TV character’
Social media users are roasting Senator Tim Scott after the South Carolina Republican delivered an animated speech at the GOP midterm convention in Texas that saw him yell and pretend to rip his heart out of his chest.
“There are no words for how over the top Tim Scott's Trumpapalooza performance is,” liberal journalist Aaron Rupar wrote on X. “It's an SNL cold open.”
Rupar added that Scott’s often impassioned tone resembled a “spoof of a preacher whose life took a wrong turn.”
Others took a similar tack in criticizing the performance at the Dallas convention, with one social media user accusing Scott of “playing a TV character.”
“Is Tim Scott OK?” filmmaker Morgan J. Freeman wrote in an X post.
Even some Republicans took note of the speech’s out-there style.
“Tim Scott is not ‘low-keying it,’” former congressman Matt Gaetz wrote on X.
The criticism was ironic, given that Scott sought to paint Democrats as the weird ones, reprising an insult Democrats used against the Trump-Vance ticket during the 2024 presidential election.
During his speech, Scott said the Democratic midterm slate had “the most dangerous, radical and frankly weird Democratic candidates in American history.”
“He believes God is non-binary,” Scott said of the Texan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico. “He thinks God needs special woke pronouns. But Texas, we know who God is. We’re talking about Jesus.”
Talarico has since walked back those comments, which he has called “cringey.” He said in a recent interview his comments about God in 2021 were meant to be deliberately provocative.
"You can't use human categories to define God,” Talarico, who has studied at a seminary and holds a master’s degree in theological studies, recently told ABC News.
Elsewhere in the speech, Scott framed the midterms as a fight for the heart of America.
“The Democrats’ extreme candidates won’t rip that heart out of chests,” he said, miming his heart being ripped out. “They hate our culture. They hate what it means to be American. Hear me, Dallas. Not! On! Our! Watch! We will not back down.”
Beyond Scott’s eyebrow-raising speech, the convention has made news elsewhere because it featured a video message to attendees from Democratic Sen. John Fetterman.
"Why am I here talking to you today?” he said in the video. “Because, well, I am a common-sense Democrat. I am always going to stand with America. I'm always going to reject the extremes [of] socialism and that anti-American way of life.”

Lawsuit challenges intimidation of DHS observers across the country
For months, Minneapolis resident Michael Khalili drove around the Twin Cities area observing and documenting the activities of federal immigration officers after they swarmed his city last winter as part of an unprecedented surge.
He points out that when federal immigration officers fatally shot fellow Minneapolis observer Alex Pretti in January, it was bystander videos that debunked inaccurate information Trump administration officials were spreading about Pretti, such as that he had committed an act of domestic terrorism and was a "would-be assassin."
"That's the only reason why the government's lies fell apart," Khalili said. "And that's why it's critical that people are out there."
But the 47-year-old father of two stopped observing ICE in recent months due to mounting risk and pressure from his family. Khalili said he follows the law when he drives behind ICE vehicles and is exercising his constitutional rights. But he said he's had repeated tense exchanges with federal officers who have taken photos of him and his vehicle, and told him to stop.
A day after one such exchange in March, Khalili's Global Entry status was revoked (until a HuffPost journalist inquired about it, and it was reinstated). On another occasion in May, he said a state trooper threatened him with a harassment charge for following ICE. Then in June, after 15 Minnesota activists were criminally indicted for conspiracy to impede or injure an officer, Khalili realized one of the counts against a defendant in that case was for following ICE vehicles across state lines in May on the same day Khalili had been warned he could be charged for following ICE. Khalili's wife became worried.
"She was concerned that federal agents could show up at our home and could arrest me in front of our children," Khalili said. "And so I agreed to stop doing this."
But Khalili hasn't given up his quest to hold the federal government accountable. He is now a named plaintiff in a new federal lawsuit filed Thursday, along with the nonprofit Common Cause, that accuses the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, the FBI and other federal agencies of violating the First Amendment and privacy rights of observers.
The new lawsuit follows a handful of other cases brought by observers arguing First Amendment violations, but it is the most sweeping to date, as it includes incidents from multiple states and seeks national relief. It is asking a judge in Washington, D.C. to bar federal agencies from intimidating or retaliating against observers.
"The right of citizens to criticize and hold our government accountable is the backbone of American democracy – and it is under attack," Common Cause's vice president for litigation, Maryam Jazini Dorcheh, told NPR. "We want to make sure we're promoting participation in the political process. And obviously, if government officials are criminalizing peaceful observation, that hinders our mission," Jazini Dorcheh said.
NPR has documented numerous instances of other people legally observing ICE describing intimidation and threats from the federal government. In Minnesota, it was a common occurrence for federal agents to tell observers they were breaking the law. NPR has previously covered how multiple activists in Maine were told by federal officers they could end up in a domestic terrorist database or on a watch list, and how a California man who runs an Instagram account tracking ICE activity was faced with an administrative subpoena seeking his identity.
NPR did not receive an immediate response from DHS or DOJ about the lawsuit's allegations. The FBI declined to comment.
The lawsuit describes disturbing encounters seven Common Cause members had with federal officers in Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey after trying to observe immigration enforcement. They include being photographed, followed, reported to police, pepper-sprayed or threatened with a visit to their home by federal officers. Federal officers did show up at one Common Cause member's Minnesota home.
In another instance, the suit alleges that ICE officers told local police to ban an unnamed Common Cause member from a public parking lot outside of an ICE facility in Maryland, where the member was observing, and told the member they knew who they were because they had put their face through a facial recognition database.
The 94-page complaint also draws from declarations filed in previous cases on behalf of observers in additional states, including Illinois, Maine and Tennessee.
The events described in the complaint are "not one-off activities. This is not about, like, 'Oh, some folks got out of hand in one place,'" said Danielle Lang, the vice president of voting rights and rule of law at the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center, which is litigating the case. "This is a top-down policy of retaliation and it needs to be addressed as such."
The lawsuit lists multiple directives from the Trump administration, including President Trump's National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7) and the DOJ's memo to operationalize it, which link impeding immigration enforcement and extreme views on migration to domestic terrorism. The NSPM-7 memo was the basis for the federal government to investigate and spy on activists in Minnesota, which ultimately led to the charges against 15 people for conspiracy to impede ICE.
Additionally, the suit lists public statements and internal memos that equate observers who record federal officers with "violent rioters" and "domestic terrorists," to argue there is a national policy in place to retaliate against observers. Furthermore, the Trump administration repealed guardrails that could have prevented federal officers from using facial recognition and license plate readers against peaceful observers, and DHS dismantled its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the suit argues.
The suit alleges that the federal government's retaliation against observers includes threatening force or arrest, collecting observers' personal information to intimidate them, using force, pursuing criminal charges, and imposing civil penalties such as administrative subpoenas or revoking observers' Global Entry or TSA PreCheck status.
Michael Khalili was eager to join the Common Cause lawsuit to help fellow observers, since in his case there is documentation of some of his encounters.
"If the paper trail for the petty things that they did to me can keep somebody else from being pepper-sprayed or murdered, like, why would I not do that? How could I not do that?" he told NPR.
Last month he requested access to his state motor vehicle records on the number of times law enforcement officials have queried his license plate, driver's license or name and date of birth. Before he started observing, there were only two such queries. But since March 2026, law enforcement queried him 55 times, a detail that is included in the lawsuit.
In addition, he has a March email from Customs and Border Protection notifying him that his Global Entry membership was revoked. Though the email only stated that the reason given for the change was "Your Global Entry has been revoked," it came one day after ICE officers stopped him, took photos of him and his license plate and told him to stop following them. Other observers in other states have also had their Global Entry status taken away, and some, like Khalili, had theirs reinstated after a reporter inquired.
Khalili still suspects he is on a federal list of some kind, or that there is a flag on him. He recently went on vacation to Ireland with his family and when returning to the U.S, he was referred for additional questioning by U.S. immigration officials.
He hopes this lawsuit can help bring about corrective changes and guardrails after what he calls a "nightmare" that the country and Minneapolis have been through.
"And so that not only will I be able to go out and observe if I so choose, but that there's no reason why I have to go out and observe," Khalili said.

Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.
“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.
The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.
That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.
“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.
In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.
The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.
Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.
The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.
Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.
Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”
Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.
But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.
“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.
“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”
After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.
He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

Universal Music Group is launching a new AI-powered platform that will allow users to draw from its catalog of licensed music to create song remixes, mashups, and new takes on tracks, according to an announcement on Thursday. The record label is developing the platform through a multi-year licensing agreement with ElevenLabs, a company that specializes in AI voice and music generation.
Universal Music is launching an AI music platform with ElevenLabs
UMG’s AI music platform will let users create remixes, mashups, and new takes on tracks.
Artists can choose whether to participate in UMG and ElevenLabs’ upcoming platform, which marks yet another AI deal for the record label. UMG is currently developing an AI music platform with Udio and has struck AI licensing deals with Spotify, Nvidia, and Klay. Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.
The study published Thursday in the journal Science involved tests on rats and certain human tissues as researchers looked at using psilocybin to fight a condition called peripheral neuropathy, which affects millions of people around the world.
It is a nerve ailment that hits about three quarters of all people who undergo chemo and commonly causes numbness and tingling, Patrick Dougherty, a co-author of the study, said in a call with reporters.
But a third of that group will develop non-stop, burning pain, said Dougherty, a pain treatment specialist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The symptoms can lead to trouble walking and other debilitating complications that can last after a person finishes chemotherapy, and even remain with them for life.
And it is not just a quality-of-life issue. This complication also affects a cancer patient's chances of survival because sometimes the side effects are so bad they force doctors to cut back on chemo or stop it altogether.
Protecting nerves
It was almost by accident that these researchers found that psilocybin can help cancer patients.
The team was initially studying how the disease manages to hijack nerve cells in order to grow.
And the researchers were surprised to see the mushroom ingredient -- it was being used to study a brain pathway regeneration concept called neuroplasticity -- actually prevented the emergence of peripheral neuropathy.
Later experiments highlighted psilocybin's role in protecting nerve cells and stimulating inside them the transport of mitochondria, often referred to as a cell's powerhouse.
This is key because chemo destroys the microscopic railroads that allow mitochondria to send energy all the way to the tips of people's hands and feet, killing off nerve endings there.
Psilocybin also seems to act on the brain, preserving electrical activity that chemotherapy thwarts.
In rodents, taking two doses of psilocybin before chemo was enough to prevent the appearance of painful hypersensitivity during as many as six rounds of treatment. And it did this without affecting the animal's immune system or hindering the cancer-fighting action.
Careful with self-medicating
"This is a highly promising finding," said Kristy Townsend, a professor of neurobiology at The Ohio State University who was not involved in the study.
And psilocybin's nerve-protecting quality does not seem to be linked to its hallucinogenic effects because a non-hallucinogenic analogue had the same effect in a lab test, she added.
Before the treatment can be made standard for people, testing will be needed to see if it is safe and effective, said Townsend.
This will be a long, slow process though it should be eased by a boom in medical research on psychedelic substances and a Trump administration executive order in April to speed up research and regulatory reviews, these scientists say.
The MD Anderson Cancer Center plans to launch clinical tests with psilocybin on cancer patients later this year.
Meanwhile it is important for cancer patients to avoid using magic mushrooms on their own as treatment, the researchers warned.
Psilocybin is legal in a few U.S. states.
The drug has an "amplifier" effect and cancer patients who take it without supervision could feel more stressed and anxious than they already are because of their cancer diagnosis, said Gregory Jones, a psychiatrist who took part in the study released Thursday.
"If you put somebody in adversity under these psychedelic substances, you can get much worse," Jones said.

Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that Donald Trump, then a New York City real estate developer, said after the attacks that he now owned the tallest building in downtown Manhattan.
For example, the self-described "pro-democracy" media outlet MeidasTouch wrote in a Facebook post:
In a television interview on the day of the attacks, Trump notably bragged how the destruction of the World Trade Center affected the ranking of his building at 40 Wall Street, claiming it was now the tallest building in downtown Manhattan.
Similar claims about Trump's alleged comments following the 9/11 attacks circulated on X (archived here and here) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us to ask about the claim.
Reminder: Donald Trump's immediate reaction to the 9/11 attacks was to brag that his building was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan after the Twin Towers collapsed. pic.twitter.com/iAkUeGafG9
— Republicans against Trump (@RpsAgainstTrump) September 7, 2026
Trump did tell (time code 2:05, archived) a reporter soon after the 9/11 attacks that 40 Wall Street, which the Trump Organization still owns, was "the tallest" building in downtown Manhattan. As such, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to Trump.
Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Fox 5 New York posted a video of Trump's phone interview with WWOR-TV reporter Alan Marcus on YouTube in 2016. Trump made the claim about owning the tallest building in downtown Manhattan after Marcus asked if 40 Wall Street had sustained any damage during the attacks. The exchange went as follows (time code 01:43 — emphasis ours):
Marcus: Donald, you have one of the landmark buildings down in the financial district, 40 Wall Street, did you have any damage or did you know what's happened down there?
Trump: Well, it was an amazing phone call I made. 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was, actually before the World Trade Center, was the tallest. And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it's the tallest.
During the 2001 interview, Marcus also asked Trump how he would have handled 9/11 if he were president given that he had considered running for the office the year before (time code 4:14). Trump said he would have taken a "very, very tough line" against "the group of people that did this."
In an interview with Politico in 2016, Marcus reportedly said that Trump's remark about 40 Wall Street was "Donald being Donald." Marcus added, "He is the brand manager of Trump, and he is going to tout that brand, and he does it reflexively."
Trump's claim that 40 Wall Street was the tallest building in downtown Manhattan following the attacks was incorrect. The nearby 952-foot tall 70 Pine Street skyscraper, which was also part of the Manhattan skyline in 2001, is 26 feet taller than 40 Wall Street.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump attacked the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York for telling him he would not be allowed to speak at its 25th anniversary commemoration.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

A wild elephant in Assam’s Golaghat district was rescued after it was found struggling with a tractor tyre stuck around its neck, highlighting the serious dangers posed to wildlife by human waste and negligence.
The elephant was spotted in distress with the tyre lodged tightly around its neck. The unusual and potentially life-threatening situation prompted a rescue operation involving the Centre for Wildlife Rehabilitation and Conservation (CWRC), Kaziranga, with support from the Golaghat Forest Division and local residents.
The rescue team successfully removed the tyre from around the elephant’s neck, giving the animal a second chance at life.
The circumstances under which the tyre became lodged around the elephant’s neck remain unknown. However, the incident has once again drawn attention to the threat that discarded human-made materials can pose to wild animals, particularly those living in areas close to human settlements.
The successful rescue was made possible through coordinated efforts between wildlife rescuers, forest officials and local people. The incident also serves as a reminder of the need for greater responsibility in disposing of waste and preventing human-made objects from entering wildlife habitats.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Delhi High Court (HC) has restrained D2C brand Beco parent entity Kwick Living from continuing its “War on What’s Hidden” advertising campaign targeting HUL’s Surf Excel and Vim products. The ad in question compares Beco’s cleaning products with Surf Excel and Vim dishwash gel. The campaign claimed that certain ingredients in HUL’s products could lead to skin irritation and allergic reactions, and asked consumers to “Switch to BECO”. Screengrab from Beco’s website showing its “War on What’s Hidden” campaign, as seen on September 10, 2026. While comparative advertising is permissible even if a rival’s product is put in an unfavourable light, it crosses legal thresholds when the overall message conveyed to consumers is false, misleading or deceptive, HC division bench led by Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani held. The HC found that Beco failed to establish the truth of the message conveyed through the campaign. As a result, the startup has been directed to pull down, remove and recall all advertisements containing the offending statements across every format and medium within one week, and file an affidavit of compliance within a week thereafter. "Just because a comparative advertisement is derisive or denigrating or unflattering of the competitor’s product or service does not necessarily imply that it amounts to disparagement in law," the Bench observed. Importantly, this is an interim order. The court has not given a final ruling on whether LAS or BIT in HUL’s products cause the effects claimed by Beco. The scientific dispute can be examined through evidence and expert testimony during the trial. The ‘War On What’s Hidden’ Campaign The case stems from HUL’s plea against Beco’s “War on What’s Hidden” campaign, which compared Beco’s products with HUL’s Surf Excel Matic Liquid and Vim Dishwash Gel. The campaign alleges that Surf Excel Matic Liquid contains 277 mg/kg of Benzisothiazolinone (BIT) and more than 10% Linear Alkylbenzene Sulfonate (LAS), while Vim Dishwash Gel contained more than 8% LAS. Beco claimed that its products do not contain LAS or BIT. In response to this, HUL alleged that the campaign amounted to commercial disparagement, trademark and trade dress infringement, copyright infringement, passing off and unfair competition. It argued that the ads went beyond pointing out the presence of certain ingredients and gave consumers the impression that Surf Excel and Vim are unsafe for use and could cause skin irritation, redness, itching and eczema. Beco defended the campaign, saying its claims were verified through independent NABL-accredited laboratories and supported by scientific literature and references from the WHO, OECD and European Chemicals Agency. It argued that the ads made ingredient-specific claims and did not directly state that HUL’s products were unsafe or toxic. The court, however, said it could not determine at the interim stage which of the competing scientific claims or laboratory reports was correct. The two sides also disputed the testing methods, which the court said would require expert evidence during the trial. The HC, however, noted that the ad campaign cannot be judged by examining each statement separately. Even if one part of an ad is technically correct, it can still be misleading depending on how its claims and visuals are presented. “A particular element of an advertisement may, when viewed in isolation, be accurate or truthful, but when juxtaposed with its other elements, the advertisement viewed as a whole may convey a false and/or misleading and/or deceptive message to an average consumer,” the court order, dated September 10, said. The court found that the use of complex chemical names, concentrations and percentages could give the impression that HUL’s products were risky to use. It believes that an average consumer is not expected to scientifically analyse an ad or examine its claims in detail, but is likely to take away the overall message presented. Therefore, the campaign went beyond simply comparing Beco’s products with HUL’s products and denigrated HUL’s products while presenting the claims as being backed by scientific evidence. The court reiterated that companies are free to highlight the strengths of their own products, including in comparison with rivals. Ultimately, the court said Beco had failed to establish at the interim stage that the material claims in the campaign were prima facie true or that they were not misleading, deceptive or misrepresentative.

Canada agrees on C$350 million air defense package for Ukraine, Carney says
Ukraine secures C$350 million from Canada for critical air defence interceptors as Kyiv runs low on Patriot missiles during intensified Russian attacks.
CALGARY, Alberta: Canada has agreed a C$350 million aid package for Kyiv to acquire air defense interceptors, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kyiv is running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia's ballistic missiles at a time when Moscow is stepping up its attacks.
"As Russia escalates its barbaric aerial warfare indiscriminately targeting civilian populations, Ukraine's air defences are critical," Carney told reporters in Calgary.
"Earlier today Canada and Ukraine finalised an agreement to deliver critical air defence interceptors...this C$350 million equipment package will help protect Ukraine's people, infrastructure, and skies," he said.
He did not give details of which interceptors would be delivered or when the aid would start flowing.
The weapons will be provided through a US program that allows third-party nations to quickly buy and supply weapons such as Patriot missiles to Ukraine.
"I thank you for this package. It's of (the) utmost importance, especially now," said Zelenskyy.
Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal defenders, has committed more than C$25.5 billion in overall aid since Russia invaded in February 2022, including C$8.5 billion in military assistance.
Carney also said Canada aimed to ramp up drone production to be able to produce millions of units within the next two years. A third of those would go to Ukraine, he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed more technology and funding to produce enough drones to fend off mass Russian attacks.
Canada is home to an estimated 1.3 to 1.4 million people of Ukrainian descent, forming one of the largest Ukrainian diasporas in the world.
As part of the deals signed on Thursday, Canada will provide nearly C$435 million in new loan guarantees to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support energy security in Ukraine, especially during the winter.

Platinum-based chemotherapy — in particular cisplatin and carboplatin — are a lifeline for children with certain cancers. These treatments, for instance, transformed the prognosis of hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is the most commonly diagnosed in childhood, from a five-year survival rate of 20% to more than 80% for localized tumors.
However, these medications work by damaging the DNA of cancer cells, and they are also known to cause mutations in the DNA of healthy cells, potentially raising the risk of new cancers later in life. The mutations have been documented in adults, but the picture is less clear when it comes to children. A new study published Thursday in Science sought a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. The researchers sampled tissues from the liver — both healthy and cancerous — and the patient’s blood, analyzing them through a sophisticated DNA sequencing technique called NanoSeq.
They then compared the sequencing results to those from children who had been treated with different drugs, or had not been treated prior to surgery, as well as to fetal liver tissue. They found that being exposed to platinum agents led to hundreds of mutations in genes (on average 2,200 per liver sample), a burden of mutation usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Mutation load also increased proportionally to platinum exposure: children who received only cisplatin had a smaller number of mutations than those who received both cisplatin and carboplatin. These mutations could increase the likelihood of liver pathologies, or the emergence of secondary tumors, the authors said.
“We found lots of cancer genes but also genes associated with long-term changes in liver metabolism,” said Foad Rouhani, one of the authors of the paper and a professor at King’s College in London. However, he stressed that “by no means does that mean that these cells will definitely become cancerous in time. All we talk about is there was evidence for potential for these cells to eventually cause problems further down the line.”
Liver cells showed many more mutations than blood cells, even though chemotherapy is a systemic treatment. “The platinum is doing something differently to liver cells than other cells. Either it’s been metabolized differently or the liver cells are repairing differently, we don’t really know yet,” said Rouhani. This could mean that the liver was more susceptible to the effects of platinum, or it could be the other way around: The extent of the mutations may explain why that liver got sick in the first place.
In a perspective article, Sanjeev Vasudevan and Donald Williams Parsons, both professors at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, wrote that the findings “provide strong evidence for conducting survivorship studies of children that have undergone treatment for liver cancer beyond their third decade of life.”
For the study authors, its primary contribution lies in establishing that the damage occurs, so clinicians can monitor these patients more closely during their lifetimes, said Rouhani, and identify issues at an earlier stage.
But there could be a prospective impact on treatment. “If we understand the mechanism, can we then eventually be able to design next-generation chemotherapies which are highly effective at treating the cancer but actually leave the background tissue largely untouched?” said Rouhani.

Fenerbahce coach announces resignation, club president tells him to stay
ISTANBUL, Sept 10 : Fenerbahce head coach Ismail Kartal announced his resignation on Thursday after a 1-1 draw with Roma in his team's return to the Champions League, but minutes later the club president said Kartal would stay in the job.
The 65-year-old Kartal told a press conference he was leaving "never to return", adding that he had taken the decision "to clear the way for the club".
Minutes after the press conference, Fenerbahce president Aziz Yildirim told reporters that Kartal "continues in his role".
"Some fans threw a bottle at the coach's head this evening during the game. He is upset about it," Yildirim said.
"I just spoke to Ismail Kartal. He mentioned the bottle incident and he also complained about being under pressure."
Asked if Kartal had told him that he would stay, Yildirim said: "There's no need for him to say (openly) that he'd continue. I am his senior, I told him to continue and that's it. We are a family."
Kartal, who spent a decade at Fenerbahce as a player, coached the club in 2014-15, then on an interim basis in 2021-22 before returning for a full campaign in 2023-24. He was assistant manager at Fenerbahce the last two times the club won the Super Lig and returned for a fourth managerial spell in June.
Fenerbahce have finished second in the Turkish top flight in the last five seasons and reached the league phase of the Champions League this season for the first time in 18 years.

Labor Day is in the rearview mirror, kids are back to school, and a squall of pumpkin spice is upon us. It’s that time again to prepare for the equally inevitable respiratory virus season with annual vaccines.
With fervent anti-vaccine activist Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as the country’s top health official, it might seem like the rollout of this year’s shots could be a disaster. For instance, one of Kennedy’s first actions as health secretary last year was to obliterate an ad campaign for flu shots amid a particularly deadly flu season. As we head into this fall, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine advisory committee—which normally sets vaccination recommendations and insurance coverage for the shots—is nonfunctioning. A federal judge ruled in March that the anti-vaccine allies Kennedy installed on the panel were illegally appointed and unfit to serve. All their changes to vaccine policy have been temporarily voided. And meanwhile, Kennedy spent last week trying to obscure the number of babies who died from measles so far this year (it was two, including a newborn).
Big picture
Despite all of that, the fall vaccine effort is looking like it will likely be somewhat smooth, potentially unremarkable even. The Food and Drug Administration has approved updatedflu and COVID-19 shots for this season. Those shots have already begun arriving at pharmacies—in case your pharmacy hasn’t already sent you multiple texts and reminders. While there are still some snags for access, it seems like it will be a lot like last year’s fall vaccine rollout.
Major insurance plans have agreed to continue covering vaccines previously recommended by the CDC’s advisory panel, including the seasonal ones, at no charge. That agreement runs at least through the end of 2027.
State and local health officials are also expecting a generally normal rollout and are keeping an eye toward improving vaccination rates.
“As we head into another respiratory virus season, state and territorial health agencies are doing what we do best: preparing early, watching the data closely, and working with our healthcare and community partners to keep people safe,” Manisha Juthani, president of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) and commissioner for the Connecticut Department of Public Health, said. “Vaccination remains one of the most effective tools we have to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death from flu, COVID-19, and RSV.”
As we saw last year, leading medical organizations have stepped in to fill the void of the CDC’s advisory committee and produced their own evidence-based vaccine recommendations, complete with a transparent scientific review explaining the basis for the recommendations.
The 2026–27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations and the evidence base behind them were released last week in a collaborative effort by the American Medical Association, the Vaccine Integrity Project, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA).
Overall, little has changed in the evidence-based recommendations from last year. But here’s the breakdown.
This year’s trivalent flu vaccines are recommended by the medical groups for all children (6 months and up) and all adults. There’s also a nasal spray for people ages 2 to 49, but it’s not recommended for people who are pregnant or immunocompromised. People age 65 and older are recommended to get a high-dose vaccine.
The biggest uncertainty this season will likely be with the new mRNA flu vaccine, approved for adults 50 and up in early August. The vaccine, Moderna’s mFlusiva, was found to be 27 percent more effective than a standard shot in trials but may have more mild side effects, like fatigue and injection-site soreness. It’s unclear how available this vaccine will be this year, given its late approval in the year. It’s also unclear what insurance coverage will look like, given its lack of a previous recommendation from the CDC’s advisory committee. Medicare is expected to cover mFlusiva, and some state Medicaid programs may cover it as well. But other federal programs, like Vaccines for Adults, may not cover it, and commercial insurance coverage is also uncertain.
The best time to get a flu vaccine is generally the span between late September and the end of October. This typically ensures the vaccine’s protection is at its strongest in the window when influenza typically peaks, between December and February. After a flu shot, it takes about two weeks for protection to kick in, but then it wanes through the flu season, which can sometimes stretch out to May.
There are some exceptions to the September–October recommendation, including if children need two shots or if a shot needs to be timed during pregnancy to provide protection to a baby after birth. These groups may want to get their flu shots earlier.
For COVID-19
Under the Trump administration and Kennedy, the FDA again approved COVID-19 vaccines for limited groups: those age 65 and older, and those age 6 months to 64 years who have a condition that puts them at higher risk. The list of qualifying conditions is long and varied, ranging from cancers to physical inactivity. Many Americans qualify.
Last year, Kennedy’s dubious CDC vaccine advisors actually voted to ease access to COVID-19 vaccines from the FDA’s restrictions (potentially accidentally); they made access based on individual decision-making instead of qualifying health conditions. This meant that, aside from a few states with restrictive laws regulating pharmacists, most people under 65 could go to a big pharmacy, like CVS or Walgreens, and self-attest that they had a reason to be vaccinated, no prescription or medical documentation needed.
This year, the federal court ruling in March that blocked Kennedy’s vaccine advisors also reversed the advisors’ vote for individual decision-making. That puts the official federal recommendation for COVID-19 vaccines in limbo. Nevertheless, vaccine access is looking pretty similar to what happened last year. Big pharmacies, like CVS and Walgreens—where most people get their COVID-19 shots—have said they’ll continue to let people under 65 self-attest, again with a few state exceptions. For instance, people under 65 in Louisiana may need a prescription to get a COVID-19 vaccine at a pharmacy. Doctors, meanwhile, can provide the vaccines off-label in any state.
Without federal recommendations, healthcare providers can turn to the medical groups’ recommendation. They urge seasonal COVID-19 vaccination for children ages 6 months to 23 months and all adults, including during pregnancy. Those age 65 and up are recommended to get a second dose six months later. Children ages 2–18 are recommended to get the vaccine if they are at higher risk or if they just want to get vaccinated.
The timing of COVID-19 vaccines can be tricky to decide because the SARS-CoV-2 virus has different seasonal trends than flu and other respiratory viruses. Waiting until cases are clearly on a sharp incline can mean protection will come too late. But getting it too early may mean protection could wane before the wave, like the flu shot.
Currently, cases are on the rise nationally in a late-summer surge but are still relatively low. For convenience, some experts recommend getting your COVID-19 shot along with your flu shot. But if you want to hold out for peak protection during a winter wave, you may want to plan for a shot as late as November.
For RSV
The respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine is not a seasonal vaccine, but it protects against a seasonal virus. As before, people 75 and older are recommended to get a one-time RSV vaccine, as are people ages 50 to 74 who are at higher risk.
Between September 1 and March 1, pregnant people should get a one-time RSV vaccine in their first eligible pregnancy between 32 and 36 weeks. The timing of the vaccination allows for protective maternal antibodies from the vaccine to be passed to babies who are then born during RSV season. This recommendation includes a notable update from the medical groups’ recommendations last year, which previously identified the RSV season from September 1 to only the end of January. The update reflects new trends in RSV transmission.
Babies less than 8 months old who were born without such maternal vaccine protection are recommended to get a monoclonal antibody drug to protect against severe disease, as are babies at high risk between 8 and 19 months.
Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes.

The National Medical Commission’s plan to create a National Medical Register (NMR), is running into rough weather again as doctors are questioning why medical practitioners are being made to pay a fee and register again for entry into the NMR when their database is already available with respective State Medical Councils.
The question assumes significance as the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the National Medical Commission (NMC) is moving to amend the Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2026.
The NMR is envisaged as a single, reliable national database that would make it easier to verify doctors’ qualifications and registration status and facilitate their practice across State boundaries. The system envisages a unique NMR identification number linked to every doctor’s State registration number.
The dispute now is over how this national database would be created -- is it the task of the State Medical Councils to provide the data for the creation of the NMR or should individual doctors have to put in application afresh, pay a fee and then await EMRB’s verification of credentials?
What the law says
Doctors point out that the NMC Act, 2019, already settles this. In Sections 31(1) , 31 (6) and 31 (7), the NMC Act says that the EMRB “shall maintain a National Register” of all licensed medical practitioners.; the State Medical Councils will maintain and update respective State Registers with the EMRB and that it will be the task of EMRB to maintain the National Register and ensure the electronic synchronisation with the State Registers.
“Nowhere in the NMC Act is it stated that it is the responsibility of registered medical practitioners to apply for NMR registration,” points out the Kannur-based doctor and RTI activist, K.V. Babu. Also, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2025, the Union Health Ministry, quoting the NMC, had said that applying for NMR registration was voluntary.
Doctors therefore argue that the NMR should be populated from the verified data already held by State Medical Councils. “Our data is already with the State Medical Council and it just needs to be handed over to the EMRB. We fail to understand why the NMR database creation should be so complicated and why doctors are being put through the registration and verification formalities all over again,” says the State President of Indian Medical Association, Kerala, M.N. Menon
A registration backlog
The concern raised by doctors is genuine. Applications submitted by several doctors for NMR registration have remained pending before the EMRB for years, raising questions about the practicality of requiring every State-registered doctor to individually apply for national registration. According to the minutes of the NMC’s 17th meeting, fewer than 32,000 registered medical practitioners had applied for NMR registration by December 2025.
The cost angle
The issue also has a financial dimension. Doctors point out that they are already paying a substantial amount as registration and licensing-related charges to State Medical Councils. The registration fee that will be charged in the name of NMR will be another burden on doctors, Dr. Babu says.
Doctors have demanded that the NMC withdraw the proposed draft amendment and ask State Medical Councils to send its database to the EMRB for creating the NMR as well as the unique ID for doctors

Jimmy Kimmel has said an interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on ABC. Kimmel accused the Federal Communications Commission of pressuring the network and its affiliates over the booking.
The interview, which was not aired on television, will be released on YouTube.
Kimmel announced the decision during Wednesday night's episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, saying the programme had faced threats from the FCC over its decision to interview Talarico, a Democrat running for the US Senate in Texas.
“Now that he is president, his FCC threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don't like,” Kimmel said, referring to President Donald Trump.
The dispute centres on the FCC's equal-time rules which generally require broadcast stations to provide comparable opportunities to legally qualified candidates competing for the same office.
For decades, daytime and late-night talk shows had generally been treated as “bona-fide” news programmes and were exempt from the requirement of interviewing political candidates. But the Republican-led FCC changed that position in January, meaning talk shows could potentially face equal-time obligations when featuring candidates.
Kimmel argued that political candidates had long appeared on late-night television without creating such problems. He pointed to previous interviews on his programme, including appearances by Trump when he was a candidate.
The host said the changed approach had now put pressure on ABC and its local affiliates, particularly as Talarico campaigns in one of the country's closely watched senate races.
ABC declined to comment to the decision, according to Reuters.
The Kimmel episode is not the first time Talarico has found himself at the centre of a dispute involving a late-night programme and the FCC.
Earlier this year, an interview with Talarico on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert was also moved away from television amid concerns about the equal-time rule. The interview was subsequently made available online, rather than airing through the programme's traditional broadcast.
That history made Kimmel's announcement particularly notable. What might once have been an ordinary late-night guest appearance has now become part of a wider argument over whether broadcast regulation is beginning to the influence editorial decision at American television networks.
Talarico is running in Texas, where he is seeking to win a Senate race that could have implications for control of the chamber after the November election. He is set to face the Republican candidate emerging from the contest involving Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Kimmel's comments come amid growing tension between broadcasters and the FCC under the Trump administration.
Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez criticised the agency's approach following the latest dispute, describing concerns over political interference in broadcasters' editorial decisions. ABC has also been engaged in a broader legal fight with the FCC over regulatory actions involving the network and its affiliates.
The White House has not been shown to have directly ordered ABC to pull the Talarico interview. Kimmel's accusation is that regulatory pressure created an environment in which the network and its affiliates were unwilling to risk airing it.
For viewers the practical outcome is - the interview has not disappeared but it will not be seen on ABC's broadcast network. Instead, it will be released online.
For Kimmel, however, the decision represents something much larger. His argument is that a routine choice over whom to invite onto a late-night programme is no longer being treated as a purely editorial decision — and that the consequences of that shift are now playing out on American television.
