Wow, that was quick.
The Supreme Court just handed Republicans a surprisingly decisive midterm loss
For the second time this week, the Court rules against Missouri’s Republican gerrymander.
At 10:03 am ET, according to the Supreme Court’s docket, a group of Republican plaintiffs filed a brief asking the Court to bless a GOP gerrymander in Missouri. Less than half an hour later, the Court issued a brief order telling these Republicans no — a rare scolding from this Court for the Republican Party, and a rejection of the party’s latest effort to skew elections in its favor.
The decision is notable for this Court, but it isn’t particularly surprising. Earlier this week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied a similar request from another set of Republican litigants. But, minutes after Kavanaugh did so, a Donald Trump-appointed federal judge issued a new order that would have forced Missouri to use the Republican Party’s maps anyway.
The Court’s new decision in People Not Politicians v. Onder places that judge’s decision on hold. As a practical matter, this means that, in the upcoming midterm elections, Missouri will almost certainly use the same maps it used in the 2024 election — which elected six Republicans and two Democrats to the US House — rather than the new maps, which were designed to give Republicans an extra seat.
Reading between the lines of the Court’s order in People Not Politicians, it appears that the justices were quite frustrated by the Republican Party’s tactics in this dispute. When Kavanaugh previously denied the GOP’s request to use its new gerrymandered maps, he did so using a process that allows a single justice to dispose of a case — a process the justices rarely use unless they view a matter as so one-sided that it’s not worth formally involving their colleagues.
Similarly, the Court’s new order was issued almost immediately after the Republican plaintiffs filed their brief — so fast, in fact, that it’s unclear whether the justices even had time to read that brief. And the order also appears to be unanimous. No justice indicated that they dissent (although it is possible that one or more justices disagree with the order but decided not to make that disagreement public).
This is how the Court behaves when they want to send a clear signal that a litigant’s arguments are entirely without merit. It’s the judicial equivalent of a spanking.
More broadly, the litigation over the Missouri gerrymander should give some assurance to Democrats, and to supporters of liberal democracy more broadly, that this Court isn’t wholly subservient to President Donald Trump or his Republican Party. The Court has a 6-3 Republican majority, and it often hands down decisions benefiting the GOP that cannot be defended using the traditional tools of legal reasoning — such as its 2024 decision holding that Trump may use the powers of the presidency to commit crimes.
But it appears that there are some lines that this Court won’t allow the Republican Party to cross.
Republicans created a “disaster” in Missouri and then demanded that the Supreme Court fix it
It is likely that the Supreme Court’s decision in People Not Politicians will lead to some serious short-term chaos in Missouri, although all of that chaos should be blamed on Republican officials within Missouri.
In September of 2025, the state’s Republican legislature enacted the new maps, as part of a broader Republican Party effort to gerrymander red states in order to give the GOP an edge in the upcoming midterm elections. But Missouri’s constitution permits opponents of a new law to put the law on hold if they collect enough signatures to trigger a ballot referendum — if a referendum is triggered, the state constitution provides that the law will not take effect unless it is approved by voters in the next election.
Opponents of the new maps submitted their petitions seeking a referendum in December of 2025, but Missouri’s Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, sat on those petitions for months — and then rejected them on the last possible date permitted under state law, August 4, 2026. As it happens, this was the same date that Missouri held its congressional primaries. So one consequence of Hoskins’s delay tactic is that many voters who voted in one district during the primary will vote in a different district in this November’s general election.
Hoskins was able to delay litigation over whether the petitions seeking a referendum are valid because a state law provides that lawsuits concerning such a referendum must be filed within 10 days after the secretary of state rules on whether a referendum should take place.
In any event, because of Hoskins’s delay, the Missouri Supreme Court did not rule on the referendum until September 3, when it determined that Hoskins was wrong to reject the petitions. That means that the law enacting the new maps is not in effect and Missouri must use its old maps in the 2026 general election — even though that means that election officials must scramble to sort voters into their proper districts before November.
In an extraordinary act of chutzpah, Hoskins argued in both the Missouri Supreme Court and the US Supreme Court that the state court’s decision came too late and should not take effect because reimplementing the old maps would be too disruptive. He even told the federal justices that “a federal-election disaster is unfolding in Missouri.”
But, as the state supreme court said in its opinion, this argument is “particularly misplaced given the secretary’s delay created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains.”
Given this background, the most surprising part of this case may be that a federal district judge then attempted to put the new maps in place, despite Hoskins’s tactics and despite the fact that Kavanaugh had already ruled against Missouri Republicans once. The Supreme Court’s new order technically only puts that district judge’s decision on temporary hold, but the hold should last through the 2026 election — thus ensuring that the old maps will be used in that election.
The GOP’s legal arguments in People Not Politicians were weak
Setting aside Hoskins’s bad behavior, Republicans made very similar arguments in both Hoskins and Onder, and those arguments were weak. I lay those arguments out in more detail here, but the short version is that they asked the Supreme Court to revive a discredited doctrine that it has rejected many times over the course of more than a century. And they also asked the justices to create a new right to vote in the same congressional district during both a primary and general election.
In light of the Court’s new order in People Not Politicians, it appears that none of these arguments persuaded the justices.
Again, that’s a reassuring sign for Democrats that this Court will not give Republicans literally anything that they ask for in an election-related case. Although it remains to be seen how the Court will rule on several other major election cases that are currently pending before the justices, including one that could potentially shut down voting by mail in many US states.

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Zelensky’s plane ‘almost hit’ by Russian drone as deadly strikes rock Moldovan border
Drone exploded 160km from main airport as Moldova forced to shut airspace due to incoming Russian drones
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's flight from Moldova to Norway was delayed after it was almost hit by a Russian drone, Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Store said.
Officials in Moldova said they had to shut down the country’s airspace because of a drone incursion as Russian forces targeted the border between that country and Ukraine this week.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Store said yesterday. The drone exploded around 160km from Moldova’s main Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were eventually lifted and Zelensky’s plane took off later than scheduled.
At least two people were killed yesterday when a swarm of Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern region of Odesa.
The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighbouring Romania, a Nato member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties.
Another Russian drone had crashed in a sunflower field on Tuesday causing four fires to break out, Moldovan police said.
Russian drones kill two at Ukraine-Moldova border crossing
Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern region of Odesa, killing two people, Ukrainian and Moldovan officials said, as Moscow targets trade and logistics routes to cause economic damage.
Two civilians were killed and three wounded in the attack on the Starokozache border crossing in southwest Ukraine, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said on Telegram.
The checkpoint, about a kilometre (half a mile) from Moldovan territory, is used daily by thousands of people and hundreds of cars. Moldovan officials said passenger and vehicle traffic was halted by the attack.
Russia has struck five border crossings in recent weeks, the Ukrainian border guards said — four on the border with Moldova and one on its border with Romania, a Nato member.
Flight carrying Zelensky to Norway delayed in Moldova because of drone incursion
A flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.
The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighbouring Romania, a Nato member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties.
Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.
Moldovan authorities confirmed the drone came down and exploded 160km (100 miles) from Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were lifted and Zelensky’s plane took off later than scheduled.
Russia says it detained a man who spied on British diplomats in Moscow for Ukraine
Russia's FSB internal security agency said it has detained a former guard at the British Embassy in Moscow who collected personal data on British diplomats, alleging that he had been working for Ukrainian intelligence.
The agency said the data collection was part of preparations for a Ukrainian false-flag operation against British diplomatic staff in Russia, aimed at accusing Russia of hostile actions at a later stage.
The UK government has yet to comment on the developments in Moscow.
Zelensky’s plane ‘almost hit’ by Russian drone as deadly strikes rock Moldovan border
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's flight from Moldova to Norway was delayed after it was almost hit by a Russian drone, Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Store said.
Officials in Moldova said they had to shut down the country’s airspace because of a drone incursion as Russian forces targeted the border between that country and Ukraine this week.

The drone exploded around 160km from Moldova’s main Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were eventually lifted and Zelensky’s plane took off later than scheduled.
At least two people were killed yesterday when a swarm of Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern region of Odesa.
The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighbouring Romania, a Nato member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties.
Another Russian drone had crashed in a sunflower field on Tuesday causing four fires to break out, Moldovan police said.
Ukraine drones spark fire at Russia's Caspian Sea port
Authorities have doused a fire ignited by Ukraine drone strikes on port infrastructure in Russia's Caspian Sea city of Makhachkala in Dagestan, the region's acting head Fyodor Shchukin said.
Both sides have exchanged major strikes on each other in the early hours today.
Four killed as Russia hits Ukraine's Black Sea port facilities
Russia's defence ministry claims it hit facilities “used for military purposes” in Ukraine's Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, two vessels near Odesa and a drone warehouse in Mykolaiv overnight.
The ministry made the comments on the Telegram messaging app.
The air strikes on Ukraine's port of Mykolaiv hit civilian and industrial infrastructure there on Wednesday and overnight, killing four and injuring 19, acting regional governor Heorhii Reshetilov said.
Trump says Putin wants to make a deal in Ukraine but says two sides 'hate each other'
Donald Trump said he had a "great" conversation with Russian president Vladimir Putin earlier in the week and that the Russian leader wanted to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine.
“He is wanting to make a deal, and if (Ukrainian president Volodymyr) Zelensky is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One en route to Dallas for the Republican National Convention.
Trump spoke over the phone with Putin on Tuesday, shortly after US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, returned from a diplomatic swing through Moscow and Kyiv.
“The holdup is two people who hate each other," Trump told reporters, referring to Putin and Zelensky.
“I think more than anything else, it's two people that hate each other."
North Korea's Kim celebrates troops involved in supporting Putin's invasion of Ukraine
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has issued a message of gratitude to his country's troops who supported Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, state media KCNA said.
Kim referred to the troops during a speech at Pyongyang's assembly hall on Wednesday, amid celebrations marking the 78th anniversary of the country's founding.
He thanks workers and soldiers for their contributions to the state, and extended what KCNA called special gratitude and respect to commanders and soldiers "participating in overseas military operations", likely referring to North Korean troops deployed for Russia's war in Ukraine.
In return for sending troops and munitions to join Russia's war effort, Pyongyang has received economic and military technology assistance from Moscow, according to South Korean intelligence assessments.
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to fight alongside Russian forces since late 2024, according to Western and South Korean officials.
Pyongyang was continuing preparations for an additional troop deployment to Russia, but there were no signs that such a deployment was imminent, according to South Korea's defence ministry in late August.
CIA chief Ratcliffe preparing for bigger role in Russia and Ukraine talks – report
CIA director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a bigger role in Washington's negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, US officials told their European counterparts, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday.
CIA spokesperson Liz Lyons denied the report, calling it "false" in a post on X.
The report, citing people familiar with the matter, said the White House is considering scaling back the involvement of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the Ukraine peace effort.
Five killed and 24 injured in Russian attack on Sumy
At least five people have been killed and 24 injured in a Russian air strike on Ukraine’s Sumy, police officials said this morning.
Regional governor Oleh Hryhorov said earlier that a Russian drone had struck a shopping centre in Sumy on Wednesday and put the toll at two killed and 20 injured.

Chubu Electric Power announced Thursday that its electricity retail subsidiary Chubu Electric Power Miraiz had mistakenly been overcharging many of its customers for more than two years.
The company said the Nagoya-based subsidiary had miscalculated the cost price that the electricity fees are based on.
At least 5,009,000 customers, half of which are households, have been overpaying. They occupy around 57% of the total number of contracts.
The value of excess payments collected totaled roughly ¥1.2 billion ($7.81 million), with the amount overcharged monthly being ¥152 per customer at most.
The money will be refunded.
Based on the change made in April 2024 to the fees paid by electricity retail firms to power distribution operators to use their transmission network, the subsidiary was supposed to set the increase in power generation costs to ¥47.4 billion over a three-year period, but it mistakenly set the cost at ¥50.1 billion.
Chubu Electric said it was not intentional.

How to watch the Flame Fatales 2026 speedrunning marathon
The fundraiser for Malala Fund runs September 13-19.
Summer is winding down, but gamers haven't turned down the heat. This Sunday is the start of Flame Fatales, a week-long charity speedrunning marathon raising money for Malala Fund. The event is run by Frame Fatales, a community under the Games Done Quick banner that spotlights and uplifts women and femmes in speedrunning.
Flame Fatales starts on September 13 at 12:30PM ET and lasts until September 19. The show will stream live on the GDQ channels on both Twitch and YouTube during the week. The Flame Fatales marathon isn't a 24/7 affair like the mainstage GDQ events; instead, each day's gaming begins at 1PM ET and usually wraps by midnight, so be sure to check each day's schedule if there's anything in particular you're keen to watch.

SC directs reputation loss compensation for compulsorily retired bureaucrat
The Supreme Court set aside the Central Administrative Tribunal and Delhi high court orders and directed his farewell
The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed the government to pay ₹9 lakh in compensation for a bureaucrat’s loss of reputation after his compulsory retirement in 2018 on the grounds of questionable integrity, and to ensure a proper farewell at his office.
A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nadu directed that all emoluments, notional promotional benefits, and the ₹6 lakh that the former Indian Trade Service (ITS) officer SS Das incurred on the eight-year legal battle be paid to him.
The court ordered the Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) to call Das back to the office and give him the fitting farewell he deserved on his superannuation.
Das was issued a compulsory retirement order in May 2018 while he was the DGFT department joint secretary, five years before he was due to retire. The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and then the Delhi high court dismissed his challenge in January 2024, prompting him to move the Supreme Court.
The bench set aside the CAT and high court orders and directed his farewell with full honour and in the manner in which he would have received on the date of his superannuation. It said Das was entitled to all service benefits, including the notional promotion gained by any of his juniors during the period that he remained out of service.
The bench found that Das’s confidential service records marked him “outstanding” and “very good” throughout his career and the Union Public Service Commission recommended his promotion as joint secretary considering his excellent track record and uncompromising integrity.
The compulsory retirement order cited the action to be in “public interest” on account of the “questionable reputation and conduct”.
The bench found that the decision was based on an additional secretary’s note which the court dismissed as not being worth the paper it was written on. “The said note is not only bizarre, but sinister in its design. The immediate and inevitable question that arises on its perusal is, was the then additional secretary acting to protect the interest of the department or to espouse the cause of the representatives of the domestic industry,” the bench said.
The bench said such a note, bereft of any credibility, was made the foundation for showing the door to an excellent public servant who, by dint of his independence, integrity and courage, stood tall to ward off pressures from the domestic industry to protect the interest of the revenue.
“It does not require great intelligence to fathom the why and what of it, and as to who orchestrated the move for the marching orders to be given to such an officer,” said the bench, citing the service records. “We deem it fit to observe that this is a fit case, in which, the order smacks of arbitrariness, perversity and mala fides, warranting the case for judicial interference in full force.”
The order was passed under Fundamental Rule 56(j) even as the government argued that this provision grants discretion to the competent officer to act in public interest. The bench underlined that discretion is not a charter for arbitrariness. It added that reputation is earned by dedicating the best years of life to the service of the nation.
The bench said dismissing such a hard-earned reputation as “dead wood” smacks of a high degree of malice and a colourable exercise of power. It added that recourse to FR 56(j) should not be exercised lightly or casually. The bench added that it must be founded on credible, cogent material worthy of being acted upon and not on mere suspicion and conjecture.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The Bhopal Municipal Corporation's (BMC) crackdown on commercial activities in residential areas has come under scrutiny over a major discrepancy in the figures in its Action Taken Report (ATR) submitted to the Supreme Court.
After the Aug 5 Supreme Court hearing, corporation officials had claimed that more than 62,000 commercial properties had been identified for allegedly carrying out commercial activities in residential zones.
The BMC's zone-wise figures show a total of 7,617 cases, while the affidavit mentions 7,951 cases, leaving a further difference of 334 cases.
However, in an affidavit prepared for the Sep 15 Supreme Court hearing, the corporation has reported only 7,951 cases in which Rule-11 notices were issued. The sharp difference has raised questions over the basis of the earlier 62,000-property figure.
Meanwhile, following the Satya Niketan building collapse in Delhi, which killed seven people and injured 12, the Supreme Court has sought affidavits and reports on compliance with its earlier directions concerning building safety.
The BMC will also have to provide details of dilapidated buildings and action taken against them. The matter is scheduled for hearing on Sep 15 at 2 pm.
190 premises reported closed
The affidavit states that 190 premises were closed and sealed for unauthorised use. Corporation records, however, indicate that only seven establishments were actually sealed, while panchnamas were prepared for the voluntary closure of 183 premises. Another section of the affidavit says 170 premises were closed, of which 165 were subsequently restored after being found compliant with sanctioned occupancy norms, while five remained sealed.
296 illegal construction cases identified
Apart from land-use violations, the corporation has identified 296 cases of unauthorised construction or deviations from sanctioned building plans. Notices were issued under Sections 302(1) and 307(2). Hearings have been completed in 124 cases, while illegal constructions or encroachments were removed in 75 cases.
3-year-old notice remains pending
An electronic showroom in Arera E-1 had received a corporation notice in 2019 over commercial use in a residential area. The High Court subsequently granted a 15-day window before action could be taken. That period expired nearly three years ago, but the corporation has yet to take action.

CUPERTINO, Calif.—Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative update that—as usual—focuses heavily on both performance and new camera features. This time around, many of the new camera features are oriented around giving the user more direct control of the image, rather than depending entirely on Apple’s computational photography assumptions.
As usual, the new iPhone has a new chip. It’s called A20 Pro, and it’s the first 2 nm chip for the iPhone. It has a 6-core CPU, with two super-cores that are up to 20 percent faster, and four efficiency cores. A 7-core GPU offers up to 40 percent improved performance and increased bandwidth.
The A20 Pro also has a new Neural Engine—the machine-learning processor on the system-on-chip—which the company says is basically two Neural Engines on one chip.
Apple spent a significant chunk of the iPhone presentation talking up Apple Intelligence, arguing that the iPhone is a perfect place to establish and maintain the context for effective AI features—for example, with access to your calendar and daily habits—but of course tried to differentiate on the basis of privacy within that context. The company also discussed the previously announced new LLM-driven capabilities of Siri. Siri AI, as Apple calls it, will arrive in October.

Five dead and 86 missing as 'heartbreaking' fire breaks out on Philippines ferry
- Published
At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.
The MV June Aster, which set off from the capital Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron in the province of Palawan when it caught fire.
The blaze, which erupted at 18:00 local time (10:00 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and poor weather were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.
A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking".
"I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," the first responder said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination.
Video clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats.
"Reports from our vessel indicate strong currents in the area," a spokesman from the coastguard tell the BBC, noting that the ferry had drifted from its initial distress location – four nautical miles off Barangay Turda – to a point 7.68 nautical miles away.
"It has been carried further out by the current. These are the challenges our personnel are facing in the search area."
The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said, adding that it had not yet spoken to any of the 43 people who'd been rescued.
The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear.
Anelyn Magbanua is among those anxiously waiting for news of their loved ones.
Her husband Marlon had spent a few days in Manila visiting their two children, who were going to school in the capital city.
Magbanua last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron, she tells the BBC.
"I was expecting that the ferry will arrive at the pier at between 18:00 and 19:00 yesterday," she said, adding that she had gone to bed early but was awakened by a cousin who told her the ferry Marlon was on had caught fire.
"I couldn't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night," Magbanua says.
She'd travelled to a hospital in Coron, hoping to find Marlon among the survivors – but he remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she says.
Rai Garcia has three family friends among those missing.
Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy.
They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire.
"We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says.
"We still hope and pray for their safety."
Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives.
Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment.
Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands.
Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air.
But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year.
Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws.
In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao.
But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately 2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only 40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders
The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.
Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.
Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs
Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down the burden of corneal blindness and make the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight. Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman.
The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions.
In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states.
“GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.”
In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play.
There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors.
“There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman.
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City.
Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.”
In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice.
For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR.
“I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.”

క్లెయిమ్: 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రతి రోజు రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పనిచేయకుండా మెటా ఆంక్షలు విధించింది.
ఫాక్ట్ (నిజం): అమెరికాలో Meta, వివిధ రాష్ట్రాల 52 అటార్నీ జనరల్స్తో ఒక ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చింది. దీని ప్రకారం 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం Instagram, Facebookలో కొన్ని కొత్త పరిమితులు, భద్రతా చర్యలు అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది. ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని ఈ ఒప్పందంలో పాల్గొన్న రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లోని 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు వర్తిస్తాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలో 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ మూసివేయబడుతుందని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు. పైగా మెటా ఇటువంటి నిబంధనలు ఇతర దేశాలకు వర్తిస్తాయని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ క్లెయిమ్ గురించి తగిన కీ వర్డ్స్ ఉపయోగించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతికితే, మెటా ఇటువంటి విధులను ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా విధిస్తున్నట్టు ఎటువంటి సమాచారం మాకు లభించలేదు.
అయితే, అమెరికాలో Meta, వివిధ రాష్ట్రాల 52 అటార్నీ జనరల్స్తో ఒక ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చింది. ఈ ఒప్పందానికి కోర్టు ఆమోదం కూడా లభించింది. దీని ప్రకారం 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం Instagram, Facebookలో కొన్ని కొత్త పరిమితులు, భద్రతా చర్యలు అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది. ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని ఈ ఒప్పందంలో పాల్గొన్న రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లోని 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు వర్తిస్తాయి. ఇవి USలో ఉన్న ఇతర మెటా వినియోగదారులందరికీ వర్తించవు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ).

అమెరికాలో Meta కుదుర్చుకున్న ఒప్పందానికి ఇప్పటికే అంగీకారం లభించింది. ఈ ఒప్పందాన్ని కోర్టు కూడా ఆమోదించింది. దీంతో 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం ఒప్పందంలో పేర్కొన్న భద్రతా చర్యలను Meta దశలవారీగా అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది అని నివేదికలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలోని చాలా నిబంధనలు 10 సంవత్సరాల పాటు అమల్లో ఉంటాయని, ఈ కొత్త భద్రతా ప్రమాణాలను TikTok, YouTube కూడా అమలు చేయాలని Meta కోరింది.
అయితే, ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని కొన్ని రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లో 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలో 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ మూసివేయబడుతుందని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ).
చివరిగా, 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రతి రోజు రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పనిచేయకుండా మెటా ఎటువంటి నిబంధనలను అమలు చేయలేదు.

What Colin Powell Did on 9/11
His insistence during an overseas trip on championing democracy in foreign policy is now a relic.
Secretary of State Colin Powell was having breakfast with Peru’s president in Lima’s historic center on September 11, 2001, when an aide passed him a note to inform him that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. Minutes later, he received a second note. “Oh my God,” Powell said aloud.
Later that morning, as the scale of the destruction in New York and Washington was starting to become clear, Powell delivered remarks in a cavernous hotel ballroom. Fears of additional attacks had forced the closure of U.S. airspace. Even senior Cabinet members remained in the dark about President George W. Bush’s whereabouts. Peru’s leaders knew that the secretary of state—the fourth in line to succeed the president—would likely need to depart. But Powell, a former chairman of the Joint Chiefs before he was picked by Bush to lead the Foreign Service, opted to stay—at least for a while.
The former general was in Peru, along with foreign ministers from across the Americas, to cement a new hemisphere-wide democracy charter that would enshrine the region’s commitment to free and fair elections and the rule of law. I was there as a Lima-based correspondent covering the visit. Countries across Latin America were emerging from a long period of despotism and military dictatorship. The United States wanted to make sure the region didn’t backslide. “A terrible, terrible tragedy has befallen my nation, but it has befallen all of the nations of this region, all the nations of the world, and befallen all those who believe in democracy,” Powell told the room full of officials, his voice grave but steady. “It is important that I remain here for a bit longer in order to be part of the consensus of this new charter.”
As the magnitude of the events in the United States washed over me, Powell’s composure and his focus on a point of principle stood out. Even at an extreme, wounded moment in America’s history, he was affirming that the country’s security was inextricably bound up with how U.S. allies represented—or didn’t represent—the will of their people. Strong democracies would support America’s ability to keep itself safe. Powell could have bolted home. But he lingered to make the point. The ministers adopted the charter by acclamation, and by 12:30 p.m. eastern time, Powell had taken his leave for Washington, D.C.—and for everything that followed from the events of that day.
This week, 25 years later, I watched a different secretary of state visit Lima. Marco Rubio is meeting Peruvian leaders today on a tour of Andean nations that have taken a turn to the political right. Given the magnitude of what followed 9/11—the wars, the excesses, the lives lost—Powell’s connection to Peru that day has receded from our collective memory. But his insistence on linking democracy promotion to national security seems remote. Donald Trump rose to power, in part, on the backlash to the post-9/11 wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. In his view, the idea of spreading democracy around the world was an expensive folly, and he’s sold his supporters on a very different approach to foreign policy.
In Latin America, the Trump administration has pushed the “Donroe Doctrine,” a 21st-century version of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that’s designed to secure “American preeminence” and allied support for the president’s priorities of shutting out drugs, migrants, and U.S. rivals such as China. Trump’s second-term National Security Strategy elevates “flexible realism” and brass-tacks interests such as access to strategic resources in the region. “Democracy” is mentioned three times, while “interests” are cited 36 times. Mutual benefits with other countries can be pursued “without imposing on them democratic or other social change that differs widely from their traditions and histories,” the document says.
In practice, that has meant partnerships with those willing to embrace Trump’s militarized approach to combating drugs, crime, and illegal migration, regardless of those countries’ governing systems. The deportation of migrants to a nightmarish prison in El Salvador is a prime example, as is the ouster of the leftist Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and the norm-busting oil deal made with Maduro’s deputy. Or consider the militarized counter-drug operations the Pentagon has pursued with Ecuadorean President Daniel Noboa, who at the same time has dissolved opposition parties and targeted rivals. Trump has enthusiastically waded into the region’s elections to endorse candidates who share his political vision: Javier Milei of Argentina, Abelardo de la Espriella of Colombia, Tito Asfura of Honduras. Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s campaign of boat strikes against alleged narco-traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which critics label as extrajudicial killings, grinds on.
“Politeness and a good bit of decorum are all to the good, but over the last generation, things have gone too far,” Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s policy chief, told Latin American defense officials in a speech in Peru earlier this year. “Our rhetoric became wildly detached from the reality of our interests. We talked about the fate of people halfway around the world as if they were as important to us as our neighbors.”
Instead of trying to build ideal societies in far-flung countries, Colby said, the United States would now advance its hard-nosed interests in its immediate neighborhood, using the U.S. military to help allies assert control over lawless areas, treating drug traffickers like the Pentagon treats jihadist groups, and blocking U.S. adversaries’ access to minerals and other key resources. What he dubbed the “Peace Corps” approach to reducing the throngs of migrants and crime headed toward the U.S. had failed, Colby said. If it’s a Latin America democracy that partners with Washington to achieve those goals, great. If it’s not, no one’s going to spend much time worrying about that.
The State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggott told me in a written statement that the United States is “working together with our allies and partners to address the shared opportunities in our hemisphere, and to confront the shared challenges, including defeating the scourge of narcoterrorism that has killed so many.”
Many Latin Americans are ready to at least entertain this shift, according to polls. Spiraling crime, ineffective governance, and the hangover of the COVID era has made trading political liberties for security and economic growth a conceivable option. One of the most popular politicians in the region is Nayib Bukele, the Salvadoran strongman responsible for some of the region’s most flagrant democratic reversals but whose taming of rampant gang violence has made him an icon to many. Democratic backsliding has also occurred on Latin America’s left. After this year’s Colombian elections, Gustavo Petro, de la Espriella’s leftist predecessor, made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud intended to sow doubt about the results.
Rubio presents a plausible case that the armed groups now fueling rampant violence across many Latin American nations are the public’s paramount concern. Those groups not only traffic drugs; they are in some places better bankrolled and armed than the state. In stops in Colombia and Ecuador this week, Rubio made an impassioned case for action. “You have to make a choice here. We’re going to choose on the side of leaders that are going to be serious about taking these groups on and eliminating them once and for all,” he said after talks with Noboa yesterday. “Otherwise, those groups—those terrorist groups—will eat these countries up.”
But the people of the region are also setting limits on how far America’s reach is allowed to extend. Noboa has allowed U.S. forces to begin joint military operations, but Ecuadoreans rejected a proposal last year that would have permitted the United States to establish military bases in the country. This week, Rubio announced that Peru, under conservative President Keiko Fujimori, will be joining the administration’s “Shield of the Americas,” Trump’s militarized counter-drug program. It’s unclear how far Fujimori, whose father, Alberto Fujimori, is both lionized and vilified in Peru for his autocratic campaign against armed leftist movements in the 1990s, will feel she can go in cooperation with Washington.
“What I see is less of a story about Trump and his government urging allies to go down this road, and more a story of these sovereign countries, these societies, having this debate about the trade-offs between political liberties and anti-crime policy,” Brian Winter, a Latin America expert who is the editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me. Based on my years of working in Latin America, the long shadow of yanqui meddling is hard to overstate. And polls show that many people in Latin America today see China, not the United States, as the more reliable superpower.
The U.S. interest in promoting democracy as a pillar of national security didn’t begin in 2001. It may have reached its peak in the 1990s. But the grand U.S.-led experiments of Afghanistan and Iraq, as well as movements elsewhere to overthrow dictators, dominated the first decade of this century—with disappointing results. Several years after 9/11, I was in Baghdad, chronicling the U.S. effort to extract Iraq from the sectarian bloodshed unleashed by the 2003 invasion. Since then, Iraq has managed to emerge as a deeply flawed but surprisingly enduring democracy. I covered Libyan rebels’ overthrow of the dictator Muammar Qaddafi in Tripoli in 2011. Libya remains a failed state, 15 years later. And I was covering the Biden administration when the two-decade effort to build a stable democracy in Afghanistan fell apart in a matter of days.
Perhaps not surprisingly, the consensus of many Americans, and certainly of MAGA supporters, is that the push to elevate democracy in the farthest reaches of the world proved to be a waste of time and money. That conclusion underpins the Trump administration’s approach in Latin America and beyond. When Trump went to war with Iran in February, democracy was an afterthought, and opponents to the country’s authoritarian regime were left to fend for themselves.
But the failures of America’s democracy-promotion experiments have eclipsed notable successes across Eastern Europe and parts of Asia. Steven Levitsky, the director of the David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies at Harvard University, told me that Latin America has proven to be a democratic success story. The chief exceptions—among them Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Cuba—need to be set against the region’s largest nations. That big countries such as Brazil and Argentina have generally stayed the democratic course despite extreme inequality, high crime, and a global democratic recession, Levitsky said, “is a sign of extraordinary resilience.”
Venezuela presents the most explicit test of how traditional U.S. values will play into Trump’s pursuit of what he sees as America’s national interest. Predictions that the country would descend into chaos after Maduro’s ouster have so far proved wrong. Yet the most tangible sign of American involvement in Venezuela’s affairs to date has been a new oil deal, which gives an office in the Pentagon a stake in the nation’s future output. Rubio has laid out a three-stage plan for shepherding Venezuela to legitimate and elected governance, and he has stressed that the country first needs to rebuild its legal and institutional structures. He argues that the oil pact will benefit Venezuelans. No date for elections—and therefore no date for democracy to return to Caracas—has been set.
Powell, who died in 2021, might have had something to say about that. In the hotel ballroom in Lima, with the U.S. homeland under its most serious attack since Pearl Harbor, he talked about a different model, one that linked democracy to achieving prosperity and peace. He noted that the countries represented around him had their own tragic histories with terrorism—Peru’s battle with the Shining Path, for instance. “It is something we must all unite behind,” Powell said. “We unite behind it as democratic nations committed to individual liberties, committed to the rights of people to live in peace and freedom in a way in which they, and not terrorists, select their leaders or define how they will be governed.” It was the means, not only the ends, that he clung to that day.

Thursday 10 September 2026 21:52, UK
Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will continue their quest to become the first American men's Grand Slam champion since Andy Roddick's 2003 triumph at Flushing Meadows as the US Open reaches its semi-final stage.
Shelton sent defending champion Carlos Alcaraz packing in the early hours of Wednesday with the pair slugging it out in the latest-finishing match in tournament history as he reached his third major semi-final, having made the final four in the 2023 US Open and 2025 Australian Open.
"That was a war," said Shelton. "The most enjoyable match that I've had in my career."

Tiafoe recovered from two sets and a break down to beat compatriot Alex Michelsen, reaching the semi-finals for a third time in a thrilling fightback.
The American has provided treasured memories for the home fans in New York, from his dragon-slaying defeat of Rafael Nadal en route to the 2022 semi-final, to his blockbuster win over compatriot Shelton two years ago.
But the Cincinnati runner-up this year is ready to write a new chapter this time around, saying: "I'm just a different person in general. Those two runs (to the semi-finals) were great, something I will cherish forever, but I'm not that person who I was when I made one in 2022 and when I made one in '24. I'm not that person. I'm excited to see what this me does," said Tiafoe.
"I have higher hopes for myself. So yeah, it's great. The tournament is still going. There's a lot more tennis to be played, a lot more sets to be played, and a lot more physical things to be done. We're going to enjoy this, but we got to keep going."
Tiafoe is enjoying a career resurgence having undertaken a big lifestyle change and fitness regime towards the end of last year.
Former world No 1 Lindsay Davenport said: "If you hear their stories about last fall, and what a dark place Frances was in, he was willing to turn over, to try and give it his best shot.
"It's not easy sometimes for players or people to do that, but he has kind of shifted everything in his life to revolve around tennis.
"Now to watch him be able to go out there and compete from two sets down, like the old Frances doesn't necessarily (do), to stick his heels in and be like 'I'm not going anywhere' - I mean, he's fighting."
Zverev going about his business
While the men's draw has fallen to pieces in the absence of Jannik Sinner and with Novak Djokovic and Alcaraz falling by the wayside, Alexander Zverev has been quietly going about his business.
Luciano Darderi, the 21st seed, is the highest-ranked player Zverev has faced, while he eased past world No 70 Botic van de Zandschulp in straight sets.
The 29-year-old is a big favourite to beat unseeded Russian Karen Khachanov in the opening semi-final on Friday from 8pm on Sky Sports Tennis.
Zverev has beaten Shelton in all five of their career meetings and has lost just one of his 10 matches against Tiafoe.
Having won his first Grand Slam title at this year's French Open and then reached the Wimbledon final, the world No 2 should be feeling at home in the latter stages of major tournaments.
But he said: "I think the more often that you get to that stage, the more normal it becomes, which is something that you should never take for granted.
"I know it can change in a heartbeat in tennis. I think confidence is something that is incredibly important, but also can go away quite quickly.
"I found that out after Wimbledon where I didn't play well throughout the two tournaments on the hard courts, and then I found it again here.
"But yeah, of course I'm happy with how things are going, but looking forward, I still hope to play two good matches here."
Khachanov has been here before
Khachanov is seeking his first major final having reached the semi-finals of the US Open in 2022 and the Australian Open in 2023.
Khachanov was unseeded in a Grand Slam tournament for the first time since 2018 after a strange season.
He reached at least the third round of all four majors for the first time but is just 10-15 in other events, with losses in the opening rounds of all three hard-court events before coming to New York.
Zverev and Khachanov, both in the 1990s generation, have met nine times, with the German holding a 6-3 edge.
Their most notable encounter came in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics final, when Zverev won in straight sets to take gold, while their only previous Grand Slam meeting came at the French Open in 2018, when Zverev fought back from a set down to win in five.

The Japanese government said Thursday that it has demanded a correction to an Equal Earth world map on a website, claiming that the map uses the same color for Russian territory as it does for four islands that Japan and Russia have a territorial dispute over.
The correction demand was made to the operator of the website via the Japanese Embassy in the United States, according to Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara.
“Displays that contradict the Japanese government’s position are seen (on the map),” Kihara said at a news conference. “We need to prevent incorrect perceptions regarding our country’s territories and geographical names from spreading,” the top government spokesman stressed.
The map contains a description stating that the islands, which Japan calls the Northern Territories, are effectively controlled by Russia but also claimed by Japan. The Japanese government maintains that the islands are part of Japan’s inherent territory.
The Equal Earth map projection accurately represents the size of each continent. Earlier this month, the U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution calling for the use of maps using the projection.
At Thursday’s news conference, Kihara noted that the U.N. resolution does not encourage the use of specific maps using the projection.

When Sen. John Fetterman’s support of Israel garnered him ill will in an increasingly pro-Palestinian Democratic caucus in May 2024, Sen. Cory Booker attempted to rehabilitate his colleague’s sudden turn toward more right-wing, moralistic positions with praise, casting the still-aphasic stroke survivor as an “inspiring figure” whose “moral voice,” despite his language impairments, had “only grown stronger.”
In September, 15 months after Booker’s statement, a Wall Street Journal investigation described a senator so checked out that he skipped 11 of 12 hearings in one stretch, dismissed Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia officials as wanting “free trips to D.C.,” and called a three-hour funeral for slain police officers “a nonstarter.” Rep. Brendan Boyle, a fellow Pennsylvania Democrat, called him “a disgrace” and “lazy.”
In all of the discourse that followed publication of the Wall Street Journal article, one thing has been largely glossed over: In 2022, toward the end of his Senate campaign, Fetterman suffered a stroke. The striking difference between the campaigning Fetterman and the legislating Fetterman, and the interpretation of that change, may be just the latest reminder of how our country is ill-prepared to deal with the complex medical matters of our politicians.
We are not diagnosing Sen. Fetterman. Neither of us has examined him, and no honest case can be built from press clippings. But as physicians who specialize in treating the behavioral outcomes of neurological diseases, which can alter fundamental aspects of human perception and personality, we can say this much: Nothing in the recent reporting is medically surprising.
Start with Boyle’s comment on “laziness.” A stroke survivor’s behavioral and psychiatric changes are often misconstrued through a moral lens as character faults. Many stroke survivors deal with “apathy.” It’s a symptom that families are significantly troubled by, as it distorts routine, agenda, and even basic activities of daily living. About a third of stroke survivors develop it in a clinically measurable form: not sadness, but a blunting of initiative, a withdrawal from effortful and immediately unrewarding tasks, distinct from depression and traceable to disrupted circuits linking the frontal lobes to the brain’s reward system. It is, almost point for point, the profile described in the Journal’s account: a senator who won’t sit through a hearing, who cancels on veterans, who finds a funeral simply not worth the hours.
None of that excuses his behavior, but a change of brain function, rather than a change of heart, is something his constituents need to consider. Lazy is a character judgment requiring atonement, while apathy is a syndrome requiring treatment.
Then there is the other Fetterman, the strident one who tore off his Harvard hood in support of Israel, feuded publicly with Sen. Bob Menendez (D) for his refusal to step down during his corruption investigation, and hardened into one of his party’s most vocal critics of loose U.S. border policy.
Exactly how much Fetterman has changed since his stroke is up for debate. But psychiatry’s diagnostic manual formally recognizes personality change due to brain injury like stroke, and frontal lobe damage has been tied to altered judgment and disinhibition since a tamping iron was driven through Phineas Gage’s skull in 1848. More recent work maps a “moral brain network” distributed across frontal, temporal, and cingulate cortex — territory that a stroke severe enough to impair speech, as Fetterman’s was, often also touches, since language and that circuitry share real estate in the front of the brain. The frontal lobes are essential for action physically and metaphysically motivated, whether that action be word or deed. When Fetterman’s words and deeds are affected, they have a broader impact than those of a patient refusing to shower for weeks or eloping from the house at midnight. Fetterman’s words become the nation’s deeds.
Brain injuries often impair a person’s abilities, but can sometimes enhance or exaggerate cognitive function. (Newfound artistic creativity with certain forms of dementia is one well-documented example.) This is because healthy brain areas, previously regulated by the injured region, are no longer suppressed through a mechanism called “paradoxical facilitation,” in which the loss of function in one faculty indirectly produces a gain of function in another. Decades of research link right brain activity to moral judgment and its inactivity to deficiencies, even to the point of sociopathy.
The left brain, by contrast, commands language processing, and following a stroke to the left brain, a person can develop not only a communication disorder but often post-stroke depression as well. (Of course, we don’t know which side of Fetterman’s brain was affected by the stroke, and again, we are not diagnosing him.)
If the senator’s moralism has been unfettered by his stroke, with a shift toward right-brain moralistic processing, that does not diminish his sincere intent or its effect. In fact, it could buffer against accusations of political expediency. Applied cautiously, this suggests that a stroke could intensify, not fabricate, the force of a person’s convictions, including ones that predate the injury.
Read together, apathy and moral zeal look contradictory. They are not. Apathy is domain-specific: Patients disengage from routine, effortful obligations while remaining fully capable of intense engagement with whatever still feels urgent or relevant. A senator who cannot be bothered with a hospital’s Medicaid concerns but will cancel a schedule to go on Fox News over Israel is not necessarily inconsistent. Both actions may derive from the same underlying changes.
None of this settles anything, and it should not be mistaken for a defense. An authentic, brain-mediated intensified focus of conviction is not the same as sound judgment, and it does not answer whether a senator who cannot reliably show up for his constituents should keep his seat. What it does is name a third option beyond “disgrace” and “inspiration”: that Fetterman’s conduct may be neither a personal failing nor a moral awakening, but a documented, and only partly modifiable consequence of surviving a stroke. A conviction with a neurological substrate is still that person’s conviction. A lapse with one is still a lapse.
The deeper problem is that Washington has no vocabulary for this, and therefore it has no apparatus to assess it. Pilots and surgeons face periodic fitness-for-duty review. Presidents have the 25th Amendment, rarely as it’s invoked. Senators have neither — only an electorate armed with anonymous staffer accounts and a word bank running from “hit piece” to “trust fund baby.” As the Senate ages, Fetterman won’t be the last case litigated entirely in that vocabulary, for want of any real capacity to evaluate, accommodate, or retire an official on medical grounds. And with at least half a dozen members of Congress having had strokes in the past decade, the public should be demanding more thorough neuropsychiatric evaluation of its politicians after illness.
To ask how much of the senator now in front of us is the man and how much is the injury is a cartoon of the Cartesian mind-body paradox. The honest and humane response to that uncertainty is not concealment but contextualization — the recognition that a brain injury which could have silenced a burgeoning political career in 2022 is still rewriting the rules by which we voters are now judging it.
Michael P.H. Stanley is a cognitive neurologist in Boston. Isaiah Kletenik is a behavioral neurologist in Boston.

The Asian Games began in Japan on Thursday when Qatar beat Iran in the men’s basketball opening group game, the first action in the continental multi-sport showpiece that has more participants than the Olympics.
Over 17,000 athletes and officials are expected to take part in 43 sports at the Nagoya-Aichi Games — which do not officially start until the opening ceremony on September 19 and will run until October 4.
Several events, such as basketball, football, cricket, hockey and modern pentathlon, will get underway before the opening ceremony.
Qatar held off a comeback from Iran to win its Group B encounter 59-35 at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya in the first match of a men’s basketball competition that will hold medal finals on September 20, the day after the opening ceremony.
Los Angeles 2028 Olympics qualifying spots are up for grabs in several sports at the Asian Games, which are returning to Japan for the first time since 1994.
Organisers hope the athletes will have a “unique experience” staying in eye-catching accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.
Officials are confident that the plan will not be affected by Japan’s typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October.
Weather has already caused disruptions, with record rainfall on Tuesday forcing hundreds of athletes briefly to evacuate their accommodation.
Rainwater also leaked into some competition venues, with more wet weather forecast for the coming days.
Among those in action at the Games will be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of world-class teenage talents in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
