A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a girl in Ladakh being abducted from her home by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) workers on the instructions of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Vinay Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.
Fact: The video shows a Jaranan performance. Also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, Jaranan is a traditional Javanese dance. The video does not show a Congress-supporting girl in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but did not find any police reports, credible news reports, or records about Vinay Kumar or RSS workers abducting a Congress supporter in Ladakh.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to the same video (archived) uploaded on the Instagram handle tubagusjakaa on 29 August 2026. The post featured similar visuals, and its caption read, “Mendem Jaranan”. The post also included hashtags such as #jaranan, #mendemjaranan, #kerasukan, #mbekes, #kudalumping, and #jatilan.
Jaranan, also known as Kuda Lumping, Jaran Kepang, or Jathilan, is a traditional Javanese dance from Indonesia in which performers dance while using flat, horse-shaped props made from woven bamboo, often accompanied by traditional gamelan music. The performance traditionally depicts horsemen or warriors and, in some forms, includes spiritual or trance elements in which dancers are believed to enter an altered state and perform unusual acts. It is performed both as cultural entertainment and as part of traditional or community events, and is regarded as an important part of Javanese cultural heritage (here, here).
The account that uploaded the video has also shared similar videos featuring people performing the same art form.
To sum up, a Jaranan performance video from Indonesia is falsely shared as a Congress supporter in Ladakh being abducted by RSS workers.

Since May 2025, the Delhi government has been setting up Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), which serve as primary healthcare centres, across the Capital. In phases, they replaced the Aam Aadmi Party government’s Mohalla Clinics, which are no longer operational. While many staff members were absorbed into the AAMs, some say they have not received their final salary dues and have been told that the budget for the payments is “under consideration”.
There were 553 Mohalla Clinics. So far, the Delhi government has set up 415 AAMs and aims to establish 1,100 in all. The centres were envisaged to provide additional services such as maternal and child healthcare, routine immunisation, free screening for non-communicable diseases and nearly 80 types of free diagnostic tests.
However, some former mohalla clinic staff who were not absorbed into the AAMs are still awaiting their dues. Dr. Amit Gupta, who worked at a mohalla clinic near Mandawali metro station, said he is owed ₹78,000. He said interviews for AAM posts were open to all staff and some were selected. He is currently practising at his own clinic.
‘Budget under consideration’
In an email to an east district health official, Dr. Gupta wrote, “It is very unfortunate that our salaries for January and February are still pending”.
He received a response from an official on August 27, seen by The Hindu, stating that the file had been transferred to the respective cell and that “the approval of budget is under consideration”.
Another senior Health Department official said, “Many of them have been retained by AAMs and have received their salaries till date. If there has been any negligence, we will look into the matter”.
Two staff members retained at AAMs told The Hindu that they had been receiving their salaries. Those who spoke of pending dues were among the staff not retained.
Pending dues
Mohalla Clinics employed four staff members each: a doctor, a pharmacist, a multi-task worker and a lab technician. AAMs have a similar staffing structure, though the number of personnel varies with the size of the centre.
A former multi-task worker at a mohalla clinic in the east district said, “I am trying to get a job in the AAM but the vacancy has not risen yet. We have been told by supervisors that the funds have not been released for our last salaries. I have been without a job since March, when the Mohalla Clinic shut.”
Another doctor said that, besides salaries, which were linked to the number of patients seen, staff had not received other dues, including cleaning and costs incurred in transporting medicines for the final month. “Authorities have said that they are doubtful that it will come through but we are still waiting.” The doctor said she was ineligible to apply to the AAMs because the age limit was 55.
Last year, Mohalla Clinic staff protested outside the Secretariat, demanding that they be retained at AAMs. Selection tests have since been conducted and several former staff members have been appointed. Some have approached the Delhi High Court over the matter, which is to be heard on September 8.

Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

Washington, Sep 10: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won't come down until after US midterm elections.
Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3 per cent, pushing international Brent crude past the USD 100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the US and Iran escalated.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
Trump, in an exchange with reporters before travelling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the US.
“They're desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
He added, “I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer.”
The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The US-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20 per cent of the world's petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.
The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the status of the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.
Trump last week downplayed the conflict as “small potatoes” even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.
The US has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.
Trump's prediction that the war won't be wrapped up until after November 3 comes after Vice President J D Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.
Vance told reporters he didn't want to set “artificial timelines” for the war's end.
“But when you ask, ‘When will this end?' You're asking me a question like, ‘When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?'” Vance said. “I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
US benchmark crude on Wednesday stood at around USD 96 a barrel, and US gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.
The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight to hit USD 4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.
Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high on Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to USD 5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.
Jet fuel has become so expensive that US and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.
The latest market gyrations come after the US military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

Smartphone maker Apple yesterday unveiled its first foldable smartphone, called iPhone Duo, at its flagship “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino. Japan’s Consumer Affairs Agency plans to comprehensively strengthen regulations over “dark patterns,” or website designs and other user interfaces that lead consumers to make decisions against their interests, sources said Thursday.
The plan is included in an interim report on dark patterns that was published by the agency the same day. The agency intends to submit related legislation, including a possible revision to the specified commercial transactions law, to next year’s ordinary parliament session.
As cases that should be regulated, the interim report cites unclear displays of payment amounts or contract periods, false displays about consumer reviews and inventory information, and displays using intimidating language to encourage consumers to file applications. It calls for administrative action against any violations.
According to the agency, dark patterns come in various forms, including methods designed to mislead consumers, and some cases are difficult to address under existing laws. In light of this situation, the interim report notes the need to consider comprehensive regulations.
The agency also released a separate interim report featuring a plan to restrict the unfair obstruction of cancellations of online subscription services and recurring product purchases. It is eyeing a revision to the consumer contract law.
Examples of such obstructions listed in the report include refusing to accept cancellation requests and unfairly delaying them.
The report also calls for encouraging businesses to notify consumers of the timing and methods for requesting cancellation when contracts are automatically renewed.

Fetterman goes MAGA in Trump tribute video at GOP convention
Democratic senator praised Republican colleague from Pennsylvania, Dave McCormick in surprise appearance
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman was a surprise virtual guest at Wednesday’s Republican convention in Dallas, Texas.
The senator’s slide to the right under the second Trump administration and the end of Joe Biden’s presidency is well-documented, but his appearance in a video explicitly for the use of Republican campaigning is still a new development for the Pennsylvania senator who won a close race to protect a Democratic Senate majority in 2022 and once took a highly oppositional tone toward Donald Trump and the MAGA-fied Republican Party.
Fetterman’s appearance came in the form of a video praising both Trump and his colleague in the Pennsylvania Senate delegation, Republican Dave McCormick. McCormick spoke Wednesday evening at the convention. In the video, Fetterman also rejected “socialism”, which he has linked to a wave of progressive candidates winning Democratic primaries in New York and other states.
"Yes, I’m Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I am a common-sense Democrat. I am always going to stand with America. I'm always going to reject the extremes [of] socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said haltingly in the video.
“Dave McCormick is the kind of senator who gets the job done,” he continued in the video.
The senator went on to make a statement that likely crossed a line for many in his party, as the Democrats are as little as two months away from potentially winning back majorities in the House and Senate: He praised the president and claimed that he would be able to work with Trump alongside Republicans.
“Right back over my shoulder, that's the iconic U.S. Steel mill, and that's exactly the kind of thing that we’ll work together and we’ll work with President Trump to fight and defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley,” said the Democratic senator.
His words drew immediate condemnations online, including at least one from a Democrat in the Pennsylvania congressional delegation who just days ago pilloried the senator over a report in The Wall Street Journal detailing Fetterman’s apparent disinterest in key parts of his job.
Rep. Chris Deluzio, a progressive from the Pittsburgh area, told reporters this week that he was considering a primary challenge against Fetterman in 2028.
“Too lazy to do it in person. Checks out,” joked the congressman on X.
Nick Field, a Pennsylvania-based elections analyst formerly with Sabato’s Crystal Ball, correctly predicted Fetterman’s surprise appearance at the convention. His reaction in the wake of the news was similar to Deluzio’s: “I was so close, should've realized Fetterman wouldn't bother to actually make the trip.”
Democrats in his party are hoping to take four seats in each of the House and Senate to win majorities in the two chambers in November. McCormick is less than two years into his first term as Pennsylvania’s junior senator and therefore not up for re-election this year, making his colleague’s video message slightly less awkward for his party — but only just.
Fetterman’s party is still trying to win key races in Maine, Texas, Alaska and a handful of other states. His endorsement of both his colleague and a Republican president with flagging approval ratings could still make that job tougher.
“Remove him from the senate democratic caucus. if he does this tonight, the removal must happen tomorrow. you don’t get to call yourself a Democrat and do shit like this,” wrote one angry Democrat on BlueSky.
The senator told The Independent in a statement Wednesday evening that he had no plans to help Republicans maintain control of the upper chamber if Democrats win four seats or more in the fall.
“My remarks introduced Dave McCormick as a great American and friend. We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA. We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life,” said Fetterman.
“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”
His presence on the campaign trail for Democrats this cycle, including those in battleground House districts in Pennsylvania, has been nonexistent this cycle. Deluzio, speaking to journalists in the wake of the Journal report, claimed it was because no one wanted him to campaign with them.
"I don’t think that Democrats want John Fetterman campaigning for them, and I say that as a guy who’s campaigning with Democrats in the most competitive and toughest districts across Pennsylvania," he said.

Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
- Published
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.
Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.
"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.
Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.
Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.
The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.
That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.
The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.
But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.
Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.
The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."
Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.
Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.
The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.
Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.
There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.
Additional reporting by Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu and the BBC Somali Service

After less than a year at Meta, the prominent AI researcher Andrew Tulloch is leaving for Anthropic.
He'll start next week, an Anthropic spokesperson told Business Insider, and work on the startup's inference and performance team, where he'll aim to optimize the training of Anthropic's AI models and how they respond to users.
As AI's talent wars steam on, Tulloch has become one of the most sought-after researchers. He had worked at Meta for 11 years prior to this latest stint, leaving for OpenAI in 2023. At OpenAI, he helped train its GPT-4o, GPT-4.5, and o3 models. He then cofounded Thinking Machines Lab in 2025.
Last year, while he was working at the AI startup, he turned down a pay offer from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg that could have totalled $1.5 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported. He ended up decamping for Meta in October.
Now, Tulloch will bring that extensive experience to Anthropic.
Tulloch and Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment. He's leaving the social media giant shortly after it launched Muse, an AI agent meant to autonomously complete tasks for users.
Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Google, and other tech companies have been in a pitched battle for AI researchers since the release of ChatGPT, giving experienced workers like Tulloch a great deal of leverage — and earning power.
Semafor first reported that Tulloch was leaving Meta.
For Anthropic, the hire may offer some calm in an intense moment. The company is preparing for its initial public offering, dueling with rivals for business, and reckoning with mounting concerns about the adverse effects of AI.
The researcher Jacob Coxon sparked a wave of concern this week when he announced that he'd resigned from Anthropic and wrote that the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

After Trump promised to pay $5,000 if Republicans win, here's what to expect Thursday
At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, President Trump made a stunning and implausible pledge: to send every American adult a $5,000 cash dividend. But only if his party maintains control of the House and the Senate in November's midterms.
"If the Republicans win, you win with us," Trump said to applause. "And it will be called the 'Trump dividend'. Congratulations. Now all we have to do is win."
That's a big "if." Republicans are facing significant political headwinds.
"We might not win," Trump admitted.
Quick math puts the bill for this proposed "dividend" at more than $1 trillion. Plus, it's illegal to pay or be paid to influence voting.
Trump's speech last night was a wide ranging, rally-style speech where he did everything from defend the Iran war to criticize the fashion sense of one Republican Senate candidate. He attacked Democrats as communist and extremists and begged Republicans to vote in November as if he were on the ballot.
"Please pretend that I'm running," he said. "If we don't have the majorities, so much can be lost."
Trump spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, far longer than scheduled.
He will deliver closing remarks tonight as well.
"But I'm not doing a big deal like this," he joked. "I gave you a lot of material. I don't have to do it twice."
The two-night event, hatched by Trump, was meant for Republicans to energize the base ahead of the midterms.
"It took a little imagination to think of it," Trump said of the first ever Republican midterm convention.
In a preview of what to expect tonight, the focus on Trump was clear as the event kicked off Wednesday, with a lineup of Republican lawmakers, candidates and everyday Americans, praising the president and his policies. It was capped off by Trump's headlining speech.
Speaking to an arena with whole sections of empty seats, Trump rallied the party faithful.
"The midterms are not supposed to be won by [the party of] the sitting president, and we're going to change that," Trump said, promising to visit the states and districts of every Republican facing a close race.
Tonight, Trump will share the convention's final hour with Vice President Vance. By the time Republicans hold their next convention in 2028, Trump will no longer be the center of the party's attention. There will be a new nominee and de facto party leader charting a course for Republicans.
The program tonight will include a tribute to the late republican activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated one year ago, and an observance of the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, which is Friday.
MAGA celebrities and cabinet members will also grace the stage tonight. Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is set to speak, along with Donald Trump Jr. and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Over the course of the convention, 19 Republicans in competitive House and Senate races will deliver short stump speeches. Many of them have used the stage to position the Republican Party as the party of the American people, painting Democrats as aligned with "socialism" and "communism."
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running to represent the state in the US Senate made those points, but also used his speech to ask for money.
"I need your prayers, your vote and your support," Paxton said. "If we lose Texas, we lose the common sense revolution. If we lose the common sense revolution, we lose America."
His Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico has a campaign cash advantage but Trump's Super PAC, MAGA Inc. just committed to spend $10 million, propping up Paxton and hitting Talarico. A Republican shouldn't be in a tight race in Texas, but Paxton has been plagued by scandal and weak fundraising.
Trump, in his remarks, urged Texans to vote for Paxton despite what the president considers to be his flaws.
"Some may not like the way he dresses. I don't," Trump said as part of a lengthy and lighthearted critique of the man he endorsed.

Dipke hits back at ‘CJP visits only BJP-ruled states to check schools’ criticism, cites Punjab, Karnataka visits
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday responded to criticism that the organisation visits only schools in BJP-ruled states.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday rejected criticism that the organisation selectively visits schools in BJP-ruled states, saying its teams had also inspected schools in Punjab, Karnataka and Jharkhand.
Citing these visits, Dipke said the organisation had raised shortcomings in the education systems of the three states with their respective governments.
“Sourav went to Punjab and spoke on shortcomings, Ashutosh went to Karnataka, Ankit went to Jharkhand,” Dipke said in a video posted on X.
Dipke said the visits had resulted in government officials taking cognisance of the concerns raised. He said the Punjab education minister called co-convenor Sourav Das for a meeting and assured him that the shortcomings highlighted by the organisation would be addressed.
According to Dipke, the Karnataka education minister similarly held a meeting with Ashutosh Ranka and assured the team that the issues raised would be worked on. He said a similar response came from the Jharkhand government.
Why Dipke's response?
His remarks came amid criticism of CJP's visits to schools in BJP-ruled states and allegations that the organisation was targeting those governments. Hitting back at the criticism, Dipke questioned why the organisation faced hostility when it highlighted poor conditions in schools.
“So when we show the condition of the schools in the BJP-ruled states, then why do they send goons? Why are you so much against education?” he said.
Dipke further accused his critics of being indifferent to the educational needs of children from poorer families. “You don't want the children of the poor to get a good school. You don't want the children of the poor to get a good education,” he said, before asking, “Why is education such a problem for the people of Pau-Pau?”

Dipke on suicide of MPSC aspirant
The CJP founder also described the suicide of MPSC aspirant Prathamesh Deshmukh as a "murder done by the system" and said the government must take steps to ensure that such incidents do not recur.
He said the growing demand for reservation was a result of the government's failure to provide quality education and employment opportunities to the youth.
Deshmukh, 28, who was preparing for the Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) examinations, allegedly died by suicide in Pune. A note left behind by him mentioned that he had a debt of around ₹2.5 lakh. A native of Paranda in Dharashiv, Deshmukh was staying in rented accommodation in the Navi Peth area while preparing for competitive examinations.
Dipke visited Khasapuri village in Dharashiv on Thursday and met Deshmukh's grieving family members.
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Dipke said Deshmukh had gone to Pune with the dream of securing a job and helping his family overcome poverty.
"He borrowed money from friends to meet his expenses. But due to paper leaks and delayed results, pressure mounted on students. This (Deshmukh's suicide) is system's fault and it is a murder done by the system," he alleged.
The CJP convenor said Deshmukh took the extreme step after becoming frustrated with the system, unemployment and the financial difficulties faced by youth in rural areas.

The iPhone Duo just might live up to the hype
It's got that Apple touch.
Apple's foldable iPhone has arrived, finally, after almost 10 years of rumors. Given how late the company was to the foldable party, many were expecting a miss or at least something that failed to excite. I think the iPhone Duo is hitting (mostly) all the right notes.
With foldables, the idea since the start was a tablet-sized screen that fits in your pocket. The best tablets are iPads, which is why the iPhone Duo matters — and not just for Apple. For the first time, the company that makes the best tablet is making a foldable.
At least with iOS 27, it's still mostly an iPhone experience, not an iPad one. Many of the features are the kind that we already expect from a foldable: app multitasking, more interface elements on the 7.6-inch inner screen and multi-camera FaceTime calls. The Duo also works with the Apple Pencil, a first for the iPhone.
But then there's that Apple touch: it does the obvious thing, and you wonder why no one else thought of it. With the iPhone Duo, Apple shifted the app dock to the side of the screen when it opens and did the same for menus. While the Galaxy Fold series has a similar feature, the Edge Panel is hidden away most of the time, housing tools and shortcuts like Now Brief and AI Select — things I use far less than core apps like Gmail or Messages.
Like Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo's screens have a more unified aspect ratio — if not precisely identical, as the company claimed in the announcement. And while it doesn't magically solve interface design complexities and wrinkles, early hands-on videos and what Apple has shown so far suggest it all looks like the UI "fits" better: it looks tidier, with more visual continuity. I like how unfolding the iPhone Duo transplants the front display screen onto the right side of the foldable display, plus the glossy transition animation that brings the other screen into focus as you unfurl.
Other Apple touches are present throughout the hardware. The iPhone Duo's volume buttons are on the upper edge, so they're always in the same place regardless of which screen you use on the iPhone Duo. On the screens themselves, a nano-coating gives a matte finish that not only reduces reflections in harsh light but also helps obscure that foldable crease that companies and some die-hard phone fans are obsessed with. Why is Apple the first to do this?
I think the asymmetric front-screen design is charming, too. With two curved and two squared-off corners, it's like a notepad or a book and looks cute either way. Did Apple sneak in a return to skeuomorphism? (Xiaomi beat Apple to the punch by a day, but its 18 Fold smartphone isn't launching globally.)
Perhaps the biggest surprise was that, despite the typical "Apple premium" and spiraling component prices, the company's first foldable will land at $2,000. I suspected it would be several hundred dollars more. This price puts it between foldable rivals like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold ($1,899) and the Galaxy Fold 8 Ultra ($2,100), and roughly matches the launch price of the Galaxy Fold 8's launch price. That's not the Apple I'm used to. (History note: Samsung's debut Galaxy Fold cost $1,980 in 2019.)
A lot of my favorite parts of the iPhone Duo are small things that add up to a better overall experience. But aside from the matte nano-coating and Apple Pencil support, there's nothing as substantial as, say, when the company ditched the home button on the iPhone X and introduced Face ID. (Funnily enough, the iPhone Duo reverts to Touch ID.)
Existing foldables already do some things better, too. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can open and run up to five apps total: three split-screen and two in floating windows. While the iPhone Duo's two-app function may seem underwhelming, it's likely a deliberate choice by Apple, not a technical limitation. I've never used more than three apps across the 10-plus foldables I've tested and reviewed over the years, because it gets messy. Also, you can just swipe to the other apps, chill.
Like Samsung's Fold 8, this is still an expensive smartphone. $2,000 is a lot for an iPhone, especially one without a telephoto camera and without the iPhone 18 Pro's headline variable-aperture camera. It's an odd look when the priciest iPhone ever lacks its best camera ever.
Despite these downsides, I'm most excited by how Apple is tackling the problems (and potential) of the foldable. Conventional knowledge (and experience) suggests holding back on a first-of-its-kind device from Apple, but this isn't its first smartphone. For those aching for a foldable that wasn't running Android, it's here, and it looks like it will deliver.

Sakshi Gallery is marking its 40th anniversary with ‘Of Being and Becoming’, an exhibition featuring over 46 artists across three generations at Travancore Palace in New Delhi.

Artist Riyas Komu, whose work will feature at the event, said he has been associated with the gallery since his student days.“Sakshi was the first gallery that responded to my work,” Mr. Komu told The Hindu. Quick Answer
Instagram uses icons for likes, comments, reposts, saves, messages, Reels, Stories, calls, profile tools, notifications, active status, and more. This guide explains what every major Instagram symbol means and what happens when you tap it.
Instagram is the most popular app with billions of users around the world. The platform has lately been getting plenty of new features and fixes.
Instagram is also one of the few platforms that are known for experimentation. Meta often changes their layout very often, which can sometimes confuse users. If you are new to Instagram, or even an existing user, the new features and some icons you never use can be confusing.
Some of the features on Instagram don’t have an undo option, so it is better to know what they do before pressing them. In this guide, you will learn everything about Instagram icons, their meanings, and what they are used for. To make it easy for you, we have included each and every icon on every page of Instagram and explained what it does.
Table of Contents
What Do Instagram Symbols and Icons Mean?
Instagram Post Symbols Meaning
Instagram posts are what we see and interact with most on a daily basis while using the app.
They come with several engaging elements. Most of them are easy to understand, but if you are confused, here is what they mean:
- Like: Wherever you see this heart symbol on Instagram, it represents a like for posts, comments, and all
- Comment: This represents a comment on the post. Tapping on it reveals all the comments, and you can also add a comment.
- Repost: Instagram has recently introduced the ability to repost. The reposted post also appears on your feed.
- Save: The save feature lets you save posts; in other words, it works like a bookmark.
Instagram Home Screen and Bottom Navigation Bar Icons Meaning
Now let’s look at what the icons mean on the home screen and on the bottom navigation bar.
You won’t find many icons on the home screen, except for the ability to create a new post and to view all your notifications.
If there is one area that Instagram constantly experiments with, it is the bottom navigation. Meta keeps changing the positions of the icons and also changes their designs frequently.
Here is what they mean:
- Notifications: The heart symbol here represents notifications. Here, you can see all the notifications you receive inside the Instagram app.
- Create: The plus symbol here represents “create,” which you can use to create a post or a story and more.
- Home: Tapping on the home icon takes you to the home screen. It is part of the main bottom navigation. Tapping on it also takes you to the latest posts.
- Reels: Instagram has added a dedicated Reels tab, where you can tap on it to go to the Reels section.
- Messages: Tapping on this icon takes you to the Instagram Messages screen, previously known as DMs.
- Search: Tapping on the search icon takes you to the Explore page.
- Profile: This is a profile icon, which takes you to your profile page.
Instagram Reels Tab Icons Meaning
Instagram offers a dedicated Reels tab where you can see all the latest Instagram Reels. It also comes with several interactive elements, some of which are already used for posts.
Here is what each and every icon means in the Instagram Reels tab:
- Create: You can also add new posts directly from the Reels page. You can tap on the Plus icon.
- Like: It lets you like the Reel you are watching. You can like it, and tapping on it removes your like.
- Comments: Lets you add a comment and see comments for the Reel you are currently watching.
- Repost: It lets you repost the Reel you are currently watching.
- Share: It lets you share the Reel with your friends. You can also copy the Reel link using this option.
- Save: You can save or bookmark the Reel using this icon.
- More options: Gives more options for Reels, including Playback controls, Meta AI, and much more.
- Audio: It represents the audio used for the Reel. Tapping on it reveals more details.
Instagram DM Page Icons Meaning
Instagram DMs are among the most feature-packed, yet Instagram somehow manages to keep them minimal. However, they do come with several icons. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram message space:
- New message: It lets you create a new message. After tapping, you can select the user and send a message.
- Notifications off: It appears if you turned off notifications for Instagram.
We missed highlighting the Instagram Instant feature that the company introduced very recently. It lets you share a random photo with other users without complex editing.
It is turned on by default, and tapping on it shares whatever your phone camera sees, so be careful before pressing it. There is also an option to turn it off completely
Instagram Profile Page Icons Meaning
Instagram profile page also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what they mean:
- Create: Lets you create a new post, Reel, or Story from your profile page too
- Menu: Lets you access main and global Instagram app settings
- Threads: Lets you open the Threads app by Instagram.
- Discover people: The icon lets you discover new friends. It appears when you have a lower following count.
- Posts: Represents the Posts tab
- Reels: It represents the Reels tab
- Tagged posts: It represents the tagged posts where you can see all the posts you were tagged in by your friends.
- Pinned post: It means the user has pinned the post. Instagram lets the user pin up to three posts.
Instagram DM Message Icons Meaning
The chat interface also comes with plenty of icons, which can be confusing for a beginner. Here is what each icon means inside Instagram chats:
- Instagram Blend Feature: This is an Instagram Blend feature where you can invite the user to the Blend, where you can see each other’s suggested Reels, new Reel suggestions based on the chat, and much more.
- Voice call: Lets you make a voice call to the user
- Video call: Lets you make a video call to the user
- Voice message: Lets you send a voice message in the chat
- Photo library: Lets you select the local photos on your phone and send them to the chat
- Stickers: Lets you access the stickers
- More options: Gives you more options, including the ability to send location, draw, and access Meta AI and much more
- Camera: Lets you access the camera, where you can quickly take a photo and share it with the user.
Instagram Share Screen Icons Meaning
The share screen on Instagram is very simple. It is very similar to the other share screens, but it comes with one unique icon that lets you create groups. Here is what that icon means:
- Create group: This is the share screen that appears when you tap on the share button under the post or the Reel. The user icon means you can create a new group.
Instagram Call Screen Icons Meaning
Instagram calling screen also comes with several icons during the call, and here is what each of them means:
- Camera off: During the video call, it lets you control the camera. If you see a cross line, it means your camera is turned off
- Mute microphone: Lets you mute or unmute your camera
- Speaker off: Lets you turn on or off sound from the other user
- End call: End the video or voice call using this button.
Instagram Story Editor Icons Meaning
If you are adding a story for the first time, it can be confusing because Instagram Stories are feature-packed and let you customize everything you upload. Here is what each icon means on the Instagram Stories screen:
- Add text: While adding an Instagram Story, tapping on this icon lets you add text
- Stickers: It lets you add stickers to an Instagram Story
- Music: Lets you add and select music.
- Effects: Lets you add effects
- More tools: More creator tools. Tapping on it lets you access more tools
- Next: Once added, you can move to the next screen while adding a Story
Instagram Profile Bio Options Icons Meaning
Instagram profile bio also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what each icon means and what it does:
- Notifications: Lets you turn on or off notifications for this account.
- More options: Gives you more options about the Instagram profile you are viewing
- Profile link: Instagram lets users add links in their bio. The link icon represents the link the creator added to their Instagram bio. It is also available for regular users.
More Instagram Profile Icons Meaning
Here are more icons that you see when you visit any Instagram profile, including icons in the top right corner of the post and the verified blue checkmark right next to the profile. Here is what they mean:
- Verified badge: Instagram has verified the account, which means it represents the official account. Also, Instagram allows users to pay for the verified badge.
- Video or Reel: If you see this on top of the post, it means the post contains a video or Reel.
- Carousel post: If you see this with a number, it means it is a carousel post.
Instagram Reels Controls Icons Meaning
In the Reels tab, when you pause the Reel, Instagram displays more icons. Here is what they mean, including the recent Friends tab icons:
- Create: The plus icon lets you create a new post or Reel
- Trending audio: If you see an arrow next to the audio file name, it means that audio is trending
- Sound: Lets you turn off sound or turn on sound for the video. It appears when you tap on the video
- Play: It appears when you pause the video. Lets you play the video again
- More options: Again, tapping on this option gives you more Reel options
- Reposted by a friend: If you see a purple arrow icon, it means the Reel is reposted by your friend. If you see the like, it means the Reel is liked by your friends.
More Instagram Messages Icons Meaning
Here is what the different icons mean in the Instagram DM space. If you have multiple accounts and unread messages, Instagram will notify you with different color badges. Here is what they mean:
- Pinned chat: It appears when you pin the chat for any user in your Instagram DMs.
- Muted chat: It means you muted the chat. You won’t receive any notifications for their messages.
- Unread message: It shows the unread messages inside the chat. If it appears, it means you have unread messages.
- Account switcher: Lets you switch between accounts, and if you see the red icon, it means you have unread notifications from the other account
More Instagram Post Icons Meaning
Instagram recently launched collaborations, which allow users to collaborate with each other and publish posts. It joins with older tags, the ability to add music, and much more. Here is what each icon means:
- Collaborative post: Instagram lets you add collaborative posts. If you see multiple profile pictures, it means it is a collaborative post from those accounts.
- More options: It lets you access more options for the posts
- Explicit audio: If you see an E icon right next to the sound or audio, it means the song contains explicit content
- Tagged people: It lets you view all tagged users for the post. Tapping on the user takes you to their profile
- Sound: It lets you mute or unmute the sound for the post.
Paid Instagram Post Icon Meaning
You don’t need a special introduction for the ads on Instagram. If you see a post and you are confused about whether it’s a regular post or not, you can find a little “Ad” label under the profile.
- Ad: If you see Ad, it means it is a sponsored post or ad inside the Instagram feed.
Instagram Story Viewer Icons Meaning
Fortunately, Instagram has kept stories minimal. They also come with several interactive elements. One is the ability to like them and also share the story with others.
- More options: Gives you more options for the Instagram Story you are viewing, which includes options like the ability to report it and more
- Like Story: Like means you can like your friend’s Story
- Share Story: You can also share the Story with others. Tapping on it lets you share the Story with your contacts.
Instagram Close Friends Story Icons Meaning
If you see a green icon in the stories, it means that the user has added you to their close friends list. It comes with an extra “Close Friends” tag, and while the rest of the elements look the same, it doesn’t come with a share option.
Here is what each icon means in the Instagram Close Friends Story screen:
- Close Friends: If you see this green star, it means they have added you to their Close Friends list and shared a Story with you
- More options: Lets you access more Story options
- Like Story: Lets you like your Close Friend’s Story.
Instagram Reels Comments Symbols Meaning
Finally, ending this guide with the post or Reels comments, it also comes with several elements which can be confusing for the beginner. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram post or Reels comments section.
- Sound: You can turn the Reel sound on or off using the icon
- Like comment: You can like any comment made by users. The number below shows how many people liked it.
- Photo: Instagram recently announced the ability to add a photo as a comment.
- GIF: You can also add a GIF in the comments.
- Gift: Send a gift in the comments. You can tap on it and buy points with real money and help the creator to make money.
Instagram Active Status Symbol Meaning
- Green dot: If you see a green dot, it means the user is active on Instagram. If you hide your active status, it won’t appear for you even if others are online.
Story Rings Meaning
- Grey colored ring: If you see a grey-colored ring, it means you have already viewed their story.
- Colorful gradient ring: It means they added a new story or a story you have not watched yet
- Green ring: If you see a green ring, it means a story for a close friend that the user added. In simple words, the user added you to their close friends list and shared a story with close friends.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

The Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) is set to shift Bengal’s Ranji Trophy home game against Delhi from Eden Gardens, as the iconic stadium is expected to host a grand Durga Puja event on Mahalaya in the presence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The game is likely to be held at either Kalyani or the Jadavpur University Ground in Salt Lake; the CAB has already informed the BCCI about the proposed change.
“Since an event of such stature will be held at Eden Gardens, we had to shift the Ranji Trophy game elsewhere. For now, we are looking at both Kalyani and Salt Lake (JU Ground). We have informed the BCCI and will take a decision soon. But there’s a possibility that we might have to zero in on Kalyani,” CAB secretary Bablu Kolay told Sportstar.
West Bengal is set to begin this year’s Durga Puja celebrations with a grand cultural programme at Eden Gardens on the evening of Mahalaya.
The programme will be preceded by a roadshow along the illuminated Red Road, featuring a grand procession showcasing 23 traditional dance forms representing the cultural heritage of the state’s 23 districts.
PM Modi and West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari are expected to attend the programme. Around 1,000 women are expected to welcome them with traditional ululation, while 10,000 dhakis will perform simultaneously.
The organisers believe the mass dhak performance could find a place in the Guinness World Records.
With Eden Gardens expected to be unavailable from the first week of October, Bengal will begin its Ranji Trophy campaign against Delhi before travelling to face Services and Kerala. It will then return home to take on Maharashtra in the final game of the first leg.
