Hong Kong signs 2 MOUs with Greater Bay Area partners to commercialise aerial technology
Deputy finance chief Michael Wong says agreements will match capabilities of bay area partners with city’s strengths in standards setting
Hong Kong signed two milestone memorandums of understanding with partners in the Greater Bay Area to harmonise standards and commercialise advanced aerial technology as the city accelerated its integration into national development plans.
Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said on Thursday the cross-border pacts would combine the production and testing capabilities of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau bay area with Hong Kong’s strengths in research and standards setting.
“These agreements will leverage the strength of our [bay area] partners in testing environment and industrial production capability, and Hong Kong’s strengths in standards setting, as well as research and development,” Wong said at the annual Belt and Road Summit.
“They will also facilitate the harmonisation of common standards and promote commercialisation of innovative [low-altitude economy] applications.”
Wong said the government was pressing ahead with a regulatory scheme to test advanced aerial projects.

The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.
Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.
Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.
The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.
However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.
In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.
He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”
According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.
A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”
Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.
Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.
Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.
Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.
According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.
Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.
That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.
In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.
During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.
Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.
The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.
Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.
“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.
“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.
“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

When Seher Hashmi speaks about mental health, her words do not stem from textbook theories or clinical observations. They carry the raw truth of a survivor. Having battled severe clinical depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), and having survived multiple suicide attempts and self-harm, Seher knows the darkest corners of anguish. Today, she is converting her trauma into a movement, traversing thousands of kilometres across India on her Royal Enfield motorcycle to shatter the silence surrounding mental illness.
Her ongoing nationwide campaign, titled ‘Beyond the Horizon – A Ride for Resilience,’ has reached Keralam after completing its north Indian leg. Together with a group of fellow riders, Seher is engaging with youth to transform societal attitudes towards mental health.
Seher’s life began under difficult circumstances. Abandoned by her biological parents at just nine months simply for being their third girl child, she was adopted by renowned social activist Shabnam Hashmi and scientist-writer Gauhar Raza. She is the niece of Safdar Hashmi, the iconic street-theatre activist who was murdered in 1989. Growing up alongside deeply committed parents whose demanding public lives sometimes left little room to process her childhood anxieties, Seher’s struggles gradually worsened into severe mental health challenges.
Path to recovery
Her path to recovery was forged through personal determination, medical intervention, and the empathy of her loved ones. Emerging from that dark space, Seher rebuilt her life as a motivational speaker, fashion stylist, and mental health advocate.
For Seher, every kilometre ridden is a step towards dismantling social stigma. By sharing her own story of survival, she offers young people across the country something far more powerful than advice—proof that resilience is possible, and that no struggle has to be faced alone.
Second journey
This motorcycle odyssey marks her second major awareness journey. Her first expedition took place in 2025, covering over 3,000 kilometres from Delhi to Kashmir and back, reaching thousands of students across 20 cities. Her current campaign—the south Indian leg—was flagged off on August 20, 2026, at the Constitution Club of India in New Delhi by veteran actor Sharmila Tagore. Spanning 55 days, 11 States, and over 7,000 km, the initiative aims at covering 100 venues across schools, colleges, and rural community spaces.
Entering Keralam on September 9, 2026 through Kasaragod, the team will cover nine districts—Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram—before heading to Kanyakumari on September 18. In Keralam, the campaign is supported by the Yuva Samithi of the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP). Parishad volunteers are accompanying the team on motorbikes throughout the State, organising mental health awareness sessions and interactive discussions in educational institutions.

Amazon discriminated against pregnant warehouse employees by denying accommodations like bathroom breaks and the option to sit while working, according to a lawsuit filed yesterday by four women who worked for Amazon while pregnant. The lawsuit is a class-action complaint that seeks to represent Amazon workers throughout the US.
“Plaintiffs Willamina Barclay, Kristina Green, Jennifer Hatch, and Dazaria Parks were formerly Amazon warehouse employees,” said the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Eastern District of New York. “All four became pregnant. All four asked Amazon for basic pregnancy-related accommodations so they could keep doing their jobs. Amazon denied them basic modifications the law recognizes pregnant workers regularly need, even in uncomplicated pregnancies: Bathroom breaks. An extra 15-minute break. Sitting instead of standing.”
The lawsuit said the four plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated from jobs at Amazon facilities in New York between April 2025 and July 2026. After the plaintiffs “took medically necessary breaks or absences to get off their feet, visit the doctor, or go to the emergency room, they were punished,” the lawsuit said. “Amazon deducted their limited bank of unpaid time off. Soon enough, they had depleted that limited bank of ‘unpaid time off,’ and Amazon threatened to terminate them.”
In a statement, Amazon said the lawsuit contains inaccuracies and denied that it violates federal law on pregnancy accommodations. “We’re limited in discussing ongoing legal matters, however we look forward to a timely resolution of these matters, as extended investigation timelines benefit neither employees nor employers,” Amazon said.
Amazon has faced similar lawsuits in previous years, but this one has the added backing of a 2022 US law called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The relatively new federal law requires “reasonable accommodations for qualified employees affected by pregnancy, childbirth, lactation, or related medical conditions and limitations so long as doing so does not create an undue hardship on the entity’s operations,” the lawsuit said.

'People were trampling me': Philippine ferry fire survivor recalls narrow escape
- Published
Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.
Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.
Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.
Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.
Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell.
"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.
He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.
He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.
"When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.
Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water.
"It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.
Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday.
But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.
The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.
The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.
Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.
The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.
Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.
Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.
Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says.
"I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.
A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".
Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.
Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital.
"He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.
She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.
Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.
But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire.
On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there.
But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone.
"I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."

Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids
They both include a giant green button to access a child's favorite content.
Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids. There's the fourth-generation Yoto Player and an updated version of the Yoto Mini.
The new Yoto Player is still a speaker with a pixel display, but the company has added some bells and whistles. Firstly, there's a big green dial that kids can twist to play their "most loved audio." This can access up to 20 pieces of content, including podcasts, stories and songs.
This is done directly from the device, so there will be no need for a kid to borrow a parent's phone. Additionally, the functionality doesn't require Yoto Cards, which are basically little NFC keys that get inserted into the player to access unique content.
The company has also upgraded the software so routines are easier to create and access. This means that parents can set up a routine just one time and the device will automatically do stuff like adjust the graphics to reflect the time of day.
Yoto promises that the hardware has been redesigned so it's "easy for little hands." The storage has been increased up to 64GB, downloads should be much faster and the nightlight panel has been upgraded.
All of this is very good news, considering an older version of the Yoto Player already made our list of the best audio gadgets for kids. However, there is a spot of bad news. The price is shooting up to $150, from $110. It's available to pre-order right now, with shipments going out on October 15.
The Yoto Mini is also getting a nice little hardware refresh. This is the company's cheaper and much smaller audio player. The upcoming Mini looks to be designed for the kind of adventures kids typically get into. It's "rugged, water and dust-resistant." The company promises it can "handle playground grass, sofa launches and rainy-day chaos without missing a beat."
The upgrade also includes the same green button that allows access to content without Yoto Cards. The device has enough storage for "1,000 hours of audio" and it integrates with both wired and Bluetooth headphones.
Sadly, there's another price increase here. The Yoto Mini is going up to $110, from $80. It's available for pre-order right now, with shipments going out on September 30.
The company is also introducing several accessories for its devices. There are scratch-proof cases for both the Mini and Player that are available in four colors. It's also working on a wireless dock and a case for Yoto Cards. We don't have pricing or availability information on this stuff just yet.

In September 2026, social media users circulated warnings about a website called VoteSafe.org, an online voter registration hub that allegedly collects and shares users' personal information.
Posts on platforms such as Facebook (screenshot), Threads and Bluesky also claimed America PAC — the political action committee tech billionaire Elon Musk founded — operates and funds VoteSafe.org. Snopes readers contacted us to verify this claim.
VoteSafe.org is, indeed, funded by Musk's America PAC, and according to the website's privacy policy, it may collect and share users' personal information. (VoteSafe.org also offers a way for users to opt out of having their personal information shared with third parties.)
As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The VoteSafe.org privacy policy page lists only one third party by name that it shares data with: a "business partner" called Western Creative Group. The company has no online presence; its Wyoming business license lists a law firm as its agent and organizer. The Washington Post reported in 2024 that Musk passed $20 million to "an advertising firm called Western Creative Group" to promote the idea that U.S. President Donald Trump "opposed a federal ban on abortion."
We reached out to the law firm, Bailey Stock Harmon Cottam Lopez, to ask about its association with Western Creative Group and will update this story if we hear back. Snopes also asked America PAC for a list of third parties the political action committee shares information with. We await a response.
It is also worth noting at least one Snopes reader asked whether Musk pays for Vote.org. Vote.org, another voter registration website, was established long before Musk's VoteSafe.org. Unlike VoteSafe.org, Vote.org is run by a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, and its tax filings and list of board members indicate that Vote.org has no affiliation with Musk.
The similarly named official government voter registration page is vote.gov, as the ".gov" domain indicates.
Elon Musk's America PAC linked to Vote Safe website
The America PAC website (archived) prominently features a description on its homepage that says, "PAC Founded by Elon Musk." According to Federal Election Commission data, the vast majority of America PAC's funds come from Musk.
The America PAC website also includes a banner that sends users to the VoteSafe.org webpage.
On the VoteSafe.org webpage (archived), there are several additional indicators that America PAC funds VoteSafe.org. For example, the copyright notice at the bottom of the webpage says "AMERICA PAC." Underneath the notice, a disclaimer reads:
Paid for by America PAC. Not authorized by any candidate or candidate's committee. www.theamericapac.org.
More on VoteSafe.org's privacy policy
VoteSafe.org's 
For example, here's the privacy policy's explanation on what America PAC may do with contact information:
Contact Information. This may include your name, physical address, email address or telephone number.
- How We May Collect It: Directly from you; passively; or from third parties.
- How We May Use It: To provide and improve our Platform; to understand your interests; to communicate with you; for marketing purposes; for legal and security purposes; to combine information; as otherwise permitted by you or as we may notify you; or as directed by you.
- How We May Disclose It: Internally; on our Platform; with our business partners; with our service providers; with third parties for marketing purposes; with any successors to all or part of our business; to comply with laws or to protect ourselves; for other reasons we may describe to you; or as directed by you.
- We may share this information with our business partners for targeted marketing purposes or sell this information to our business partners. For more information about your right to opt out, please click here.
While the VoteSafe.org privacy policy references selling user information, it's unclear whether America PAC directly sells information to third parties for monetary gain. That's because — as the privacy policy notes — some U.S. privacy laws have broadened the "sale" of information to mean more than just a monetary exchange.
In California, for example, the "sale" of information can involve any exchange of a consumer's information "by a business to a third party" for any "valuable consideration."
There's no clarification in the VoteSafe.org privacy policy about whether America PAC sells consumer information for money or for other reasons, aside from "targeted marketing purposes."
It is unclear how many third parties have received information from America PAC. The political action committee's privacy policy notes that under California law, the state's residents have the right to ask once a year "whether we have shared personal information with third parties for their direct-marketing purposes."
"To make a request, please submit a request via info@theamericapac.org," the policy says.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). In this context, a video is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods.
Fact: The video has been available online since at least 11 June 2023 and predates the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google keyword search but found no credible reports stating that Nepali citizens converted to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to multiple social media posts featuring the same visuals (here, here, and here). The earliest post we found dates back to 11 June 2023 and claims to show 41 Nepalis converting to Islam at a mosque in Saudi Arabia, confirming that the viral video is unrelated to the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal and has been available online since at least June 2023.
We also found a set of photos showing the same venue and a similar event. The caption identified the location as the Al-Da’wah Association in Badi’ah, Saudi Arabia, and stated that 44 Nepalese people converted to Islam.
A subsequent Google Maps search led us to Masjid Ghazwa Al-Mutairi in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia. Photos of the mosque’s interior available on Google Maps matched the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the footage was filmed in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
However, we could not independently verify the identities or nationalities of the people seen in the footage or the other details surrounding the incident. Based on the available evidence, it can be concluded that the video has been available on the internet since at least June 2023 and is therefore unrelated to the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
To sum up, this viral video does not show 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam after the 2026 Nepal floods; it has been online since 2023.

A probe has been ordered by Bhopal Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, a day after at least four MBBS intern doctors suffered injuries due to water cannons that were used against them during their protest in the campus of government-run Gandhi Medical College (GMC) to demand a hike in their stipend.
On Monday (September 7, 2026), hundreds of interns of the GMC, Bhopal, protested at their campus over their longstanding demand that their stipend be increased from the current ₹14,437 to ₹30,000. However, as they planned a march to the Chief Minister’s residence, the police used water cannons on the protestors, visuals of which appeared on the internet.
The protestors also alleged that as they continued their march later in the day, the police also resorted to baton charge on them near the campus. The march was stopped less than 2 kilometres from the CM house, prompting them to launch a sit-in at the site.
The sit-in in Bhopal’s Kamla Park area continued through the night and on Tuesday (September 8) even as they boycotted the OPD and routine operation theatre (OT) services, while emergency services remained operational. Services were also interrupted at Gwalior’s Gajra Raja Medical College in support of the protest.
Four interns injured in the police action
Speaking to The Hindu, Siddhartha Kumar Rai, undergraduate student wing president of the Junior Doctors’ Association (JDA), Madhya Pradesh, said that at least four interns got seriously injured in the police action, including one person suffering a broken arm and another an eye injury.
“It was a completely peaceful protest inside the campus but still the interns who perform 36-hour-long duties and contribute the most in handling the heavy patient load at government hospitals were treated like goons by the police. They even targeted the girl interns who were standing on the side,” he said.
Meanwhile, various other doctors’ bodies in the State have also come out in support of the interns’ protest while condemning the police action.
Mr. Rai said that if a written assurance was not given by Tuesday night, the JDA and various other bodies will boycott medical services across the State from Wednesday (September 9).
Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean and CEO, GMC, Bhopal, also slammed the use of force in a letter to Commissioner Kumar while seeking an inquiry into the matter and action against responsible officers.
“Water cannon was used and lathicharge was done on the intern students at the emergency gate in which two students were injured.
Taking such action against intern students on the hospital campus without prior notice is completely inappropriate,” she wrote.
In an order, Mr. Kumar said that the matter was brought to attention by Deputy Chief Minister and Health Minister Rajendra Shukla and that Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Zone 2, Vikas Sahwal has been appointed to conduct an “impartial investigation of the whole incident”.
“It has been brought to the notice by Shri Rajendra Shukla, Deputy Chief Minister, that during the protest of intern doctors in Bhopal on September 7, 2026, the police sprayed water using water cannon near the gate of Hamidia Hospital, due to which some doctors were injured,” the order read.
Mr. Rai also claimed that Madhya Pradesh ranked 28th in the country in the amount of stipend given to MBBS interns, after the Uttar Pradesh increasing the amount from ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 in August.
“But in terms of MBBS fee at government colleges, we are at the third position with about ₹1.15 lakh. How is this fair,” he asked.
Meanwhile, Mr. Shukla also held a meeting with senior officials and the management of the GMC to discuss the issue and interns’ demand and said that a resolution will be reached soon.
“I am aware of the issue raised by intern doctors in Bhopal regarding an increase in stipends. The expectations and problems of young doctors in the state are being taken seriously. I am in constant touch with representatives of the intern doctors on this matter,” he wrote on X.
“Our effort is to engage in positive discussions with all parties and arrive at an appropriate and practical solution to this issue. Young doctors play a vital role in strengthening the health services of the state, and the government is sensitive to their rightful expectations. Following discussions and necessary deliberations, appropriate and necessary decisions will be taken in this regard,” he added.

In Summary
- The Redmi Turbo 5 sees the Redmi brand return to a higher price point. It had earlier released the K series in this segment.
- The Redmi Turbo 5 follows Redmi’s classic formula of offering very good specs at surprisingly affordable prices. Its highlights are a powerful chip and a large Silicon Carbon battery.
- Priced at Rs 41,999, the Redmi Turbo 5 is one of the best options for those looking for something close to a budget flagship in an era of rapidly rising prices.
Redmi is mainly known for its budget-friendly devices, mostly in the mid- and lower-mid segment. It has occasionally released slightly more expensive devices, most notably in its K series, but has then gone back to the comfort of the Redmis and Redmi Notes. Now, as phone prices get on an upward-heading escalator, Redmi is getting back into the higher price zone with the Redmi Turbo 5. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 41,999, and while that may seem a bit on the premium side for a Redmi smartphone, it brings an equally premium spec sheet to the table. But can it help Redmi stretch beyond Note-land? Let’s find out!
Table of Contents
Redmi Turbo 5 design and appearance: Classy, yet not-so-loud appearance
The Redmi Turbo 5 does not come with a radically new design – it looks very similar to its cousin, the Poco X8 Pro. And that is a good thing. The phone has all the design elements that make up a trendy smartphone in today’s day and age – a tall, display dominated front which is surrounded by razor thin bezels, a flat back with two circular camera rings jutting out just a little parked on the top left side, and has those flat sides that have become an essential part of a modern day smartphone’s anatomy.
While not out of the box, the Turbo 5 still has a few distinct design touches that catch attention, the kind that are not obvious or scream for attention, but do not get lost completely either. The right side of the back comes with a thick vertical strip filled with very dainty checkered patterns, and the cameras seem like two independent lenses stacked together, but there is a subtle capsule outline encasing them. The two camera lenses also have LED rings inside them, which is a nice conversation starter.
We received the Turbo White variant of the smartphone, which has a red Redmi logo near the base of the back. The cameras and the power/lock button also come with a very distinct red accent. These subtle touches make the design of the Redmi Turbo 5 give it a personality of sorts, making it stand out in the crowd. The back comes with a matte finish, which keeps smudges and scratches at bay and keeps the phone relatively clean. The metallic frame (a pleasant surprise at this price) is home to a handful of features as well. The top carries an infrared port while the base holds a SIM card tray, a USB Type-C port, and a speaker grille. The left side is bare while the right one bears the volume rocker and the power lock button.
Although relatively light for the size of the battery it carries (more about that later), the phone is not exactly light. It weighs 204 grams, and you can feel the weight in hand and even when the phone is in your pocket. At 157.5 mm, the Redmi Turbo 5 falls somewhere between large (160 mm and above) and compact phones (153 mm and below). It is 75.2 mm wide and, at 8.18 mm, is impressively slim, again considering the size of its battery. It is quite a sturdy phone with Gorilla Glass 7i protection on its front and back, and with IP68 and IP69K ratings for dust and water resistance, which means it can easily survive a fall in the water.
At first glance, the Redmi Turbo 5 might seem routine, but give it more attention, and little details start to pop up, and you start appreciating it for its classy, yet not-so-loud appearance.
Redmi Turbo 5 Specs: Ticks a surprising number of boxes
At a time when brands are cutting spec corners, the Redmi Turbo 5 ticks a surprising number of boxes. The phone is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra processor, which is considered to be in the budget flagship zone, and is paired with 8 GB and 12 GB RAM options and 256 GB of storage. What’s more, the 12 GB RAM variant comes with LPDDR5X RAM, and the storage on both variants is UFS 4.1. On paper, this is a very powerful setup for the price, which can not only run your everyday smartphone tasks but even handle high-end gaming.
The phone comes with a 6.59-inch AMOLED full HD+ (2756 x 1268) display with 120 Hz refresh rate and a peak brightness of 3500 nits, which can actually cover as much as 25 per cent of the display, instead of being isolated to a tiny section. Photography is handled by a dual camera setup on the back comprising a 50 megapixel Sony IMX882 main sensor with OIS, and an 8 megapixel ultrawide sensor, while a 20 megapixel sensor on the front handles selfies.
The Turbo 5 also packs in some very impressive battery numbers – it brings a sizable 7540 mAh Silicon Carbon battery (a rarity at this price, actually at any price) with support for 100W charging and 27W reverse charging. Also on board are stereo speakers, an in-display fingerprint scanner, and an IR blaster. Like all Redmi devices, the Turbo 5 also runs on Android 16 topped with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3. Xiaomi promises four years of software and six years of security updates.
In sheer spec terms, this is one of the best specced devices out there in its segment. Some might find the display a little small, but the power of that processor and the RAM and storage options will attract gamers on a budget.
Redmi Turbo 5 Performance: A smooth, powerful operator
The Redmi Turbo 5’s speedy processor+ RAM+ storage set up, reflects in its performance as well. The phone sails smoothly through everyday duties. It moves from app to app smoothly, handles multi-tasking without a hiccup, keeps going through intense social media scrolls, and binge sessions on OTT. The phone can also handle high-end games like Call of Duty and BGMI at 120 fps for long-ish sessions. Although it does get warm while going through power-hungry tasks, the temperature comes down quickly enough.
The AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate does not disappoint. It delivers a very rich contrast with vibrant colors and is bright enough not to dull down against a very harsh sun either. The 120 Hz refresh rate kept scrolling through social media breezy. The in-display fingerprint scanner works smoothly as well. This, combined with the loud and clear stereo speakers, makes the phone a multimedia master. We did not face any call drops or connectivity issues with the phone either.
Redmi Turbo 5 Cameras: One sensor show (censor the others)
Cameras are not the forte of the Redmi Turbo 5. There are three sensors on the phone, but all the photography weight rests on the 50-megapixel main sensor’s shoulders. This performs well in daylight conditions, capturing a good amount of detail and producing sharp images, so much so that the photos look decent even after a little zoom-in. The colors seem slightly more vibrant than reality but never to a point of looking unnatural. The details do take a very marginal hit in low light, but the presence of OIS helps, and Night mode on the device also improves results a fair bit. A number of other modes are built right into the native camera app, which offer a lot of scope for creative photography.
The 8-megapixel ultrawide sensor is capable of capturing a wider area, but it does not really do an impressive job. The colors remain nice and vibrant, but the details take a nose dive, resulting in images that look noisier, especially when compared to the main sensor. Matters only get worse as the light dims down. The sensor is usable and will allow you to take some quick snaps for social media in good light conditions, but do not pin your photography hopes on it. The 20-megapixel sensor on the front delivers social media-ready snaps but has the tendency to smooth out skin texture even with no ‘beauty mode’ on. The colors also lean towards being a little oversaturated, but you can get good casual snaps, and video calls are handled well.
The main camera supports 4K video at 60 fps, but the other two cameras are limited to 1080p at 60 fps. The video performance of the main camera sensor is good in daylight and even in low-light conditions, but the others miss the mark a bit. Overall, the 50-megapixel camera is the star of the Redmi Turbo 5’s camera show, while the other two are just supporting staff.
Redmi Turbo 5 software and UI: Very nice HyperOS, but loaded with third-party apps
The Redmi Turbo 5 runs on HyperOS 3. Now, HyperOS has been one of the most intuitive, simple, and functional Android skins since its MIUI days, and while that still largely remains true, the phone comes loaded with a plethora of third-party apps. This really makes the experience feel very cluttered and might even seem overwhelming to those new to the UI. Most of these third-party apps can be uninstalled, thankfully.
That said, features like Xiaomi Interconnectivity that not only allow you to connect your smartphone with other HyperOS products but with other gadgets as well, letting you create a hybrid ecosystem, give HyperOS its productivity edge. Top this with add-ons like Hyper Island (similar to Dynamic Island on the iPhone), and AI features like AI Translate, writing assist, call transcription, and a range of customizations, and HyperOS comes across as a very functionality-forward UI. The LED rings around the camera sensors that light up when you get notifications or calls were actually very handy, even while being a nice party trick as well.
Redmi Turbo 5 Battery: Lasts for days, gets charged in a jiffy
The phone’s massive 7540 mAh battery can see you through even the heaviest work days. Emails, messaging, gaming, photography- we did all of that and more with the smartphone, and it still had some juice left even after a day. If you are someone who does not push their device as much, the phone would easily see off more than two days on a single charge. It comes with 100W fast charging support with a 100W brick in the box, which means you get a fully charged phone in slightly over an hour, while the phone goes from 0-50 percent in about 30 minutes. This makes the Redmi Turbo 5 a device that will not only last for day(s) but will also get charged in a jiffy. The reverse charging feature is quite handy too and charges our TWS at a very decent speed.
Redmi Turbo 5 Price: Typically Redmi!
The Redmi Turbo 5 is available in two RAM variants – 8 GB and 12 GB, while the storage remains 256 GB for both options. Although the phone was initially launched at Rs 37,999, this price has since been revised, given rising costs of inputs. The 8 GB/ 256 GB version of the phone is now priced at Rs. 41,999, while the 12 GB/ 256 GB version is priced at Rs. 46,999.
It might have a much higher starting price than the Redmi Note series, but the Redmi Turbo 5 brings a solid spec sheet to the table at a price tag that is typically Redmi. While there are other devices in its price range, at the time of writing, none quite match its price-to-spec equation.
Perhaps the one that comes closest is its own cousin, the Poco X8 Pro, which comes with a similar processor and a similarly sized display at Rs 39,999, but has a smaller battery. Devices like the OnePlus Nord 6 come with a comparable Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 chip, but are more expensive at Rs 46,999, while the recently launched Vivo S2 brings a sleeker design and bigger display to the table at Rs 39,999 but loses out in terms of processor muscle.
Redmi Turbo 5 Review Verdict: A phone that does everything well
It might come with a higher price tag, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a typical Redmi smartphone in more than one aspect. It delivers a very consistent performance across multiple segments, making it one of the most reliable and powerful options at its price point (typical Redmi!). Its gaming and general performance are both quite smooth; the main camera delivers good snaps, its battery is perhaps its biggest USP, and the display combined with the stereo speakers make it an entertainment master. The price tag is a little higher than some might expect, but the Redmi Turbo 5 is a device for those who are looking for a very good everyday phone that does almost everything well.
- Smart design, sturdy build
- Gorgeous display
- Very good speakers
- Long battery that charges swiftly too
- Good gaming and multimedia performance
- Smooth overall performance
- Ultrawide camera is average
- Bloatware in UI

Hamilton and Leclerc 'squash' Monza controversy
- Published
Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them after a difficult Italian Grand Prix.
Leclerc forced Hamilton into the gravel at the first chicane at Monza on Sunday, and then crashed two laps later. Hamilton recovered to finish a disappointed sixth.
It was the second flashpoint between the Ferrari drivers in two races, after an argument over the radio during the Dutch Grand Prix when Leclerc resisted a request to move aside for Hamilton.
Hamilton said: "What's great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion. We sat face to face, just him and I, and talked about it.
"We were just both open and honest, and we squashed it. We can move on. I think that one shows the maturity from him."
Speaking at the media day for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, the seven-time champion added: "It's healthy. It's a relationship we have built over time. Of course, there's going to be frustrations and I'm sure there'll be more times where we're close because we're very close in pace.
"We both want to win just as much as each other, and we both want to do well for the team as well."

Leclerc said: "It's kind of clear that we never want to see a car of the same team in the grass.
"After reviewing, we spoke with Lewis. I obviously know I went too far in turn two and I said it to Lewis and I think it's very clear what we should do or should avoid going forward.
"But I won't go into much more details of what we've said. The only thing I can say is that it definitely did not affect the good relationship that we have and it will not affect anything going forward. And that is the most important for me, really.
"I know we are driving for Ferrari and if there's one race where you don't want that to happen, it's in Monza and when these things happen at our home race, then it does a huge mess outside.
"However, looking at the race from outside, there's been also some friction between other team-mates and the only thing we end up speaking of is Lewis and me, which I don't think is quite right. But that doesn't mean we did everything perfect."
Hamilton acknowledged again that Ferrari had to improve their operations, after three consecutive race weekends where qualifying has not gone to plan.
"It's really just making sure we're executing to make sure we get the best result for the team," he said. "Instead of us working against each other and finish fourth and fifth, maybe we can work together and get a podium and pull off more points.
"It's a longer term process. It's not something we can just change into this weekend. There's a huge amount of moving parts, there's a lot of people, there's a culture that's been there for a long, long time and moving big pieces is not so easy."
Madring 'one of the most risky circuits'
F1 faces a fresh challenge this weekend at the first Spanish Grand at the new Madring, a hybrid street circuit built on the Ifema complex near the city's international airport.
Hamilton said: "It's a massively challenging circuit. Of all the new tracks that I've gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines and such."
Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's a crazy circuit, I would put it. Arguably one of the most risky circuits of the whole calendar.
"Because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque, the walls are very close, so there's no margin for error, but then you have other corners... where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone, you're braking and turning at the same time, so locking tyres are going to be easy and if you lock up you'll be straight in the wall.
"So, excited to try that out, I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers, the race is going to be challenging to overtake, so on the whole it's not an easy one."
Russell heads into the race 66 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli after the Italian's landmark victory in Monza from 19th on the grid.
The Briton acknowledged that his title hopes with nine or 10 races left, amid uncertainty about the end of the season, were fading fast.
"I would definitely need some luck and I need some good performances," Russell said. "It's not really something I'm thinking about, because he's performing better than me, so he deserves to be leading the championship.
"There's still a long way to go, but he's yet to have a bad weekend in terms of performance.
"So he's performing exceptionally well, my performances are better, but if I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck on the way. But it's not something I'm focused on. I'm focused on driving faster and just finding more performance."
Antonelli said: "I don't really want to try thinking about the championship. I think Monza was the proof that I wasn't driving thinking about, or worrying about the championship. I was just driving to win, to do my best. So that's the mindset."
The Italian said his win in Monza was "so far the best day of my life and definitely one I will remember forever".
He said a day karting with Mercedes on Monday helped him move on from the excitement of the day before.
"After Monza, that night, that day overall, I was very excited. But then going karting on Monday helped me to go back to earth, just go back to the ground.
"It was a good day, good fun day with the team. It was also a way to remind myself where I came from, all the journey that was done.
"And then about pressure, I try to embrace it as much as possible. And I try to see it as a positive thing and try to see it as an opportunity too. That's also what is helping me to stay calm under difficult situations."

President Donald Trump on Wednesday said that he would pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retained control of the US House and Senate in the midterm elections, seemingly in an effort to incentivize votes for his party.
“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”
“That alone should win the midterms,” he added.
The outlandish remarks came midway through Trump’s at times freewheeling speech at the Republican midterm convention the GOP is holding in Texas, as part of an effort to drive turnout among Trump’s base this November, and were quickly shot down as unaffordable.
It’s unclear whether the “Trump Dividend,” as he’s calling it, was a serious proposal or an attempt to galvanize the president’s base to turn out on election day, after he also previously promised payouts like a $5,000 “DOGE dividend” or a $2,000-per-person tariff check—neither of which has happened. Any attempt to make real on the offer would need congressional approval.
Vice president JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s offer in an interview following the speech, saying it wouldn’t go to wealthy Americans, but also suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues. “A one-time payment of this size would wipe out about a decade’s tariff revenue at current tariff levels,” wrote Erica York, senior economist at the Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy, on X.
Responding to a Fox News question that “critics will say the president is bribing voters and he’s bankrupting the country,” Vance said: “Tariffs have generated a lot of revenues. The president is saying, if you keep us in power, then you will share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating.”
The rough total cost of paying out $5,000 to about 240 million adults in the US would amount to $1.2 trillion, a price tag that exceeds the roughly $284 billion in gross customs revenue collected between January 2025 and June 2026, according to the University of Pennsylvania.
The shortfall would be even greater after accounting for tariff refunds the Trump administration is compelled to pay after the US Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump had unlawfully imposed tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977.
Following orders from the Court of International Trade, the administration has started to refund some of the $160 billion collected from tariffs, plus interest, which is accruing at an estimated rate of about $650 million per month.
After accounting for refunds, the administration’s net revenue from tariffs will come out to roughly $118 billion, meaning Trump would need to have Congress approve an additional $1.08 trillion, on top of the president’s proposed $1.86 trillion discretionary budget request for fiscal year 2027.
The principal concern for the Republican National Committee has been that the midterm elections will be decided in large part by voter turnout, which could be depressed for Republicans because Trump will not be on the ballot.

Mumbai has seen a surge in H1N1 (swine flu) cases over the last three months, as the number of cases have jumped to 441 this year from 62 during same period last year. This marks a 612% rise, while for malaria the cases have seen a 20% rise.
According to Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)’s monsoon data for June, July, and August, 441 cases of H1N1, and 4,485 malaria cases were recorded between June and August as compared to 3,733 last year.
To curb the surge of swine flu, BMC has been screening suspected H1N1 patients, and prescribing Oseltamivir. Further, surveys are being conducted in the affected regions, where the H1N1 positive cases have been located.
The BMC said suspected H1N1 patients are being screened and treated with oseltamivir wherever required. Close contacts of infected patients are being monitored for 10 days, while door-to-door surveys are being conducted in affected areas. BMC also clarified that they have prepared ventilators, PPE kits, reserved beds and medicines to manage patients for hospitalisation.’
Mumbai’s E-ward, K-West ward, G-South ward, F-South ward, and H-West ward have so far recorded the highest cases of malaria. To combat the vector-borne disease, BMC has increased the field-level monitoring in most affected areas. They have surveyed 52,197 potential breeding sites for malaria control. Anopheles mosquito breeding sites were detected at 8,055 locations, along with 12,55,469 potential mosquito breeding sites for dengue control, and Aedes mosquito breeding at 27,352 areas.
Decline in monsoon related illnesses.
Mumbai saw a decline in dengue cases,leptospirosis cases, COVID-19 cases, Chikungunya, and Gastroenteritis. According to BMC data, COVID-19 cases dropped drastically by 77% this year, as 151 cases were recorded compared to last year’s 668. For dengue the fall has been by 20% — 1,563 patients recorded this year in June, July, and August. For chikungunya, cases have dropped from 370 to 46, a decrease of 87%.
Leptospirosis cases declined by 37% — from 406 to 255, while gastroenteritis cases dropped from 2,197 to 1,954, this year.

Citing the 'Deep State,' Trump overhauls the intelligence community
John Sipher spent nearly three decades at the CIA focused on the Russians, a core part of the agency's mission. That changed dramatically after the al-Qaida attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
"Frankly, tracking and hunting terrorists, finding people, finding a needle in a haystack was not something that we trained for," said Sipher, who served in Moscow and later ran the agency's Russia operations at CIA headquarters.
The CIA and the larger intelligence community had to adapt quickly.
"We did that by by learning, and actually even developing new technologies, computer power, data collection, drones, communications, means to defeat networks, terrorist networks," he said.
There were real successes, such as locating Osama bin Laden in 2011 and destroying his group, al-Qaida, and later, dismantling the Islamic State.
More broadly, the Department of Homeland Security was created, and now has a quarter-million employees, making it the second-largest government agency, trailing only the Pentagon. Military and intelligence budgets soared.
By most all accounts, the U.S. is safer at home. The country has not been hit on U.S. soil with anything remotely comparable to the 9/11 attack, which killed nearly 3,000 people.
Trump targets the "deep state"
Yet 25 years later, U.S. national security industry is undergoing another dramatic change.
President Trump is waging an ongoing campaign against the so-called "deep state," which he describes largely as national security officials trying to undermine him.
"We will clean out all of the corrupt actors in our national security and intelligence apparatus, and there are plenty of them," Trump said in announcing his plans for his second term.
Critics say Trump is tearing down the national security infrastructure with no clear vision of what comes next, aside from protecting the president's personal interests.
"Since the re-inauguration of Donald Trump, the architecture of American national security is being destroyed, just like the east wing of the White House," said author Tim Weiner, who's covered the U.S. intelligence community for decades. This includes a book last year, The Mission: The CIA in the 21st Century, that examines the CIA since 9/11. "Trump has deliberately swung a wrecking ball through American national security and has in great part worked to dismantle the systems set up after World War II to protect the United States.
Weiner said Trump consistently selects loyalists with limited experience to lead national security agencies.
"The people he has put in charge, [Pete] Hegseth at the Pentagon, Kash Patel at the FBI, John Ratcliffe at CIA, are sycophants," said Weiner. "They will tell the president what he wants to know rather than what he needs to know."
Cutbacks at home, strained relations abroad
While many officials have been dismissed under Trump, some left on their own.
Steven Cash held multiple national security posts — at the CIA, the Senate Intelligence Committee and the Department of Homeland Security.
He resigned when Trump began his second term.
"I could not in good conscience keep working for a president who was going to take what I was working on and what others had spent careers working on, and turning it against Americans, which is exactly what he has done," Cash said.
Cash now leads the Steady State, a private group of more than 400 former national security officials. They were career officials who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, but are now highly critical of Trump's policies.
Cash believes the intelligence community made important advances over the past quarter-century, particularly in information sharing. But he acknowledges it's been an imperfect process.
The post of director of national intelligence, or DNI, was created to coordinate the work of what are now 18 separate intelligence agencies.
"The original idea was it would be very small," Cash said. "We sort of joked that the new DNI would get a deputy, he'd get a big conference table with 18 chairs, and the biggest, best coffee machine he could find. And other than that, he'd get nothing."
The office quickly swelled and is often criticized for not functioning as intended. There are periodic calls for the office to be abolished.
Trump cut back the office, along with other national security agencies, as part of his larger government reductions.
Cash said these moves have gone way too far.
"We took a dive off the cliff in 2025. All the gains, I think, are gone, and we are in the process of destroying our intelligence community," he said.
Shifting agendas
U.S. successes in fighting terrorism have made it less of a priority these days, leading to cutbacks, according to Marc Polymeropoulos, a former CIA officer who spent much of his career in the Middle East.
"Counterterrorism is getting second fiddle to the threats from China and Russia, and the current administration's focus on the border and narco-trafficking means a shift of resources to the Americas," said Polymeropoulos. "I am afraid that counter-terrorism will not be a priority until a mass casualty event, and then it very much will be once again."
John Sipher says one of the most damaging ideas that's taken root is that career intelligence officials actively take sides in partisan politics.
"We have allowed our partisan anger, and specifically the Trump administration, to create this narrative that there's a deep state and that the intelligence services work for one party or another. I think it's a real danger," he said.
Tim Weiner said the damage has also been inflicted abroad as Trump repeatedly antagonizes U.S. allies.
"The CIA in particular relies or depends on intelligence sharing with friendly and not so friendly foreign intelligence services," Weiner said. "It it is still only 20,000 people, and they cannot cover the entire world. They need the British. They need the Dutch. They need the Saudis. They need help."
That help, he says, is much harder to come by today than in the aftermath of 9/11.

Apple's new boss starts with big gamble on $2,000 first folding iPhone
- Published
John Ternus has entered his second week as Apple's chief executive and the company has revealed the first major change to the iPhone since it was released almost 20 years ago.
Ternus, who took on Apple's top job after Tim Cook stepped down, was onstage on Wednesday at the company's annual product release event in front of huge images of the first foldable iPhone.
With a book-style format, the new iPhone, dubbed the Duo, is the largest ever size of the product. And with a US starting price of $1,999 (£1,475) going up to $3,200, it is also the most expensive. UK prices start at £1,999.
Ternus said the Duo was "inspired by the iPad" but called the folding features "fluid and completely intuitive."
The foldable phone has been a work-in-progress inside Apple for several years.
When unfolded, the new Duo has the look of a small iPad. When folded in half, it has the look of a wider iPhone.
Ternus said during the event that Apple wanted to avoid the look and feel of other foldable smart phones on the market, which he said "feel like two phones stuck together... making a larger screen feel much smaller."
The Duo, he said, is the "result of a series of remarkable innovations that we think will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone."
Ternus was directly involved in developing the foldable iPhone as he spent many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division before being tapped earlier this year as Cook's successor.
Ben Wood, chief analyst at technology research firm FDM CCS Insight, said it was likely Ternus's promotion was timed specifically "to coincide with what will be arguably one of the biggest iPhone launches for many years".
"Nothing happens by accident at Apple," Wood added.
Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies who attended the Wednesday presentation, said the spotlight on Ternus made it feel "almost like he was a product himself."
Altering the design of the iPhone may address some criticism that Apple has yet to land a major product hit or truly exciting innovation since the first iPhone came out in 2007.
"The foldable risks becoming a premium-priced ornament in the portfolio, imparting badge value but not meaningful growth," said Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester.
Previously, the highest starting price of the newest iPhone was $900 (£664). Apple also revealed on Wednesday the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which in the US start at $1,199 (£855) and $1,299 (£959) respectively.
Chatterjee said the foldable iPhone could go the way of Apple's Vision Pro headset, which the company priced at $3,699 (£2,729) and has not been a hit with buyers. Or, he said, it could be the company's next Apple Watch which, while not as popular as the iPhone, is bought by millions of people each year.
The way people have become accustomed to the way the iPhone operates is another potential hurdle to Apple seeing big sales of the new design.
"Foldables are interesting devices", Milanesi noted. "A lot of people are intrigued by it, but the software and the learning curve that you have from moving from a traditional phone to a foldable is real."
Wood noted that the current market for foldable smartphones from the likes of Samsung and Huawei make up only 2% of smartphone sales. Even with Apple's version likely driving interest and demand, sales are only expected to reach 4% of the total market in the next decade, according to data and analytics firm FDM CCM Insight.
The iPhone has been Apple's top-selling product and accounts for more than half of the company's sales each year.
In recent quarters, the company has boasted that the iPhone is more in-demand than ever, with the most recent version of the device becoming its most successful product launch.
The company also revealed more about the coming relaunch of its audio and chat assistant Siri, which it now calls Siri AI.
Starting with the iPhone 18, the bot will now be able to go across information on a person's phone, like messages and emails, to find information, answer queries and take action on a person's behalf.
Some Siri AI features will also be available on the new Apple Watch, including the ability to take notes of conversations and transcribe them, should a wearer enable that feature.
Ternus referred to new AI-enabled capabilities on the iPhone as an "intelligent personal hub", and admitted that Apple would be making use of "the most private details of your daily life."
He insisted that all of it will remain private, with the AI features often running "on device", meaning not through third-party companies. And when a third-party is required for a function, Ternus said it will remain private in a remote server, or cloud.
"Others see that data as something to collect and store", Ternus said. "Here, not even Apple can access what's yours."

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”
The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.

“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.

He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.
Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

Plea in Bombay High Court challenges Maharashtra religion law over marriage rights
A petition in the Bombay High Court challenges key provisions of the Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026. The plea says the law intrudes on personal choice in faith and marriage and blurs consent with coercion.
A fresh legal challenge has been mounted before the Bombay High Court against the newly enacted Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026, with a petitioner alleging that several provisions of the law are vague, overly broad and arbitrary and interfere with the fundamental right to marry a person of one’s choice.
Maulana Halimullah Farooque Ahmed Khan, a 70-year-old Islamic scholar from the Bhiwandi area of Maharashtra’s Thane district, has filed a writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of the Act. The plea, filed through advocate Mateen Shaikh, alleges that the legislation infringes fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution.
The petition specifically challenges Section 2(a), which defines “allurement”. Khan argues that the provision uses excessively broad terms, with phrases such as “better lifestyle” and “divine healing” potentially bringing routine religious instruction and social work within the ambit of criminal law.
The plea also challenges Section 6, which requires individuals seeking to convert to give 60 days’ prior notice. According to the petitioner, the requirement exposes deeply personal decisions about faith to public scrutiny and executive control.
Khan further challenges Section 13, alleging that it shifts the burden of proof onto the accused. The petition argues that this undermines procedural fairness and the constitutional presumption of innocence.
Section 9(2), which provides for stiffer penalties where women are converted, has also been challenged as gender-discriminatory.
The petition further points to instances of what it describes as premature police action. It argues that while the state can prohibit or penalise marriages or relationships brought about through force, fraud, coercion or deception, that power cannot extend to placing consensual inter-faith relationships, marriages or voluntary changes of faith under state surveillance or heightened scrutiny merely because the individuals profess different religions.
The petitioner contends that choosing a life partner and deciding one’s faith are matters of personal autonomy, dignity, privacy and decisional freedom protected by the Constitution.
Khan has urged the High Court to declare the Act unconstitutional, arguing that its provisions could have a “chilling effect” on citizens’ fundamental rights and fail to adequately distinguish between consent and conversion.
Alternatively, he has asked the court to read down the provisions so that they apply strictly to cases involving actual force, fraud or coercion.

Orange Shirt Day founder says her truth is being 'pushed aside' by controversial shirts
Orange shirts with slogans like 'Dig deeper' and 'Still no proof' being sold online
The founder of Orange Shirt Day says she was sick to her stomach when she learned orange shirts with slogans like "Dig deeper" and "Still no proof" were being sold online.
Holding back tears and speaking from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc in B.C., which announced a discovery of potential unmarked graves near a former residential school site in 2021, Phyllis Webstad said her campaign was being used in a "hateful way."
"I've been trying to understand why they believe that it's OK to hurt people," she said.
In 1976, Webstad wore a present from her grandmother, an orange shirt, on her first day at a residential school at St. Joseph's Mission, in Williams Lake, B.C. The shirt was taken from her by school officials and never returned.
Webstad founded Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30, 13 years ago, to honour Indigenous children who were forced to attend residential schools.
In late August, Rebel News announced it was selling orange T-shirts on its website for the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and that the shirts are about "challenging the identity politics that Canadians are increasingly pressured to accept and standing up for the whole truth in our complex Canadian history."
Statements printed on the shirts include "Still no proof," "You can't handle the truth," "Buried Truth" and "Dig Deeper," as well as "Canada was built not stolen."
Webstad called the sales a direct attack on her work with the Orange Shirt Society.
"It's my truth and what I know is the truth," Webstad said.
"It seems like this truth is not being respected. It's not being understood. It's being pushed aside."
In an emailed statement, Ezra Levant, founder and owner of Rebel News, pointed CBC News to a video on its website launching the sale of the shirts, saying their reporter "approaches these issues with compassion."
"The stated purpose of the National Truth and Reconciliation Day is noble – to honour residential school survivors and their communities by recognizing the lasting impacts of Canada's residential school system, so Canadians can better understand its legacy as part of our ongoing journey toward truth, healing, and reconciliation," Levant quoted what was said in the video.
In the video, the Rebel News reporter goes on to say "But five years later, Canadians are still being told that there are some truths they're not allowed to question."
Levant added in the statement that Rebel News staff are "dedicated to freedom of expression including the right to seek the truth" and "these orange shirts are a response for people who are forced to wear orange shirts at school or at work, as part of an 'official' political narrative."
"No Canadians should be compelled to support any political view, including Orange Shirt Day’s politics."
In the video promoting the shirts, the Rebel News reporter says "what's more than likely underneath the apple orchard soil at the Kamloops site is probably an old septic plot."
Webstad pointed to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which has so far documented more than 4,000 deaths of Indigenous children in Canada's residential school system.
She said her own auntie, Agness Jack, shared a personal story about what it was like living in the Kamloops Indian Residential School in a book published in 2001, Behind Closed Doors: Stories from the Kamloops Indian Residential School.
Webstad also said her grandmother and her grandmother's 10 children including Webstad's mom were all forced to attend residential school.
"My mother was so traumatized that she could not take care of me; thank God my Granny was there, thank God my auntie was there," said Webstad.
"I want to say that we aren't liars. Indian Residential School survivors are not liars. Have some respect and give us the space and time to do what we need to do as individuals, as family, as a community, as a nation."
The orange shirts available on the Rebel News website are listed in youth sizes as well as adult.
"That is a whole new level of every word in the book: disgusting, unbelievable, sickening. Where are their minds?" said Webstad about the youth sizes.
MPs and ministers condemn shirts
Last week, the Liberal Indigenous Caucus published a statement that said merchandise "that mocks survivors' experiences and dismisses their truths is reprehensible and beneath any organization."
A request for comment from Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party's shadow minister of Indigenous Services, was not returned by time of publishing.
Morin told APTN News last week, “I find it racist and I find it absolutely disgusting that they’re attempting to make a profit off the pain and suffering of residential schools."
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, who is a member of the Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, said people across the country have raised concerns about the shirts to her.
"Not just people living in my riding but also from Canadians who are appalled about this really disgraceful and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering for financial gain," said Gull-Masty.
Gull-Masty's mother and grandmother were both forced to attend the La Tuque Indian Residential School in Quebec.
Gull-Masty said she expressed her concerns to Justice Minister Sean Fraser, but didn't say what avenues the government would explore. She said she felt Fraser understood how serious the matter is.
"I think this is one of the areas where we are seeing behaviour that is not only being perpetuated more commonly but it is reaching a level that is unacceptable," said Gull-Masty.
In a statement to CBC Indigenous, a spokesperson for Fraser said, "Seeking to profit from Indian residential school denialism is deeply disgraceful and represents a cruel and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering."
"Residential school denialism is a serious and distinct issue, and our government has said this issue warrants dedicated further parliamentary study," the statement said.
"Any legal response should be developed carefully in consultation and co-operation with Indigenous Peoples and the communities most affected."
Earlier this year, Canada's Senate voted down an amendment to Bill C-9 that would have criminalized residential school denialism, by making it illegal to wilfully promote "hatred against Indigenous Peoples by condoning, denying or downplaying the Indian Residential Schools System."
Webstad said she supports the idea that residential school denialism should be added as hate speech to Canada's Criminal Code.
"I believe what Rebel News is doing right now is what is needed to convince our Canadian government that yes, a law needs to be passed," said Webstad.
Shirts designed to provoke conflicts in schools, says academic
Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, said he feels the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering.
"Thousands of Indigenous children died, we know that," said Carleton.
"So what [Rebel News] is trying to do is cast doubt, shake public confidence and are trying to convince Canadians that maybe we shouldn't care about Indigenous people and reconciliation anymore."
Carleton said the easiest way to understand denialism is to look at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's simple formula.
"We've got to have truth first," he said.
"Truth will lead to healing and justice. Healing and justice will lead to reconciliation. Denialists know that and what they're trying to do is keep us stuck in the truth part."
Carleton said he believes the inclusion of youth sizing is a tactic designed to provoke conflicts within schools where parents may be influenced by denialist rhetoric and use their children to challenge school policies.
He said the slogans on the shirts not only defend the colonial status quo but promote colonization as a compassion project, and said they question survivors' lived experiences.
NDP MP Leah Gazan tabled a private member's bill in Parliament last fall to criminalize residential school denialism.
In a letter to the Indigenous Liberal Caucus on Tuesday, Gazan said anti-Indigenous racism and denialism are growing and have now resulted in "the production of merchandise denying genocide and mocking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. We must respond to this as what it is – the incitement, monetization and promotion of hate."
Gazan called on the Indigenous Liberal Caucus to table her bill as a government bill.
