Nandan Nilekani, Kamath brothers on Karnataka SIR notice list over mismatches
Prominent Karnataka voters, including Nandan Nilekani's family and the Kamath brothers, were placed on a verification notice list during the electoral roll revision. Officials said no notices were served in these cases and the discrepancies are being handled directly.
Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani and his family, along with Zerodha founders Nithin Kamath and Nikhil Kamath, are among the prominent names on the notice list generated during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Karnataka, official sources said.
Nilekani’s wife and children have reportedly been flagged as “unmapped with the last SIR (2002 rolls)”, while Nithin Kamath, Nikhil Kamath and their mother Revathi Kamath have been flagged for a “parents’ name mismatch” in the Bengaluru South Assembly constituency.
Sources said notices have been generated in several such cases, but prominent personalities and VIPs are not being inconvenienced during the verification process. Officials are expected to visit them, wherever required, to complete the formalities. Sources added that notices generated in these cases had not been served on the individuals concerned.
NOTICES GENERATED FOR PROMINENT NAMES
A notice was also reportedly generated for Bharat Ratna awardee Professor CNR Rao over a name-related mismatch, while actor Shivarajkumar was flagged because his name was not mapped with the 2002 electoral rolls. However, the notices in these cases were also not served, with officials resolving the discrepancies at their level.
The ongoing SIR has flagged voters for several discrepancies, including mismatches in names or parents’ names and failure to map their details with the 2002 electoral rolls.
CLARIFICATION ON SHIVAKUMAR’S MOTHER
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar’s mother, Gowramma, was also reported to have been flagged for a “self-name mismatch” in the Kanakapura Assembly constituency.

The official said two other voters with the same name within the jurisdiction of her polling station had been issued notices.

Lonnie Bunch Protected the Smithsonian From More Than Trump
As pressures bore down on an American institution, its secretary held firm.
Americans may not realize for many years just how lucky they were that Lonnie G. Bunch III led the Smithsonian Institution from 2019 to 2026. Bunch has announced that he will step down at the end of this year. He insists that the timing is his own, and we should do him the honor of believing him—notwithstanding the immense pressure the administration has applied to the Smithsonian generally and Bunch personally since Donald Trump returned to office last year.
Bunch, 73, would likely have chosen to retire earlier if not for his sense of duty—his conviction (which few dispute) that he was the best person to guide the Smithsonian through a turbulent period. The Smithsonian is the world’s largest museum, education, and research complex. It’s also “part of the glue,” as Bunch himself said shortly after taking office, “that holds the country together.”
Since his appointment as the Smithsonian’s top official—its 14th secretary and the first historian and Black man to hold the position—in June 2019, Bunch has been the glue holding the Smithsonian together. Through a combination of principled stances and deft political skills, he has kept the sprawling institution on mission and aligned with its public. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said in a statement that Bunch has “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian has “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision, and leadership.”
Bunch is a fighter, but a smart one. He has often struck me as a master of institutional jiu-jitsu—a leader who knows instinctively when to hold the line, when to yield, and how to convert yielding to the advantage of the institution he has done so much to advance and protect. “When you’re Black in America,” he told The New York Times earlier this year, “you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right? You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”
Bunch has worked at the Smithsonian since 1978, interrupted by stints at the California African American Museum in the 1980s and the Chicago Historical Society in the early 2000s. His tenure as secretary included the upheavals of 2020 and 2021, when—after the killing of George Floyd and amid the coronavirus pandemic—activists on the left were accusing museums across the country, including the Smithsonian, of being bastions of white privilege, colonialism, and cultural theft. Bunch remained calm and compassionate in the face of these critiques, compromising when appropriate, but never giving in to bullying.
It surely helped that his greatest achievement prior to becoming the Smithsonian’s top official was planning, raising funds for, and launching the National Museum of African American History and Culture. The museum, which opened to great fanfare in 2016, has been hugely popular. Under Bunch’s leadership, the museum balanced a forthright, profoundly moving description of slavery and its long aftereffects with exhibits that bear witness to the extraordinary flowering of African American culture, celebrating a panoply of achievements by Black Americans across many fields of human endeavor.
The Smithsonian was founded by an act of Congress in 1846. During the Civil War, it created a controversy by refusing to host a lecture series presented by abolitionists. The institution’s leadership eventually relented, but Frederick Douglass, the most prominent abolitionist of the day, was still not permitted to speak. At the 2019 ceremony installing him as secretary, Bunch referred back to those days: “Today we are here speaking in a place as an African American, where Frederick Douglass could not speak, but we are a different institution.”
Bunch’s leadership, and the Smithsonian’s resilience, has been severely tested since Trump’s return to power. Efforts by the institution to tell what Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, described as “a fuller, more American story” and “one that fosters connection, reflection and understanding” came into conflict with White House officials who felt that the “fuller story” being told was overly focused on moral failure, hypocrisy, and oppression.
The new administration was quick to target the Smithsonian. Some of what gave Bunch moral authority during the Biden years now threatened to work against him.
In March 2025, an executive order noted that the United States had witnessed “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” The Smithsonian, it stated, had, “in recent years, come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology.” Trump announced that he was firing Sajet. The Smithsonian regents asserted that only Bunch had authority over such personnel decisions, but she resigned anyway.
More recently, the administration has ramped up pressure on the Smithsonian, demanding an overhaul of its presentations to rid them of perceived liberal bias and attempting to force its hand with explicit threats, such as pulling funding and erecting warning signs in front of the National Museum of American History. (Although it is independent, the biggest share of the institution’s budget comes from the federal government.)
Bunch has had to figure out how to handle these various assaults without allowing the Smithsonian’s mission to be compromised. He has said plenty on the public record—all of it sage and diplomatic, yet consistently firm on questions of principle. I can only imagine what private conversations he has been having on a daily basis.
Thanks to the double whammy of COVID and activist pressures, few leaders of any prominent organization have had a fun time since 2020. But Bunch has been the leader of an enormous—and enormously important—institution that’s explicitly in the business of (among other things) telling the American story at a time when the question of how to tell that story has become so fraught and divisive.
What to do in such circumstances? Perhaps Americans could all begin by just agreeing that the pandas in the National Zoo (which is part of the Smithsonian) are very, very cute. And then, perhaps, that the Apollo 11 command module in the National Air and Space Museum—the one that carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin to the moon and back—is really cool. If so, perhaps they can next agree that Bunch, during his tenure at the helm of the Smithsonian, has been the exact combination of resolute leader and compassionate and good-humored public servant that America needed him to be.

Several videos have gone viral on social media following the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, 2026. Some users shared a video claiming that after the disaster, the world’s largest Shaligram, said to be more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath.
In this context, Zee News put out a report with a screenshot from the viral video and, along with the hashtags #Nepal, #Flood and #Shaligram, wrote: “Viral Video: Floods have revealed a secret, a 170-million-year-old Shaligram has been found.”
Shaligrams are naturally formed stones traditionally found in Nepal’s Kali Gandaki River, and revered by Hindus as representations of the deity, Vishnu.
Right-wing X user Amitabh Choudhary (@MithilaWaaala), who has been found spreading misinformation and comminal propaganda several times in the past, shared a video and wrote: “Stone older than dinosaurs. Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal.”
Kisi ne sahi hi kaha hai, “शुरुआत भी वही, सफ़र भी वही, और अंत भी वही।”
Stone older than dinosaurs !!
Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal 🇳🇵 pic.twitter.com/GIv851LJbV
— Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala) August 29, 2026
X user Shashank Shekhar Jha, who claims to be a Supreme Court lawyer, and others such as @Nalanda_index, @CodexZeroTR, @Krishnavallabhi, @bhaktSenapati, along with several Facebook and Instagram users, too, shared videos and photos with similar claims.
Fact Check
To find out the truth behind the viral claim, we performed a relevant keyword search. This led us to reports published on June 30, 2026, by Himalaya Times and Online Khabar featuring images of the giant sculpture seen in the viral video.
The reports stated that a 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Nepal’s Mustang district was gradually becoming a centre of religious faith. According to the reports, sculptors from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts carved a huge rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom in Gharpajhong rural municipality area and created the 22-foot-tall Shaligram replica between April 20 and May 4, 2026.
During our investigation, we found a report by a website called Desh Sanchar. According to the report, the 22-foot-tall sculpture had been unveiled on the evening of May 28, 2026, after religious rituals on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River.
We also located a video uploaded on April 23, 2026 on the Facebook page, Nepal Raibar, in which artists could be seen carving a rock to create a Shaligram statue.
We also geolocated the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video. It’s located on the Kali Gandaki River, opposite ‘Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom. When we compared Google Street View images from 2025 with the viral video, we found that the 2025 image only showed a large rock.
This makes it clear that the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video is not a natural or ancient stone. Rather, it is a statue created by carving a rock.
We also tried to look for the sources of all the variants of the now-viral visuals. We found the original version of the video and the screenshots shared by Zee News on the Instagram account of a user named Durga Prasad Poudel. It was posted on June 2, 2026.
View this post on Instagram
Similarly, we found the second viral video uploaded on June 30, 2026, on the Instagram account of a user named Rijan Dongol.
View this post on Instagram
The third viral video was shared on June 8, 2026, on the Facebook account of a user named Arjun Singh. Its caption reads: “A huge 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue is located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom, Mustang. This monumental work, inaugurated by Jagadguru Shankaracharya Mahaswami Vidushekara Bharati, attracts a large number of pilgrims and stands as a major spiritual and cultural site in Nepal.”
Thus, all three viral videos featuring the Shaligram statue have been available on social media since June 2026. They have absolutely no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal in August.
Overall, the claim by Zee News and other users that after the recent disaster in Nepal, the world’s largest Shaligram, more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath is completely misleading. In reality, the 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue seen in the viral video was created by carving a rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Mustang district, during April–May 2026. The videos of the Shaligram statue circulating on social media are also from June 2026 and have no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal.

With Chumbak now streaming on Netflix, the show’s writer-director Aatish Kapadia has opened up about which character from the ensemble he would have loved to play if given the chance. His answer? Gulshan Tarapurwala, the lively and memorable character brought to life by Delnaaz Irani.
Aatish Kapadia picks his favourite Chumbak role: “Gulshan Tarapurwala, without a doubt!”
When asked which role he would pick from the show’s colourful cast, Kapadia didn’t hesitate, “Gulshan Tarapurwala. Without a doubt! I would play Gulshan very well! 'Aye Hutoxi' and the way she says it, I would have so much fun and make everyone have fun that everyone would say, ‘For Gulshan, there is no one better than Aatish Kapadia to cast for the role,’” Kapadia said.
His enthusiastic response highlights the playful spirit behind Chumbak, a series that revolves around five interconnected families and their quirks, conflicts, and camaraderie. For the unversed, the character of Gulshan played by Delnaaz Irani is that of a dominating mother-in-law of a Mumma’s boy played by Anant Joshi as Freddie while Amyra Dastur plays the latter’s wife Hutoxi.
Created and produced by Jamnadas (JD) Majethia and Aatish Kapadia under Hats Off Production, Chumbak is a warm, multi-generational comedy set in a neighbourhood where everyone knows—and influences—each other’s lives.
The series features a star-studded ensemble including Neena Gupta, Deven Bhojani, Arjun Bijlani, Helly Shah, Sumeet Raghvan, Sandeepa Dhar, Sumeet Vyas, Manasi Parekh, Anant Joshi, Amyra Dastur, and Delnaaz Irani in key roles.
While audiences are just beginning to explore the dynamics of the Chumbak universe, Kapadia’s casting choice offers a fun glimpse into the joy and creativity that went into shaping the show’s vibrant characters.
Chumbak is now available to stream on Netflix as it premiered on the streaming platform on September 10, inviting viewers into a world where humour, heart, and human connections take centre stage. With its relatable storytelling and a cast known for delivering memorable performances, the series is poised to resonate with fans of family-driven comedies.

East Zone retraced the footsteps of history as it broke its 14-year Duleep Trophy drought on the same ground it won its last title on, defeating South Zone on a first-innings lead in the final at the M.A. Chidambaram Stadium on Thursday.
Holding a 584-run lead coming into the final day, Ishan Kishan’s side knew that it simply had to dot the i’s and cross the t’s to take home its third title in the zonal competition in front of a morning crowd, diminished on the final day by a lack of stakes and ominous weather overhead.
Having notched a half-century stand the previous evening, Mohammed Kounain Quraishi (116 not out, 190b, 13x4, 4x6) and Kumar Kushagra added 26 more through the first session. Kushagra seemed set to celebrate his India-A call-up by adding a half-century to his first innings ton, but nicked C.V. Milind behind on 46, attempting a booming drive to reach the milestone.
From the other end, Quraishi followed his solid first-innings 40 with a knock to savour. The 23-year-old was compact in defence and put bad balls away, looking unflustered as he completed his fifty from 84 balls with a six against Tripurana Vijay
Once he was past his half century, he opened up with a pair of sparkling drives for four against M.D. Nidheesh, and looked in supreme control as he sauntered his way to a maiden First-Class ton from 179 balls. He was visibly emotional as he reached the milestone with two through covers, pumping his fist as the helmet came off.
With the game over in all but name, Mohammed Siraj bafflingly sent down a nine-over spell to start the day, and though he beat the edge on a couple occasions, he continued to look largely ineffective despite relatively cooler conditions.
After Kushagra’s dismissal, Quraishi was joined in the middle by Anukul Roy (64, 112b, 4x4, 2x6), who recovered sufficiently from a finger injury that kept him out of the bowling innings. He played some stylish shots, lofting Vijay down the ground for two sixes over the sight screen.
Anukul reached his half-century in 83 balls after Lunch, but as focus drifted away from the game, the biggest cheers of the afternoon came when Kishan walked down to the boundary to sign autographs. Soon after Quraishi’s ton, Anukul clipped Milind for two through mid-wicket to take East Zone to the highest aggregate score in a Duleep Trophy match.
Anukul’s essay came to an end when he edged Nidheesh to Devdutt Padikkal at first slip, and the end came soon after. Mohammed Shami came out for a brief stint at the crease before handshakes were offered to confirm a long-awaited triumph for East Zone.

Trump’s Smithsonian vendetta, briefly explained
After a resignation announcement, what comes next for the Smithsonian?
Welcome to The Logoff: The head of the Smithsonian Institution will resign after weathering nearly two years of attacks by President Donald Trump.
What’s happening? Lonnie G. Bunch III, the secretary of the Smithsonian, announced on Tuesday that he will step down at the end of 2026 after more than seven years in the role.
Bunch’s retirement isn’t entirely about Trump; he’s 73 and has already served longer as secretary than his two most recent predecessors.
But the president, who has waged a relentless campaign against what the White House has described as “improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology” at the Smithsonian, is indisputably part of the story. As Bunch put it to the New York Times on Tuesday, “at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”
What has Trump done to the Smithsonian? Since last spring, Trump has gone after the Smithsonian system for promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive.” He has threatened its funding, forced out the director of the National Portrait Gallery, and attempted to meddle with its exhibits. His ability to successfully make changes has been limited by the Smithsonian’s structure — but a new secretary could give Trump far more control.
The president also, unsurprisingly, wants more Trump: administration officials have reportedly pressed for a new Portrait Gallery exhibit focusing on the president.
What’s next? Trump doesn’t officially have a role in selecting Bunch’s successor, who will be chosen by the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents — but that board does include Vice President JD Vance and multiple Republican members of Congress, so he might as well.
Trump will surely want to install a loyalist, which means — as the Washington Post’s art and architecture critic Philip Kennicott explained on Tuesday — that the Smithsonian’s fate could depend on the ability of the rest of the board, and especially its chancellor, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, to resist.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
Don’t miss my colleague Rachel Cohen Booth’s new piece on the “smartphone trap”: the way in which phones have become not just ubiquitous, but required for many parts of daily life (reading a menu, parking a car, signing into an account — the list goes on).
As Rachel argues, it’s not too late to preserve, or claw back, the option of going through life phone-free. “Pushing for a non-smartphone option is about accessibility, affordability, and agency. It’s about demanding the kind of freedom in a society we deserve to have,” she writes.

The latest update suggests that Adani Group might have already begun working on the massive restoration work of the Writers' Building in Kolkata. According to a report by Jagran, the Group has commenced a preliminary assessment of the heritage building. The Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department (PWD) and his team reportedly inspected the historic building, which is due for renovation and restoration work. Adani Group advisor and retired IAS officer Sanjay Thade was reported to be with the inspection team during the visit. The inspection is said to be focused on assessing the building’s current condition while looking into structural issues and the scope of restoration work. Based on the preliminary assessment, a detailed restoration proposal is expected to be prepared. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari had asked the Adani Group to undertake the renovation project of Writers' building, sources told Times of India. It is believed that the preliminary assessment has indicated that the restoration could cost ₹100-120 crore, which the group may consider funding as its corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative. According to the same report by Times of India, the primary inspection has found major sections of the Writers' Building in poor condition. It is expected to require extensive restoration before functioning again. However, the government has not yet officially confirmed these details. The decision to renovate the Writers' Building arrived after the BJP came to power in the state. The current government shared its intention to shift the state administration back to Writers’ Buildings, instead of operating from Nabanna in Howrah. It expressed its desire to make the iconic building the main centre of Bengal’s administration. In 2013, the West Bengal state secretariat was temporarily shifted to Nabanna. The move to Howrah was initially said to be a brief transition by the Trinamool Congress-led government to allow for the renovation of the historic complex. However, even after a decade, the state secretariat continued to operate out of Nabanna. Fresh restoration proposals, including an alleged interest by the Adani Group, are reportedly facing the challenge of balancing modern administrative needs with strict heritage conservation rules in the city. For the unversed, Writers’ Buildings is among Kolkata’s premier historic landmarks. Conservation guidelines restrict altering its classic façade, historic character, or original architectural framework under the pretext of modernisation. As AI reshapes the nature of work and raises concerns about job displacement, startups and small businesses will become the key engines of employment creation, Infosys cofounder Nandan Nilekani said at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 today. Nilekani said large companies, with their structured roles and processes, are better positioned to deploy AI for automation and reduce their workforce. Smaller businesses, on the other hand, have more dynamic roles that are harder to automate. “If you want to AI-proof an economy, you actually should create a situation where job creation is done by millions of small companies,” Nilekani said. He pointed to the rapid expansion of India’s startup ecosystem, saying that the country had about 10,000 startups in 2015 and around 1.5 Lakh in 2025. He expects the number to reach 10 Lakh by 2035. “Both the new startup world as well as the traditional world, they will be the employers of the future,” he said. Nilekani added that technology should make it easier for these businesses to access capital, markets, and capabilities traditionally available to larger enterprises, thereby creating a more level playing field. Tokenisation Push For SMEs Nilekani said tokenisation has reached a stage where it is moving beyond an emerging technological concept to practical applications, with the RBI and SEBI working on tokenised financial assets. While the RBI is exploring the tokenisation of certificates of deposit, the two regulators are also working together on tokenised corporate bonds, he said. Financial tokenisation involves creating a digital representation of an asset that carries information about its attributes and the rules governing it. This allows the asset and the information required to verify it to move together. Nilekani, who has been closely involved in building India’s digital public infrastructure, said tokenisation represents the next layer of this evolution. While systems such as Aadhaar and UPI made identity and payments digitally accessible at population scale, tokenisation can similarly make productive assets and economic rights identifiable, verifiable, and portable. This could allow such assets to be used across lenders, insurers, fintech platforms, and marketplaces. Nilekani highlighted three pilots being developed using the Finternet architecture, an open and interoperable digital financial infrastructure designed to connect financial systems and different classes of assets. One pilot involves tokenising cattle by capturing information such as an animal’s identity, ownership, health, and milk productivity in a digital credential. The credential can be shared with lenders, which can then provide credit against the asset. Another use case involves tokenising warehouse receipts by recording details such as the quantity and quality of the stored produce in a portable token that can be shared with lenders. The third pilot focuses on tokenising loan documents across marketplaces to make them interoperable, with smart contracts used to standardise transactions. Nilekani said all three pilots use common infrastructure designed to work across asset classes and public blockchains. AI Agents To Create Demand Nilekani said tokenised assets would also need interoperability and liquidity to become useful at scale. AI agents could help create demand for such assets by executing transactions on behalf of businesses, he added. For instance, an AI agent could convert an invoice into a token, identify potential lenders, and offer the asset to them. “Tokenisation by itself will only handle issuance. But tokenisations on public chains supported by agentic transactions will also create demand,” Nilekani said. He added that the larger opportunity lies in using tokenisation to expand smaller businesses’ access to capital and financial services. A token that establishes an asset’s identity and value, combined with an AI agent that continuously looks for financing or market opportunities, could give small businesses access to capabilities previously available mainly to large enterprises. His remarks came a day after Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis said the state is working to establish India’s first state-level legal framework for the blockchain-based tokenisation of land and other immovable assets under the proposed Maharashtra Digitisation and Exchange of Land Token Asset (DELTA) Act.

Walk into any major teaching hospital in India and look at the signboards. You are likely to find Cardiology, Neurology, Nephrology, Gastroenterology, Endocrinology departments—and, somewhere among them, a General Medicine. Now travel outside India and ask for the corresponding specialty. In most countries and in much of international medical literature, you will be directed to Internal Medicine. Are these two different specialties? No.
The Indian ‘general medicine’ physician and the international ‘internal medicine’ physician belong, essentially, to the same broad specialty: the discipline concerned principally with the diagnosis and non-surgical management of disease in adults. The question, therefore, is not whether Indian general medicine is different from internal medicine; it is whether India should continue using a name that has become increasingly ambiguous when a more precise and internationally intelligible name is available.
A name that understates
The first problem is the word ‘general’. To the ordinary patient, a ‘general physician’ can sound like a doctor who treats common ailments—a doctor one sees before being referred to a specialist. But that is not what an MD or DNB physician in General Medicine represents. An internist (one who practices general medicine or internal medicine) has undergone intensive specialist training in the diagnosis and management of complex adult diseases. The internist is expected to integrate information from multiple organ systems, recognise patterns that may not fit neatly into one specialty and manage patients with several simultaneous illnesses.
Consider an elderly patient with breathlessness, anaemia, kidney dysfunction, diabetes, weight loss and abnormal liver tests. Which specialist should he be treated by? His condition falls within the specialities of haematology, nephrology, endocrinology and gastroenterology/hepatology -- all of which are sub-specialties of internal medicine in most other parts of the world. But in India they continue to be called super specialties.
For our patient with breathlessness, the specialist trained to look at the patient as a whole and ask whether the abnormalities are connected, is the right specialist: an internal medicine consultant. Integrative function is at the heart of internal medicine, and the word ‘general’ does not adequately convey it.
General Medicine also creates confusion with Family Medicine. India recognises Family Medicine as a distinct medical specialty. Family Medicine and Internal Medicine are not the same thing. Family Medicine is concerned with comprehensive and continuing healthcare across the lifespan—from children to older adults—and across a broad range of health problems. Internal Medicine, by contrast, is fundamentally the specialist discipline of adult medical care.
There is also a common misunderstanding about the word ‘internal’. It does not simply mean ‘medicine of organs inside the body’. The modern concept of internal medicine has deep roots in 19th-century European medicine, particularly German medicine, when advances in physiology, pathology and bacteriology transformed clinical practice. Physicians increasingly applied scientific knowledge to the diagnosis and treatment of diseases that were managed medically rather than surgically. The term ‘Innere Medizin’ emerged from this tradition. Internal medicine, therefore, describes a method and discipline of adult medical practice, not merely a list of internal organs.
Why ‘general’ medicine?
Why does India say ‘general medicine’ then? The answer lies partly in history. British medicine developed a strong tradition of general clinical medicine. Even as specialisations increased, the general physician retained an important role in British hospitals and broad clinical knowledge remained highly valued. Britain was an important source of the medical terminology inherited by India. There is, therefore, a historical explanation for India’s terminology.
The terminology subsequently became part of Indian medical law and was reinforced by Indian institutions. The Indian Medical Council Act of 1956 formally recognised Doctor of Medicine (General Medicine) as a postgraduate medical qualification. By the 1990s, the nomenclature had become even more firmly standardised. The Medical Council of India’s 1993 regulations explicitly stated that the nomenclature for postgraduate degree courses should be uniformly adopted and prescribed M.D in General Medicine. Thus, what may have begun as part of a British medical tradition became entrenched in India’s own regulatory system.
Why the nomenclature matters
The word ‘general’ is increasingly misleading in the age of sub-specialisation. When the term ‘general medicine’ became entrenched, medicine was far less specialised than it is today. Today, internal medicine is the parent discipline from which numerous subspecialties have emerged: cardiology, gastroenterology, nephrology, endocrinology, rheumatology, pulmonology, infectious diseases, haematology, medical oncology and others. The existence of these subspecialties does not make the internist a non-specialist: quite the opposite. The internist’s expertise lies in understanding the patient when disease does not respect these boundaries. That is a specialty in its own right.
Indian medicine is no longer operating in an isolated linguistic environment. Indian doctors train abroad; foreign doctors train in India. Indian postgraduate qualifications are evaluated internationally. Medical journals, conferences, guidelines and clinical research operate across national boundaries. A doctor introducing himself or herself internationally as a specialist in internal medicine is immediately understood. The title general medicine may require explanation. That may appear trivial. It is not. Specialty names communicate the scope of a physician’s expertise to patients, colleagues, hospitals, universities, regulators and international institutions. A clear professional vocabulary matters.
Formalising usage of an exisiting term
The proposed change would not introduce an alien concept into Indian medicine. The term ‘internal medicine’ is already widely used in Indian hospitals, medical departments, academic literature and postgraduate teaching. The Indian Armed Forces Medical College, for example, has a Department of Internal Medicine. And Indian postgraduate curricula routinely use ‘internal medicine’ to describe the discipline being taught. Even India’s medical regulatory ecosystem is not completely uniform in terminology. The National Medical Commission’s own records contain doctors in general medicine departments whose qualifications are described as M.D., Internal Medicine. The transition, therefore, would not be from an unfamiliar term to a new one. It would be a formal recognition of terminology that is already in partial use.
What should change ? The proposal need not be complicated. India could gradually adopt: MD (Internal Medicine) instead of MD (General Medicine); DNB (Internal Medicine) instead of DNB (General Medicine); Department of Internal Medicine instead of Department of General Medicine and Specialist in Internal Medicine or Internist instead of relying on the ambiguous description General Physician. Existing degrees would, of course, remain completely valid. There is no need to alter the training, scope of practice or professional standing of existing physicians. Only the nomenclature would change. A change of name, not a change of specialty. The proposal is therefore not about prestige. It is about precision. It is not about rejecting India’s medical history; it is about allowing medical terminology to evolve with medical practice.
Looking ahead
Every profession periodically has to ask whether the language it inherited still accurately describes what it does. Indian medicine has changed enormously since the terminology of its postgraduate specialties was first codified. We now practise medicine in an era of molecular diagnostics, precision medicine, artificial intelligence, genomics, transplantation, complex multisystem disease and unprecedented sub-specialisation. Yet one of our principal adult medical specialties still carries a name that essentially says: general. Perhaps it is time to be more specific.
(Dr. Abraham Ittyachen M. is professor of medicine, M.O.S.C Medical College, Kolenchery and chairperson – Association of Physicians of India, Kerala Chapter. abyliz@rediffmail.com)

Kenya's chai lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
- Published
Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.
A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.
But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.
The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.
But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.
Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity.
"Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.
Macharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not.
"If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.
Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.
A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.
Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.
The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.
According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.
The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.
It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.
Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre.
"This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.
The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.
Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down.
"Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.
It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.
This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".
In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.
Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.
Customers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs.
"Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.
Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.
On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.
The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.
He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.
Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.
According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.
In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.
For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.

The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has sealed at least 56 jewellery shops in Chandni Chowk on 10 September, PTI reported, citing traders. The shops are located in Kucha Mahajani, a bullion market in Delhi. Traders said gold and silver jewellery worth crores remained locked inside the sealed shops. The action reportedly followed stricter checks against dangerous and illegal buildings across Delhi. These checks increased after seven people died in the Satya Niketan building collapse. Yogesh Singhal said officials sealed the shops around 11.30 AM after posting notices. Singhal heads the All India Bullion and Jewellers Association. Quick answers to key questions The MCD sealed at least 56 jewellery shops in Chandni Chowk due to stricter checks on dangerous and illegal buildings, a response heightened after a recent building collapse in Satya Niketan. Traders have reported that gold and silver jewellery worth crores remains locked inside the sealed shops, raising concerns about the valuables and the impact on traders. Traders expressed frustration, claiming MCD officials arrived without prior notice and alleged that the sealing process was conducted simultaneously across multiple locations. The increase in enforcement actions follows the tragic collapse of a building in Satya Niketan, which resulted in seven fatalities and raised alarm about unsafe structures across Delhi. Traders and the All India Bullion and Jewellers Association have questioned whether accountability extends beyond traders to include government departments and politicians in light of the Satya Niketan tragedy. "The question to consider is whether, after the Satya Niketan tragedy, only traders will have to bear the brunt of this tragedy or whether action will also be taken against any government department and politicians," PTI quoted the association as saying in a statement. Traders alleged that MCD officials and police had arrived without giving them advance notice. They claimed officials pasted notices and sealed shops in several buildings at the same time. Some traders said they only understood the situation after arriving at their shops. The association also alleged that the notices carried earlier dates. One shared notice was dated 12 May. It asked owners to stop unauthorised commercial use of basements within 48 hours. Trump’s midterm strategy: More Trump
The Republican midterm convention gets underway in Dallas.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is bound for Dallas to kick off Republicans’ midterm convention — which is likely to be all about him.
What’s going on? If you haven’t heard of a midterm convention before, you’re not alone. They’re not common: The last one was in 1982 and, as the New York Times notes, it “went so poorly” that a subsequent Democratic Party chair described them as “places for mischief” and canceled the next one.
Nonetheless, Trump has decided to hold one this year to tout his and his party’s (but mostly his) record leading into the 2026 midterms. The event will span two days — today and Thursday — in Dallas, Texas, and Trump is set to get the prime speaking slot on both nights.
The event won’t have any of the features that make a traditional presidential-year convention, such as formally selecting a candidate or setting a party platform; instead, it will look more like a multi-day GOP infomercial.
Is this a good strategy? If you’re a Republican politician, probably not. The Republican National Committee chair is explicitly billing the event as a “Trumpapalooza,” and with Trump in attendance, that’s what they’re sure to get.
The only problem is that polling suggests Trump is radioactively unpopular right now, with his overall approval hovering near record lows and dragging down Republican candidates across the board. Some Republican candidates are staying away from the convention entirely, while those who are attending may not see much benefit.
(Democrats, unsurprisingly, are thrilled by the Trump-centric convention, as the Washington Post reported on Wednesday.)
How else is Trump getting involved in the midterms? He’s spending heavily, or at least starting to: His MAGA Inc. super PAC has about $400 million on hand and (indirectly) made $49 million in ad buys earlier this week in key states, plus another $10 million in Texas.
He’s also asked voters to “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.” It remains to be seen whether that will yield the result he’s hoping for.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

France wants to transform Fifa after withdrawing Infantino support
- Published
France's football leaders have proposed to seek ways to transform how Fifa is run after its national association became the latest to withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's presidency.
On Thursday, the French Football Federation (FFF) followed England, Italy, Republic of Ireland and Scotland in withdrawing support for Infantino over his aborted plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors.
The FFF had pledged its support for Infantino in June before his investment proposal came to light.
Infantino's plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions.
Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and North American governing body Concacaf have called for Infaninto to step down, though he retains the backing of South America's Conmebol and African governing body CAF.
Fifa has confirmed Infantino will stand for a fourth term in the Fifa presidential election in March.
"A project with such a significant impact on the future of football could not be envisaged without comprehensive information, in-depth consultation and a fully transparent decision-making process," FFF president Philippe Diallo said in a statement.
"Fifa's governance does not live up to the standards that football represents."
Despite Infantino abandoning his proposal, the FFF said that "Fifa's governance cannot be considered resolved".
The FFF has pledged to start consultations with confederations, national associations, players, supporters and governance experts about reforming Fifa.
"The aim of these consultations will be to foster collective reflection and to draw up proposals for a far-reaching transformation of Fifa's governance, with a view to restoring confidence, enhancing transparency and ensuring the independence and exemplary conduct of world football's governing body," the FFF said.
"The FFF, a founding member of Fifa, thus intends to contribute to a debate that is vital for the future of football, its regulation and its development."

NASA has carried out some notable rescue missions over the past few years, including bringing home the astronauts stranded on the International Space Station last year. More recently, the agency sent up a probe in hopes of saving the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite first launched in 2004 that began falling out of our planet’s orbit.
The plan was for robotic arms on the probe, known as LINK, to grab onto the aging satellite and—with a powerful set of thrusters—drag the observatory back into position. The rescue robot was launched into space this past July but soon after suffered issues with its altitude systems, a key set of controls for moving in space. The mission had to be canceled.
“Swift wasn't designed to be serviced,” Ghonhee Lee—CEO of Katalyst Space, the company that developed LINK—stated just before the probe’s launch. And as Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s astrophysics division, also noted at the time, this was “a high-risk, high-reward mission.”
Now, Swift will continue sinking. Like all low-orbit satellites, the observatory experiences air resistance from Earth’s upper atmosphere, causing it to gradually descend. Originally, scientists predicted the telescopes might not reach critical depths until 2030, but in recent years, intense solar activity has caused the Earth’s atmosphere to expand, increasing drag. Swift is expected to reenter the atmosphere as soon as the end of this year, though it may still capture some fascinating information about our cosmos before burning up on its descent.
The satellite has been NASA’s eyes on some of the most explosive and short-lived phenomena in the universe. Equipped with three primary telescopes, it’s capable of observing multiple wavelengths, including visible light, ultraviolet, x-rays, and gamma rays. Over 21 years, this has made the observatory indispensable for recording and alerting ground teams about supernovas, gamma-ray bursts, and black holes shredding stars.
The Swift operations team has announced a plan to conduct as many observations as possible during the remaining lifetime. Prior to the rescue mission, the observatory had shut down its telescopes to conserve power, to keep its solar panels oriented, and to minimize air resistance.
But shortly after the rescue mission was abandoned, two of the three telescopes aboard were successfully restarted, and the x-ray telescope captured images of the Tycho supernova remnant, located approximately 13,000 light-years away. Adjustments are also underway for the Burst Alert Telescope, which is still powered down, with the goal of resuming observations within a few weeks.
Once Swift’s altitude falls below 185 miles above the Earth’s surface, operating the telescopes becomes increasingly challenging, and its descent will further accelerate. But researchers are looking forward to what else it might capture before finally expiring.

“From the outset, reproduction is a collaborative venture,” writes Anna Louie Sussman, a journalist who has spent years reporting how people all over the world try, and too often fail, to build the families they want. Her work explores how the collaborators of reproduction keep multiplying: doctors, employers, legislators, insurers, and a fertility industry that increasingly promises not just a baby but a better one.
Is it harder to have kids today? Or is it harder to want to?
A new book unpacks why so many people struggle to build the families they want.
In her new book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty, Sussman traces the economic, political, and psychological negotiations that stand between people and the children they say they want. Her reporting challenges the assumption that falling birth rates can be fully explained by metrics like income, marriage and education that demographers tend to focus on. She argues the answers are much more personal and resistant to measurement.
I wanted to better understand what Sussman meant by this idea of “impossibility of family” — and how one would even determine that, whether as a prospective parent or as a policymaker. What are the biggest barriers to having kids and how do people tell the difference between what they can’t afford and what they’ve come to believe they need? How much does the media conversation about these issues inform people’s choices?
I spoke with her about what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s egg freezing reveals about women who aren’t running for president, what countries that subsidize fertility treatment tell us about the demand going unmet here, and why she hesitates to say outright that having children is good. Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
You started working on this book seven years ago. What has most surprised you about how the conversation around fertility and family formation has changed in that time?
There are some people on the left who have always paid attention to family issues, like Elizabeth Warren with her work on bankruptcy and the “two-income trap,” but I do think we’ve been seeing a lot more movement there, with groups like the Congressional Dads Caucus [in 2023], and care infrastructure ideas like those in the Build Back Better Act. There’s also been all this movement around paid leave in the states, 3-K and pre-K, and attempts for more affordable child care.
On the right there’s been the rise of this strange pronatalism and the turn that’s taken with what I’ve wound up calling “kid-maxxing.” Plus this embrace in Silicon Valley and among the super rich with so-called super babies and the really overt embrace of technology to make children on this industrial scale. I also did not expect Roe to be overturned. I would have hoped that would’ve come with a lot more attention on the right to support for mothers and children, but that really hasn’t come to pass in a big way.
I was startled to read that you found some philosophers attempting to reclaim the term “eugenics.” You cite one who wrote a paper called “Defending eugenics,” which sets out to “reclaim the spirit” of eugenicists like Charles Darwin and Francis Galton. You cite another who calls for “liberal eugenics” grounded in the freedom of parents to choose how to enhance their children in accordance with their own values.
One Oxford philosopher even says parents have a duty of “procreative beneficence” and should select embryos or fetuses “most likely to have the best life” based on the genetic information they have.
That was also surprising to me. Like you, I also thought it was a discredited and taboo word. It’s hard to know how widespread those views are. I mean to be clear, eugenics has always been part of our culture in the US. I think people forget that a lot of Nazi policy was inspired by American eugenic policies, and it’s an attitude that has never really gone away. We still see it in a lot of subtler forms that I mention in the book. I mean, even just how people are choosing embryos and terminating pregnancies based on certain genetic conditions.
“Clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.”
This eugenicist rhetoric is gaining steam at a moment when some people are also really hard at work on developing technologies that could enable this sort of thing. While some of these philosophers will definitely make a distinction between parents making some individual choices vs. a state sponsored program, I think it’s the attitude that’s at the root of this, and that’s what we really need to work on criticizing and dismantling.
So the book is arriving just as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been documenting her egg freezing journey, and talking about how she wants to push to expand insurance coverage and federal support for fertility treatments. What does her experience — and the reaction to it — say about our current moment? Some on the right were so mad, as if she should just throw in the towel or eschew hope and agency at age 36.
What’s so interesting about her experience that I think that people miss is, yes, is it exceptional that she’s contemplating a run for president? Sure. Not many of us are doing that. But on many other levels, she’s doing what a lot of women who can afford to do in their late 30s do when they’re still single. In the book I mention the research of Marcia Inhorn, who interviewed about 150 women who sought to freeze their eggs. And what’s interesting is if you look at their profiles, they were city-dwelling professionals who were on average nearly 37 at the time of freezing.
That is AOC to a tee, and if you asked those study participants why they were doing it, most were not doing so because they felt like they needed to put their families on hold to pursue careers. A full 82 percent cited their lack of a partner as the prime motivation. They wanted to have a family at some point and didn’t want to rule that out.
What do you think we should take from other countries that do subsidize egg freezing?
So the city of Tokyo has subsidized egg freezing and they were totally oversubscribed. So many women took up the city’s offer, and France has also started offering it. More places offer IVF coverage for people who need it because they treat infertility like a disease, which is how the World Health Organization defines it.
What’s interesting is when you look at places where there is more coverage, it also gives you a sense of the scale of need for it. So in Denmark, where you can get something like up to six rounds of treatment publicly funded for your first child and another six rounds for your second child; I believe about one in nine children is born there with assisted reproductive technologies. If you compare that with the US, it’s closer to one in 36. So clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.
In the book you cite historian Sara Matthiesen, who argues that since legal abortion helped transform having a child into more of a personal choice, pregnancy thus became understood as chosen, with parents then sacrificing or forfeiting some of their claim on societal help. I couldn’t tell where you landed on that argument. Do you find it persuasive?
So I find it persuasive in the sense that I feel like conservatives will grab onto any argument to avoid state responsibility towards families and children. The fact that you can terminate a pregnancy is one more reason that can be provided to individualize the responsibility of parenthood.
But I think that we’re also seeing the mirror image of that — where the choice to remain or not remain pregnant has also been taken away in so many places post-Roe. And I don’t think that has resulted in the converse of her argument, which is that when that choice is taken away and you can no longer sever pregnancy and motherhood, then states and society will step up to acknowledge that reality.
In the middle of your book you recall an ex-boyfriend, who was divorced and felt it would be impossible to afford a second kid. You were surprised by this, and later cite a pregnant woman in Venezuela you met while traveling, who was worried about money but excited about parenthood. She told you the Venezuelan proverb that “a baby comes with a loaf of bread under his arm.” The subtext was that they believe things will work out. The subtitle of your book is The Impossibility of Family in Age of Uncertainty. So where do you land? Is it impossible, as your ex said?
I think that’s what people are trying to negotiate with themselves. That’s where things like faith, agency, and disposition come into play. One of the reasons I wanted to write this book was I feel like birth rates and demography are always discussed in terms of these data points that people can measure, like how many people are married and how old are they, and do they have college education or not? Do they earn X, Y, Z income, or not? Do they have a job?
But it’s just all so personal. So the Venezuelan woman was an optimist, whether that’s culturally or dispositionally, and she did believe things would be okay. And I think we all know stories of people who’ve grown up who came from very challenging backgrounds and wound up achieving some sort of fame, fortune, success…so we know that things are always possible. And that’s where questions of what one is prepared to sacrifice come into play, or what expectations do you have of what you want to provide a child.
The thing I really want to highlight is how individual these negotiations are, whether you come down on it being impossible or whether you want to lower your standards and maybe your child doesn’t get in-home violin lessons or if music’s really important to you and you can’t imagine a universe in which your child doesn’t play an instrument.
I cover these issues too and I think about a lot about what our role in the media is. I share your view on reproductive justice, and wanting to help people live the lives they want. But you also wrote about experiencing what you called “money dysmorphia” — when someone is feeling insecure about their financial situation even when they are in fact okay. What role do we have as journalists to help people distinguish between genuine financial impossibility and the fear that they can never be secure enough? And if we don’t do that, how do we not end up in a world where only rich people are encouraged to have kids?
So I try to be optimistic, but I also feel like as a country, there’s no bottom to how far someone can fall in America. As Elizabeth Warren found, having a child is a huge predictor of bankruptcy. I would like to be more positive. And I do believe that there’s so many easy policy fixes, so many ways to make parenting easier. But for people I know who’ve gone through serious financial distress because of things in their life changing, there’s a limit to what I can do or say without giving them all my resources.
Regardless of our job as media, I wish I could say that everything will work out fine. And in some cases it can. Again, people do really great jobs being parents with so much less than I have, which is something I try to keep in mind all the time. But I also would say as a society that we let people fall all the way through the floor and then some. We just don’t have a safety net. So I find it hard to say that everything will work out and you’ll wind up fine.
At the beginning of your book you talk about how having children is an intensely personal decision and you’re not interested in writing about if it’s “good” or “bad” or “worth it.” One of the critiques conservatives make about people like us is that we can be so averse to making any kind of normative statement about having kids that we’ve lost the plot. I’m curious for your thoughts on that. In a book arguing that we need more family-friendly policies, do you think you need to more explicitly say that having kids is a good thing to do?
What I would say is loving relationships are good, and having kids is one of those. I think parenthood is an exceptional one just in the level of responsibility that you’re inviting. Having kids for people who want to have kids is good. But I don’t know, I do hesitate to privilege that relationship above all others because of what doing so means. If you say having kids is good, well, who has kids? That immediately has gendered implications and instantly puts an onus on women.
Though we say public libraries are good and that doesn’t mean we have to make libraries against people’s will. But yeah, I guess I wonder if that position avoids the ways this kind of relationship is different from other loving relationships. While this isn’t what personally motivates me, I think one can definitely make a case that having kids is more of a social good than some other kinds of relationships.
When we say society should be more family-friendly and fund it with tax dollars, it’s not just so everyone can live out the lives they want, but also so we can support our society now and in the future.
Lyman Stone I think gets at this, he says children are good because people are good. Again, I would say if you feel like you might be a good parent and enjoy that relationship, that specific relationship, the whole point of my book is I want that to be more accessible because from what I’ve seen and now in my own experience, it is an amazing relationship. It’s not a relationship like any other one I’ve ever had. But I guess it’s not clear to me what the corollary is of saying having kids is good. It’s definitely good for people who want to have kids, but it’s definitely not good for people who don’t want to have kids.
Though I’m not someone who always wanted to have kids myself. And while I’m strongly against coercing people into having children, I think there are millions of people like me who are like, “I don’t know. I’m not sure. I can’t really picture it.”
There are people on the right who say, “Therefore, just do it because you’ll like it.” And I don’t think that’s appropriate. But it’s also true that for most of human history, people were simply not asked to come down on this question of: “Do I want it or not?” Now today I’m so glad I have a child and the choice to decide, but if you had asked me five years ago I would have said, “I don’t really like little kids. It’s never been my thing.”
So the identity question becomes interesting and confusing to me, and I think it leaves me more uncomfortable with the idea that we should just support whatever anyone’s choice or desire is today when we know that our choices and desires do change, including based on what people absorb in the media.
I think a lot of young people are just really struggling. I see this all the time on Reddit threads or listening to young people talk about their lives who say, “If I can barely take care of myself, how can I take care of someone else?” We don’t have a society that makes any form of caregiving easy, and people are really struggling to find work. We have a society that doesn’t make it easy to care for oneself, for one’s parents, for one’s friends, for one’s partner.
I mean I did have a kid before I felt totally comfortable and I was just really fortunate that it worked out. I do agree with some of the people on the right who say that a lot of the things you think you need to become a parent, you don’t. And we know that really great people grow up all over the world where they have much fewer resources and infrastructure and everything. So I do think kids need a lot less than we often imagine they need. And that is part of thinking about your own expectations and what you want for a child and also, again, what you’re prepared to sacrifice.
I joke that I go to an annual yoga class fairly regularly. I don’t really cook anymore. I had a single mom who was just resourceful, though she was lucky to be in New York City, where there actually are resources to access. If you’re living in Tennessee or Mississippi those types of resources would probably not be available.

Finally available in the US! Repairable with long-term software support. Five-year warranty. Good performance. Daylong battery life. Distraction-free mode. Expandable storage. Capable cameras.
TIRED
Feels very plasticky. Not supported on Verizon, with caveats on other carriers. Not waterproof. Cameras still don’t match the competition.
It’s time to vote with your wallet.
The US has long had fewer smartphone options than the rest of the world. The Apple-and-Samsung duopoly, supported largely by carriers—where people buy most smartphones—has made it hard for other phone brands to break through. It’s partly why the Dutch manufacturer Fairphone hasn’t sold its repairable, ethically made smartphone in the US in its 13-year existence—until now.
Fairphone finally made it across the pond with a new model, the Fairphone (Gen. 6+). If you’ve complained about the lack of repairable smartphones, the inability to self-replace a battery, or even the idea of a more ethically manufactured phone, the Fairphone should be on your list (if it’s time to upgrade).
I’ve been using this $650 Android handset for several weeks, and it’s pretty good.
Fairer Phone
There isn’t much of a difference between the Fairphone (Gen. 6) I reviewed last year and the (Gen. 6+). The phone comes in a new cobalt blue color to commemorate people who work in the cobalt mines (a crucial component in smartphones) and the Fair Cobalt Alliance, a nonprofit cofounded by Fairphone.
Chiefly, the Fairphone has a slightly more souped-up processor—the Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4—alongside 12 GB of RAM. That last part is important, as many of the new software features in our smartphones, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence, demand a lot of memory; the 12 gigs here should give the Fairphone a longer shelf life in being able to take advantage of those capabilities.
Performance has been plenty satisfactory, whether I was using Google Maps to navigate, doomscrolling through Instagram Reels, or playing PokémonGo while waiting for a doctor’s appointment. My benchmarks show the tiniest of performance bumps over the processor in the Gen 6. You may see a slight stutter here and there, but it barely affects day-to-day use. The software is also more polished this time around; I haven’t run into notable bugs, which I can’t say for last year’s model.
I don’t mind the look of the new Fairphone—the blue and the yellow-accented button is a fun combo—but it does have a very plasticky feel. You might like Fairphone’s accessory system, which lets you replace part of the backplate with accessories like a wallet or phone grip by removing two screws (you can use the included screwdriver). I haven’t bothered, as it feels a little clunky; I don’t want these items permanently on the back, and unscrewing them is a hassle. Hopefully, Fairphone can move to a MagSafe-like system in the future.
The 6.3-inch AMOLED, 120-Hz screen is more than adequate. It’s colorful, sharp, and bright enough to read in sunlight. Fairphone’s adaptive brightness mode can be a little aggressive, so I often manually adjusted the brightness slider, but I don’t have much else to complain about.
Battery life from the 4,415-mAh cell isn’t impressive, but it won’t have you running to a wall outlet all the time either. I typically ended most days with around 20 percent by bedtime; that’s with around five to six hours of screen-on time. It’s a shame there’s no wireless charging, but that’s a nice-to-have not necessarily a deal-breaker. Oddly, the phone doesn’t come with a USB-C cable (the lack of a charging block is standard across phones these days), but the idea is that you probably have one lying around in a drawer. Less e-waste!
The dual-camera system, powered by a 50-MP main and a 13-MP ultrawide, is solid. No, Fairphone can’t really compete with the big tech giants like Google, Apple, and Samsung on this front. Low-light scenes suffer the most, with details lost in shadows—stay very still to avoid a blurry image. Photos from the 32-MP selfie camera can also look a little soft. Still, it’s not so poor that you won’t use it. You’ll get perfectly adequate results, but if you rely heavily on your smartphone’s camera for video and photos, you may want to look elsewhere.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
Main camera
Fairphone doesn’t meddle too much with the base Android 16 software, except for Fairphone Moments, which is tied to the yellow switch on the right edge of the phone. Flick the switch and the phone’s interface goes minimal, only offering access to a handful of apps. You can create your own Moments—up to five apps—to help you focus on the task at hand. For example, if you’re driving, you can flick the switch and have it only let you access Google Maps, Spotify, and Phone. It’s a neat system, though its practicality completely depends on your willpower to use it.
I’d have liked to see Fairphone win some brownie points with a headphone jack, but alas. You’ll at least appreciate the microSD card slot to expand on the already generous 256 GB of internal storage (unusual at this price). You might even prefer the capacitive fingerprint sensor baked into the side power button, rather than the under-display fingerprint sensor in most Android phones.
Long-Lasting
People are holding onto their phones for longer. But manufacturers can do several things to make it easier. Software and security updates are crucial, and thankfully, Fairphone promises seven years of updates through 2033. It also comes with a five-year warranty, virtually unheard of for a phone.
A big part of the Fairphone is repairability (iFixit gave it a 10/10 score). With the included screwdriver, you can remove that same backplate mentioned earlier to access the battery. Fairphone has instructions on its website for accessing the 11 other components you can replace, from the speakers and display to the USB-C port. Fairphone will sell these parts through 2033, and they’re cheap, too! Replacing the display, for example, will cost just $90. (You can also access most of this information in the preinstalled My Fairphone app.)
There are some caveats. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) only has an IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating, meaning it’ll be fine in the rain, but a drop in the pool may wreck it. That’s the trade-off for having such easy access to the device’s internals for repairs.
And while the Gen. 6+ works on T-Mobile and AT&T, it doesn’t support Verizon (which includes all the smaller MVNOs that rely on Verizon’s network, like Visible). Fairphone’s website has a chart showing carrier compatibility, and you’ll see that some MVNOs on AT&T’s network are only partially supported, like Boost Mobile and Cricket. Other limitations include the lack of millimeter-wave 5G or missing eSIM support on T-Mobile. For what it’s worth, I’ve used it with an eSIM on Google Fi—the phone dips to 4G more often than other phones, but it hasn’t been a big issue for me. Your mileage may vary.
Can you find better specs for the money? Sure. The Pixel 10a will easily give you a better camera system. For $50 more, the new Samsung Galaxy S26 FE delivers flagship-grade performance and a telephoto camera. But you’ll also be out of pocket if you drop either phone and need a screen replacement. The Fairphone doesn’t have that problem, and you’ll have a little more peace of mind that your phone was made sustainably, with fair wages paid out to folks in the supply chain. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) proves you no longer have to make massive compromises just to take a stand.
