Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season
- Published
The NFL is notoriously difficult to predict and last season was no different.
Seven of the eight division winners were different from 2024, with two of the Super Bowl favourites missing out on the play-offs entirely - the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.
Two outsiders then made it all the way to the big game, with the Seattle Seahawks beating the New England Patriots for their first NFL championship in 12 years.
So, who will be this season's surprise package? Who will be playing at Super Bowl 61 next February? And who will be the main men?
Here, the BBC's NFL experts make their picks for the 2026 season, which begins this week. Plus you can predict your Super Bowl winner at the bottom of this page.
Who will reach the Super Bowl?
Rob Staton: I think the NFC will be another battle between the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks. I'm going to go with the Rams, simply because only two teams have repeated since the turn of the century. I have them facing the Buffalo Bills. Josh Allen finally gets to the big game.
Hugh Ferris: You could argue that, aside from an underwhelming head coach hire, there's little reason the 2026 Bills will be any different to the recent incarnations. I'm picking them to finally get over the line, though, and reach the Super Bowl, but to lose nonetheless. It's incredibly difficult to choose anyone else rather than the Rams, isn't it?
Haydn Parry: Surely the Bills can convert Allen's talent and make it to the season showpiece? Joe Brady's promotion to head coach might prove to be the missing ingredient. From the NFC, I think the Rams look most likely to have a strong tilt this campaign, and I see them winning it.
Joe Bradshaw: The last time the Super Bowl was at SoFi Stadium in 2022, the Rams won on home territory and they look primed to repeat next February. From the AFC, surely Bills quarterback Allen is overdue a trip to the NFL's biggest game, even if it will ultimately end in defeat.
David Brindle: After losing Bo Nix to injury in last season's play-offs, I expect the Denver Broncos to use that as motivation and at least go one further this season. As for the Rams, it's very difficult to look past the consensus predictions for the Super Bowl.
Ben Collins: Full disclosure, I'd seen the above before writing this so here's some leftfield picks... imagine if it's the Los Angeles Chargers that actually get to play in the Super Bowl in their own stadium, and it's former Rams quarterback Jared Goff that leads Detroit to victory.
Who will be the NFL's MVP?
Rob Staton: I'm going with Josh Allen. He now has an offensive-minded head coach running the team. Everything will be geared towards him having a big season.
Hugh Ferris: In an attempt to think outside the box, I'm picking Justin Herbert of the Chargers. You might suggest a quarterback in a Jim Harbaugh team isn't likely to get the chance to have an MVP-level season, but the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator might change that.
Haydn Parry: I might be wearing my blue-star goggles here but Dak Prescott has the ability and the weapons to have an outstanding season. Offence was not the Dallas Cowboys' problem last year and it certainly wasn't Prescott's fault that the team failed to deliver. Dallas just need to find a 'D'.
Joe Bradshaw: Buffalo's new head coach Joe Brady has stepped up from offensive coordinator so knows how to get Josh Allen purring. If the Bills make the Super Bowl, their quarterback will be the obvious candidate for his second MVP award.
David Brindle: If it wasn't to be a quarterback, I fancy Jahmyr Gibbs. He's signed a new deal and now has no running back competition at Detroit so expect him to see lots of action on a Lions team who are NFC contenders.
Ben Collins: Cincinnati have remedied their defence and still have a top offence. After twice winning comeback player of the year, quarterback Joe Burrow stays fit long enough to bag the award he really wants as the Bengals make a deep play-off run.
Who will be coach of the year?
Rob Staton: It could be Joe Brady if he can help Josh Allen reach MVP status, but in order to mix things up I'm going for DeMeco Ryans. The Houston Texans are going to lead on their defence and I think they'll be really strong.
Hugh Ferris: If the Bills reach the Super Bowl, then it stands to reason Joe Brady gets the nod as a first-year head coach, putting to shame people (like me) who called him an underwhelming hire.
Haydn Parry: I have always been a big fan of John Harbaugh. He will start from a comparatively low base in New York with the Giants, but with their passionate fanbase and the enormous potential of Jaxson Dart lift-off could be achieved early.
Joe Bradshaw: There has been such turnover on the NFL's coaching carousel, it has been hard to keep up this off-season. In the face of such instability, I'll opt for Sean McVay as he steers the Rams to their third Super Bowl title.

Melania’s top aide reveals their true thoughts about Natalie Harp
Natalie Harp, a close aide to Donald Trump, has made headlines in recent weeks over her unusually personal relationship with the president
Melania Trump’s top aide has revealed their true thoughts about Natalie Harp, whose close relationship with her boss, Donald Trump, has fueled recent speculation.
Harp, Trump’s executive assistant, has been thrust into the political spotlight in recent weeks with reports that she slept in the locker room at Trump’s Bedminster golf club and even hopped in the trunk of an SUV to stay close to the president.
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat from Georgia up for re-election, made headlines for his quip about Trump, telling a crowd in Atlanta last month, “He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie.”
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania, dismissed any rumors that her husband’s relationship with Harp is anything but above board on an episode of conservative media personality Stella Escobedo’s YouTube show released Tuesday.
“The mainstream media…they’re endlessly obsessed with garbage tabloid gossip about Natalie Harp, who, by the way, is a hard-working, loyal White House aide to President Trump—a cancer survivor—who POTUS helped get off labeled treatment for and saved her life. I mean, what do you make of that?” Escobedo asked Beckman.
Harp, who says she was diagnosed with bone cancer, gained national attention in 2019 for crediting Trump for saving her life with a law he signed in 2018 that provided her access to experimental treatments.
“The liberal media is ridiculous. They don’t know anything about the first lady’s personal and private life,” Beckman told Escobedo. “They don’t even take the time to put us on air to cover these incredible achievements that our first lady has accomplished.”
“What they need to do is look in the mirror because they’re all attacking this hardworking, very talented, very intelligent person in Natalie Harp,” he said, adding that the mainstream media is “obsessed with the gossip with the first family. And I can tell you firsthand that it’s time for them to become journalists and stop looking at the gossip.”
The public started to pay closer attention to Harp after The Washington Post reported last month that she was one of the select few who got to ride with Trump in a catering truck that transported them from Air Force One to a smaller jet amid a potential assassination threat from Iran while they were leaving the NATO summit in Turkey. During Trump’s escape, Air Force One, which carried unsuspecting D.C. reporters and senior Trump officials, served as a decoy.
Harp —who reportedly received a $45,000 holiday cash gift from Trump — wrote in a letter to Trump in 2023, “You are all that matters to me,” The New York Times reported shortly after the president’s 2024 election victory in an article announcing that she would follow him to the White House after joining his team in 2022.
While Harp seems to never leave Trump’s side, Melania has been largely absent from the public eye during her husband’s second term.
Over the summer, Melania missed Senator Lindsey Graham’s funeral, the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner, and the dignified transfer of the remains of four service members killed in the Middle East.
NBC News reported on August 17 that Melania has made about half as many public appearances as she did at that point in Trump’s first term.

Jimmy Kimmel will be interviewing Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico “under unusual circumstances,” posting the interview directly to YouTube, rather than airing it on TV during Jimmy Kimmel Live. In Wednesday night’s episode, Kimmel said this was out of concern for retaliation from the Trump administration’s FCC:
Another big James Talarico interview is punted to YouTube due to FCC threats
Jimmy Kimmel is the latest talk show host to move an interview with Talarico online after the FCC “threatened” him.
[Trump’s] FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings, it would seem they don’t like. And so, out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV.
Kimmel’s announcement comes almost a year after his show was taken off the air in response to threats from FCC chair Brendan Carr. In February, Stephen Colbert also had to move an interview with Talarico to YouTube, claiming CBS barred him from airing it over worries about upsetting the FCC, citing the FCC’s equal time rule. The FCC also took aim at The View after an interview with Talarico earlier this year.
ABC, which airs Jimmy Kimmel Live and The View, filed a lawsuit against the FCC last month claiming it has “waged a retaliatory campaign” against its networks, “punishing” ABC by threatening to pull its broadcast licenses.

Nintendo's latest sale is 'made possible' by the tariff refunds it's hoarding
The Customer Appreciation Sale starts this weekend after Nintendo recouped $300 million in tariff refunds.
Rather than giving any of the tariff refunds it obtained from the US government back to players, Nintendo has opted to run a Customer Appreciation Sale. The sale, which Nintendo claims is one of its "largest promotions ever," starts at midnight ET on September 13 and it runs until September 26.
"The Customer Appreciation Sale is our way of saying thank you to Nintendo players for their continued support and is made possible in part by tariff-related refunds," the company said. "While Nintendo absorbed most tariff-related costs, the refunds helped make promotions like this one possible."
The sale will run across the eShop, Nintendo Store and retailers. It includes 30 percent discounts on dozens of digital games and bundles, as well as DLC, physical games, Amiibo, accessories and other merch.
The company increased Nintendo Switch 2 pricing in the US, Canada and Europe just last week owing to "changes in market conditions." It jacked up prices of the Switch and other products in August 2025 for similar reasons in the wake of tariffs being imposed on imports to the US.
Earlier this year, Nintendo sued the US government in an attempt to claw back tariff payments after the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration's global levies were illegal. In an earnings report last month, the company said it had received around $300 million in tariff refunds, adding that "the tariffs related to the refunds were primarily borne by the company rather than passed on to consumers through product prices."
Like PlayStation parent Sony and Amazon, Nintendo is facing a consumer lawsuit after declining to pass along tariff refunds to customers. In a motion to dismiss that Nintendo filed in July, the company argued it's not legally required to give those refunds back to consumers, claiming the plaintiffs "received exactly what they bargained and paid for" when they bought its products following tariff-induced price increases.
Framing the sale as a thank you to players — whose money Nintendo wants to get its hands on during said event — while touting the tariff refunds as a reason for making the discounts possible is deeply gross. Panic, on the other hand, did the right thing by simply giving tariff refunds back to Playdate owners.

Barcelona began its Champions League campaign in commanding fashion with a 5-1 win over Feyenoord on Wednesday, with Raphinha continuing his strong start to the season by scoring twice.

This week, Lyft riders in Nashville, Tennessee, who request a ride on the app might get matched with a new driver: a robot.
A new partnership between the ride-hail company and Waymo, the self-driving-vehicle developer, will integrate self-driving rides into Lyft’s platform. (Riders can also request a driverless ride through Waymo’s own app; service there started in April.)
The rollout marks a new milestone for Lyft, which has worked with other, smaller self-driving vehicle companies in the US, but never with a partner as big as Waymo, which operates in 14 US metros. Lyft executives also see the partnership as a continuation of a conversation the ride-hail company has been having for a few years now with its hundreds of thousands of US drivers.
Lyft, like its competitor Uber, insists that its platform will be a “hybrid network” for a long while yet, as human drivers work alongside robot ones. But it’s hard to imagine the transition won’t upend life for some of the millions of professional drivers who work in the US today.
“We've got to make sure we're honest, we're open. We have conversations with drivers and bring them into the journey with proactive communication,” says Jeremy Bird, Lyft’s executive vice president of global growth. “We've done AV [themed] driver forums; we've done driver appreciation events to make sure we're having a conversation. But we're embracing the transformation in the future of AVs.”
A glimpse of what the future might look like can be found in Lyft’s provisional operations depot in Nashville, where employees of its longtime car rental service called Flexdrive now clean, prep, repair, and position Waymos in the right parts of the city so they're ready for passengers. (An 80,000-square-foot, purpose-built depot is set to open in October.) Waymo, which focuses on building autonomous vehicle technology, partners with several companies around the US to help manage and operate its driverless fleets. Of the 72 people who work at this Nashville depot, half of them are former Lyft drivers, the company says.
One of those former drivers, Jonathan Baines, started picking up Lyft riders in 2016 to help support himself as he worked as singer-songwriter. He liked the extra cash but also the people he drove—tourists, locals. “It kind of felt like you were hanging out with your friends more than anything,” he says. Now Baines works as a fleet operations lead, which means he oversees workers cleaning the Waymos, making sure they hit their metrics and standards. It’s the best operations job he’s ever had, he says, “more fun than retail.”
And Baines has to admit: There’s something nice about being alone in a Waymo. “As much as I love to talk to people, to be able to be in the car and relax and not have an obligation to talk with anyone is a nice feature,” he says.
Bird says having Waymos on the Lyft platform will give riders more choice, which is a good thing. Also, more vehicles on the platform means more supply means lower fares. (In a recent earnings call, Lyft executives used data from San Francisco, where it doesn’t offer driverless rides, to suggest that the presence of autonomous vehicles won’t affect the number of rides that human drivers see.) Bird says Lyft intends to continue partnering with different robotaxi companies.
But it may be near-impossible for the new jobs maintaining and directing self-driving cars to neatly replace the driving ones lost. In Washington, DC, where Waymo has fought for months to start service, the company has said that it expects to employ “hundreds” of people if its cars launch there; some 3,200 taxi and ride-hail drivers work in the District (likely many of them part-time). To compensate, Waymo has proposed diverting some of its DC revenue to a fund dedicated to vocational training and workforce development for drivers, to help them transition to other jobs. Waymo did not respond to a request for comment on this story.
Former drivers make up 35 percent of Lyft’s Flexdrive workforce, which is currently in 30 US cities. Hiring former drivers “is an effort we will continue to be very intentional about as AVs become a growing part of the fleet,” Lyft spokesperson Cristian Delgado writes.
Baines is already looking ahead, even beyond that sprawling Waymo depot set to open in October. Part of him misses the “small business” part of being an independent contractor for Lyft. Eventually, he’d like to own his own autonomous vehicle, so it can go out to pick up and drop off passengers without him. “There's the fear of AI taking over,” he says. “I think you can learn how to use AI as a resource.”

A debate examines the funding and functioning of registered unrecognised political parties across India, raising questions over alleged money laundering, hawala transactions, and tax evasion through poll donations. Former Chief Election Commissioner Dr S.Y. Quraishi pointed out that while registration remains simple, the Election Commission of India lacks statutory powers to de-register political parties following a Supreme Court ruling, making actions like de-listing ineffective. Transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj questioned the silence of central enforcement agencies, including the Income Tax Department, the Enforcement Directorate, the Central Bureau of Investigation, and the Lokpal, despite significant donations flowing into unrecognised parties that often become untraceable. The discussion highlighted concerns regarding audit compliance, 100 percent income tax exemptions on political contributions, non-implementation of the Central Information Commission order bringing parties under the Right to Information Act, and the need for stricter accountability mechanisms.
An India Today investigation exposes registered unrecognised political parties across Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, and Bihar that collect hundreds of crores of rupees in donations despite having no visible operational ground presence. The Rashtriya Vikas Party received 207.63 crore rupees over five years according to ADR analysis, yet its listed Delhi address operates as a dance school whose owner denies knowledge of the outfit. In Jabalpur and Delhi, residents at addresses listed for the Bharatiya Jan Kranti Dal Democratic were entirely unaware of the party. Similarly, Prabal Bharat Karti in Sitamarhi, Bihar, gathered 103.84 crore rupees in donations, but ground checks revealed no physical party office, raising serious questions over tracking and oversight of electoral funding.
In an interview ahead of the BRICS Summit in India, Columbia University Professor Jeffrey Sachs shared his perspective on India-China relations, the global economic order, and multilateral diplomacy. Highlighting Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India, Sachs described the bilateral relationship between New Delhi and Beijing as the most critical in the world, stating that both nations can foster a stable multipolar framework. Sachs argued, "The bilateral relationship between India and China is the most important bilateral relationship in the world," suggesting both countries should resolve historical border disputes peacefully. He emphasized that the center of gravity of the global economy has returned to Asia and dismissed the effectiveness of Western unilateralism. Commenting on strategic alliances, Sachs advised against Indian participation in the Quad and cautioned against strategic over-reliance on the United States and Israel.
An India Today special investigation reveals that registered unrecognised political parties in Gujarat collected over two thousand crore rupees in donations between 2019 and 2024, based on data analyzed by the Association for Democratic Reforms. Ground checks across Gujarat, Delhi, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh showed that several of these parties exist primarily on paper. The Bharatiya National Janata Dal received 957.44 crore rupees, while The New India United Party secured over 600 crore rupees, though its registered Ahmedabad office was locked without any signboard. The Satyavadi Rakshak Party, which collected over 330 crore rupees in 2023-24, fielded just one candidate in Vadodara who finished last, operating from a locked flat in Anand. Similarly, the Aam Janmat Party collected over 220 crore rupees while its registered office remained shut, and Saurashtra Janata Paksha received over 200 crore rupees. ADR noted that 90 percent of donations come from individuals and large donors despite poor electoral participation and minimal vote shares.
At the India Today Global Aaj Tak BRICS Roundtable, former Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal R.K.S. Bhadauria and Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi analyzed geopolitical security, defense diplomacy, and economic resilience surrounding the 18th BRICS Summit. Discussing Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India and bilateral relations along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), Air Chief Marshal Bhadauria noted that high-level talks directly impact bilateral ties and regional stability. Admiral Tripathi described BRICS as a pragmatic multilateral platform rather than a military alliance, emphasizing that the path to peace requires strategic power. Both military leaders evaluated maritime security, counterterrorism, critical infrastructure protection, supply chain localization under the Atmanirbharta initiative, and defense exports. The panel also addressed non-traditional security threats, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and energy security risks along global trade choke points such as the Strait of Hormuz, while affirming the enduring strategic foundation of India-Russia bilateral defense relations.

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

Commentary: The changing face of terrorism 25 years after 9/11
Twenty-five years after the September 11 terror attacks, Singapore and the region face a rapidly evolving landscape of terrorism and extremism threats, says RSIS’ Kumar Ramakrishna.
SINGAPORE: The attacks in New York and Washington on September 11, 2002, that killed nearly 3,000 people were a catalyst for transnational terrorism.
Southeast Asia felt its repercussions through the terror bombings of two nightclubs in Bali, Indonesia on Oct 12, 2002, perpetrated by the Al-Qaeda-linked Jemaah Islamiyah (JI) terrorist network.
The threat of organised terrorist networks gripped regional governments throughout the 2000s, but risks have evolved significantly. Since the mid-2000s, militant groups like Islamic State have exploited the internet and social media to spread propaganda, leading to the radicalisation of vulnerable youth.
The landscape is now also defined by the rise of far-right extremism and “salad bar” extremism, which adds complexity to counterterrorism efforts by states and watchdogs.
BEWILDERING RANGE OF EXTREMIST ONLINE CONTENT
The threat from Islamic State-linked regional groups persists, especially in Indonesia and the southern Philippines, though at a generally lower level than in the past.
The bewildering and diverse range of extremist content on social media has enabled even further ideological mutation. Disaffected youth worldwide have idiosyncratically combined individual grievances and diverse ideological elements, producing “composite violent extremism”, or “salad bar extremism”.
In Southeast Asia, young individuals are being influenced by Islamic extremism, far-right extremism, antisemitism, and most recently, nihilistic violent ideas. Nihilistic violent extremism appears to be of increasing importance. Violence is carried out for non-ideological, personal reasons, with the violence often being the end in and of itself.
This trend has been particularly apparent regionally in the form of the so-called True Crime Community – an online community of supporters of mass shooters and serial killers.
Such supporters idolise school shooters and have attempted to carry out similar attacks in real life. For instance, in November 2025, an Indonesian youth attempted to bomb his high school in Jakarta. While he had inscribed on his fake rifle a slew of far-right extremist concepts and names, Indonesian police assessed that the youth had been influenced by the True Crime Community.
In addition, Singapore has experienced a few cases of “salad bar” extremism involving youth. While these cases had been variously influenced by a diverse mix of jihadist, far-left, far-right and misogynistic ideas, they had also been exposed to nihilistic True Crime Community ideas online.
THREE LESSONS LEARNED
Three key lessons emerge from this survey of the ever-evolving terrorism and extremism terrain since 9/11.
First, while for the past decade there has been much policy attention on the youth radicalisation issue, it is clear that transnational militant networks remain a challenge in the region.
It is generally understood today that a judicious mix of military or police power and softer measures addressing extremist narratives and underlying grievances is needed to deal with the threat.
Hence while Indonesian authorities have applied kinetic force against Islamic State-linked networks, they have complemented these with persuasion and negotiations. Through such a mixed strategy, the old JI network formally disbanded in 2024.
Likewise, in the southern Philippines, militant violence has declined since the longstanding issue of Bangsamoro political autonomy was addressed with the setting-up of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region of Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in 2019. Counterterrorism legislation, cross-border intelligence sharing and operational cooperation have also been vital for dealing with the physical terror threat across the region.
Second, in the increasingly complex domain of countering youth radicalisation, simply debunking extremist ideologies alone is insufficient. With the rise of composite, nihilistic violent extremism, broader measures are required to build overall youth resilience to violent ideologies.
Such broad-ranging resilience includes building digital literacy among youth; embedding them in stable family, peer and community relationships; providing balanced perspectives on hot-button geopolitical issues like the Gaza conflict; and shielding them as far as possible from online extremist propaganda and disinformation – increasingly AI-enhanced – through legislation like the Online Criminal Harms Act.
Counterterrorism agencies aside, such a holistic approach must involve other stakeholders, including civil society groups, social media firms, think tanks, religious bodies, educators, counsellors and rehabilitated extremists.
Finally, the boundary between counterterrorism and other national security domains such as cybersecurity for instance, may be blurring. A 19-year-old Singaporean youth recently detained under Singapore’s internal security legislation had planned cyberattacks against the websites of local and foreign Muslim organisations he considered deviant.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Singapore and the region face a rapidly evolving terrorism and extremism threat environment. They will need to apply strategic clarity and a diverse suite of policy tools on a whole-of-society basis.
Kumar Ramakrishna is Professor of National Security Studies, President’s Chair in National Security Studies and Dean of the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
- Published
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.
But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.
The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.
The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).
"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.
"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."
Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.
The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.
Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.
"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.
"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."
That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.
Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.
For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.
Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.
"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."
"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."
"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".
Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.
And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.
American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".
Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."
McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.
"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.
"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,
"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.
"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."
The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.
"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."
Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.
She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.
"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.
While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.
Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.
But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.
"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".
Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.
The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.
"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.
And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,
"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.
"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

Most people associate heart disease with men, and generally elderly men. This, however, is far from the real picture. Heart disease is a serious health problem in women as well, but still remains underdiagnosed and sub-optimally managed in our country. One of the main reasons for this is that in many cases, women may not have the ‘classic’ symptoms of a heart attack. This can result in symptoms being overlooked or misdiagnosed as acidity, stress, tiredness or other minor health issues.
Warning signs in women
Chest pain or pressure is common in women, but they can also get other, more subtle, symptoms. These may occur suddenly or slowly.
The following signs should be watched out for:
- Unusual shortness of breath, even without much exertion
- Abnormally excessive fatigue
- Nausea, vomiting, dizziness or sweating
- Back pain or discomfort in the back, jaw, neck, shoulders or arms
- A sense of pressure, weight or unease in the chest
Sometimes, both women and healthcare providers may ignore these symptoms or dismiss them as fatigue or digestive issues, particularly when there is no severe chest pain. But continued or atypical symptoms should never be left to self-diagnosis.
Understanding heart disease in women
The risks of heart disease can vary for women of different ages. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and high cholesterol contribute to the risk. Heart health can also be impacted by smoking, inactivity, poor diet and chronic stress. Some conditions that can occur during pregnancy are also likely to be factors in heart risk, and should be discussed with a doctor, including high blood pressure and diabetes during pregnancy. Hormonal changes may also play a role. Once women reach menopause, the risk of cardiovascular disease rises, as there is less protective oestrogen in the body.
Also, coronary artery disease is not always obstructive: a normal angiogram does not necessarily exclude heart disease. as women have a higher incidence of microvascular angina, and so, it is important to not stop evaluations.
What is also of great concern is that women might not seek medical treatment if symptoms are atypical. During a heart attack this delay can be fatal, as every minute counts.
Steps to make a difference
Protecting your heart health does not always mean making big changes in your lifestyle. Simple daily practices and regular health checkups can make a big difference.
These are some steps that women can take:
Know your numbers: Be aware of blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol—especially if there is a family history of heart disease.
Diet : Follow a balanced, nutritious diet, preferably a Mediterranean/DASH diet.
Be physically active: Walk, exercise or do something you enjoy regularly, to help maintain your heart health.
Stop smoking completely: This protects the heart and the rest of the body as well
Do not ignore unusual symptoms: Sudden difficulty in breathing, sudden weakness, chest discomfort or pain in the jaw, back or arms should be promptly evaluated.
Women don’t always experience noticeable symptoms when they have a heart disease. Sometimes, symptoms may not be obvious. For women to own their heart health, it is crucial to be aware of these symptoms, understand their risk factors, and seek timely medical attention. Women’s heart health should be also given increased importance in healthcare settings because their symptoms may be less apparent at times, and early detection and prompt medical intervention can make a huge difference.
(Dr. Saurabh Juneja is director & head, CTVS, cardiac sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. dr.juneja@gmail.com)

Quick food delivery startup Swish has raised $24 Mn (about ₹228.4 Cr) in a funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments (BII), as it looks to expand its kitchen network and enter new cities. Existing investors Accel, Bain Capital Ventures, and Hara Global also participated in the round. Swish plans to use the funding to deepen its kitchen network across its existing markets, expand into new cities, strengthen its supply chain infrastructure, and increase its order-handling capacity. The startup is looking to build a network of more than 1,000 kitchens over the next five years. The startup claimed that its monthly order volume has tripled since March 2026 and crossed 1 Mn orders. Founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja, and Saran S, Swish owns and manages its kitchens, technology, and last-mile delivery operations. Its neighbourhood kitchens typically serve customers within a one-kilometre radius. The startup promises food delivery in around 10 minutes and currently operates across Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida, Delhi, and Ghaziabad. It said it covers nearly 50 pin codes and delivers more than 80% of its orders within 15 minutes. Swish’s kitchens use dedicated preparation, cooking, and assembly stations, along with automated equipment. The company claimed that its kitchens process thousands of orders a day, with an average preparation time of under four minutes. Its menu has expanded to more than 250 stock-keeping units (SKUs) across over 20 food categories. According to the startup, lunch and dinner have overtaken snacks and late-night orders as its biggest consumption occasions. Swish cofounder and CEO Aniket Shah said the company intends to make quick food delivery available to 100 Mn consumers. Quick Food Delivery Race The latest funding comes less than six months after Swish raised $38 Mn in a Series B round led by Hara Global and Bain Capital Ventures. Accel also participated in the round, while Alteria Capital and Stride Ventures provided venture debt. Including the latest round, Swish has raised $78 Mn in external funding to date. The fundraise comes even as the viability of ultra-fast food delivery remains under scrutiny, with several companies recalibrating their operations in the segment. Deep-pocketed quick commerce players have also experimented with the segment. Blinkit operates Bistro, while Zepto runs Zepto Cafe. However, some companies have pulled back from quick food delivery. Swiggy shut down its standalone 10-minute food delivery app SNACC earlier this year amid profitability concerns. Zing, which entered the segment around the same time as Swish, has also moved away from quick food delivery, citing weaker-than-expected demand and the model’s high operating costs. Meanwhile, Rapido and Flipkart are exploring opportunities in food delivery, potentially intensifying competition in a market dominated by Swiggy and Eternal-owned Zomato.

A nearly identical exploit kit that targets critical vulnerabilities in both Chromium-based browsers and older versions of Windows is being actively used by at least four hacking groups, some of which have ties to the Chinese government.
Researchers from security firm Proofpoint said Wednesday that BlueMoon, the name they gave to the kit, chains three vulnerabilities together so the attackers using it can install malware of their choice. BlueMoon exploits two Chromium vulnerabilities and one in the kernel of Windows 10 (Oct 2018 Update), Windows Server 2019, Windows 10 2004, Windows Server 2022, and the initial release of Windows 11. All three vulnerabilities have received patches in the past 24 hours.
Deployed rapidly, widely shared
The attacks lacked the stealth found in many campaigns. More often, hackers want to exploit newly discovered vulnerabilities sparingly to lengthen their longevity. Proofpoint hypothesized that one reason for the widely used and visible exploit chain was to take advantage of a “patch gap” in the Chromium supply chain, which spans the time a patch is available from developers and the time that patch is incorporated into browsers such as Chrome and Edge. Another likely contributor was the use of AI, which can often spot vulnerabilities faster than discovery performed solely by humans.
Both these factors likely pushed the attackers to move quickly before a window of opportunity closed. Proofpoint said:
A fully weaponized Chrome exploit chain has historically been a high-value, rare capability. BlueMoon was developed, deployed rapidly, and shared across multiple threat actors within days in a manner that had high detection signals. This may reflect a reduced cost and barrier to entry for this class of capability, as AI agents increasingly enable threat actor exploit development. This is particularly relevant for open source codebases, such as Chromium, where upstream patches are publicly accessible prior to downstream consumers of the codebase applying the patch. This creates a window for threat actors to attempt to rapidly reverse engineer patches and develop exploits ahead of downstream stable releases.

Presidential pardon for controversial Sri Lankan monk overturned
- Published
Sri Lanka's Supreme Court has overturned a presidential pardon granted to a hardline Buddhist monk and ordered him to serve the remainder of a six-year prison sentence for intimidating the wife of a missing political cartoonist.
Galagodaatte Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 for contempt of court and intimidating Sanya Eknaligoda, the wife of Prageeth Eknaligoda who disappeared in 2010.
The monk had interrupted a court hearing to speak in support of military intelligence officials who were accused of abducting the cartoonist.
Gnanasara served less than a year of that sentence because he received a pardon from Maithripala Sirisena, who was the country's president at the time.
In his cartoons, Prageeth Eknaligoda depicted issues of media freedom, political power and social disadvantage.
His work was critical of the former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, a nationalist credited with the defeat of the Tamil separatist rebels in 2009 after a bloody civil war.
Eknaligoda went missing in 2010 and has not been seen since. His wife has led a campaign to trace his whereabouts, and accuses the authorities of not doing enough to investigate his disappearance.
Gnanasara, who leads the Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) or "Buddhist Power Force", was a supporter of Rajapaksa and his brother Gotobaya, who also later served as president.
In 2025, he received a separate nine-month prison term for insulting Islam and inciting religious hatred.
Sri Lanka rarely convicts Buddhist monks, and it is almost unheard of for one to receive a custodial sentence.

A high-level official at Anthropic posted on Tuesday evening that he believes there is a greater than 10% chance that “AI could kill all humans” within the next decade.
While I am not deep enough in the code to comment coherently on our impending extinction, I *am* qualified enough to say: if you want award-winning coverage of the risks (and benefits!) of AI in our current health systems, you should sign up for a STAT subscription.
OK, here’s the news, including three AI-related items.
Oz says ‘AI-based avatars’ can help rural communities. Some leaders disagree
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services head Mehmet Oz and other Trump administration officials are touting artificial intelligence as a game-changing force for rural health. But some rural hospitals are skeptical the tools will close the funding gaps they face from Republicans’ Medicaid cuts, STAT’s Daniel Payne reports in the latest installment of STAT’s Unraveled series.
Rural health care providers have struggled for years and are now staring down $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts over the coming decade. While there are places where AI could shine — sending nudges on prescriptions or helping providers determine which patients need care and when — rural health leaders worry that investing in AI will only exacerbate existing inequalities between urban and rural communities.
AI tools perform well with clear determinations from large data sources. It may struggle with more subjective calls, such as which patients qualify for “medical frailty” exemptions, could be harder.
Daniel talked with dozens of health officials and trekked to Maine and Louisiana for this eye-opening story. Read more.
Feds invest $62 million to develop AI for heart failure treatment
Are “autonomous prescribing cardiologists” coming to a clinic near you?
ARPA-H, the government agency that funds cutting-edge health research, plans to commit $62.7 million to develop artificial intelligence bots that direct treatment of heart failure. The program aims to produce AI devices that can perform several functions, including assessing symptom severity, prescribing drugs, and ordering lab tests.
Federal officials hope that these AI agents will help many of the 6.7 million Americans with heart failure, who often struggle to get optimal treatment because of difficulty accessing specialists, especially in rural and other underserved settings. It’s the latest example of the Trump administration trying to use AI to solve health care problems.
STAT’s Mario Aguilar breaks down the new program (ADVOCATE) and dishes the details on the initial health tech companies and teams that were awarded grants.
It’s not just U.S. health officials …
… that are discussing how to use AI tools for medicine.
A U.K. commission on Thursday unveiled recommendations for how the country should regulate artificial intelligence in medicine, the latest country to try to get a handle on a quickly changing technological landscape.
The authors write that they want to ensure that the U.K. takes advantage of AI’s potential in medicine — the ability to review the millions of scans that are generated each year to track the eye health of patients with diabetes, for example — while still prioritizing safety and treating patients equitably.
The report details 44 recommendations, including some that call for a staged authorization of new AI models and others that would build a system for providers to report how tools are performing in their clinics.
Read more about the report from STAT’s Andrew Joseph.
The vaccine election
Vaccine policy has become a central issue ahead of the November midterm elections as the White House pushes states to revamp their immunization policies and state-level Republican politicians campaign on ending school vaccine requirements.
The majority of states have already departed from national, unified vaccine guidance set by the federal government and are pursuing their own rules. But the midterms could have major consequences for whom the public looks toward for guidance on which shots they and their children should get.
To understand this emerging patchwork of vaccine policy, STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo looks at five races in November. What’s the situation in states like Florida, Arizona, and Iowa? What has Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, said about federal officials’ approach to vaccine policy? Read more.
To sleep, no more
Two scientists who identified the role that a key neuropeptide plays in the uncontrollable sleepiness of narcolepsy were one of three recipients of the prestigious Lasker Awards, announced Thursday.
Starting in the late 1990s, Emmanuel Mignot and Masashi Yanagisawa began research that separately arrived at the same conclusion: that orexin, a neuropeptide, was critical to narcolepsy. These findings laid the foundation for the development of new sleep drugs that biotech companies are racing to bring to market in their bid to capture a $5 billion market. Read Elaine Chen’s excellent story from last year if you want the skinny on these drugs, and then read her recent update about the company whose narcolepsy drug just gained approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
Two other groups received Lasker Awards, which are often precursors for Nobel Prizes. A team of Japanese scientists won for their development of treatment for hemophilia A. Michael J. Fox won an award for his philanthropy and advocacy for Parkinson’s disease research.

The US department of homeland security (DHS) on Thursday released a draft proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period, currently available to certain non-immigrant workers (such as H-1B and L-1 visa holders) following termination of employment. While the proposal covers several employment-based non-immigrant visa categories, from the perspective of the Indian diaspora, the most significant impact would be on H-1B visa holders, L-1 visa holders (those on intra-company transfers) and O-1 visa holders (this visa is given to those who are recognised for extraordinary ability).
Under the existing framework, following a layoff or other termination of employment, these visa holders are typically granted a discretionary grace period of up to 60-days, or until the end of their authorised stay, whichever comes first. The grace period can provide valuable time to find another employer, seek a change of status (say transition to a B-visitor visa) or make arrangements to leave the US.
The proposal marks a significant reversal of a policy DHS itself introduced in 2016. At the time, the agency recognised that the abrupt loss of employment was not necessarily the worker's fault and that allowing highly skilled workers time to find new employment could benefit both foreign workers and US employers.
The proposed rule now argues that the 60-day provision goes against the employment-linked nature of these immigration classifications. DHS states: “The up to 60-day discretionary grace period disconnects the alien’s lawful status from the very basis of eligibility under these employment-based non-immigrant classifications.” The agency also says the earlier rule “did not sufficiently consider the negative impacts of the grace period provision.”
Notably, DHS acknowledges that scrapping the grace period would carry human and economic costs. The department says some affected workers could suffer monetarily because they would have to leave the US and subsequently seek readmission rather than remain in the country while looking for new employment. It also acknowledges that some workers could receive Notices to Appear (NTAs) and potentially enter removal proceedings.
DHS further recognises the extent to which foreign workers and their families may have put down roots in the US. In the proposal, it notes that such workers and their dependents may have “purchased houses, paid taxes, and may have otherwise invested in the local community in reliance on the alien’s continued stay in the US.” They may also have made career and personal plans on the assumption that they could remain in legal status for up to 60 days after their employment ended while seeking a new status.
Despite such acknowledgement DHS concludes that the costs of retaining the grace period are outweighed by what it describes as the need to restore the employment-linked nature of the non-immigrant classifications and reduce the administrative burden on US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
The proposed rule is open for public comments and the entire process up to issue of a final rule could take several months.
Cyrus D. Mehta, a US immigration attorney, states “If the discretionary 60-day grace period is eliminated, foreign nationals whose employment ceases prematurely (and their dependents) would no longer be maintaining status and would generally be required to depart the US immediately, unless USCIS exercises its separate discretion to forgive the lapse in status and allow the foreign national to change status or change employers within the country.”
The potential impact on Indians is significant. According to the latest USCIS data for fiscal year ended Sept 30, 2025, 57,747 India-born beneficiaries accounted for 50.3 percent of the 1,14,806 H-1B petitions approved for initial employment. The concentration was substantially higher among continuing employment cases: 2,26,359 India-born beneficiaries accounted for 77.6 percent of the 2,91,542 H-1B petitions approved for continuing employment.
Immigration attorneys point out that the Trump administration had already begun tightening the net around laid-off foreign workers in recent months. Workers using the 60-day period to seek a change to B-1/B-2 visitor status allowing them to remain lawfully in the US while looking for new employment, have increasingly faced Requests for Evidence (RFEs) and, in some cases, Notices of Intent to Deny (NOIDs).
Thus, while currently the 60-day grace period currently remains until a final rule is introduced, transiting to a new visa status remains challenging.

For years, drugmakers have offered free meals, samples, gifts, and speaking fees to physicians, a widely studied issue due to concerns such largesse may unduly influence prescribing habits.
But to what extent have interactions between doctors and pharmaceutical representatives changed behaviors over time?
A new analysis attempts to provide some answers. A group of researchers surveyed 283 physicians who were among more than 1,300 medical students and residents queried in 2011. They compared the responses to an updated effort that was undertaken two years ago, and the results suggest the topic is likely to remain contentious.

Apple Watch Series 12 hands-on: New sensing system, health features and audio intelligence
There was a lot more new stuff than expected.
I wasn't expecting Apple to have a ton of interesting updates to the Apple Watch this year, but somehow it managed to surprise me. Some of the new features coming to the Apple Watch Series 12 are things the competition has already offered, like Readiness scores and increased sampling rates. But others, like the Audio Intelligence suite of tools and even the new finishes and materials, are novel. I'm also not against AI wearables that listen to your surroundings and conversations, as long as done responsibly and with accountability, so I'm intrigued by things like Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
Unfortunately, I wasn't really able to test out most of these features at the demo area right after today's "Surprise and shine" keynote ended. But I did get to spend a bit more time with some Apple Watch demos, and carefully scrutinize what exactly is different on the Series 12. I also got a bit more detail on how the new Audio Intelligence features work and whether Apple is listening to your conversations. (Short answer: No.)
One of the main changes in the Apple Watch Series 12 is in the sensing system, which Apple says it has re-architected. I actually got to compare my Series 11 to the new smartwatch, and their undersides certainly look quite different. I could go into greater detail on how the photodiodes and the LEDs have been upgraded and rearranged, but suffice to say that on the newer model, you'll notice a ring of 12 lights compared to the four LEDs laid out in a diamond shape on last year's device.
New health sensing system on the Apple Watch Series 12
If you look really close, you'll notice differences in other components as well, like the number and layout of the diodes and electrodes around the LEDs. What all this leads to is an increased surface area that's in contact with your skin, which together with the updated hardware should lead to more accurate and consistent readings. Apple is also increasing its sampling rates so it's getting measurements of your heart rate (and therefore related data like your VO2Max and heart rate variability) much more frequently. Apple goes as far as to say that it conducted its own study of wearables and found the Series 12 to be the most accurate in heart rate sensing.
That data feeds into a few health-related features on the Apple Watch Series 12, including the updated heart rate app, which has a new HRV metric. That's now measured at up to every five minutes, compared to every two to four hours or so on older watches.
The HRV information is a key part of the new Readiness app on the watch, and factors into your readiness score each day. This is delivered daily on a scale of 0 to 10, and takes into account your activity, sleep and vitals. Of course, I wasn't able to test this myself as I'd have to wear an Apple Watch for at least seven days for it to work. But the number I did see on a company rep's watch was a concerning "3," and upon closer investigation the Health app said that poor sleep and HRV performance brought the score down.
Apple also made some tweaks to the Vitals app, changing up some of the language it uses around performance. But the biggest update to the Apple Watch experience might be outside of the watch itself. The Health app is getting quite a significant makeover, which might sound like welcome news to longtime users who never quite enjoyed how to make sense of their data in that app.
Since Apple Intelligence summaries are part of the redesigned Health app, you'll have to have a compatible iPhone to use it. (If not, you'll see the current version.) This updated version is coming later this year, with the first thing you see being a summary generated by Apple Intelligence at the top. This considers the time of day to deliver your most relevant information at the time. Then come tiles that show your metrics like activity, heart and sleep, and these will also change order throughout the day.
Swiping sideways on the home screen will take you through sleep, fitness and heart pages, while the bottom navigation bar shows you options to go into the Longevity and data tabs. The Longevity tab is a new interface that not only measures your wellbeing across seven different areas including the ones I already mentioned, but also shows your "health age." It's a bit confusing to me all the different names for what I think should be the same thing, but I'm sure after I spend some time with the app later this year I'll understand the distinctions better. I'm also intrigued and keen to try out some of the new assessments in the app, like the one for VO2Max where you'll have to follow along instructions to jog in place, while the Health app studies your heart rate from your Apple Watch or compatible AirPods to evaluate your performance.
While the refreshed Health app isn't going to be available for a while, nor is it exclusive to the Apple Watch Series 12, it certainly impacts a lot of your experience. It is where you'll spend a lot of time looking at your health data, after all. But more features coming to the Series 12 are around AI, performance and "audio intelligence."
Audio Intelligence, AI and privacy concerns on the Apple Watch Series 12
One thing that's important to keep in mind when thinking about the new Apple Watch's sound and listening-related features is the S11 chip. It's designed with what Apple calls the "secure exclave," which is where the raw audio coming in from the watch's microphone is being processed. That's where the sound is transcribed and processed, and only the results of that interpretation leave the exclave. It won't store any of the audio it gets, Apple says.
With this, there are four updates related to sound. First up is the most straightforward: Improvements to Shazam on your watch. Right now, if you want to pull up Shazam to identify a song playing around you, you might scroll through the smart stack on your watch and whizz past or land on the Shazam widget. Then you'd tap it and wait for the system to listen and guess the tune. On the Series 12, because it has a buffer of the previous 15 seconds of audio information to work with, it can already start looking up the song once you scroll past the Shazam widget. This means it can potentially recognize music much more quickly.
Next is the sound recognition tool that has long been an accessibility feature in iPhones. This uses the mics in your iPhone, for instance, to alert people to important sounds like alarms, sirens, babies crying or glass breaking. The Series 12 will be able to deliver alerts about these sounds even if a companion iPhone isn't close by. For people who are deaf or hard of hearing, this could be a handy expansion.
More interesting of the suite of updates here are the Live Rewind and Siri Recap features. Live Rewind can basically deliver a transcript of the last 15 seconds of what someone near you might have said at any given time. You just double click the dial on your Apple Watch Series 12, and a screen pops up, while the microphone indicator appears at the top right corner to show it's pulling audio data. In my demo, I saw all these cues followed by onscreen text that certainly seemed to accurately transcribe what the Apple rep had said just seconds earlier.
I don't really have the time at the moment to break down all my thoughts, concerns and understanding of the way this works just yet. The takeaway is that the Apple Watch is not technically recording audio and is instead producing a rolling buffer of audio that's constantly overwriting itself inside its Secure Exclave. It's then transcribing at the Secure Exclave level, and everything else it produces is based off that transcript, which means the effectiveness of these features has a lot to do with the quality of the models behind that process. Plus, it only starts transcribing when the button is pressed twice, so it's not always transcribing.
Finally, Siri Recap creates "high-level" summaries of events, rather than a full transcript. It's something you'd more actively set up to listen to your surroundings on either a schedule or manually each time you're in a meeting, for instance. I wasn't able to test this, but I saw the Recaps in a companion iPhone's Siri App, under the new Recaps tab. Apple does specifically say that Recap does transfer audio from your Watch's exclave to the iPhone's exclave in its 11-page privacy overview, though it notes that the encrypted file will be "inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user or Apple."
The last thing I want to point out for now is that I am enamored with the Ceramic variant of the Series 12. It felt smooth, and unsurprisingly almost like porcelain. I didn't spend enough time with it to know if it will feel sturdy over time, but I definitely liked the way it looks.
I'm sure I'll learn more about the new Apple Watch Series 12 features when I get to test out a review unit, but for now, I'm sure we can agree there were a lot more updates than can be quickly covered in a relatively brief article. I'm intrigued by the audio intelligence features and how they'll perform in the real world, and how they might impact performance and battery life. Stay tuned, as I'll go over that in my full review.

Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
- Published
A bitter succession dispute has erupted in one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms, days before the burial of its late king, who until his death had been the world's youngest reigning monarch.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled the Tooro Kingdom for more than three decades, was undergoing cancer treatment in the US when he died last month aged 34.
Royal clan elders have named popular TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, as the next monarch, but this has been rejected by Oyo's close family.
His sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will written in 2022 naming his young son, whose identity has never been disclosed, as his successor.
"My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.
Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".
She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.
"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."
Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.
His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.
Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.
Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.
No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.
The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.
Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.
At a press conference in the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.
The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.
The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution.
Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.
Another royal, UK-based Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, was initially considered for the throne but declined, citing other responsibilities, according to the succession committee.
It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.
Oyo's family quickly called a press conference to denounce the announcement, insisting the late king's written wishes should be respected.
Princess Komuntale said Oyo had left "very strict instructions" on his succession, naming his son as first in line and also setting out alternatives if the boy could not take the throne - a position backed by her aunt, senior royal Princess Elizabeth Bagaaya.
But clan representatives said that reports of Oyo having a son were not sufficient because the child had not been formally presented to the royal clan as dictated by Tooro tradition.
One committee member told Uganda's NTV station that a royal child must be formally introduced to elders and then must undergo ceremonies and others preparations if they were to be considered for future leadership.
Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde has stepped in to say he will be overseeing mediation efforts, with an outcome expected after consultations with President Museveni and cultural leaders.
