On food labelling and misleading claims, weight loss drugs, climate change, rabies, cancer care, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.
Climate change will also never be further than a beck and call away. It has dominated headlines periodically, and likely will be even more frequent in future. Jacob Koshy writes: Global warming will exceed limit, UN says in a report that maps path to get back below danger zone. UNEP’s detailed ‘overshoot, peak and decline’ pathway seeks to hold the peak as low as possible and then bring temperatures back down below the 1.5°C limit; report terms it ‘best remaining option’.
Yet another new study highlights the life-saving role of air conditioning, but indicates that it comes at a cost. Do check this story out, for the details: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say.
On the rabies front, there was some exciting news in the region. I record how Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem. The WHO also validated Bhutan’s claim and explained that this was achieved through conscious of deployment of the One Health approach, affording some key lessons for neighbour India too.
Meanwhile, Authorities are probing ‘counterfeit’ rabies vaccine, and the counterfeit ‘Abhayrab’ rabies vaccine batch remains under investigation. Why is this important? With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.
On dogs, segueing into cancer, we had an interesting article this week on whether dogs can sniff cancer? Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs’ brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data. Click on the link to learn more.
Dr. Jayanth Reddy meanwhile wrote on how transplant oncology is rewriting the story of liver cancer, and why surgeons, instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one.
In the In Focus podcast, there’s a discussion with Dr. Narayana Subramanian about cancer ‘vaccines’ and if will they revolutionise treatment. What are these new therapies and what cancer do they treat? Why are they called vaccines when they don’t actually prevent cancer? How does mRNA tech work and how is AI helpful in this? Will these personalised treatments be available in India any time soon and how expensive will they be?

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
- Published
Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.
Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong.
Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.
The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials.
They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored.
Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road.
"The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said.
"The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway."
The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry.
Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days.
A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said.
Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old.
Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said.
Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years.
The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha.
There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN.
Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws.
Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors.
This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India.
In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

A fossil feather from the age of dinosaurs may explain why only some birds survived
Paleontology can be quite physical.
In 2016, David DeMar was doing field work in the rocky badlands of Montana in what's known as the Hell Creek Formation.
"We all get down on our hands and knees," he recalls. "And I start crawling up the hill and I noticed this little dark, round object on the ground. It was kind of odd."
DeMar, the lab manager at the Burke Museum in Seattle, picked up the cherry-sized fossil.
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
"I start looking at the surface of it," he says. "And then I rolled it over and I was like, 'You got to be kidding me.'"
Embedded in a small crack on the surface was a tiny fossilized branching structure. As it turned out, this was the first fossilized feather from this part of the world.
In addition, "it is, without a doubt, the best feather we've ever found from the age of dinosaurs," says Jingmai O'Connor, a bird expert and an associate curator of fossil reptiles at the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
The researchers say the plume, which they describe in the journal Current Biology, is part of a fossil assortment that may reveal part of a late Cretaceous food web from some 66 million years ago. And they speculate it could help explain why, around that time, many types of ancient birds died out alongside the dinosaurs after a giant asteroid collided with the Earth — while others survived to give rise to the birds we know today.
Excremental progress
After first spotting the round nodule, DeMar quickly radioed his colleagues. At first, no one responded.
"They probably thought I was kidding," he says.
"But I got back on the walkie about five minutes later. I was like, 'No, hey guys, I think I found a bird feather.'"
Subsequent analysis confirmed DeMar's conclusion. The feather dates back to the late Cretaceous, right before the great extinction event that wiped out the dinosaurs and a large swath of other species.
When O'Connor joined the project, very little was known about the feather, except that it looked quite modern. "My goal was to try to figure out what animal this feather belonged to," she says, "and then in the grand scheme of evolution to try to say, 'Well, what can this exceptional feather tell us?'"
The round object that the feather was sitting in turned out to be a chunk of coprolite — that is, fossilized feces — produced by a large meat-eating dinosaur. "So I would argue that Tyrannosaurus rex or Nanotyrannus are the more likely candidates," says O'Connor. (This coprolite had actually broken off from a few larger, softball-sized pieces where additional clues may later be found.)
The team CT-scanned the small coprolite and found it contained still other feathers, a couple of bone fragments, and two tiny fish scales. After studying the feathers and bones, O'Connor concluded they likely came from the same animal adapted to life in the water.
She believes it was an ancient aquatic, swimming bird, "kind of like a loon or a grebe," she says. "They're foot-propelled divers."
"It's certainly impressive that this amazing feather morphology could be detected in dinosaur poop," says Richard Prum, an ornithologist at Yale University who didn't contribute to the research. "That is remarkable, unexpected. There's nothing of that age that's so beautifully preserved, [including] evidence of individual cells."
The researchers argue that the fish scales also preserved in that coprolite might have been remnants of the ancient bird's last supper before it too became a meal for a predator like T. rex — and that that animal later defecated out the fragments that would be discovered by DeMar roughly 66 million years later.
A Cretaceous turd-ucken
This bird was one of many types of birds that went extinct with the dinosaurs, when the Chicxulub asteroid smashed into the planet and sent ash and soot into the air, clouding the skies and causing a dramatic planet-wide cooling.
"You have all these birds during the Cretaceous," says O'Connor. "And only one group of birds survives when the asteroid impact happens." That group was the one that gave rise to modern birds.
Researchers have wanted to know what provided the surviving birds with the edge they needed to make it through the drop in global temperature. O'Connor thinks it may have to do with the fact that they were better insulated. Building on her previous work, she noticed that some of the fossilized body feathers inside the coprolite from the ancient bird (whose relatives ultimately died out) appeared to lack the insulation of their modern counterparts.
"How do they stay warm when it gets cold, when this [asteroid] impact winter happens?," she says. O'Connor isn't arguing that plumage differences are the sole reason behind the extinction of these birds. "I'm saying it's a contributing factor."
Not all researchers agree with the conclusion, however. "I think it's a stretch to explain the survivorship of some [species] and the extinction of others from that evidence," says Julia Clarke, an evolutionary biologist at UT Austin who wasn't involved in the study. "The fragments themselves are incomplete."
Still, she's taken by the snapshot of a food chain apparently captured by this piece of poo. "A dinosaur ate an aquatic bird that ate a particular type of fish," she muses. "Almost like they've discovered a Cretaceous turducken."
What O'Connor believes they've discovered is a new way of gaining access to crucially important specimens since telltale features don't usually preserve very well.
"Now that we know that coprolites of some carnivorous dinosaurs can preserve soft tissues," she says, "we now have this whole potential to find fossilized not just feathers, but fur and other soft-tissue structures."
O'Connor considers the work worthwhile. Understanding past extinctions says something about the current extinction crisis — and who may survive and who may not.

A report published by the US Census Bureau last month purported to uncover evidence backing up President Donald Trump’s baseless claims that noncitizens voting cost him the 2020 election. It was the latest salvo in Trump’s broader assault on the safety of US elections. “I WON THE ELECTION,” Trump quickly declared on Truth Social after the publication of the report.
However, though Trump and other government officials quickly shared and praised the report, a WIRED investigation has uncovered significant flaws in the data used to compile the report, as well as in the approval process used prior to publication. WIRED has also learned that a number of the report’s authors have links to the Trump administration and the Republican party. They include one former affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency and two researchers from the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a highly influential think tank founded by veterans of Trump’s first administration.
The report, titled “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis,” claims that an analysis of over 128 million voter records from the 2020 election identified 24,000 people tied to administrative records indicating noncitizen status. The numbers range from 4,300 in California to fewer than 15 in Wyoming—not nearly enough to have affected the outcome of the presidential race. But even these figures seem extremely questionable, and experts and Census Bureau employees who spoke to WIRED allege it is much likelier that they represent basic analytical errors than actual instances of noncitizen voting.
The Census Bureau did not respond to a request for comment. The White House directed WIRED to President Donald Trump’s post on Truth Social and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s post on X, where both officials praised the report.
The number of noncitizens voting in US elections has been repeatedly shown to be vanishingly small. In Utah, for example, the state’s top election official, Lieutenant Governor Deidre Henderson, reviewed the state’s approximately 2.1 million registered voters. The result was the discovery of 27 “confirmed noncitizens,” none of whom was ever confirmed to have voted. Studies in Pennsylvania and Idaho have returned similar outcomes. Still, the idea that a flood of noncitizens have been voting in US elections for over a decade, skewing the outcomes, has remained one of the central conspiracy theories promoted by Trump and his allies.
John Abowd, former associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist at the Census Bureau, called the Census report “statistical nonsense” and wrote on LinkedIn that “it is extremely uncommon for the US Census Bureau to publish a research report, even one of blog length, without the authors explicitly listed.”
Census Bureau sources who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity could not say what prompted the report. Records reviewed by WIRED, though, show it originated at the Center for Economic Studies, a division within the Census Bureau that uses confidential data to conduct research.
According to those records, one of the authors was Dan Sweeney, currently a deputy general counsel at the Department of Commerce overseeing the Census Bureau. He previously worked as the “DOGE legal liaison and deregulatory attorney” at the Environmental Protection Agency, according to his LinkedIn profile. Michael Lachanski was also an author, according to two sources with knowledge of the report’s origins, and he was appointed to his current role as the deputy director for data, policy, and science at the Census Bureau just two months ago. Previously, he was a fellow at the Trump-aligned Claremont Institute.
The two America First staffers involved in authoring the report, according to records reviewed by WIRED, were Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea. McCrea previously served as campaign manager for former congresswoman Cathy McMorris Rodgers of Washington, who has expressed a belief in creationism and signed an amicus brief contesting the 2020 election results. Jensen previously worked for the American Enterprise Institute, where, according to his bio on the America First Policy Institute website, “contributed to the design of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act,” the tax law passed during the first Trump administration.
Sweeney, Lachanski, Jensen, and McCrea did not respond to requests for comment.

|---|
| Are you a current or former government employee who wants to talk about what's happening? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at velliott88.18 or davidgilbert.01. | 
Sources who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity confirmed that Jensen and McCrea are working in government on loan from America First through what is known as the Intergovernment Personnel Act. The IPA is meant to allow people with specialized skill sets from certain institutions, like nonprofits and universities, to work for the government for up to two years on a temporary appointment.
Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, says that the Bureau has long used IPAs for scientific work. “But they do what the civil servants require them to do, not what the political [appointees] require them to do.”
Boyd says that the group of people who records indicate authored the noncitizen voting report appear to be of a different stripe. “These ultimately appear to be people coming from a Republican operation that’s pretending to be a 501c3,” she says. “Rather than doing the work for the agency, it appears they’re doing work in political interest.” The AFPI did not respond to a request for comment.
The report was approved by the Census Bureau’s disclosure review board on August 7 through an email vote, which is typically used for publications with tight deadlines or in response to demands from Congress or the White House. The members of the review board who approved the report were shown the three tables contained in the final publication, but not the analysis that accompanied them, according to one source within the bureau who had access to the materials submitted to the review board.
The report concludes that the author’s analysis “readily determined with high confidence that over 128 million of these voter records represented citizens, and that over 24,000 of these voter records represented noncitizens at the time of the election. Over 32 million voter records remain to be analyzed.”
According to documents viewed by WIRED, the authors used data from the DataClear 2020 voting file—a commercial dataset—as well as USCIS immigration records (both the 2025 extract and the February 2026 A-number and case files); USCIS DACA approvals from 2025; State Department immigrant and nonimmigrant visas for 2017 through 2023; ICE student, removal, and national-docket records; IRS form 1040 for 2020; Social Security Numident (2019 and 2020); and State Department passport issuances across 50 vintages from 1978 through 2025.
Former Census officials say the breadth of data used, as well as the lack of clear explanation of the methodology employed to analyze it, raises significant red flags.
“We don't know whether or how the sources are updating their citizenship info,” Amy O’Hara, a former official who used to run the administrative data linkage unit at Census, tells WIRED. “It is really hard to join and deduplicate these files, especially across a range of years.”
In order to match people between surveys and records without revealing their identities, the Census Bureau uses what are known as Protected Identification Keys (PIKs), which replace identifying information with a unique code. Sources who spoke to WIRED say that they are unsure which data points were used to match PIK data across the many datasets, though something like an address could be used for cross-referencing.
Though PIKs have been used for years to allow academics and government employees to conduct studies without compromising the privacy of the people whose data it is, they are not foolproof. A January 2026 study published by the Census earlier this year found that “while PIK assignment is generally accurate, some person records are not successfully assigned a PIK, which can lead to sample selection bias in analyses of linked data.”
“The brief says ‘high confidence,’ which indicates some probability,” one bureau source who spoke on the condition of anonymity over fears of retribution by the administration, tells WIRED. “However, no confidence intervals in the tables of the brief are shown. The supposed count of non-voters is small relative to the total state population.” The source alleges that there are probably PIK errors and not actual noncitizens who voted.
Abowd says that false match rates—in this case, when a voting record is assigned the wrong PIK, and then when it is “matched” with citizenship data–are likely to be higher when using commercial data like those used in the report. This means that the analysis is more likely to return a “false positive” showing that a noncitizen had voted. “You can’t estimate the false positive rate without more technical details” that were not included in the report, Abowd tells WIRED. “Because the false match rate is much greater than the estimated noncitizen voting rate, the alleged noncitizen voters are more likely to be data errors.”
All of this, Boyd worries, could undermine more than just trust in voting and elections—it could make academics and researchers doubt the quality and reliability of the products and data that the Census Bureau produces. “They're putting it out with the imprimatur of the Census Bureau so it looks legitimate,” she says. “But there’s no authors, no methods, no discussions of the limitations of the data, or the Bureau's approach.”
Republicans have already attacked the accuracy of the 2020 census, alleging that an algorithmic process used by the Bureau to protect data privacy had disproportionately favored Democrats in terms of the drawing of congressional districts. In August, WIRED reported that an internal memo circulated by the Department of Commerce, which oversees the Census Bureau, proposed excluding immigrants from the count, a move that could radically reshape how congressional districts are apportioned.
The report is also just one part of a broad attack on the integrity of American elections by the Trump administration, which includes weaponizing the Department of Justice, dismantling voter protections, attempting to wrest control of election administration from states, and pushing an endless barrage of baseless conspiracy theories about voting in America.

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.
"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.
However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.
The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.
Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to City
As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.
Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.
Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.
He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.
"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.
"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."
After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.
Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.
Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.
A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.
Is £65m a fair price for Ndiaye?
In a summer of highly-inflated transfer fees, value has become increasingly hard to determine.
On one hand, the Senegal international is a player of superlative skill, evasive, quick and wonderfully entertaining with the ball at his feet.
Ndiaye was responsible for 73 of Everton's 250 completed dribbles last season, the highest share of any Premier League player.
Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.
On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.
In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more.
It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.
He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.
Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side.
Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.
As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.
But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

Jeanine Pirro unloads on reporter who pressed her about Trump’s Reflecting Pool case
The president’s top federal prosecutor in DC refuses to answer questions about his demands to re-open vandalism case against ex-Olympian
Donald Trump’s top prosecutor in Washington, D.C. unloaded on a reporter who pressed her about the president’s demands to prosecute a former Olympian accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
The case against 67-year-old David Hearn collapsed this summer after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro dropped charges in a stunning court filing that appeared to blame the Trump administration’s own “botched” construction for damage to the monument.
Trump, however, has demanded that Pirro re-open the case while accusing her of having “folded like an umbrella” and “choking.” Her office agreed to dismiss the case but is asking a judge to leave open the possibility of retrying Hearn again.
During a press conference on cryptocurrency fraud on Wednesday, a reporter asked Pirro about Trump’s efforts to “revisit the reflecting pool case.”
“Ugh, why did I know that was coming? That’s why I didn’t call on you first,” Pirro fired back. “Well, first of all, I’m here to talk about one of the biggest problems that American people have right now. And I’m not going to talk about any other issue. I know you’d love to, but I’m not going there.”
The reporter then noted that the case is important to Trump.
“The president has the right to decide what he wants to do and what is important,” Pirro shot back.
“And what he’s shown us already is that through the executive order, that this cryptocurrency fraud on Americans is a priority,” she added. “There is an executive order, and there is a focus with resources for us to do it.”
She then counted for the next question — “not on the pool.”
When a reporter tried again to bring up the case, Pirro lost her cool.
“No! No, and no!” she shouted.
“How many times do I have to say no?” Pirro said. “I am not talking about that. Anyone want to talk about this case?”
The judge overseeing the case against Hearn appears prepared to block the Department of Justice from charging him again.
Prosecutors initially accused Hearn of tearing out the recently applied “American flag blue” liner that started to flap to the surface shortly after it was installed.
Just weeks after she publicly accused Hearn of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the liner, Pirro’s office admitted that the sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed. Contractors left behind “widespread damage,” according to her office.
It was not until after the indictment was filed that the Department of Interior determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” according to her filing.
Hearn has asked a judge to dismiss the case with prejudice, which would prevent prosecutors from reviving felony charges against him for the same alleged crime.
On Truth Social, Trump called Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen a “Political Hack” and “TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG” as he pushed Pirro to “re-visit her hastily made decision” to drop the case.
The legal team behind Hearn — a champion canoeist who represented the U.S. at the 1992, 1996, and 2000 Summer Olympics — has argued that Trump’s comments suggest the administration is trying to charge him again.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman hauled lawyers to court last week to hear why prosecutors would want to keep the door open after admitting there isn’t any evidence to do so.
If someone like Hearn can be charged for a crime they didn’t commit, “then every American is at risk,” Eisen told reporters outside the courthouse last Friday.
“Davey Hearn is innocent. He's got nothing to do with the toxic contamination of the reflecting pool and the algae farm that is growing in it,” Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told reporters. “That is a problem with the Trump administration. They should deal with it without bringing my constituent into it.”

BANGOR, Maine — Rural health care providers, which have struggled for years, are facing nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts over the coming decade. The Trump administration is pointing to a cutting-edge, if unproven way to save them: artificial intelligence.
“The best way to help” rural communities, is “AI-based avatars,” Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said at an event on mental health this year.
His comments are among the grand promises administration officials have made about AI. They’ve also touted the prospect of concierge care for every American and AI nurses as good as any doctor, for example. Their argument is that AI, fueled by the $50 billion rural health transformation fund that came along with the Medicaid cuts, could remake rural care in the U.S.
The technology could lower the cost of delivering care, Oz has said, and could be a deflationary force across the health care economy.
But providers serving rural communities aren’t so sure.
“I don’t think AI is going to make health care costs go down in the near term at all,” said Lori Dwyer, president and CEO of Penobscot Community Health Care, a system that stretches across Maine. “I don’t think it’s going to save us.”
Her system has already started using ambient scribes, an AI technology that listens to a clinician’s conversation with a patient and then helps document it in the electronic health record. While that’s had plenty of benefits, saving money isn’t one of them, Dwyer said.
“It’s allowed us to off-load work, administrative burdens from our providers and our care teams so that they can focus on patients and patient care and so that they don’t burn out,” she said, adding that documentation time is down, and communications are improved. “But that doesn’t reduce costs.”
Other ways the system is using AI, such as for patient communications or to aid in remote patient monitoring, have been helpful, she said — but only create marginal economic efficiencies at a time when years of work to stabilize the system’s finances is essentially being wiped out by the looming cuts.
A troubling reality on AI
Across dozens of interviews with rural health providers, hospital system leaders, and health AI experts, a troubling reality was repeated: Investing in AI technology would be costly, especially for already at-risk systems, and its savings potential hasn’t yet been proved. Despite the tools holding promise, they’re expensive — and buyers are facing a wave of new financial pressures.
Rural health system leaders are excited about the technology’s potential in the distant future and feel the need to invest in it in order to keep up with the nationwide advancement.
But the large-scale, system-altering changes that promise huge savings and a fundamental shift in health care delivery seem well out of reach for many rural health systems.
Health AI leaders and rural health providers alike are concerned those gains will go largely to the big systems with money to invest in AI-native infrastructure — a costly, time-consuming endeavor. In the end, the technology could increase health inequities in the U.S. instead of shrinking them, they worry.
Despite the challenges, some rural health leaders see adopting AI technology as their only way forward in an exceedingly difficult environment.
A few system leaders told STAT they’re accelerating their adoption of AI tools — because of the cuts — even beyond what they were doing at the start of the ChatGPT age. Finding new efficiencies has become a mandatory task, and more than 70% of hospitals are estimated to be using predictive AI, according to one survey, and companies that create electronic health records software are grappling with how to make the most of the technology.
“We’re accelerating it probably faster than I thought we would,” said Trampas Hutches, the Mountain Region president at MaineHealth, who noted the technology was one of the top priorities in MaineHealth’s three-year plan. “The only way to meet the demand is technology and AI.”
Hutches said the system is in the process of making AI a “care team member,” as well as using the technology for ambient notetaking and in administrative work.
“We’re really trying to push the envelope on acceptance of AI as a care team,” he said, though he added that the cost of the technology is a concern. “We’re doing everything we can to make sure our cost structure does not go any higher than it is today.”
AI’s rural limits
Medical technology doesn’t have to be on the cutting edge to come up against challenges in rural America. Telehealth, for instance, which often uses tech from a decade ago or more, still has trouble getting traction in remote areas at times, because internet infrastructure can be weak or missing — or because the regulatory and payment structures are still unsettled.
AI faces those problems — and more.
Low access to broadband in Maine, for example, could keep internet-dependent systems from being reliable, said hospital leaders in the state. Others may not have the data infrastructure needed to take advantage of new systems: Forms that are faxed or handwritten aren’t always easily entered into digital systems.
Even some digitized systems aren’t easily or reliably digestible by AI systems. Even advanced hospital systems have had to undergo lengthy, tedious reorganizations to prepare for the technology.
“If you’re employed by a big health system, you’re much more likely to have that opportunity,” James Jarvis, president of the Maine Medical Association, said of the new technology. “If you’re at a private practice, you’re much less likely to have that advantage.”
Many rural providers — including those trying to accelerate their adoption of the technology — are finding it difficult to figure out which AI products are worthwhile.
“There’s a lot of garbage out there,” said James McHugh, a managing director at Berkeley Research Group who focuses on health technology and automation and helps clients implement the technology. Many AI implementations in health care haven’t gone particularly well so far, and adoption has taken substantial resources, he said.
Many system leaders look to invest in AI in the hopes that it will lower their labor costs, but that “usually doesn’t happen,” he said. There’s potential for it in the future, he added, but it’s not as simple as the grand claims being touted by AI vendors and administration officials.
The calculus for hospitals goes beyond just whether the tech that vendors are selling will actually improve their bottom line. It also includes whether the tools are safe for patient data and care.
“There are so many out there,” Hutches, who works at a relatively well-resourced system, said of the tools being sold, comparing it to the dot-com bubble. “You don’t know where to go.”
Small practices and clinics, especially those in the middle of a struggle to stay afloat, may have an even harder time landing on the right adoption strategy or finding the cash to invest.
“It still creates inequities for sure, as does the education and ability to use the tools themselves,” Dwyer said.
Even so, some AI vendors have reported expansion in rural areas. Aidoc, a radiology AI company, has seen “definitive growth” in more remote areas, Jesse Ehrenfeld, chief medical officer at the company and past president of the American Medical Association, told STAT.
“As you’d expect, a lot of those places are not well resourced: They don’t have AI governance in place, they don’t have the bandwidth to do deployment at scale,” he said. “It looks very different.”
Ehrenfeld said he sees a future where Aidoc’s technology can make sense of patient imaging to help under-resourced systems figure out how to deploy clinicians and medical transportation. But for now, rural leaders say fundamental issues of financial sustainability will have to be solved before an AI-powered medical system can come to many Americans.
“If you’re technology challenged,” Jarvis said, “it doesn’t help that someone comes up with a technology-based solution.”

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Tobacco use is linked to infertility in women as well as poorer sperm quality and sexual function in men, according to the latest World Health Organisation (WHO) report, which further warned that second-hand smoke may also affect fertility. Women who quit smoking may have a 25% lower infertility risk than continuing smokers, it said.
The report highlighted evidence that tobacco use is associated with potentially lower chances of success for some fertility treatments. It said that evidence on newer products, including e-cigarettes, waterpipes, and smokeless tobacco, is still emerging, stating that while evidence is strongest for cigarette smoking, other tobacco and nicotine products may also pose risks to fertility and require further research.
Globally, one in six people of reproductive age will experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex.
40% rise in risk
The publication cites decades of evidence showing that smoking can harm women’s reproductive health. A systematic review of studies conducted between 2000 and 2026 found that women who currently smoke tobacco have a 40% higher risk of infertility compared to those who do not smoke.
The publication also notes that women who smoked tobacco in the past but are not currently smoking may have a 25% lower risk of infertility compared with women who continue to smoke, suggesting that quitting tobacco can make a meaningful difference.
The WHO stressed that infertility is not only a women’s health issue. "A recent review of 44 studies involving more than 60,000 men found that smoking was associated with reproductive dysfunction, including semen abnormalities and sexual dysfunction. The evidence indicated that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, ejaculation problems, and related issues such as absence of sperm in semen, poor sperm motility and abnormal sperm shape," it said.
Impact on treatments
For people using fertility treatment, tobacco smoking may reduce the chance of success. The publication cites earlier research from 21 studies, showing that cigarette smoking was linked to fewer live births and fewer pregnancies following assisted reproduction, such as in vitro fertilisation, with findings suggesting that the chances of successful outcomes may be roughly halved by cigarette smoking.
The WHO has recommended that healthcare providers inform individuals and couples planning a pregnancy about the reproductive risks of tobacco use and offer evidence-based support to help them quit. It also recommended that brief advice on quitting be consistently provided to all tobacco users in all healthcare settings.
